Title: Exploration of Climate Smart Organic Farming in Nepal: Impact of Cover Crops on Rice Growth, Yield and Soil Health in Organic Management System
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Authors: Gaire, Achyut; Kumar Shrestha, Ram; Dahal, Kishor; Nandwani, Dilip
Keywords: Cover crops; Organic agriculture; Rice; Soil properties
Abstract_Text: A two-year field experiment was conducted at the Organic Agriculture Farm in Chitwan, Nepal, during the 2023 and 2024 to compare the effects of different cover crops on soil properties and rice productivity in an organic farming system. Four replications of six cover crops as a treatment: Control, Soybean, Sesame, Cowpea, Sesbania, and Mungbean grown in field plots were arranged in randomized complete plot design (RCBD). Sesame plots recorded significantly lower soil temperatures across intervals, and cover crop biomass varied significantly, with mungbean producing the highest biomass. After cover crop incorporation, 25-day-old rice seedlings (cv. Ramdhan) were transplanted, and growth and yield attributes were recorded. Significant differences were observed in plant height of rice across different growth stages, with mungbean consistently producing the tallest plants. In both years, significantly higher effective tiller density of rice was observed in sesame (278 m⁻²) and mugbean (275 m⁻²) plot. Grain yield was significantly higher under mung bean cultivated plot (5.66 MT ha⁻¹). Residual soil analysis following rice cultivation indicated that all cover crop treatments contributed to enhanced soil health between 2023 and 2024. The greatest increases in soil pH were observed under soybean and sesame, while organic matter and nitrogen levels were most enhanced by sesame and cowpea. Mungbean led to the highest improvement in available phosphorus, and both mungbean and sesbania significantly increased available potassium. Thus, cover crops appeared to differ not only in their effects on the soil properties, but also has potential to influence the performance of organic rice.

Title: Securing Nepal’s Vulture Future: From Policy Success to Action
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Vulture, NAIDs, Restriction, Coordination, Policy
Abstract_Text:
Nepal’s vulture conservation journey demonstrates how science-based advocacy, progressive policy, and sustained field action can reverse a severe biodiversity crisis. Home to all nine Asian vulture species, Nepal experienced population declines of over 90% in the 1990s and early 2000s, largely driven by the veterinary drug diclofenac. In response, Nepal restricted veterinary diclofenac in 2006, promoted meloxicam, developed successive Vulture Conservation Action Plans, and established Vulture Safe Zones, including Asia’s first formally declared VSZ in Gandaki–Lumbini in 2021. These measures have contributed to population recovery and stronger provincial engagement.
As of now, Nepal has made remarkable progress in vulture conservation through strong policies, scientific advocacy, Vulture Safe Zones and sustained community engagement. Recently, in April 2026 Nepal also restricted acceclofenac, nimesulide and ketoprofen.  A ploicy advocacy from BCN for over decades has resulted in this outcome.
However, these gains remain vulnerable due to weak inter-agency coordination, continued access to vulture-toxic veterinary drugs, open-border risks, and gaps between policy and implementation. Addressing these challenges requires stronger coordination among wildlife, veterinary, health and drug-regulation authorities; effective regulation and enforcement of harmful drugs; cross-border cooperation; and consistent implementation and monitoring of conservation measures. Sustaining Nepal’s vulture recovery will depend on turning established policy commitments into coordinated, timely and accountable actions.
Nonetheless, the emerging threats and policy gaps still remain prominent. Weak inter-agency coordination, delayed administrative decisions, and the continued availability of vulture-toxic drugs could undermine conservation gains. Urgent regulatory action, stronger coordination, effective implementation, and sustained monitoring are essential to secure Nepal’s vulture recovery and maintain its leadership in vulture conservation.

Title: Rising Sustainability Ambitions, Evolving Policy Mixes? China’s Industrial Parks in Transition
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Li, Yuxi; Fransen, Jan; de Jong, Martin; Faure, Michael
Keywords: Climate governance, policy accumulation, policy mixes, industrial parks, sustainability transitions
Abstract_Text:
Sustainability ambitions have become increasingly prominent in industrial-development policy, connecting environmental protection and resource efficiency with industrial decarbonization. Yet successive ambitions are pursued through policies that interact with existing goals, instruments and implementation arrangements. Understanding this interaction matters because the introduction of new policies does not, by itself, explain how they work alongside earlier ones or what their combined implementation requires.
China’s industrial parks provide a longitudinal case, with national initiatives spanning eco-industrial development, circular transformation, low-carbon development, green manufacturing and zero-carbon development. This study asks whether China’s national industrial-park sustainability policies accumulated between 2006 and September 2026 and, if so, how this accumulation is reflected in their policy mixes. It also considers when accumulation may support or complicate implementation, and for whom.
The study employs longitudinal document analysis of five national initiatives, drawing on formal policy documents and associated standards. Policy mixes are examined through three components: policy goals, policy instruments and formal implementation arrangements. The analysis first reconstructs changes within each initiative, then traces continuity, additions and revisions over time, and finally compares recurring characteristics and explicit connections across initiatives. Particular attention is paid to changes in policy instruments and how their use is specified, alongside the implementation arrangements that define the conditions, procedures and responsibilities for their application.
By examining these arrangements together, the study seeks to explain how successive sustainability ambitions reshape both the means available for implementation and the tasks expected of parks and public authorities. Its contribution is to clarify when policy accumulation may facilitate further improvement and when it may create difficulties for particular actors. This perspective can inform industrial decarbonization and sustainable development by and beyond 2030 by connecting policy ambition with participation opportunities, implementation capacity and coordination.

Title: Agroecological Practices for Soil Restoration in Ecuador and Colombia: Systematized Lessons and Directions for Post-2030 Sustainability Agendas
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Agroecology, PRISMA systematic review, Soil restoration, Post-2030 SDGs, Andean-Amazonian ecosystems
Abstract_Text: Soil degradation caused by intensive agricultural and livestock activities threatens ecosystem stability and food security across the Andean and Amazonian regions. As the deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) approaches, particularly SDG 15 (Life on Land) and SDG 13 (Climate Action), evaluating the real-world effectiveness of nature-based solutions is crucial for designing post-2030 sustainability strategies. Using the PRISMA systematic review protocol, this study analyzed 45 peer-reviewed scientific articles (Colombia: 76%, Ecuador: 24%) to assess how agroecological practices influence biological, chemical, and physical soil quality indicators across major land-use systems, focusing on silvopastoral and agroforestry models. The synthesis demonstrates that silvopastoral systems (predominant in 57% of Ecuadorian and 46% of Colombian reviewed studies) and agroforestry systems (29% and 38%, respectively) consistently enhance organic carbon sequestration, improve water infiltration, reduce soil compaction, and foster edaphic biodiversity. Tree root dynamics and organic matter incorporation via leaf litter effectively act as natural subsoilers, accelerating soil recovery in tropical and Andean ecosystems. However, adoption remains constrained by high initial establishment costs and technical management requirements. A decade of SDG implementation shows that technical agroecological solutions are highly effective for ecological restoration, but their scalability depends on targeted economic incentives, land-tenure security, and regional policy integration. Moving beyond 2030, sustainable land management policies must transition from passive conservation to active support for integrated socio-ecological systems.

Title: Strengthening the Role of National Human Rights Institutions in Advancing the Sustainable Development Goals: The Experience of Komnas HAM Indonesia
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Indonesia, Komnas HAM, human rights, SDGs, NHRI
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a global framework for achieving inclusive and sustainable development, while human rights provide the normative foundation, accountability mechanisms and principles necessary to ensure that development leaves no one behind. Recognizing the close relationship between the SDGs and human rights, the National Commission on Human Rights of the Republic of Indonesia (Komnas HAM) conducted research to examine and strengthen the position and role of Komnas HAM in supporting the achievement of the SDGs in Indonesia.
The research starts from the premise that human rights are not merely an outcome of development but also a framework for designing, implementing and monitoring development policies. Although Komnas HAM has often been associated primarily with SDG 16 on peace, justice and strong institutions, its constitutional and statutory mandate extends across virtually all SDGs, including poverty, health, education, gender equality, decent work, inequality, environmental protection and access to basic services. This reflects the recognition that the achievement of all SDGs has significant human rights implications.
The research examines the institutional mandate, existing practices and potential contributions of Komnas HAM through a human rights-based approach (HRBA) to development. It identifies opportunities for Komnas HAM to contribute through human rights monitoring, research, policy advice, public participation, data development, advocacy and accountability mechanisms. Particular attention is given to the principles of participation, equality and non-discrimination, accountability, transparency, and the principle of leaving no one behind.
The research argues that National Human Rights Institutions (NHRIs) can play a strategic bridging role between human rights obligations and development commitments. By integrating human rights standards and data into SDG planning, implementation and monitoring, Komnas HAM can help identify groups that are marginalized or excluded from development, assess structural inequalities and policy gaps, and strengthen government accountability for SDG commitments.

Title: Traditional water management knowledge for sustainable climate change adaptation for dry zone of Sri Lanka
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Piyadasa, Prof. Ranjana | University of Colombo
Keywords: water, food, climate change, Adaptation, environment
Abstract_Text: In Sri Lanka, dry-zone regions is traditionally harvested and managed through man-made, interconnected cascade tank ecosystems for paddy cultivation. Ancient cascade ecosystems across the country are now under unprecedented pressure, posing serious threats to their sustainability and long-term development prospects. All cascade-based irrigation systems were traditionally operated and managed by local communities, with responsibility vested in the village leadership and community-based organizations. This study was conducted in the Horivila cascade system in the dry zone of Sri Lanka, to identify the present status of community-based management of cascade water systems. The findings reveal that several key ecological components and natural ecosystem types are still being maintained by the community, contributing to the sustainability of the system. Community organizations are adapting to increasingly precarious climatic conditions through the application of indigenous knowledge, diversified cropping systems, the use of drought-tolerant paddy varieties, changes in food consumption patterns, and reliance on locally derived agro-inputs. Many indigenous and traditional farming practices demonstrate significant potential for wider application in enhancing climate change adaptation. With increasing unpredictability in rainfall seasonality and variability in the study area, community organizations actively promote drought-tolerant crop varieties to ensure food security during drought periods. A defining feature of Sri Lankan community-based Ecosystem-based Adaptation to climate change is that, beyond environmental and adaptive benefits, it actively pursues social co-benefits for local communities. These include enhanced household incomes, economic diversification, expanded livelihood opportunities, improved access to education, strengthened gender equality, and inclusive benefits for women, youth, and other vulnerable populations.

Title: Climate-informed resilience: Integrating rainfall variability, geospatial analysis, and data-driven evidence for sustainable development in Nepal
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Rainfall variability, climate change adaptation, climate resilience, geospatial analysis, sustainable development
Abstract_Text:
Nepal's monsoon-dependent socioeconomic systems are becoming more vulnerable to hydroclimatic fluctuations, and the country's complicated topography causes noticeable spatial variations in precipitation, which have an impact on infrastructure, agriculture, water, and local adaptability. This study assesses how observable hydroclimatic signals might guide climate-resilient development and describes the spatiotemporal variability of rainfall throughout Chitwan District, a strategically significant agricultural region in the central Himalayan foothills, between 2014 and 2024.
Daily rainfall observations from 10 meteorological stations operated by the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology were examined at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales. Temporal characteristics and monotonic trends were assessed using the Mann–Kendall test and Sen’s slope estimator, while geographic information system-based inverse distance weighting interpolation was used to resolve spatial patterns in rainfall distribution. Results demonstrate a strongly seasonal precipitation regime, with the monsoon contributing approximately 78–83% of annual rainfall. July consistently recorded the highest rainfall, whereas November represented the driest month. Annual rainfall exhibited a declining tendency, with an estimated Sen’s slope of approximately −0.82 mm/year, while spatial interpolation revealed substantial heterogeneity across the district. These findings indicate that climate-sensitive planning based on district-wide averages alone may obscure meaningful local hydroclimatic differences. Integrating station-based observations, robust non-parametric trend analysis, and spatial rainfall characterisation therefore provides an evidence base for geographically differentiated adaptation, particularly for water-resource management, agricultural planning, infrastructure development, and disaster-risk reduction. The study demonstrates how routinely collected hydroclimatic information can be translated into locally actionable resilience intelligence, supporting risk-sensitive development and contributing to climate adaptation objectives under the Paris Agreement, the Sendai Framework, the Sustainable Development Goals, and the post-2030 sustainability agenda.

Title: Renewable Energy for MSME Transformation in Nepal: Turning Energy Challenges into Opportunities for Sustainable and Inclusive Growth
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Federation of Nepal Cottage and Small Industries (FNCSI)
Keywords: Renewable Energy; MSMEs; Green Transformation; Energy Transition; Sustainable Development; Inclusive Growth; Green Finance; Nepal
Abstract_Text:
Objective:Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are the backbone of employment, local economic development, and livelihoods in Nepal. However, many MSMEs are facing challenges arising from high energy costs, unreliable and unequal access to energy, dependence on imported fossil fuels, limited access to clean technologies, and inadequate green finance. This paper examines how renewable energy can transform these challenges into opportunities for sustainable, competitive, and inclusive MSME growth.
Methods:The study adopts a practice and policy oriented approach, drawing on the experience of the Federation of Nepal Cottage and Small Industries (FNCSI), stakeholder consultations, policy reviews, and evidence from Nepal’s renewable energy and MSME sectors. It examines opportunities for solar energy, bioenergy, micro hydropower, energy efficiency, battery energy storage, and decentralized renewable energy systems across productive sectors, including agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, and services.
Key Findings:The analysis indicates that renewable energy can reduce exposure of MSME to imported fossil fuel price volatility, diversify the energy mix, improve energy reliability, increase productivity and competitiveness, create green jobs, and stimulate local value chains. Distributed renewable energy can further support enterprises in rural and underserved areas by enabling the productive use of locally available resources. However, significant barriers remain, including limited access to affordable finance, clean technologies and technical skills, unstable policies, inadequate market linkages, and weak mechanisms for scaling successful solutions.
Conclusion:Nepal needs an integratedGreen MSME Transformation Frameworkthat links renewable energy deployment with energy efficiency, green finance, technology transfer, skills development, circular economy approaches, digitalization, and market access. Strong public private partnerships and locally adapted financing mechanisms are essential to accelerate and scale this transformation.
Relevance for Sustainable Development by 2030 and Beyond: Accelerating the renewable energy transformation of MSMEs can simultaneously contribute to climate action, affordable and clean energy, decent work, inclusive economic growth, and reduced inequalities.

Title: Clean air in the Anthropocene
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Organisations: Lelieveld, Prof. Jos | Max Planck Institute for Chemistry, Germany
Keywords: Anthropocene, Clean air, Health, Human rights, SDGs
Abstract_Text:
Massive anthropogenic emissions in the Anthropocene have transformed atmospheric composition to such an extent that biogeochemical cycles, air quality, and climate have changed globally and, in some regions, profoundly. Air pollution is estimated to cause 7–8 million premature deaths annually, corresponding to 120–200 million years of life lost every year. Worldwide, air pollution is the leading environmental risk factor for human health, and achieving the World Health Organization’s air quality guidelines could substantially reduce morbidity and premature mortality.
Clean air should be recognized as a human right and is fundamental to achieving many of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including good health and well-being, climate action, sustainable cities and communities, affordable and clean energy, and the protection of life on land and below water. Yet clean air itself is not explicitly represented among the Sustainable Development Goals. This is remarkable because, like clean water, clean air is a fundamental prerequisite for human health and well-being, while exposure to ambient air pollution is largely involuntary and affects nearly the entire global population. Moreover, the burden disproportionately affects vulnerable populations and low- and middle-income countries.
Reducing air pollution simultaneously benefits human health, climate and ecosystems, making clean-air policies among the most effective means of advancing multiple Sustainable Development Goals. Given its universal importance and the need for measurable targets and accountability, clean air should be adopted as a Sustainable Development Goal in its own right.

Title: Justice as a Foundation for Resilience: Transitional Justice, Equity, and Sustainable Transformation in The Gambia
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Nzally, Dr. Jimmy | University of Antwerp
Keywords: ransitional justice; Equity; Community resilience; Sustainable transformation; The Gambia
Abstract_Text:
Objective. This paper examines how unresolved transitional justice undermines community resilience in a small post-conflict state. It argues that historical accountability is a structural precondition for sustainable transformation and resilience, rather than a separate human-rights process.
Methods. The study draws on documentary analysis of The Gambia’s Truth, Reconciliation and Reparations Commission (TRRC), focusing on the implementation of its recommendations. It is complemented by a forthcoming programme of 20–25 semi-structured interviews with victims of political violence during Yahya Jammeh’s 22-year rule (1994–2016), using purposive nonprobability sampling. The study builds on the author’s doctoral research, which included 75 semi-structured interviews in The Gambia, examining how victims’ interpretations of past violence shape perceptions of justice, state legitimacy, and institutional trust.
Key Results. TRRC reporting indicates that transitional justice remains substantially unresolved nearly a decade after Jammeh’s departure. By 2025, only a minority of recommended measures had been fully implemented. A Special Tribunal established through an ECOWAS framework in December 2024 remained unfunded as of April 2026, while victims continue to express concern that they may die without seeing justice.
Conclusions. Resilience-building that treats accountability as a separate and time-bound process risks overlooking its continuing influence on institutional legitimacy and social trust. Justice and accountability should therefore be integrated into resilience and development strategies.
Relevance beyond 2030. A justice- and equity-centred approach to resilience, consistent with Leave No One Behind, requires unresolved historical accountability to be recognised as a structural component of sustainable transformation in post-conflict societies.

Title: Indigenous Peoples and local communities; Community resilience; Social equity
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Nzally, Dr. Jimmy | University of Antwerp
Keywords: Indigenous knowledge; Griot tradition; Community resilience; Social equity; The Gambia; Decolonisation
Abstract_Text:
Objective. This contribution examines the Gambian griot (jali) oral tradition as an indigenous knowledge system with direct relevance to community resilience. It argues that the continued marginalisation of griot knowledge from formal heritage, education, and development planning constitutes an equity gap in resilience-building.
Methods. The analysis draws on a review of existing scholarship on the Senegambian griot tradition, colonial administrative and heritage documentation, and a forthcoming programme of community-based interviews with griot lineages and elders in the Albreda–Juffureh–Barra corridor. Access is grounded in the author’s decade of engagement in Gambian public life and current teaching of decolonial and oral studies at the University of The Gambia.
Key Results. Existing scholarship reveals a substantial documentation and recognition gap. Griot tradition represents a structured system of historical, genealogical, ethical, and social knowledge that predates colonial rule. Yet colonial administrative practices and subsequent heritage-tourism development have largely privileged written and externally produced accounts, positioning griot knowledge as supplementary cultural material rather than recognising it as an authoritative knowledge system. This marginalisation limits its visibility within contemporary resilience and development frameworks.
Conclusions. Resilience approaches that treat indigenous knowledge primarily as cultural heritage overlook functioning systems of knowledge transmission, social cohesion, community governance, and intergenerational learning. Recognising griot knowledge as a legitimate institutional resource can therefore strengthen locally grounded approaches to resilience and sustainable transformation.
Relevance to sustainable development by and beyond 2030. Consistent with the principle of Leave No One Behind, a post-2030 development agenda should recognise Indigenous Peoples and local communities as knowledge holders and resilience actors. Integrating indigenous knowledge into development and resilience planning can advance equity, decolonisation, and more locally legitimate pathways to sustainable transformation.

Title: Rescaling and Reconfiguring Environmental Crisis Deadlocks: Pathways Toward Security–Sustainability Transformations in India–Pakistan Relations
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: environmental peacebuilding; India–Pakistan relations; Indus Waters Treaty; smog diplomacy; conflict transformation
Abstract_Text:
The India–Pakistan conflict remains one of the world’s most enduring interstate rivalries, unfolding in a region that is simultaneously among the most climate-vulnerable. Drawing on Johan Galtung’s concepts of negative peace, positive peace, and transcendence, the study examines how climate change can either reinforce adversarial security practices or catalyse novel forms of cross-border cooperation. Using qualitative comparative case analysis, the article compares three climate-security episodes: the 2025 Indus Waters Treaty crisis, the emergence of “smog diplomacy” between Indian and Pakistani Punjabs, and proposals for Indo-Gangetic airshed governance. The findings demonstrate that climate-related crises within
the same rivalry can produce divergent pathways. While water insecurity was securitised and deepened geopolitical confrontation, transboundary air pollution created practical, technocratic collaboration based on shared environmental risks. The Indus crisis remained embeded in national-level zero-sum politics whereas smog diplomacy emerged through subnational actors who reframed the issue around public welfare. Airshed governance extends this logic by shifting cooperation to a broader regional, multi-country scale that can dilute bilateral tensions. These cases demonstrate that climate risks can either entrench conflict or create pathways
toward more cooperative regional governance, depending on how they are framed, scaled, and institutionally managed.

Title: From decolonisation to decarbonisation: self-interest and material incentives as drivers of global competitive cooperation for a fairer climate future
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: competitive cooperation; climate action; decarbonisation; climate incentives; climate cooperation; game theory;
Abstract_Text: Mainstream frameworks for climate and economic governance remain shaped by the colonial foundations of the global economy, yet these legacies are seldom placed at the centre of debates over how decarbonisation might be achieved. This article situates global climate politics within a postcolonial political economy of structural dependency, showing how colonial extraction, unequal exchange, external debt, and technological hierarchy continue to constrain the fiscal and policy space of states across the Global South. Empirical analysis of UNFCCC and COP processes demonstrates that climate ambition is routinely diluted by democratic short-termism and an anarchic international order, yielding lowest-common-denominator agreements that privilege consensus over ambitious decarbonisation target. Calls for climate justice and rights-based approaches supply vital normative legitimacy but rarely achieve systemic transformation when decoupled from the material structures of the world economy. By contrast, the Montreal Protocol’s phase-out of ozone-depleting substances shows that robust, redistributive cooperation becomes feasible when environmental goals align with technology transfer, productivity gains, and predictable, targeted financing. Building on this analysis, the article advances the concept of ‘competitive cooperation’: a reframing of climate governance in which durable decarbonisation emerges when climate ambition is made economically rational and technologically enabling for structurally diverse states, generating a “race to the top” in green investment. Just as empires unravelled primarily for strategic, economic, and security reasons rather than through a sudden embrace of human-rights norms, climate action is most likely to advance when institutional designs realign material incentives in ways that are equitable across diverse geopolitical spaces.

Title: Reconstructing Urban Air Pollution and its Mortality Burdens: Historical Health Inequalities in Maastricht 1864-1950.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Historical, Urban, mortality, Air Pollution, Inequality
Abstract_Text:
Ambient air pollution remains a leading global driver of cardiometabolic, cancer, and respiratory mortality, yet most exposure-response evidence comes from twentieth- and twenty-first-century monitoring data, limiting our understanding of health effects under the extreme, largely unregulated exposure levels of early industrialisation. This study addresses that gap by reconstructing ambient air pollution in Maastricht, the Netherlands, across a critical 86-year window of industrial growth and early governance response (1864–1950), and linking it to individual-level cause-of-death records to estimate historical premature mortality attributable to pollution exposure.
Using newly developed historical ambient pollution estimates alongside spatial mortality data, this study tests whether industrial pollution produced observable, spatially patterned health inequalities across the city. This topic is of direct relevance to current environmental justice research, where it remains contested whether pollution control narrows or simply displaces exposure disparities. Contrary to expectations, citywide analysis reveals no significant spatial variation in respiratory mortality. This study proposes three explanations with implications beyond this case: (1) domestic rather than industrial combustion may have driven particulate exposure; (2) exposure may have been sufficiently uniform across the city to flatten spatial health inequality even as pollution burden remained severe, suggesting that spatial homogeneity in exposure does not equate to equitable outcomes; and (3) socioeconomic mediators (healthcare access, education, social infrastructure) may buffer pollution's mortality effects independently of exposure level, a mechanism difficult to isolate in contemporary, already-regulated settings.
By spanning nearly a century of shifting fuel use, industrial practice, and governance, this study also offers a long-run temporal baseline for research into the cumulative health impacts of urban air pollution, and provides a historical anchor point for studies examining how energy transitions reshape exposure and mortality patterns over time.

Title: Firm-Level Marginal Abatement Cost Heterogeneity in Indian Manufacturing: A Convex Quantile Approach
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Marginal abatement costs; Industrial decarbonization; Carbon markets; Firm-level heterogeneity; Partial frontier estimation; India
Abstract_Text: India faces the challenge of decarbonizing its energy-intensive manufacturing sector while sustaining industrial growth. Exploiting differences in energy-use adjustment costs across firms and inputs could substantially lower mitigation costs. Using a panel of 504 firms across seven energy-intensive and trade-exposed industries over 2012-2018, this paper estimates input-specific marginal abatement costs (MACs) for coal, purchased electricity, diesel-generated electricity, and furnace oil. We employ a convex quantile regression directional distance function (CQR-DDF), which estimates local partial frontiers rather than imposing a common frontier and allows MACs to vary across firms with different production and energy-use characteristics. Results reveal a highly asymmetric cost structure: most firms have zero or near-zero MACs, indicating substantial low-cost adjustment opportunities, while significant costs are concentrated among a smaller subset. Coal is the least costly input to reduce, with a median MAC of approximately Rs. 55/tCO₂, whereas purchased and diesel-generated electricity involve substantially higher costs. Furnace oil exhibits particularly high costs for some firms, highlighting technological rigidity in selected combustion-based processes. A stylized simulation of India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) shows that cost dispersion, rather than average costs, drives market outcomes. Trading reallocates mitigation toward lower-cost firms and reduces compliance costs by 39-58% under stringent targets, equivalent to approximately Rs. 214 billion, although gains decline as low-cost opportunities are exhausted. These findings show that effective CCTS design requires recognizing firm- and energy-input-specific cost heterogeneity in benchmark design and targeting complementary support toward high-cost technologies and energy transitions.

Title: The Invisible Plateau: Experience Curves, Artificial Intelligence, and the Terminal Cost of the Green Transition
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Keywords: experience curves, macroeconomic learning, directed technical change, artificial intelligence, climate policy
Abstract_Text:
Integrated assessment models, national decarbonisation plans and the ratchet
mechanism of the Paris Agreement all rest on a projection of where clean
energy costs eventually stop falling --- the technological plateau that follows
an exponential growth cycle. This paper asks whether that plateau can be seen
in the data at all, and what artificial intelligence does to it. We first
establish a theoretical result: when a technology's cost is the sum of
components with heterogeneous learning rates, its measured learning elasticity
must decline monotonically, at a rate exactly equal to the share-weighted
variance of component learning rates, converging to the slowest component's
rate. Saturation is generic, not exceptional. In the data, however, the
opposite happens. Using seven energy technologies over 1975--2024, we find that
measured learning elasticities are rising: for onshore wind the
fifteen-year rolling elasticity climbs from 0.09 to 0.81. We show this is an
identification artefact rather than an acceleration of technical progress. The
experience-curve slope is arithmetically the ratio of the cost-decline trend to
the deployment-growth trend; the correlation between the estimated elasticity
and that ratio is 0.999, and deployment growth has decelerated significantly in
every technology we examine. We draw out what an unidentified plateau implies for the treatment of endogenous technical change in climate-economy models and for the design of international environmental agreements.

Title: Navigating the Climate-Development Nexus: Frameworks for Equitable Infrastructure and Just Energy Transitions
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Keywords: Climate-development nexus, just transition, resilient infrastructure, climate justice, equitable adaptation
Abstract_Text:
Abstract
The interplay between climate action and socioeconomic development presents a critical challenge for achieving long-term sustainability beyond 2030 which we have just faced due to Bhotekoshi floods in Nepal on 26th August, 2026. I also mention that across the Himalayas, more than 200 potential “glacial time bombs” may be hidden in river basins and mountain valleys like the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli. We do not yet know when or where a massive ice–rock collapse or GLOF could occur, potentially sending destructive flows from above 5,000 metres downstream at extreme speeds and causing devastation like the recent Rasuwa disaster. So, we must urgently collaborate on comprehensive Himalayan hazard research, monitoring and early-warning systems before the next disaster strikes. While rapid decarbonization and climate adaptation are essential to prevent irreversible environmental degradation, top-down policy interventions often risk exacerbating social inequalities and disproportionately burdening vulnerable populations. This study examines how integrated, community-centered civil engineering and development frameworks can bridge the gap between climate resilience and social equity. By evaluating case studies of infrastructure development and energy transition initiatives across diverse regions, this paper highlights key mechanisms for balancing structural adaptation with equitable development. The analysis demonstrates that climate interventions are most effective when aligned with local development priorities, transparent decision-making, and targeted resource allocation for marginalized communities. Furthermore, we outline actionable policy and engineering guidelines designed to ensure that sustainable infrastructure investments strengthen institutional capacity while fostering social inclusion.
Ultimately, my paper will contribute evidence-based strategies to the post-2030 sustainability agenda, demonstrating that navigating the climate change–development nexus requires moving beyond simple mitigation metrics toward systemic, just, and equitable transformations across human and built environments.

Title: Manufactured Doubt and Climate Governance Failure
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: climate agnotology, climate misinformation, manufactured doubt, climate governance, sustainable transformation
Abstract_Text:
Climate misinformation is often treated as a communication failure or a stock of mistaken beliefs. This paper instead theorises climate agnotology—the deliberate, socially organised production of ignorance—as a supplied political-economic good that obstructs climate action and weakens the institutional foundations of sustainable transformation. It develops a three-component model of manufactured doubt. First, ideologically predisposed citizens and elites provide a receptive population whose uncertainty can be mobilised. Second, algorithmically curated and ideologically homogeneous media environments confine misinformation, recirculating rather than correcting it. Third, fossil-fuel interests, partisan entrepreneurs, think tanks, and platform-native amplifiers sustain the system through strategic investment. Together, these conditions transform diffuse scepticism into coherent and durable public doubt.
The model predicts a threshold effect. Below a critical level of organised investment, scepticism remains fragmented and largely self-cancelling; above it, mobilisation and communicative confinement reinforce one another, making doubt production self-sustaining even as its marginal cost falls. The paper constructs and stress-tests this argument through comparative-static reasoning, specifying its actors, mechanisms, scope conditions, rival explanations, and falsifiable propositions. It selectively draws on threshold models of collective behaviour, alongside information theory’s distinction between signal and noise, while grounding the analysis in political economy, democratic theory, and research on organised climate denial.
This framework links epistemic disruption to both governance and finance. It predicts that sustained agnotological coherence increases policy polarisation, lengthens legislative timelines, weakens international climate commitments, raises the transaction costs of coordination, and distorts price discovery. By explaining how organised interests convert information asymmetries into durable obstacles to mitigation, the paper identifies misinformation as a structural barrier to resilient and equitable climate transformation. It therefore advances agnotology from historical description toward a predictive theory of when climate-governance systems become vulnerable to manufactured doubt and where interventions may most effectively disrupt its amplification before hardening into persistent governance and market failure.

Title: Climate Change, Water & Agriculture Sector in Nepal: Management and Adaptation Strategies in the Framework of Agricultural Engineering
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Chand, Dr. Jeet | Government of Nepal
Keywords: Agricultural Engineering; climate-smart agriculture; precision agriculture; resources conservation technologies; water
Abstract_Text: The focus of this study is to document major impacts of climate change in water and agriculture sector, and key adaptation management strategies applied at farm level from agricultural engineering perspectives focusing food security. Climate change is causing Nepal to experience a number of negative effects, including unpredictable rainfall patterns, a significant and rapid temperature rise, an increase in the frequency of extreme events, and rapidly melting glaciers with an average retreat of more than 30 meters per year. Agriculture, water, forest, health and biodiversity are the hardest-hit sectors from changed climatic pattern in Nepal. Nepal's temperature is rising at a rate of roughly 0.06°C per year, which is faster than the global average. Glaciers in Nepal melted 65% faster in recent years compared to prior decades. Nepal is the 10th most affected country from 2000 to 2021 on the long-term Global Climate Risk Index. More than 80% of property loss due to disasters is attributable to climate hazards, particularly water-related events such as floods, landslides & GLOF. Water availability, quality, and stream flow have significantly changed across the nation, mostly as a result of changes in weather patterns. It is predicted that 14.5% national GDP in Nepal will be lost by 2100 due to climate change related issues if proper adaptation strategies would not be applied. Since agriculture is the backbone of national economy, its reliance on rainfall, water and irrigation makes it particularly vulnerable to climate change. Climate-smart agriculture, resources conservation technologies, farm mechanization integrated with automation, application of precision agriculture, and enabled climate-friendly policy are key adaptation strategies from agricultural engineering perspectives to manage adverse effects of climate change in Nepal. “Nothing Goes Right if Agriculture Goes Wrong”- and it is recommended that “agriculture can’t go right if engineering goes wrong because modern agriculture is engineered agriculture”.

Title: From Relief to Resilience: Sustainable Water and Energy Support in Conflict-Affected Lebanon
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: water, energy, agrifood systems, war
Abstract_Text:
How can sustainability be advanced amid intersecting crises, including war, unprecedented drought, and a prolonged socioeconomic crisis? This session sheds light on the research and implementation work undertaken by Oxfam in Lebanon over the past three years, during which the country witnessed an exponential deterioration in security conditions. This period was marked by recurrent Israeli attacks on water, energy, and other critical infrastructure, alongside the widespread burning and degradation of approximately 56,000 hectares of agricultural land.
The session addresses two key issues. First, it examines how humanitarian interventions can respond to urgent needs while building the foundations for sustainable water and energy systems. It explores how Oxfam’s provision of clean solar energy to water institutions in communities affected by attacks on water and energy networks simultaneously supported immediate service continuity and longer-term resilience. These interventions demonstrated their efficiency both during escalations, when conventional services were severely disrupted, and during periods of relative de-escalation, when they continued to strengthen access, institutional capacity, and preparedness.
Second, the session discusses Oxfam’s research, policy, and advocacy efforts to document the environmental and sustainability-related impacts of war and connect resilience and sustainability to international humanitarian law and policymaking processes. It is grounded in the philosophical conviction that multilateral efforts toward sustainable development cannot be separated from protecting international legal standards and advancing just security arrangements.
The session contributes directly to discussions surrounding SDGs 6, 7, 13, and 16 by connecting access to water and clean energy with climate resilience, accountable institutions, peace, and justice. Lebanon’s experience, and that of the wider region, offer an important lesson for the post-2030 agenda: sustainability frameworks must account for conflict, infrastructure destruction, and institutional fragility while supporting solutions capable of functioning across both crisis and recovery contexts.

Title: Sustainable Pathways for Recycled Fibre-Reinforced Concrete: A Life Cycle Assessment Perspective
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Organisations: Shafique, Dr. Muhammad | Brunel University of London
Keywords: Sustainable Pathways, Recycled Fiber-Reinforced Concrete; LCA
Abstract_Text:
The construction industry faces increasing pressure to reduce resource consumption, greenhouse gas emissions, and environmental impacts while maintaining the performance and functionality of infrastructure. In this context, the integration of recycled materials into cement-based composites offers an opportunity to support more circular and sustainable construction practices. Fibre-reinforced concrete composites are increasingly promoted as a circular alternative to virgin-material-based construction, providing a pathway for diverting waste from disposal and reducing dependence on virgin resources. However, the environmental performance of recycled fibre-reinforced concrete depends not only on the material itself but also on the processes used to recover and prepare the fibres.
A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) was conducted to evaluate the environmental impacts of virgin and recycled fibres. Compared with the conventional steel-fibre benchmark, mechanically recycled fibres reduced climate impacts by 28 to 61%, with bio-based fibres demonstrating the greatest environmental benefits. The study provides insights into circular material strategies and supports the development of more environmentally responsible fibre-reinforced concrete for future construction applications.
Importantly, circularity is not environmentally beneficial by default: the recovery pathway, rather than the recycled label itself, determines whether a material genuinely closes resource loops or merely shifts environmental burdens. Low-intensity mechanical recycling therefore warrants greater consideration in procurement criteria, material standards, and design guidance.

Title: Strengthening Climate-health Governance and Societal Engagement for Resilient Sustainable Development in Africa
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Organisations: Mawanda, Dr. James | Net Zero Hub Ltd
Keywords: Climate Policy, Public Health Governance, Societal Engagement, Africa CDC, Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract_Text: The intersecting crises of climate change and public health pose a profound threat to global progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Extreme weather events continue to devastate global health, with projections indicating that climate-induced health shocks could drive over 44 million people into extreme poverty by 2030, according to World Bank studies. In Africa, the situation is particularly critical: national implementation remains fragmented, and only 35% of countries explicitly prioritize health within their climate policies, according to the African Institute for Development Policy. In response, the Africa CDC Strategic Framework calls on African Union member states to build climate-resilient health systems, strengthen disease surveillance, and secure dedicated implementation budgets through 2029. Utilizing a secondary research methodology, this desktop study analyzes climate-health governance across the continent to provide actionable integration frameworks that foster active societal engagement for resilient, sustainable development. The study will contribute to evidence-based policy harmonization through practical methodologies to embed environmental and epidemiological risk data directly into municipal and local development planning. The study will strengthen institutional capacity building through evaluation of historical barriers, such as financing gaps, weak data infrastructure, and political silos, to strengthen health system governance. The study will also enhance community-led engagement through actionable strategies to catalyze localized dialogue, integrating indigenous knowledge and traditional governance into climate adaptation. The investigation will promote climate finance alignment through integrated roadmaps demonstrating how health-resilient policies and green infrastructure simultaneously advance SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action).

Title: From Monopsonistic Traps to Decoupled Value Chains: An Extractive-Agrarian Framework for Post-Mining Resilience in Indonesian Nickel Frontiers
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Widhagdha, Dr. Miftah Faridl | Sebelas Maret University
Keywords: Nickel mining, Community empowerment; Post-mining resilience; Market decoupling; Sustainable livelihoods; Creating Shared Value (CSV); Extractive-Agrarian Decoupling Framework (EADF)
Abstract_Text: As the global energy transition accelerates demand for nickel, mining corporations in Indonesia deploy agricultural Community Empowerment Programs (PPM) to secure their Social License to Operate (SLO) and mitigate the local resource curse. This study critically compares two divergent agricultural PPM models operating in Sulawesi’s nickel frontiers: PT Vale Indonesia Tbk’s integrated pineapple farming in Wasuponda (Luwu Timur) and PT Hengjaya Mineralindo’s short-cycle vegetable program in Makarti (Morowali). Employing a qualitative comparative case study design based on Most Similar Systems Design (MSSD) and grounded in critical realism, this research utilizes the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework (SLF) and Creating Shared Value (CSV) concepts. Empirical data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews, focus group discussions (FGDs), field observations, and documentary analysis. Findings reveal a fundamental structural divergence driven by corporate operational maturity (brownfield vs. greenfield) and commodity time horizons. PT Hengjaya’s short-cycle horticulture model delivers immediate financial liquidity, rapid cash flow, and gender inclusion via Women Farmer Groups (KWT), yet locks farmers into a monopsonistic dependency on mine catering supply chains. Conversely, PT Vale’s integrated agro-industrial model transforms pineapples into high-value secondary processed products managed by Village-Owned Enterprises (BUMDes), successfully achieving market decoupling from mining operations and establishing post-mining economic resilience despite facing local institutional capacity bottlenecks. This paper conceptualizes the Extractive-Agrarian Decoupling Framework (EADF), a novel four-quadrant typology explaining how corporate operational maturity and value-added commodity processing determine rural autonomous resilience versus monopsonistic dependency. It recommends that mining regulators integrate "Market Decoupling Indices" into official community development evaluations to prevent the cliff effect upon mine closure.

Title: Understanding Climate Change and Climate Action for Human Security
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Keywords: Climate change, human security, resource conflict, equity and justice.
Abstract_Text:
Climate change not only impacts the environment surrounding humans but also affects security, which can threaten the economy and influence access to resources, social stability, human mobility, and interregional relations. The increase in natural disasters caused by climate change-such as droughts, floods, rising sea levels, and clean water scarcity-has the potential to spark competition over limited resources. Climate change can also drive population displacement-both internally and across national borders-raising critical questions about responsibility, protection, and the distribution of burdens among communities and nations.
This paper aims to understand the relationship between climate change, climate action, and human security from the perspective of justice and equity. This paper also analyses mitigation and adaptation strategies that can be implemented to ensure human security. The central argument of this article emphasizes that human security in the face of climate change cannot be understood solely from the perspective of national security or control; rather, it requires a human security-oriented approach that places the rights, vulnerabilities, and capacities of communities at the centre of climate change response efforts. To address climate change, there must be transnational cooperation, equitable resource management, and a fair distribution of responsibilities so that the burden does not fall solely on poor communities or nations. Through this approach, it is hoped that climate actions can be developed that are not only ecologically effective but also promote justice and strengthen security in the face of increasingly complex climate change challenges.

Title: Digital Twins for Climate-Resilient Development: Integrating SEEA Energy Accounting with AI to Unlock Green Climate Finance in Developing Economies
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Organisations: Indian Institute of Forest Management Bhopal
Keywords: Digital Twins, SEEA Energy Accounting, Green Climate Finance, AI for Sustainability, Climate-Resilient Development
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals have underscored the critical need for integrated data systems to track progress on climate action (SDG 13), clean energy (SDG 7), and sustainable finance (SDG 17). However, developing economies face persistent barriers in mobilizing green climate finance due to fragmented environmental and economic data, limited institutional capacity, and the absence of transparent, real-time decision-support tools. This research addresses these gaps by proposing a Digital Twin framework that integrates the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) for Energy with Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enable evidence-based climate finance decisions.
Drawing on empirical insights from a pilot project in Bhutan—where the SEEA-Energy framework was operationalized with Green Climate Fund support—this study demonstrates how AI-powered Digital Twins can model climate-resilient development pathways. The framework integrates natural capital accounting, energy flow data, and climate vulnerability indices to simulate green investment scenarios, track environmental-economic trade-offs, and enhance policy coherence. The pilot engaged over 25 stakeholders across eight ministries, achieved 95% satisfaction, and directly influenced Bhutan's 5th National Development Plan.
Methodologically, the research employs a hybrid approach combining AI-based predictive modeling, geospatial analysis, and stakeholder-validated scenario planning. Key outputs include dynamic ESG dashboards, climate risk heatmaps, and automated reporting aligned with TNFD and CSRD. The Digital Twin architecture enables real-time updates, transparent audit trails, and participatory co-design—addressing critical gaps in trust, data autonomy, and governance identified in post-2030 agenda discussions.
Findings reveal that AI-integrated SEEA frameworks unlock green finance by improving investor confidence, reducing transaction costs, and aligning national priorities with global climate commitments. The study concludes by proposing a scalable Digital Twin model for other developing economies, offering a replicable pathway for the twin green and digital transition. This research contributes to the broader discourse on reimagining sustainability governance and monitoring beyond 2030.

Title: Reimagining Water Governance in the Age of Climate Change: Positioning Johads as Indigenous Pathways to Urban Water Resilience in North Delhi
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Johads, Indigenous Knowledge Systems & Practices, North Delhi, Geo-cultural Mapping
Abstract_Text:
The paper argues that the water crisis in the current context of global climate change cannot be addressed only through technological and infrastructural interventions, and that the revival of traditional water bodies and the knowledge systems associated with them is critical for building climate-resilient cities in India. There is a growing importance of blue infrastructure in responding to climate change, particularly amid rising heat, flooding, water scarcity, groundwater depletion, and shifting rainfall patterns. The paper also examines the mounting recognition of Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Practices in global climate governance. It argues that India’s climate politics have nevertheless continued to privilege modern knowledge systems and economic interests in water governance, while ignoring traditional water bodies such as Johads (traditional earthen reservoirs) in Delhi, which were economically regenerative and ecologically sustainable.
While applying the political economy approach to the case study of Johads in North Delhi district, the paper draws on focus group discussions with local communities and in-depth interviews with water experts. The paper argues that the Johads are socio-ecological structures that contribute to physical, psychological, social, cultural, and ecological well-being. Their restoration can support groundwater recharge, flood mitigation, reduction of urban heat, biodiversity, and community well-being. It signifies an epistemological standpoint that respects the indigenous connection between humans and water, grounded in values of peaceful coexistence. Finally, the paper proposes three steps for protecting Johads: identification, demarcation, and notification, while introducing a tool called geo-cultural mapping, based on a participatory approach that integrates GIS data with local knowledge and cultural practices to document and reviatize johads.

Title: From Digital Access to Digital Justice: Rethinking SDG 4 through the Experience of South Asian Higher Education
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Mukherjee, Dr. Abirlal | University of the People
Keywords: Digital inequality; Digital justice; SDG 4; Higher education; South Asia; Digital inclusion
Abstract_Text:
The digital transformation of higher education has become increasingly central to the achievement of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4), particularly its commitment to inclusive and equitable quality education. Yet the experience of South Asian higher education institutions suggests that expanding digital access does not necessarily produce equitable educational participation. This paper critically examines what the SDG era has revealed about the relationship between digitalisation, educational inclusion, and structural inequality in higher education.
Drawing on the literature on digital inequality, higher education and sustainable development, the paper develops a multidimensional framework for evaluating digital educational equity beyond the conventional measurement of connectivity and device ownership. It distinguishes between infrastructural access, affordability, digital capability, quality of participation, institutional support, and the ability to translate digital access into meaningful educational outcomes. Particular attention is given to socioeconomic, geographical, gendered and institutional inequalities that shape students’ experiences of online and technology-mediated learning across South Asia.
The paper argues that the SDG approach has often treated digital technology as an enabling infrastructure without sufficiently addressing the unequal social conditions under which that infrastructure is accessed and used. Consequently, measures of technological penetration may obscure persistent inequalities in educational opportunity. The experience of South Asian higher education offers an important lesson for the post-2030 sustainability agenda: digital inclusion should be understood not merely as connectivity but as a question of digital justice.
The paper proposes that future global development frameworks integrate measurable indicators of meaningful digital participation, institutional capacity, affordability, accessibility and educational outcomes. Such a shift would reposition digital equity from a peripheral concern within SDG implementation to a foundational condition of sustainable and inclusive development beyond 2030.

Title: Generative AI and Educational Inequality in the Global South: Who Gains from the AI Revolution?
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Mukherjee, Dr. Abirlal | University of the People
Keywords: Digital inequality; Higher education; Social mobility; Student well-being; Sustainable development
Abstract_Text:
Generative artificial intelligence has introduced a new phase of digital transformation in higher education. Students can now access tools capable of generating text, translating information, explaining complex concepts and supporting research. However, these capabilities may not be equally distributed or equally usable. This paper examines the implications of generative AI for educational inequality in the Global South.
Focusing on South Asian higher education, the paper develops a conceptual framework for analysing differential access to generative AI across socioeconomic, institutional and linguistic dimensions. It considers how differences in connectivity, devices, AI literacy, language capabilities and institutional policies may influence students’ ability to derive educational value from generative technologies.
The paper argues that generative AI creates a paradox. It has the potential to democratise access to forms of intellectual assistance previously available mainly to students with substantial educational resources, while simultaneously creating new advantages for students who possess stronger digital capabilities and access to more sophisticated technologies.
The paper therefore proposes that AI inclusion must move beyond universal availability towards equitable capability. Institutions should provide students with opportunities to develop critical AI literacy, understand algorithmic limitations and use AI responsibly within educational contexts.
The paper contributes to discussions of AI as an enabler of sustainable development by examining the distributional consequences of technological innovation. It argues that the sustainability of the AI transformation will depend substantially on whether educational systems can prevent new technological capabilities from becoming mechanisms of social reproduction.
The paper concludes by proposing an equity-oriented model for integrating generative AI into higher education in the Global South.

Title: From Digital Divide to AI Divide: Emerging Inequalities in the Intelligent University
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Mukherjee, Dr. Abirlal | University of the People
Keywords: Artificial intelligence; AI divide; Digital inequality; Higher education; Equity and justice
Abstract_Text:
The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence is transforming the technological landscape of higher education. While AI tools promise personalised learning, automated feedback, research assistance and expanded access to knowledge, their benefits depend upon unequal technological and human capabilities. This paper asks whether the digital divide is evolving into a more complex “AI divide”.
Using South Asian higher education as a critical context, the paper conceptualises the AI divide as a multidimensional inequality encompassing access to AI tools, digital literacy, AI literacy, institutional infrastructure, quality of outputs and the capacity to use AI strategically. These inequalities may exist between institutions as well as among students within the same institution.
The paper argues that the AI divide differs from earlier forms of digital inequality because access to technology alone is insufficient. Meaningful participation increasingly depends upon the ability to evaluate, interpret and critically use AI-generated information. Consequently, inequalities in educational benefit may persist even when basic access to AI tools becomes widespread.
The paper proposes an AI equity framework integrating access, capability, critical literacy, institutional governance and educational outcomes. It suggests that universities should evaluate AI adoption through an explicit sustainability and equity lens.
The contribution lies in extending digital inequality research into the emerging AI era. Rather than asking simply whether AI is accessible, the paper asks who can use AI effectively, who can critically evaluate it, and who gains the greatest educational advantage from its integration.
The paper concludes that addressing the AI divide will be essential if digitalisation is to function as an enabler rather than a multiplier of educational inequality beyond 2030.

Title: asugetme@gmail.com
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: JAISWAL, Dr. ASTHA | INDIAN INSTITUTE OF SCIENCE
Keywords: Responsible Innovation; GM Crops; Agricultural Innovation Governance; Regenerative Agriculture; Climate Resilience; Sustainable Agriculture; Stakeholder Governance; India
Abstract_Text:
India’s agricultural sector faces growing pressures from climate change, resource constraints, environmental degradation and the need to ensure long-term food security. At the same time, agricultural innovation remains highly contested, particularly in relation to genetically modified (GM) crops. The Indian experience demonstrates that debates around agricultural biotechnology can become polarised between GM and non-GM positions, potentially overlooking the wider range of technological, ecological and knowledge-based pathways available for sustainable agricultural transitions.
Drawing on ongoing research on the “Governance of Genetically Modified Crops in India: Mapping Stakeholders and Embedding Responsible Innovation,” this paper examines what lessons India offers for governing contested agricultural innovation in ways that support sustainable development, health equity and societal well-being. The study adopts a qualitative case-study approach, drawing on policy documents, scientific literature, regulatory materials and stakeholder perspectives relating to agricultural innovation governance in India. The analysis is informed by the principles of Responsible Innovation—anticipation, inclusion, reflexivity and responsiveness—and the Purpose–Process–Outcomes framework.
The paper argues that India’s experience offers three important lessons. First, agricultural innovation governance should be problem-oriented rather than technology-centred, beginning with the social, ecological and agricultural problems that innovation is intended to address. Second, sustainable transitions require consideration of a diversified innovation portfolio, including GM crops alongside crop diversification, millets and locally adapted crops, agroecological practices, conventional and molecular breeding, gene editing, and technologies improving soil, water and resource efficiency. Third, decisions about agricultural innovation should incorporate the perspectives and interests of farmers, consumers, scientists, regulators and other affected stakeholders, while considering social, environmental and economic consequences.
The paper proposes Responsible Innovation as a governance approach for moving beyond polarised technology debates towards inclusive, anticipatory and context-sensitive agricultural policy. India’s experience offers broader lessons for aligning agricultural innovation with climate resilience, natural-resource conservation, health, livelihoods and sustainable well-being in the post-2030 sustainability agenda.

Title: “INDIAN CLIMATIC SCENARIOS ALIGNED TO GREEN GROWTH AND ENVIRONMENTAL LAW AMID GLOBAL HEADWIND
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: *Keywords:*  India Climate Scenarios, Green Growth, Environmental Law, Carbon Credit Trading Scheme [CCTS], EU CBAM, PARIVESH Portal, Green Credit Programme, EPR, NGT, Precautionary Principle, Polluter Pays, Absolute Liability, Digital Public Infrastructu
Abstract_Text:
ABSTRACT - 250 Words.
The relationship between digitisation and productivity in India is moderated not by access to technology but by contextual factors — export orientation, workforce composition and market structure. Export-oriented firms facing EU CBAM and CSRD adopt AI for carbon accounting due to competitive pressure, while firms with higher skilled workforce translate digital tools into gains; low-skill firms see only costs.
Digitisation pressure varies across industries. Sectors most at risk of digital lag are construction, agriculture and low-margin traditional manufacturing, marked by informality and low data maturity. International evidence from Germany's Mittelstand-Digital and Denmark's MADE shows generic subsidies fail; effective interventions are sector-specific data cooperatives and applied-tech intermediaries providing competence development.
Banks must evolve beyond credit to advisory and ecosystem-building. Our questionnaire finds banks offering carbon accounting APIs, subsidised IoT and cluster advisory can de-risk adoption for MSMEs, but Indian commercial banks have low readiness — lacking tech talent and advisory trust. Viability requires RBI and SIDBI to enable fee-based advisory decoupled from lending, risk-sharing guarantees for green-tech loans, and incentives for bank-incubated digital hubs as in DBS Singapore.
The digital-ESG intersection risks green-washing. Genuine environmental co-benefits from AI occur only when investments are tied to measured resource KPIs with third-party MRV and absolute reductions — e.g., AI forecasting cutting renewable curtailment or digital twins for ZLD in textiles. Efficiency narratives without baseline disclosure are green-washing.
Thus, green growth requires a triad: Law provides trust via CCTS, Green Credit Rules and NGT enforcement; DPI provides scale via PARIVESH portal, National Carbon Registry and open environmental data; AI provides intelligence for predictive governance — transforming environmental law from compliance burden to competitive advantage for a resilient, just and equitable transition.

Title: Beyond Goals to Financing: Lessons from Mozambique for the Post 2030 Sustainable Development Architecture
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Post 2030 Agenda, Development Finance, SDG Implementation, Domestic Public Finance, Africa
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals established an ambitious global framework for sustainable development, but their implementation has exposed a persistent gap between global commitments and the fiscal, financing and institutional conditions required for delivery. This paper uses Mozambique as a country case to examine what this implementation gap implies for the design of the sustainable development architecture beyond 2030.
Using a policy and institutional case study approach, the paper synthesizes evidence from national development planning, public finance, debt, official development assistance, climate finance and sector financing processes. It examines how international commitments are translated through domestic budgets, fiscal institutions, external financing arrangements and implementation systems, and where these relationships constrain delivery.
The Mozambique case highlights four recurrent weaknesses. First, financing remains insufficiently integrated into global goal setting. Second, domestic and external financing systems remain fragmented, weakening alignment with national priorities. Third, global commitments often insufficiently reflect fiscal space, debt pressures and institutional implementation capacity. Fourth, accountability for financing and delivery is dispersed across multiple actors and instruments. These challenges are becoming more acute as countries such as Mozambique confront changing development cooperation, climate related financing demands and competing public expenditure priorities.
The paper argues that the post 2030 framework should embed financing and implementation architecture within the design of global development goals rather than treat financing as a parallel enabling agenda. This requires stronger links between global commitments, national planning and budgeting, debt sustainability, development cooperation, climate finance and institutional delivery. Mozambique illustrates a wider lesson: sustainable development goals are credible only when accompanied by realistic, nationally grounded pathways for financing and implementation. The post 2030 architecture should therefore be assessed not only by the ambition of its objectives, but also by whether countries possess the fiscal, institutional and financing conditions required to achieve them.

Title: Beyond Climate Finance Commitments: Financing a Just and Equitable Transition in South Africa
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: Just Energy Transition Climate Finance Development Finance Climate Justice South Africa
