Abstract_Text:
South Africa has become one of the most prominent test cases for aligning climate finance with development objectives through its Just Energy Transition. Yet the scale of announced international support has also highlighted a critical question: whether headline climate finance commitments translate into financing that is sufficiently accessible, additional, concessional, transparent and aligned with national development priorities to support a genuinely just transition.
This paper examines the climate development nexus through the financing architecture of South Africa’s energy transition. Using a policy oriented case study approach, it analyzes public information on international climate and development finance, financing instruments, sector allocations, implementation arrangements and the evolving development cooperation landscape. Particular attention is given to the distinction between pledges, commitments, allocations and disbursements, and to how the terms and structure of finance affect implementation capacity and distributional outcomes.
The analysis identifies several tensions. Large aggregate financing commitments can mask differences in concessionality, additionality and accessibility. Fragmented financing channels can weaken alignment with national institutions and priorities. Financing for infrastructure and decarbonization may also advance faster than support for employment, local economic development, social protection and other dimensions of justice. At the same time, fiscal pressures and changing official development assistance increase the importance of how climate finance interacts with broader development finance.
The paper argues that effective climate development finance should be assessed not only by volumes mobilized, but by its quality, allocation, institutional alignment and contribution to equitable development outcomes. South Africa demonstrates that a just transition requires a financing architecture capable of connecting decarbonization with jobs, livelihoods, public investment and local development. These lessons are relevant beyond South Africa as countries seek financing models that reconcile climate ambition with fiscal realities, development priorities and social justice.

Title: Advisories for Whom? Digital Early Warning Systems and the Reproduction of Vulnerability in Indian Agriculture
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Drought, Early Warning, Farmers, Agromet Advisories, Digital Literacy, Just Transformation
Abstract_Text:
As climate crises intensify, digital early warning systems have become a central node in the climate change–development nexus, reshaping disaster risk communication and, with it, expectations of resilient and equitable adaptation. India has introduced digital initiatives like SACHET for rapid-onset hazards (cyclones, floods, heat waves, lightning), yet slow-onset drought remains peripheral to these otherwise effective initiatives, posing structural challenges that existing frameworks for drought are ill-equipped to address. Drought early warnings for farmers are generated through monitoring and forecasting, disseminated as layered agro-meteorological advisories — historically via print and extension services, and increasingly via digital modes in recent years. However, fragmented institutions and the lack of a unified framework trap these advisories in complex digital dissemination channels, undermining last-mile reach and, with it, the promise of a just transformation in climate risk communication. This study examines advisory dissemination among progressive and non-progressive farmers in Rajasthan this El Niño year through telephonic surveys, revealing distinct inequalities: progressive farmers face technology-centered rather than user-focused services, while non-progressive farmers confront deeper issues of accessibility, comprehensibility, and trust. Thus, despite rising Information and Technology adoption, simply disseminating advisories digitally without accounting for existing inequalities in access and understanding between progressive and marginalized groups fails to ensure equitable reach, and risks reproducing the very vulnerabilities that resilient development is meant to reduce. The study identifies key dissemination challenges and argues that navigating the climate change–development nexus toward resilient, just, and equitable transformation requires inclusive institutional architecture, not technology alone.
Keywords: Drought, Early Warning, Farmers, Agromet Advisories, Digital Literacy, Just Transformation

Title: Climate Extremes and Urban Slums: Heatwave Impacts, Health Vulnerabilities, and Community Adaptation in Jaipur
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Heatwave, Health, urban, Slums, Resilience
Abstract_Text: According to the Medical Health and Family Welfare Department of Rajasthan, a total of 6,069 heat stroke cases were reported in 2024, reflecting the severe health implications of extreme temperatures in the state. This raises critical questions of who is being impacted, why certain groups are more vulnerable, and how they cope with such extreme conditions. Slum populations, already burdened by livelihood insecurity and inequality, are disproportionately exposed to climate impacts and extreme events like heatwaves. This study was undertaken during the summer months of 2024 with two objectives: first, to assess the impacts of heatwaves and the associated vulnerabilities in the slums of Jaipur city; and second, to explore the adaptive strategies and the key challenges and propose pathways for policy interventions. Personal interviews and focus group discussions were conducted with residents of five slum settlements in Jaipur, alongside interactions with institutional stakeholders. The adaptive capacity is categorised in generic and specific strategies, supported by a SWOT-based assessment of policy and field realities. Heatwaves severely affect community health, water resources, and livelihoods, with disproportionate impacts on vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children, the elderly, and women, often leading to unreported deaths. The findings underscore the persistent vulnerability of marginalized populations, challenging the current policy emphasis on resilience-building without adequately addressing underlying vulnerabilities. The study argues that focusing narrowly on specific adaptive capacities is insufficient for sustainable resilience. Instead, the state must engage more deeply with marginalized communities to design inclusive strategies that genuinely strengthen resilience by first acknowledging and addressing their structural vulnerabilities. By identifying who is most affected, how, and why, such studies can inform long-term transformative solutions that address both climate change vulnerabilities and entrenched social inequalities.

Title: Climate Extremes and Farmers: Impacts of Drought and Rising Temperatures, Adaptation and Mitigation Measures
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Farmers, risk perception, drought, temperature rise, adaptation action, societal resilience, community, household survey
Abstract_Text: As climate extremes intensify, building societal resilience depends on grounding adaptation action in how communities themselves perceive and respond to risk. This paper explores the concept of 'Risk and Vulnerability' by investigating farmers' perceptions of the risks associated with drought and heat waves, and their corresponding adaptation strategies, in the dry-land region of India. The research concentrates on an area of grassroots investigation, meticulously chosen through a vulnerability assessment carried out using the IPCC framework, with specific emphasis on the state of Rajasthan. Through a primary survey of 150 rural households within the agricultural community, the study elucidates the perceptions of the agriculture community in Sikar district regarding the occurrence of drought and heat waves in the region. It further explores the impact of these events on their livelihoods and examines the adaptation actions and mitigation strategies employed by the community in response. Analysis of secondary data reveals an insignificant decrease and increase in drought and heat wave days, respectively, for the region. The household survey indicated that farmers perceive highly variable rainfall and increasing heat intensity due to climate change, giving rise to locally understood conditions such as Akal, Trikal, and Bhujkal. Farmers in the region have responded to these events primarily through adjustments in agricultural practices, a shift toward non-farm activities, migration, and fodder storage — adaptation actions that vary from household to household based on social and economic status. Moreover, government initiatives to help these farmers cope with such adverse situations remain limited. The findings underscore the importance of capturing micro-level grassroots perceptions, which offer valuable insight into locally evolved adaptation strategies and the institutional gaps that constrain them. Understanding these perceptions is essential to identifying effective, locally grounded actions for climate change adaptation and to building a more resilient society in the face of increasingly extreme climate disasters.

Title: A Comprehensive Assessment Framework for Biofuels Integrating Sustainability and Circularity Dimensions
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Arias Calvo, Dr. Ana | Imperial College London
Keywords: biofuels, sustainability, circularity, decision making, framework
Abstract_Text: Transitioning to low-carbon energy systems requires biofuels that are demonstrably sustainable and circular, yet existing assessment frameworks lack an integrated approach that simultaneously addresses circularity alongside the three conventional sustainability dimensions, environmental, social, and economic, and none provides a structured classification of requirements across minimum and advanced performance tiers. This study develops a comprehensive, evidence-based decision-support framework for biofuel sustainability and circularity assessment, organized across four hierarchical levels: pillars, areas of concern, criteria, and requirements with associated indicators. The framework was developed considering a systematic review and analysis of voluntary certification schemes recognized under the EU Renewable Energy Directive, alongside EU directives, international regulations, technical standards, and globally recognized institutional reports, to identify sustainability and circularity requirements and indicators. In a second stage, requirements were classified into minimum and advanced performance tiers through the application of a structured five-question decision matrix, ensuring a transparent and accurate classification procedure. The resulting framework encompasses 4 pillars, 23 areas of concern, 101 criteria, 139 requirements, and associated quantitative and qualitative indicators. A coverage analysis reveals that circularity and economic sustainability remain critically underrepresented across existing certification schemes and regulatory instruments, confirming the need for the integrated approach proposed. The framework provides a structured, transparent basis for assessing biofuel performance and supports the design of practical tools toward best practices to make informed, evidence-based choices when selecting sustainable biofuels.

Title: Geoinformation Technologies and UAVs as Cross-Domain Enablers of the SDGs: Evidence, Gaps, and Governance Implications
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Arias Calvo, Dr. Ana | Imperial College London
Keywords: Geoinformation; Sustainable Development Goals; Governance; Environmental monitoring; UAVs
Abstract_Text: The achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) demands integrated, multi-scale approaches capable of capturing the complexity of socio-environmental systems. This contribution examines how geoinformation technologies, including Geographic Information Systems (GIS), remote sensing, and Earth observation, alongside Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), function as cross-domain enablers of sustainable environmental management and SDG implementation across natural, agricultural, coastal/aquatic, urban, and Arctic environments. Drawing on a systematic cross-domain analysis of 84 reviewed applications across 13 SDGs, the study reveals a concentrated but uneven distribution of sustainability contributions. SDG 13 (Climate Action) emerges as the most cross-domain SDG (n=18), spanning agriculture, coastal/aquatic/Arctic, and urban contexts. SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) ranks second (n=16), driven by urban and coastal applications in flood risk mapping, air quality, and disaster risk reduction. SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) demonstrates the highest domain specificity (n=14), concentrated in precision agriculture and food security applications. SDG 12 (n=10), SDG 15 (n=7), and SDG 14 (n=6) further reflect the resource-efficiency and ecological dimensions of these technologies. Critically, SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals) records the lowest representation (n=1), signalling a significant governance gap in data-sharing and international cooperation frameworks. Despite their multi-SDG contributions, persistent structural barriers constrain broader operationalisation. EU drone regulations restrict deployment in sensitive and transboundary environments, while data standardisation deficits limit cross-institutional comparability. Furthermore, high computational demands and limited open data infrastructure in low- and middle-income countries risk deepening geospatial inequalities. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated investment in open data ecosystems, inclusive governance frameworks, and capacity-building initiatives, imperatives directly relevant to equitable SDG implementation and the post-2030 sustainability agenda.

Title: Where, when, and how should EV charging infrastructure be deployed in the Netherlands to reduce transportation emissions and optimize electricity-system integration?
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: ayatallahbouramdane, Prof. Ayat-Allah Bouramdane | Independent researcher
Keywords: EV charging infrastructure, the Netherlands, transportation emissions, electricity-system integration.
Abstract_Text:
The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) in the Netherlands creates an opportunity to reduce transportation emissions while also challenging the electricity system. This study investigates how the Dutch electricity system can support EV charging infrastructure and where charging stations should be deployed to maximize environmental and energy-system benefits.
First, the study examines the Netherlands’ transportation emissions, focusing on road, maritime, and aviation sectors, and assesses the existing EV charging network, including station location and utilization. Second, it evaluates whether the electricity system can accommodate additional EV charging demand by analyzing the generation mix, merit-order curve, and temporal electricity dispatch. Particular attention is given to identifying electricity sources supplying EV charging and determining whether optimized charging times can increase the use of low-carbon electricity and reduce grid pressure.
Third, the study develops a spatial assessment of EV charging potential across the Netherlands. Regions are classified into low-, medium-, and high-potential zones based on technical, economic, environmental, transportation, and social criteria, including EV adoption, traffic, population density, existing charging infrastructure, grid capacity, electricity prices, renewable-energy availability, and proximity to highways and urban centers.
The results aim to identify where and when EV charging infrastructure should be expanded to reduce transportation emissions, support cleaner electricity use, and minimize grid stress. The study provides a basis for policymakers, electricity-system planners, and infrastructure developers to prioritize charging investments and support sustainable electric mobility.

Title: Navigating Sustainable Performance through the Lens of Green Shared Vision
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Organisations: Raheel yasin, Dr. Raheel yasin | International University of Rabat
Keywords: Sustainable leadership, Connectedness to nature, Green shared vision Green ambidexterity
Abstract_Text: Grounded in the green resource base theory, this study delves the impact of sustainable leadership on sustainable performance. In addition to that, in this study we measure mediating role of green shared vision along with that we also measure the moderating effect of connectedness to nature and moderating role of green ambidexterity. Data were collected from the Vietnam hospitality sector using a three-wave research design and hypotheses were tested using Lavaan package of R software. The results confirmed existence of positive correlation between sustainable leadership and green shared vision. Green shared vision mediates the nexus between sustainable leadership and sustainable performance. Finally results confirm the moderating role of connectedness to nature and green ambidexterity. We also examine the machine learning application, specifically the random forest algorithm by using Random Forest package of R Software, to augment objectivity and reliability in performance evaluation. Results confirm that sustainable leadership is most important for economic performance, whereas green shared vision is most important element for environmental performance and sustainable leadership is most important for social performance. This study extends the green resource base theory by elucidating mechanisms through sustainable leadership and becomes a source of sustainable performance in the hospitality context.

Title: WOMEN'S ROLES AND FAMILY GENDER DYNAMICS IN REDUCING STUNTING AT YOGYAKARTA CITY: A SCOPING REVIEW
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: Rizky, Redhita; Nurhayati, Ida; Pudyastuti, Rita Rena; Saputra, Andika
Organisations: Health Polytechnic of the Ministry of Health, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
Keywords: stunting, women's role, gender equality, family empowerment
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study aims to map scientific evidence on women's roles and family gender dynamics in reducing childhood stunting in Yogyakarta City, and to identify research gaps and family empowerment strategies based on pro-equity gender roles.
Methods: A scoping review was conducted following the Arksey and O'Malley framework and PRISMA-Scoping Reviews guidelines. Literature covering 2016 to 2026 was searched across national and international databases, including Google Scholar, Scopus, PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Garuda, using combinations of keywords related to stunting, women's role, gender equality, and family empowerment. From 150 records initially identified, 120 remained after duplicate removal and screening, and 10 studies met the inclusion criteria for thematic analysis.
Key results: Five key aspects of family-based stunting prevention were identified: nutritional fulfilment, parenting practices, utilization of health services, environmental sanitation, and household decision-making. Women, particularly mothers, held strategic roles in nutrition provision and childcare, while paternal involvement as an active partner within a gender-equitable support system remains underexplored. A family model built on pro-equity gender roles has the potential to strengthen collaboration between women and men, consistent with the decline in Yogyakarta City's stunting prevalence to 9.13 percent by October 2025, below the government's 10 percent target.
Conclusions: Optimizing women's roles alongside greater paternal involvement, guided by pro-equity gender principles, offers a promising family-level pathway to reduce stunting and its long-term impact on children's growth and cognitive development.
Relevance to sustainable development by and beyond 2030: These findings support progress toward gender equality (SDG 5), good health and well-being (SDG 3), and zero hunger and malnutrition reduction (SDG 2), demonstrating that gender-responsive family empowerment is essential to achieving equitable and sustainable health outcomes by and beyond 2030.

Title: AI, Big Data and Digital Taxation: Indonesia’s Emerging Framework for Sustainable Fiscal Capacity
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Coordinating Ministry for Economic Affairs Indonesia
Keywords: Digital taxation; artificial intelligence; big data; digital economy; fiscal capacity; sustainable development
Abstract_Text:
The rapid digitalization of economic activity is reshaping how value is created, delivered, and consumed. Digital platforms and data-driven business models allow economic value to be generated beyond boundaries. This creates challenges for conventional tax systems, which were designed around identifiable businesses, locations, and transactions. The availability of Big Data and artificial intelligence (AI) provides governments with new opportunities to understand economic activity, improve tax administration and fiscal governance. This study explores how Indonesia can use these capabilities to develop a digital tax framework, strengthen fiscal capacity, and support sustainable development by 2030 and beyond.
The study adopts a prospective policy-analysis approach, drawing on the digital economy, Indonesia’s tax architecture, international tax reforms, and sustainable development objectives. It develops a Digital Fiscal Capture Framework connecting digital value creation with domestic resource mobilization, digital tax instruments, data-driven tax administration, international tax cooperation, institutional capacity. The study examines how Big Data and AI-enabled analytical capabilities can support taxpayer identification, risk-based compliance, monitoring digitally generated activity, and responsive fiscal decision-making. The framework is assessed against revenue potential, feasibility, efficiency, investment incentives, equity, and sustainability.
The analysis identifies a growing gap between the expansion of digital economic activity and the capacity of fiscal arrangements to capture digitally generated value. It also highlights an opportunity: digital data and AI can strengthen governments’ ability to identify economic activity, analyze compliance risks, and improve fiscal administration. It proposes a phased pathway to 2030 combining digital tax instruments, data-driven compliance, AI-enabled analytical capacity, institutional strengthening, and international cooperation.
Digital taxation should not be viewed as a new revenue instrument, but as part a transformation of fiscal governance. Indonesia’s emerging approach is presented as a policy-learning case that may offer lessons for developing economies seeking to strengthen domestic resource mobilization while balancing revenue, innovation, investment, equity, and sustainable development.

Title: Financing Local Development Beyond 2030: Native Philanthropy and Sustainable Financing Pathways for Local NGOs in Bangladesh
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: zihady, Md Shumon; Ahmad, Mokbul Morshed
Keywords: Native philanthropy; Local NGOs; Sustainable financing; Local development; Post-2030 development
Abstract_Text:
As the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) approach 2030, an important question concerns not only what development priorities should follow, but how locally driven development can be sustainably financed. Local non-governmental organizations (NGOs) play an important role in translating development priorities into community-level action. However, most of them remain dependent on external development finance. Bangladesh provides an important context for examining whether locally embedded resources, particularly native philanthropy, can complement external funding and contribute to a more resilient financing architecture for sustainable local development.
This study investigates the dynamics between native philanthropy and local NGOs in Bangladesh, examining the possibilities and constraints involved in transforming locally embedded traditions and practices of giving into sustainable financing pathways for local NGO. Empirically, the study focuses on Sylhet, Bangladesh, and draws on in-depth interviews, key-informant interviews, focus group discussions, observation, and document analysis involving local NGOs, philanthropists, community and religious actors, civil society representatives, and relevant institutional stakeholders. Guided by critical realism, the research combines inductive analysis with retroduction to identify the underlying institutional, relational, and structural factors that shape the relationship between native philanthropy and local NGOs.
The study examines the financing challenges of local NGOs and the motivations and practices of native philanthropy. It also explores the gaps between philanthropic preferences and local development priorities and how these two areas can be better connected.
By bringing the financing of local development into the post-2030 sustainability debate, the study contributes to broader scholarship on SDG localization and locally led development. It suggests that lessons from the SDG era should extend beyond identifying development goals toward the unexplored potentials of local knowledge and resources. In this pursuit, the Bangladesh case shifts attention from what sustainable development should achieve to how locally driven development can be institutionally and financially sustained beyond 2030.

Title: HPV Vaccine Communication on Social Media: A Systematic Review of Platforms, Messages and Outcomes
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: HPV vaccine, social media, health communication, vaccine communication
Abstract_Text:
In 2023, Thailand reintroduced its nationwide Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme for girls and young women, generating greater public discussion about HPV vaccination and cervical cancer prevention. Social media has become an important environment for health communication, providing opportunities for vaccine promotion while also facilitating misinformation, safety concerns, and negative narratives.
Based on this background, this systematic literature review examines global research on HPV vaccine communication through social media, focusing on the platforms studied, message and content characteristics, and reported communication and behavioural outcomes.
Following PRISMA guidelines, Scopus was searched for peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2016 and 2026 using terms related to HPV vaccination and social media. The search identified 66 articles. Following title, abstract, and full-text screening against predefined eligibility criteria, 41 articles were included in the final review.
The findings show that research has examined HPV vaccine communication across platforms including Twitter/X, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. Social media performs a dual role: it supports health-information dissemination, vaccine promotion, and communication interventions, while also enabling the circulation of misinformation, vaccine-safety concerns, personal narratives, and mistrust of health authorities. Reported outcomes include knowledge, perceptions, trust, vaccine hesitancy, acceptance, vaccination intention, and uptake.
The review demonstrates that effective HPV vaccine communication requires platform-sensitive strategies that account for information sources, message characteristics, and audience responses. By strengthening vaccine confidence and equitable access to reliable health information, such strategies can support cervical cancer prevention and progress towards SDG 3 on health and well-being.

Title: Valuing visible urban greenery for sustainable housing and urban transformation in Bengaluru
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Roy, Sayan; Dey, Arijit; Ramachandran, Parthasarathy
Keywords: Green View Index, Housing Prices, Spatial Econometrics, XGBoost, Urban Greenery, Hedonic Pricing
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Urban transformation requires better measures of environmental quality that reflect how residents experience their neighborhoods. This study examines whether visible street-level greenery is associated with apartment prices in Bengaluru, India, and evaluates its relevance for sustainable housing and urban planning.
Methods: The study combines 4,663 apartment transactions from January to August 2024 with Google Street View imagery, remotely sensed environmental indicators, and neighborhood accessibility measures. Visible greenery is measured using the Green View Index (GVI) derived through a Grounding DINO and Segment Anything Model (SAM) computer vision pipeline. Hedonic pricing models are estimated using Ordinary Least Squares, Spatial Error, and Spatial Lag models, while Extreme Gradient Boosting and SHapley Additive exPlanations assess nonlinear relationships and variable importance.
Key results: Visible greenery is positively and significantly associated with apartment prices across the econometric specifications after controlling for housing characteristics, accessibility, and environmental conditions. In the preferred Spatial Error Model, a 0.1 increase in the GVI corresponds to an approximately 2.7% increase in apartment prices. Satellite-derived vegetation and land surface temperature also show significant relationships with housing values. Machine-learning results further demonstrate that visible greenery contributes to housing-price prediction alongside structural and neighborhood characteristics.
Conclusions: Pedestrian-scale greenery represents an economically valued dimension of urban environmental quality. Integrating street-level and satellite-based measures can strengthen the evidence base for evaluating urban green infrastructure and sustainable housing.
Relevance to sustainable development by and beyond 2030: The findings demonstrate how digital environmental measurement and housing-market evidence can support sustainable urban transformation. Because environmental amenities are capitalized into housing values, urban greening strategies should consider both environmental benefits and equitable distribution to avoid reinforcing spatial inequalities.

Title: "A Solar–Biogas Hybrid Mini-Grid for Off-Grid Coastal Bangladesh: Technical, Economic, and Socio-Environmental Feasibility — A Case Study of Galachipa Upazila"
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Solar–biogas hybrid mini-grid; Renewable energy; Off-grid electrification; Climate change mitigation; Energy access; Coastal Bangladesh; Techno-economic feasibility; Sustainable development.
Abstract_Text:
Bangladesh sits in South Asia and is home to about 161 million people across roughly 29 million families, spread over 147,570 square kilometers. Around 15 million people live in rural areas, many of them far inland and out of reach of the power grid. Extending the grid to these areas is expensive and slow. (Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics [BBS], 2023)
At the top of the atmosphere, Earth receives about 175 petawatts of solar irradiance. Roughly 30% of it bounces back to space, and the rest is absorbed by land, clouds, and water. In Bangladesh, solar insolation ranges from 3.8 to 6.4 kWh per square meter per day, peaking in March and April and dropping to its lowest in December and January. That range makes solar power a realistic option for the country. (NASA POWER, 2024; Das et al., 2020).Bangladesh is largely an agriculture-based, temperate country with good conditions for poultry farming and dairy cattle, which means a steady supply of cow dung and poultry droppings, the starting material for biogas. Poultry farming has long been a self-sustaining part of rural economies in many developing countries, and Bangladesh is no exception: the sector has grown at an average rate of 20 percent a year over the last two decades, supporting rural livelihoods and giving families a path to higher income. (Rahman et al., 2018; Saha et al., 2025)

Title: Prioritizing Climate-Induced Hazards in a Vulnerable Coastal Delta: Evidence from Galachipa Upazila, Southern Bangladesh
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Coastal area, disaster risk, risk analysis, risk reduction, Galachipa Upazila
Abstract_Text:
The coastal area of Bangladesh is highly vulnerable to climate change and climate-induced natural hazards. The coastal community is suffering from different forms of natural hazards such as floods, tropical cyclones, tornadoes, tidal surges, droughts, and river erosion almost annually. The main aim of the study was to identify, analyze, and prioritize the dominating climate-induced hazards of the study area. The research was carried out in Galachipa Upazila of Patuakhali District of the southern coastal region of Bangladesh. Data were collected through direct observations, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, and literature review.
The research establishes the hazards' ranking according to their level of impact and severity as perceived. Salinity is ranked number one, reflecting high risk. Close behind are Flood, Storm Surge, and Storm winds, which are ranked two, three, and four, respectively. River bank erosion and high tides are ranked moderate at five and six, respectively, in light of their possibilities to inflict damage, but to a lesser degree. Irregular rainfall, Pest attack and cyclones are ranked middle level of severity and positioned at seven, eight, and nine, respectively. At the rear is the Hail storm at ten.
The research recommends that the same disaster risks be taken into account in planning and decision-making for any development project for disaster risk reduction. In addition, the research can be used as a guideline for prioritizing mitigation and preparedness measures and resource allocation to address ranked higher hazards of greater consequence to the community or environment.

Title: Traditional Security to Human Security: A Case Study of SDG-3 in India
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Keywords: Traditional Security, Human Security, Health Security, Sustainable Development Goal 3, India
Abstract_Text: India’s vision of good health goes beyond the absence of disease; it encompasses physical, mental, and social well-being for all. In India, the paradigmatic shift from traditional security to human security is most clearly reflected in the recognition of health as a strategic domain, where pandemics, healthcare inequities, and climate-sensitive diseases pose greater threats to human survival than conventional military dangers. Yet the literature on these two areas remains disconnected: human security scholarship treats health as one of seven core dimensions but rarely translates this into indicator-level analysis, while India’s SDG-3 policy literature tracks health outcomes in detail without framing them as security concerns. We aimed to critically assess India’s progress toward SDG-3 targets between 2015 and 2025 through a human security framework, and to identify the structural gaps in healthcare financing, workforce availability, and inter-state disparities most likely to prevent India from meeting its 2030 health security commitments. SDG 3 addresses key health issues, including reproductive, maternal, and child health, as well as communicable and non-communicable diseases. SDG 3 helps identify priority areas and targets, and design evidence-based policies and interventions to effectively achieve the other SDGs.

Title: Climate change adaptation for seaports and airports
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Ching-Pong Poo, Dr. Mark | Liverpool Hope University
Keywords: Climate change adaptation, Seaports, Airports, Transport resilience, Critical infrastructure
Abstract_Text:
Seaports and airports are critical nodes in global transport and supply chain networks, yet their fixed locations, complex infrastructure systems, and dependence on interconnected transport networks make them increasingly vulnerable to climate-related hazards. Rising temperatures, sea-level rise, extreme precipitation, flooding, storms, and other climate extremes can disrupt infrastructure, operations, accessibility, and the wider economic systems that depend on these transport hubs.
This presentation synthesises insights from previous research on climate risk, resilience, and adaptation in major transport infrastructure, with a particular focus on seaports and airports. It examines the similarities and differences in climate exposure, operational vulnerability, and adaptation requirements across the two sectors. Particular attention is given to how climate hazards interact with infrastructure characteristics, operational dependencies, and existing resilience capacity, highlighting the need to move beyond hazard-specific assessments towards integrated and system-level approaches.
The presentation reviews emerging approaches for assessing climate risks and supporting adaptation decision-making, including expert-based assessment, multi-criteria decision analysis, probabilistic risk modelling, and scenario-based evaluation. It also discusses a range of adaptation strategies, from physical infrastructure protection and drainage enhancement to operational preparedness, monitoring, redundancy, and long-term planning.
The findings highlight that effective climate adaptation requires not only stronger physical infrastructure but also adaptive management, cross-sector coordination, and consideration of interconnected transport and supply chain networks. By comparing seaports and airports, the presentation identifies transferable lessons between the two sectors and proposes directions for developing more integrated, evidence-based, and forward-looking climate resilience strategies for critical transport infrastructure.

Title: Governing the food–water–energy nexus: Community resilience in Bali and lessons for European water policy
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: nexus approaches, sustainable resource management, food system transformation, water resilience, multi-level governance
Abstract_Text: Water scarcity increasingly exposes the limits of sectoral approaches to sustainability because pressures on water availability simultaneously affect food production, energy use, livelihoods, and institutional resilience. This study examines how community-based water governance shapes resilience within the food–water–energy nexus in Bali, Indonesia, and considers its relevance to emerging European water-resilience policy. It addresses a gap in nexus scholarship by shifting attention from technical resource optimisation toward the institutional processes through which competing demands are negotiated and coordinated. The research employs a qualitative case-study design based on semi-structured interviews with community water managers and users, field observations, local institutional documents, and policy analysis of the European Water Resilience Strategy and the Water Framework Directive. The findings show that nexus resilience depends not only on resource availability, but also on institutional capacity to allocate water, distribute costs and benefits, adapt rules, coordinate infrastructure, and maintain legitimacy under environmental and socioeconomic pressure. Community-based arrangements can strengthen resilience through collective management and locally legitimate allocation, but their effectiveness weakens when scarcity, infrastructure dependence, and external resource competition exceed local institutional and financial capacity. These findings resonate with the European Union’s shift toward restoring the water cycle, improving water efficiency, strengthening governance, and integrating water resilience with wider economic and security objectives. The study argues that European water policy can benefit from greater attention to locally embedded governance, while the Bali case illustrates how broader policy frameworks can support community institutions without displacing them. By and beyond 2030, resilient food–water–energy systems will require multi-level governance that combines resource efficiency, infrastructure investment, equitable allocation, institutional adaptability, and meaningful local participation.

Title: Agroecological Transition and Food Security in Benin: Lessons for Sustainable Agricultural Transformation beyond 2030
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Laboratory for Research on Innovation for Agricultural Development (LRIDA)
Keywords: food security; smallholder farmers; resilience; agricultural transformation; Benin.
Abstract_Text:
Agroecological transition offers a pathway for improving food security, strengthening farming-system resilience, and advancing sustainable agricultural transformation. However, adoption remains limited among smallholder farmers due to constraints related to technical knowledge, appropriate inputs, markets, finance, and institutional support. Understanding these dynamics is essential for informing agricultural policies and shaping sustainable transformation beyond 2030.
This study examines the relationship between agroecological transition and food security among smallholder farmers in the Donga Department of Benin, focusing on Djougou, Ouaké, and Copargo. A mixed-methods approach combining household surveys, semi-structured interviews, and field observations was used to compare conventional, transitional, and agroecological farming systems. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, multivariate analysis, and qualitative content analysis were used to assess differences in agricultural practices and food-security outcomes.
Preliminary results indicate that18.0%of farmers are engaged in agroecological farming,36.5%are in transition, and45.5%remain predominantly conventional. Crop diversification is reported by64.8%of agroecological farmers, compared with48.6%of transitional and34.7%of conventional farmers. Organic fertilizers and locally available soil-fertility resources are used by69.4%,46.8%, and27.9%of farmers, respectively. Relatively favourable food-security conditions are reported by71.2%of agroecological,59.6%of transitional, and48.3%of conventional farmers. Key constraints include limited technical support (56.2%), insufficient agroecological inputs (48.7%), and limited remunerative markets (44.5%).
The findings suggest that agroecological transition can contribute to more diversified, resilient, and food-secure farming systems, while highlighting the importance of institutional, technical, and market conditions for accelerating sustainable agricultural transformation beyond 2030.

Title: Agroecology, Food Safety and Well-being: Rethinking Sustainable Food Systems for Healthier Communities in Benin
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Organisations: Laboratory for Research on Innovation for Agricultural Development (LRIDA)
Keywords: food safety, well-being, pesticide exposure, sustainable food systems, Benin.
Abstract_Text:
Agroecological transition is increasingly recognized as a pathway towards more sustainable and healthier food systems. Beyond environmental benefits, agroecological practices can contribute to reducing exposure to synthetic pesticides, improving food safety, supporting dietary diversity, and strengthening household well-being. However, the links between agricultural production practices, food safety, nutrition, and well-being remain insufficiently documented in Benin, particularly within rapidly changing urban and coastal food systems.
This study examines the contribution of agroecological practices to food safety and household well-being in Benin, focusing on Houéyogbé, Cotonou, and Grand-Popo. A mixed-methods approach combining household surveys, semi-structured interviews, and field observations was used to assess production practices, pesticide use, food-safety practices, dietary diversity, and perceived well-being. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and qualitative content analysis were used to compare agroecological and conventional production systems.
The results indicate that 18.0% of surveyed producers were engaged in agroecological production, while the majority relied on conventional or mixed practices. Among agroecological producers, 67.4% reported avoiding or significantly reducing synthetic pesticide use, compared with 32.6% who continued to use them. Furthermore, 61.8% of agroecological producers reported respecting recommended pre-harvest intervals, compared with 38.5% of conventional producers. On the consumer side, 72.3% perceived agroecologically produced food as safer, while 58.7% reported paying greater attention to the origin and production practices of food. Household dietary diversity was reported by 64.2% of households associated with agroecological production, compared with 45.8% among conventional production systems. In addition, 69.5% of respondents associated agroecological practices with improved household well-being.
The findings suggest that agroecological transition can contribute simultaneously to safer food, reduced pesticide exposure, improved dietary diversity, and enhanced well-being. Strengthening farmer training, consumer awareness, local markets, and institutional support could therefore help position agroecology as an important pathway for healthier and more sustainable food systems in Benin.

Title: Digital Agriculture and Food System Resilience: Opportunities and Challenges for Smallholder Farmers in West Africa
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Organisations: Laboratory for Research on Innovation for Agricultural Development (LRIDA)
Keywords: food system resilience, digitalization, agricultural innovation, digital inclusion, West Africa.
Abstract_Text:
Digital agriculture is increasingly recognized as a pathway for strengthening the resilience, productivity, and inclusiveness of food systems in West Africa. Mobile phones, digital advisory services, weather information platforms, digital marketplaces, and mobile financial services can improve farmers’ access to information, markets, inputs, and financial resources. However, unequal access to digital technologies, limited connectivity, and low digital literacy remain major constraints.
This study examines the opportunities and challenges associated with digital agriculture among smallholder farmers in Benin, Nigeria, and Togo. A mixed-methods approach combining household surveys, semi-structured interviews, and a review of digital agricultural services was used to assess farmers’ use of digital technologies for agricultural information, climate information, market access, financial services, and farm management. Descriptive statistics and comparative analysis were used to identify patterns of digital adoption and key constraints.
The results indicate that 22.0% of smallholder farmers use digital technologies for agricultural purposes. Among these users, 61.5% access agricultural information, 52.8% use digital tools for market information, 47.6% access weather and climate information, and 35.4% use digital financial services for agricultural transactions. Furthermore, 58.7% report that digital tools have improved their farm-level decision-making. However, 51.9% identify limited digital literacy, 46.3% poor internet or mobile network connectivity, and 39.7% the cost of smartphones, data, or digital services as major barriers.
The findings highlight the potential of digital agriculture to strengthen food system resilience. However, inclusive digital transformation requires improved rural connectivity, digital literacy, affordable services, farmer-centred innovation, and supportive institutional frameworks across West Africa.

Title: Drivers, barriers, and outcomes of eco-innovation: a qualitative investigation of manufacturing industries in Pakistan
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Authors: Shaukat, Sadia; Rehman, Zainab; Rasheed, Haroon
Organisations: Shaukat, Dr. Sadia | University of Sargodha
Keywords: Eco-Innovation Adoption, Drivers, Barriers, Sustainable Business Outcomes, Manufacturing Firms, Pakistan
Abstract_Text:
The purpose of this study is to identify key drivers and barriers influencing the adoption of eco-innovation and to explore its contribution to sustainable business outcomes across manufacturing sector of Pakistan by adopting qualitative research approach. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with key informants from 15 of manufacturing companies actively engaged in eco-innovation practices.
The main insights of this study are three fold. First, companies seem to be primarily influenced by external factors in implementing eco-innovation. Among the internal drivers, the most emphasis has been placed on cost saving and cost reduction, cleaner technology, organizational capacities and cultural legacy, while the most important external drivers are customer green demand, competitive pressure, and compliance with international standards. Secondly, barriers to eco-innovation are also derived from external and internal pressures. Cost (High upfront and capital cost), lack of managerial commitment and limited resource availability prevail within internal barriers, while legislation, inadequate regulatory and government support, weak absorptive capacity and market uncertainty seems to be the most commonly experienced external barriers. finally, the outcomes of eco-innovation that firms most often experience are improved resource efficiency, reduced operational costs, and adoption of greener production technologies are coherent with reported outcomes.
Conclusion- The study concludes that successful implementation of eco-innovation in Pakistan’s manufacturing sector depends on addressing both external institutional and market conditions as well as internal firm-level constraints. The result underscores the need for more institutional and regulatory support, improved organizational capabilities, investment in technical skills, and increased managerial commitment to eco-innovation, all of which have practical implications for policymakers, practitioners, industry leaders and manufacturing firms. Overall, the study adds to the growing literature on eco-innovation by providing empirical insights into eco-innovation drivers, barriers and sustainable business outcomes within the framework of developing economy.

Title: Integrated Social Capital and Functional Community Contracts: Introducing Growth Cooperatives as Societal Foundations for Collective Well-Being and Resilience in Climate-Vulnerable Bangladesh
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Keywords: Social Capital, Alternative Adaptive Mechanisms, Development For Profit, Collective Resilience, Social Contracts, Alternative Governance
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
This research examines how climate-vulnerable communities can build locally governed institutions for collective well-being, social harmony, and resilient growth without depending primarily on donations, debt-based microfinance, or externally prescribed solutions. It investigates whether purpose-oriented community contracts can convert existing trust, knowledge, relationships, aspirations, and reciprocal responsibilities into durable cooperative institutions, and whether such institutions can respond differently to distinct social, cultural, and ecological contexts.
Methods:
The study adopts a comparative, practice-based and participatory research design across two contrasting landscapes of Bangladesh: Tanguar Haor, a distinctive wetland ecosystem that supports fishing, boating, tourism, and seasonal agriculture, and the lower Teesta River basin in Lalmonirhat, characterised by river dynamics, char settlements, and seasonal cropland. Through community consultations, participatory observation, institutional mapping, and case-based comparison, the research examines community aspirations, cultural and livelihood patterns, existing relationships, locally negotiated contracts, cooperative purposes, and decision-making practices. This design enables comparison of how a common institutional approach is adapted to different landscapes and community realities.
Emerging Field Findings and Innovation:
Field evidence indicates an emerging innovation: Growth Cooperatives, structured as non-credit and purpose-oriented community institutions, can transform informal social relationships into accountable systems of collective action. Instead of distributing external resources, the model begins with community-defined purposes and contracts that establish responsibilities, mutual commitments, resource mobilisation, leadership, and collective benefit. Early experience across the two landscapes suggests that this approach can strengthen local organisation while supporting economic initiative, mutual support, dignity, participation, and social peace and harmony.
Implications:
The research proposes Growth Cooperatives as an alternative institutional pathway for climate-vulnerable communities—one that treats communities as producers of their own social and economic infrastructure rather than passive recipients of assistance. It offers a transferable, landscape-sensitive model for strengthening collective well-being and resilience through locally generated cooperation.

Title: Scaling Information Access: Evidence from a Nationwide Digital Policy in China
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Zhao, Shilong; Naeher, Dominik; Liu, Juan; Ma, Junqiao
Organisations: Naeher, Dr. Dominik | University of Goettingen
Keywords: Economic growth; Information access; Spatial disparities; Factor mobility; China
Abstract_Text: Access to information, particularly in digital form, is increasingly recognized as a driver of economic development, yet the evidence comes mostly from small-scale studies whose scalability to national policy remains unknown. We address this gap by exploiting the staggered rollout of China’s Information Access to Villages and Households (IAVH) program across counties. Using a panel of 17,172 county-year observations for 2009–2020 and a difference-in-differences design, we estimate the effect of IAVH on rural economic activity, proxied by rural nighttime light intensity isolated from satellite imagery. IAVH adoption is associated with a 1.5% increase in rural nighttime light intensity, and the estimate is robust across specifications. The effect is larger in counties with (a) deeper information barriers, reflected in poorer transport accessibility and greater administrative and cultural fragmentation, and (b) more uneven spatial endowments, a pattern suggesting that IAVH narrows rather than widens spatial disparities. Individual-level panel evidence is consistent with IAVH lowering the transaction costs that fragment rural land, labor, and capital markets, with the association ending at each market’s non-informational boundary. Because IAVH was implemented after broadband coverage was largely in place, the findings indicate that the marginal benefit of a large-scale digital policy depends not only on how much connectivity it adds but also on whether it converts existing connectivity into use.

Title: Recommend or Simplify? Digital Information Design with Cross-Category Spillovers
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Organisations: Naeher, Dr. Dominik | University of Goettingen
Keywords: Digital Information Design, E-Commerce, Information processing, Welfare effects
Abstract_Text: Digital markets are increasingly shaped by AI-based technologies that curate and prioritize information. Firms use these tools to facilitate product search and steer consumer attention, yet their effects remain poorly understood when consumers choose across multiple product categories. We develop a theoretical framework of a multi-category seller facing buyers with heterogeneous information-processing capacities, contrasting two instruments: simplification, which reduces learning costs, and recommendation, which increases the share of fully informed buyers. Category-specific information provision generates cross-category attention and pricing spillovers and can induce non-monotonic attention responses. The two instruments have sharply different effects on prices and market coverage. Simplification typically raises willingness to pay and prices within a pricing regime, reducing buyer surplus while increasing total welfare; at discrete thresholds, however, it can expand market coverage, lower prices, and raise buyer surplus. Recommendation instead leaves prices unchanged within regimes and typically benefits buyers, but can contract market coverage at discrete thresholds, causing prices to jump and both buyer surplus and total welfare to fall. Our results offer new insights for the design and regulation of information systems and highlight potential risks of AI-driven information provision in multi-category markets.

Title: Beyond Engagement: Within-Person Dynamics of Environmental Action, Recovery, and Psychologically Sustainable Agency
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Psychologically Sustainable Agency; Within-Person Dynamics; Pro-Environmental Behaviour; Environmental Engagement; Behavioural Recovery
Abstract_Text:
Environmental engagement is often studied as a relatively stable characteristic, with research asking why some individuals are more environmentally concerned or behaviourally active than others. This between-person perspective, however, leaves an important temporal question unresolved:how does environmental engagement change within the same person, and what enables it to persist, decline, or return after disengagement?I approach pro-environmental behaviour as a dynamic trajectory rather than a fixed individual attribute.
This research examines whether within-person changes in psychological agency and adaptive capacity predict subsequent environmental engagement, while accounting for prior behaviour and stable differences between individuals. I further propose a conditional model in which perceived climate threat is processed through emotional and coping responses that shape agency, willingness to act, perceived feasibility, and subsequent engagement. The focus therefore shifts from whether people are environmentally engaged to theconditions under which engagement is maintained, interrupted, and recovered.
Repeated National Climate Action Survey data will provide the primary longitudinal basis for examining these trajectories. Where measures permit, I will distinguish psychologically sustainable persistence from persistence accompanied by substantial emotional or psychological costs. Cross-national robustness will be assessed through the International Climate Psychology Collaboration, while the Bath dataset will provide an India-focused and broader Global-South perspective.
I developPsychologically Sustainable Agency (PSA)as a framework describing the capacity to remain responsive to environmental threats while preserving efficacy, emotional functioning, and the psychological resources required to continue or recover constructive action.
By shifting the analytical unit fromthe engaged individual to the changing trajectory of engagement, this research seeks to explain not only why environmental action lasts, but also why it falters  and how it can be renewed.

Title: When Symbolic Responses Become Consequential: Digital Impression Management and Corporate Sustainability
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Keywords: digital impression management; institutional theory; symbolic management; sustainability; analyst coverage; ownership balance
Abstract_Text: Organizations face pressure to demonstrate digital transformation, yet their digital representations may outpace substantive action. We examine whether this divergence—digital impression management (DIM)—affects corporate sustainability. Drawing on institutional theory, we theorize that symbolic digital responses translate into sustainability outcomes through external evaluation, resource access, and organizational action. We further distinguish two governance conditions: external supervision (analyst coverage breadth) and internal governance (ownership balance). Using a longitudinal sample of Chinese listed firms, we find that DIM is associated with lower energy consumption, mediated through external evaluation, resource access, and organizational action. The resource-access pathway accounts for the largest share of the total effect. Broader analyst coverage weakens, whereas greater ownership balance strengthens, the DIM–sustainability relationship. By shifting attention from whether symbolic responses are decoupled from substantive practices to how such responses become consequential, this study extends institutional research on decoupling and symbolic management. More broadly, the findings suggest that the consequences of digital transformation arise not only from what firms substantively do, but also from how their digital actions are represented, evaluated, and translated into organizational outcomes.

Title: INTEGRATED AGRICULTURE-AQUACULTURE SYSTEM AS AN ALTERNATIVE TECHNOLOGY TO IMPROVING SMALL-SCALE FOOD PRODUCTION IN LEYTE SAB-A BASIN PEATLAND, EASTERN VISAYAS, PHILIPPINES
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Authors: Silvano, Brandon Briggs; Lauzon, Quenstein; Madeja, Mary Ann; Domingo, Chrizhane; Merro, Shereen
Keywords: Peatlands, Integrated Agriculture-Aquaculture System, Income
Abstract_Text: The Leyte Sab-a Basin Peatland, the second-largest peatland in the Philippines and the largest water catchment basin in Eastern Visayas, represents a critical ecosystem of ecological and socio-economic importance. Encompassing approximately 3,088 ha, of which about 1,740 ha (44%) have been reclaimed for agriculture, the basin supports predominantly low-income households engaged in agriculture and small-scale aquaculture as sources of food and supplemental livelihood. However, low production among fishpond operators in the municipalities of Alangalang, Santa Fe, and San Miguel, Leyte, is constrained by limited financial resources, remoteness from urban centers, inadequate knowledge of resource utilization, limited awareness of nature-based production technologies, and increasing climate-related pressures. This study introduces the Integrated Agriculture–Aquaculture System (IAAS), a resource-efficient production model that integrates aquaculture with crop or livestock production to maximize the productive use of available land and water resources while maintaining peatland integrity. The system utilizes locally available and peat-adapted plant and animal commodities, providing opportunities to enhance household food production, diversify income sources, and improve resilience to climate-related production risks. In this context, IAAS contributes particularly to SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) and SDG 13 (Climate Action) by strengthening local food production and promoting climate-responsive livelihood strategies while supporting responsible resource utilization. The technology introduction, initiated in November 2024, followed a systematic process involving site assessment, targeted capacity building, validation of site suitability, and phased implementation, complemented by scientific interventions to improve productivity and system sustainability. To date, 15 participating fishpond operators have adopted IAAS configurations, including rice–fish, vegetable–fish, root crop–fish, fruit–fish, and livestock–fish integrations. Preliminary outcomes indicate improved household food security and diversified income opportunities. The study aims to establish an evidence-based, locally adaptable, and environmentally responsible production model for sustainable livelihood development within the Leyte Sab-a Basin Peatland.

Title: Whose knowledge is recognized and sustained? Indigenous Knowledge, Women Artisan and Systematic Recognition in Local Sustainability Governance in Nepal.
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Indigenous knowledge, Equity, Gender, Local governance, Community resilience
Abstract_Text:
Indigenous Knowledge systems are increasingly recognized as important for sustainable and resilient communities, and yet the institutional processes to recognise, support and sustain them remain uneven. This paper examines how local government recognition of Indigenous Knowledge and the contribution of women who sustain it in the Prajapati community of the historic town of Madhyapur Thimi, Nepal, as a case study. It asks whose knowledge and labour are recognized within the local governance, how women’s contribution as a knowledge holder of indigenous pottery are perceived and recognized. Additionally, what these patterns of recognition reveal about equity and community resilience.
Drawing on a qualitative interpretive case study, the research analyses municipal annual planning, policy and budget documents, alongside interviews with municipal representatives, focus groups with community members and women potters. Reflective thematic analysis is used to examine how indigenous pottery is framed within local government priorities and how the contribution of women artisans are represented.
The findings identify a gap between symbolic representation of pottery as part of Madhyapur Thimi’s heritage and its institutional recognition requiring systematic and sustained support. Similarly,while pottery remains closely interconnected to communities' identities, intergenerational knowledge, and livelihood, the labor through which women contribute are frequently embedded within households and support the production process rather than explicit recognition in local governance. This creates an important equity question: while cultural practices may be celebrated as heritage but the knowledge holders and gendered labour who are sustaining them remain insufficiently visible in development plans.
The paper argues that community resilience cannot be understood merely as the preservation of cultural practices. It depends on whether the governance system recognizes the knowledge, labor, and agency of the communities sustaining them. It contributes to the debate on sustainable transformation, through understanding, whose knowledge is visible, and whose contribution counts in local sustainability processes.

Title: Sensory Characteristics of Cookies Formulated with Fish Protein Concentrate Powder Produced from Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus Linnaeus, 1758)
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Silvano, Brandon Briggs; Cerena, Justine; Cabillo, Rolaine; Eyana, Johndie; Solano, Daniel
Keywords: Fish Protein Concentrate, Hedonic scale
Abstract_Text: In Leyte, Eastern Visayas, Philippines, a significant portion of small and large-scale fish pens and fishponds culture Nile Tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus Linnaeus, 1758). However, due to unsustainable aquaculture practices which include poor knowledge on tilapia culture breeding practices resulting to unintentional inbreeding, concerns have arisen regarding the poor quality of Nile Tilapia produced in terms of size and weight. To utilize this affected species, this study was conducted to evaluate the sensory characteristics of the traditional cookies supplemented with fish protein concentrate (FPC) extracted from Nile Tilapia. A total of four treatment samples with varying FPC levels were evaluated in terms of color, aroma, taste, texture, and overall acceptability using the 9-point Hedonic Scale. Treatment 2, the cookie formulation containing 10% FPC, received the highest acceptability score of 6.96, corresponding to a "like moderately" rating. Acceptability scores across all treatments ranged from 6.45 to 6.94, falling within the "like slightly" to "like moderately" categories in the Hedonic scale. A two-way ANOVA revealed significant interactions for sensory attributes. Consumer preference testing further demonstrated that the majority of evaluators favored FPC-enriched cookies over commercially available options, indicating potential market opportunity. Therefore, this study demonstrated the potential for developing fishery products from aquaculture waste, such as Nile Tilapia produced from unintentional inbreeding practices, thereby enhancing the value of the resource that would otherwise be discarded or used for low-value purposes.

Title: Does Carbon Emission Disclosure Influence the Profitability of Listed Firms in Thailand?
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Organisations: THONGTAI, Dr. CHANON | Faculty of Economics
Keywords: Carbon emission disclosure, Firm profitability, ESG reporting, Emerging markets
Abstract_Text:
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) has been encouraging companies to publicly disclose sustainability information with GRI standards including greenhouse gas emissions since year 2021 under voluntary period, with a compulsory phase planned in 2030. Certain are under impression that doing so can damage their profitability due to time and costs of collecting data, reporting, and validating. This study examines whether the disclosure of carbon emission information affects the profitability of companies listed in SET by collecting ESG statistics, including scope-1 and scope-2 emissions data from sustainability reports as well as the profitability data from their official financial reports. Studied companies are in the energy, property and construction, and industrial sectors. Study period is during 2021-2025 subject to availability of data and sources. Panel regression models with firm fixed effects were employed to analyze the influence.
The regression results indicate that carbon emission disclosure has negligible effect on profitability of the studied firms among Thai listed companies. This implies that the negative influence on profitability in terms of costs of sustainability reporting is not scientifically observed in practice. It can also be regarded that market participants may consider incorporate ESG disclosure practice and include in their investment decisions, but some firms might not fully incorporate unless the benefits of disclosure balance outbalance the costs. As Thailand mostly provide primary products as a downstream within the global supply chain, it is essential for Thai firms to align their practices with international sustainability and disclosure standards. Such alignment not only enhances their competitiveness and credibility in global trade but also ensures that businesses should create value not only for their shareholders but for all stakeholders—employees, suppliers, customers, partners, the local community.

Title: Beyond the SDGs: Hybrid Development Goals for an Age of Natural and Artificial Intelligence.
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Keywords: Agency; double literacy; ProSocial AI; Hybrid intelligence
Abstract_Text:
Objective. The Sustainable Development Goals were designed for a world in which human institutions remained the principal agents of development. That premise is changing. Artificial intelligence increasingly influences how knowledge is produced, decisions are made, resources are allocated and behaviour is shaped. As the international community prepares for the post-2030 agenda, this paper proposes Hybrid Development Goals (HDGs) as a framework for development in societies increasingly shaped by interaction between natural and artificial intelligence.
Methods. The paper combines systems thinking, sustainability governance, human-AI interaction and emerging evidence on cognitive offloading and agency decay. It examines where the SDG architecture becomes insufficient when AI is treated mainly as an instrument for accelerating existing targets. The proposed HDG framework is operationalised through Double Literacy, which combines technological literacy with critical reasoning, judgement and responsible action, and ProSocial AI, which evaluates technological choices across Purpose, People, Prosperity and Planet.
Key results. The analysis identifies human agency as a missing dimension of contemporary sustainability governance. AI can expand analytical capacity, access to knowledge and coordination while also shifting cognitive effort, judgement and decision-making away from individuals and institutions. Development metrics must therefore assess not only outcomes, but also the quality of human-AI relationships: who retains meaningful agency, whose knowledge shapes decisions, how technological systems affect future generations, and whether they strengthen social and planetary resilience. This reframes agency preservation as an enabling condition for sustainable development in increasingly hybrid societies.
Conclusions. The post-2030 agenda requires goals designed for a hybrid age. Hybrid Development Goals would extend sustainable development beyond what societies achieve to include how human and artificial intelligence interact in achieving it. Their purpose is to ensure that technological capability expands alongside human agency, social legitimacy and planetary responsibility.

Title: “Navigating the Intersection of Gender Identity in the Informal Economy: Exploring the Case of Gay Men Providing Home-based Beauty Services
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Home-based beauty service, Informal Economy, LGBTQIA+, Intersectionality Theory, Rational Choice Theory
Abstract_Text:
This study explored the experiences of gay men who provide home-based hair,
makeup, and nail services in the informal economy in Davao City. Using a
qualitative case study design, data were gathered through in-depth interviews
with seven gay men engaged in home-based beauty services for at least five years.
Guided by an integrated framework of Intersectionality Theory and Rational
Choice Theory, the study examined the factors influencing their entry into the
field, challenges and risks encountered, and how economic, social, and cultural
factors intersect with their social identities. It also explored the rational coping
strategies they employed to navigate the precarious nature of informal work. The
thematic analysis revealed that gay men's engagement in the home-based beauty
work is shape by both economic practicality and social benefits, such as passion
and identity. They encountered multiple challenges, including economic
insecurity, toxic competition, and the emotional labor of managing difficult clients.
They are expose to economic, emotional, and physical risk while working in the
