field. These challenges and risks intersect with poverty, limited education, gender
identity and discrimination, and family responsibilities that lead to participants
normalizing their vulnerabilities, while weighing the benefits and costs of
informal work. To cope with the challenges and risks, they maintain
professionalism, regulate their emotions, develop their skills, build referrals, and
expand their social media advertising skill. This study contributes to the sociology
of labor in the informal economy, and fills a gap in the literature by focusing on
the marginalization, vulnerabilities, and agency produced by the intersection of
LGBTQIA+ social identities and informal labor conditions. Ultimately, it challenges the inclusivity of current global frameworks, offering a vital critique for the post-2030 sustainability agenda regarding "decent work" and social equity for marginalized informal workers.

Title: Social Inequalities and Multidimensional Exclusion Undermine the Sustainability of Local Communities in Developing and Underdeveloped Countries
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Social Inequality, Multidimensional Exclusion, Community Sustainability, Marginalized Communities
Abstract_Text: The sustainability of local communities refers to their ability to survive, adapt, and develop while ensuring sustainable social, political, and economic conditions for present and future generations. Despite global commitments to equality and justice, many communities in developing and underdeveloped countries continue to experience persistent social inequalities and multidimensional forms of exclusion. These challenges are particularly evident across South Asia and Africa where they undermine both community sustainability and national development. This study asks: how do social inequalities and multidimensional forms of exclusion undermine the sustainability of marginalized local communities in Bangladesh? Marginalized communities live in remote rural areas, riverine regions, coastal zones, hill tracts, and urban slums. They have limited access to education, healthcare, public services, and economic opportunities and depend largely on low-income traditional occupations including fishing, sanitation work, tea garden labor, jhum cultivation, and begging. Persistent poverty forces many children into labor, restricting their education and future opportunities. Consequently, these communities remain excluded from political participation, social decision-making, and public policy. Poor health awareness, inadequate healthcare, and malnutrition further reinforce their vulnerability, while weak economic structures and insufficient policy support leave their basic needs unmet. This study employs a qualitative research design based on semi-structured interviews with members of the River Gypsy (Bede) community, tea garden workers, coastal communities, Hill Tracts communities, and urban slum dwellers. The research also incorporates a qualitative review of reports published in Prothom Alo and The Daily Star. The findings demonstrate that social inequality and economic, social, and political exclusion are the principal barriers to the sustainability of local communities. The study contributes to the sociology of local communities by providing empirical evidence from Bangladesh and argues that targeted, inclusive, and context sensitive public policies are essential for overcoming structural barriers and promoting sustainable local community development in developing and underdeveloped countries.

Title: Commercialization of vehicle-to-grid technology across passenger vehicles requires localized policies
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Organisations: Sun, Dr. Xin | University of Groningen
Keywords: Vehicle-to-grid, techno-economic analysis, passenger vehicle
Abstract_Text: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology could transform electric vehicles into distributed energy storage resources, but its commercial viability remains highly heterogeneous across regions and poorly understood. Here we develop a bottom-up techno-economic framework to evaluate V2G commercialization across 337 Chinese cities, incorporating city-level differences in electric passenger vehicle markets, driving behavior, climate, electricity tariffs, and ancillary service compensation. The levelized cost of storage estimated ranges from 1.2–6.1 CNY/kWh for frequency regulation and 1.1–8.1 CNY/kWh for peak shaving and valley filling, while benefit-cost ratios vary from 9–22% and 15–136%, respectively, meaning V2G in most cities remain unprofitable. Achieving profitability would require frequency regulation subsidies to increase by 4.7–22.3 times and the time-of-use price spreads to increase by 1.0–45.1 times. Our analysis shows that V2G commercialization is most favorable in southeastern China for large battery electric vehicles, highlighting the importance of localized rather than uniform national policies for accelerating V2G deployment.

Title: Shifting Northern Hemisphere snowfall extremes and their physical drivers
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Authors: Bintanja, Richard; Romein, Nick; van der Linden, Eveline
Keywords: Snowfall, extreme, climate change, Greenland
Abstract_Text: Northern Hemisphere extreme snowfall changes are studied using the Large ENsemble TIme Slice (LENTIS) model. Extreme snowfall frequency and amount are projected to increase more strongly than light snowfall in several regions. The sign and magnitude of change depend on the regions present-day seasonal mean climatological temperature. While light and extreme snowfall are projected to decline significantly, particularly in maritime and mid-latitude regions near the melting point, increases are expected in high-latitude maritime, select high-altitude and continental areas. Compared to light snowfall, extreme snowfall only begins to decline at seasonal mean temperatures roughly 7 °C higher. Consequently, increases in light snowfall are limited to the coldest regions, whereas increases in extremes already occur in relatively warmer, yet still freezing regions. In sufficiently cold regions, warming enhances extreme event frequency (up to 278%) and amount (up to 271%) more strongly than light snowfall (up to 101% and 152%). Regions near the melting point are thermodynamically controlled due to climate warming, while colder regions are likely influenced by both thermodynamic warming and dynamical circulation changes, evident for Greenland. Extreme Greenland snowfall is found to be associated with a sea level pressure anomaly dipole between Greenland and Northern Europe, promoting warm moist Atlantic air advection. Using the Greenland Oscillation Index (GOI) – which measures the strength of the dipole – it is found that increases in extreme snowfall events are linked to a higher frequency of favorable circulation patterns with above-median GOI, particularly over Eastern, Central and Northern Greenland.

Title: Socio-Technical Characterization of Urban Quarters for Municipal Heat Planning: A Spatial Cluster Analysis of Energy and Socio-Demographic Milieus in Bremen, Germany
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Keywords: municipal heat planning, urban transformation, socio-spatial analysis, citizen participation, GIS
Abstract_Text:
Municipal heat planning in Germany identifies suitable neighbourhoods for centralized or decentralized heat supply mainly on energetic and urban-structural grounds. The socio-cultural composition of residents and their potential to engage with this transformation are rarely considered systematically. Citizen participation is nevertheless a key precondition for implementation.
This contribution presents a GIS-based framework that links energy-related and socio-demographic data. It characterizes urban quarters along two dimensions: technical suitability for heat supply options (individual, district, or low-temperature network heating) and societal activation potential. The analysis uses a 100m x 100m grid for the city of Bremen. It combines milieu-based social-geospatial data (Sinus-Milieus) with seven indicators from the 2022 census. These indicators cover home-ownership rate, building age, vacancy rate, and household structure. A spatial cluster analysis identifies spatially coherent quarter types. These types are then intersected with previously derived suitability areas for heat supply options.
The resulting two-dimensional quarter typology is explorative and hypothesis-generating. It offers municipalities and energy utilities an empirical basis for prioritizing quarters and tailoring citizen-activation strategies. This links technical infrastructure planning with the social dimension of urban transformation. The approach is transferable to other cities with comparable data availability. It contributes to Theme 2.4 by showing how socio-spatial analysis can inform urban transformation measures beyond purely energetic planning criteria.

Title: Investment Opportunities in Solar PV, Battery Storage and Distributed Energy in Nepal
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Federation of Nepal Cottage and Small Industries (FNCSI)
Keywords: Solar PV, Battery Energy Storage, Distributed Energy, MSMEs, Renewable Energy Investment, Nepal, Green Enterprise, Nepal China Cooperation
Abstract_Text: Nepal is entering a new phase of renewable energy development in which hydropower, traditionally the backbone of the national electricity system, can be complemented by solar photovoltaic (PV), battery energy storage systems (BESS), distributed renewable energy, and smart energy management. This paper examines Nepal’s emerging renewable energy market and highlights opportunities for investment, technology transfer, enterprise development, and international partnership. Particular attention is given to utility scale and rooftop solar PV, commercial and industrial solar plus storage, agricultural energy applications, mini-grids and microgrids, electric mobility, and digital energy solutions. Battery storage is identified as an important market enabler for renewable energy integration, system flexibility, commercial and industrial backup, peak management, resilient mini grids, and EV charging. The paper further argues that Nepal’s energy transition should move beyond conventional energy access towardproductive energy use, where clean electricity directly supports enterprises, employment, income generation, and local economic development. Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are positioned as critical actors in this transformation, particularly in agriculture, manufacturing, tourism, services, and green industries. Accordingly, renewable energy investment should not focus solely on large infrastructure projects but should also enable thousands of productive enterprises across Nepal. Potential investment and cooperation models include foreign direct investment, joint ventures, public private partnerships, EPC plus-finance, Energy-as-a-Service, local assembly and manufacturing, and technology licensing and transfer. Nepal–China cooperation offers particular potential by combining China’s technology, manufacturing capacity, investment, and supply chains with Nepal’s renewable resources, growing energy demand, local enterprises, and emerging market opportunities. The proposed pathway is thereforeTechnology → Partnership → Investment → Enterprise → Prosperity, transforming Nepal’s renewable energy potential into reliable energy, competitive enterprises, green jobs, and sustainable economic growth.

Title: The Effect of Utility Services to Child Health in Indonesia
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Arina, Shahnaz Natasya; Masron, Tajul Ariffin; Nugroho, Kusumo Bambang
Keywords: child wasting; clean water; electricity access; utilities; child health; Indonesia; dynamic panel data; system GMM
Abstract_Text: Child wasting remains a significant public health concern in Indonesia, while existing research has largely focused on stunting and child mortality rather than wasting. This study examines the relationship between access to basic utility infrastructure—particularly clean water and electricity—and the prevalence of wasting among children in Indonesia. Using balanced panel data covering 33 provinces over the period 2012–2022, the study employs a dynamic panel-data approach using the Generalized Method of Moments (GMM). Child wasting is used as the dependent variable, while utility indicators include the volume and value of clean water distributed, household access to improved drinking-water sources, electricity distributed, and household access to electricity from the State Electricity Company (PLN). The models also control for provincial economic conditions, protein consumption, consumer prices, government health expenditure, and carbon dioxide emissions. The results from the two-step system GMM indicate significant negative relationships between child wasting and several utility indicators. A 1% increase in the volume of clean water distributed is associated with a 5% reduction in the wasting rate, while a 1% increase in the value of clean water distributed is associated with a 4.8% reduction. A 1% increase in the proportion of households with access to improved drinking-water sources is associated with a 41.4% reduction in child wasting. For electricity, the volume of electricity distributed is not statistically significant, but a 1% increase in the proportion of households with access to electricity from PLN is associated with a 26.5% reduction in wasting. These findings highlight the importance of addressing child wasting through an integrated approach that combines nutrition interventions with improvements in essential infrastructure. Strengthening access to safe drinking water and household electricity should therefore form part of broader multisectoral strategies to improve child health and reduce wasting in Indonesia.

Title: Digital Regional: Innovative Tools to Increase Local Food Choices in Online Grocery Retail
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Spieker, Svea; Herrmann, Lisa; Herzig, Christian
Keywords: production and consumption, value chains, business models, sustainable resource management, food system transformation
Abstract_Text:
OBJECTIVE: The import-dependent food system is environmentally and socially vulnerable to opaque supply chains, geopolitical uncertainties and climate change, highlighting the need for organic-regional value chains. Addressing convenience and knowledge barriers, the project „Bio-Regional-Development” (BiRD) examines two digital measures at the online store Ökokiste Boßhammersch Hof (food-box supplier): a recipe tool highlighting (less-in-demand) regional foods with one-click cart additions and gamified regional bonuses with points and discount challenges.
METHODS: In a mixed-methods design (recipe tool: May/June 2025; regional bonuses: May–July 2026), think-aloud tests captured cognitive processes, evaluated via content-structuring qualitative analysis after Kuckartz and Rädiker. A full census of A/B-test sales data assessed cart-level economic success descriptively. Additionally, customer surveys based on the extended Theory of Planned Behavior before (February/March 2025) and after implementation (November 2026) evaluate intention-behavior gap changes via structural equation modeling addressing test-situation and generalizability limitations.
KEY RESULTS: The recipe tool significantly increased intervention-group sales and shows that full-recipe purchases localize vegetable consumption, though absolute sales remain low. For regional foods with low demand (e.g. less-known varieties), no effect emerged, presumably due to limited recipe coverage. Usability tests revealed an inspiration effect driving post-viewing purchases - observed overall, but particularly pronounced for non-regional products.
CONCLUSIONS: Digital recipe tools can effectively nudge consumers toward local food when purposefully designed.Practically, prominent placement, more recipes with regional niche products and convenience optimizations are recommended. How regional bonuses support this effect and whether both tools jointly reduce the intention-behavior gap is currently evaluated; final results will be completed in Q1/2027.
RELEVANCE TO SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT BY AND BEYOND 2030: Digital platforms for organic-regional food systems strengthen local circular economy and resilience against crisis. This directly supports the 2030 Agenda (SDGs 2, 12, 13), providing practical insights into how digital innovations advance the socio-ecological transformation of food systems beyond 2030.

Title: Street-scape visual features, sustainable mobility, and low-carbon urban transformation: Evidence from urban park visits in Shenzhen, China
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Zhang, Wenting; Cheng, Yiming; Hua, Li
Organisations: Zhang, Dr. Wenting | Huazhong agricultural university
Keywords: low-carbon urban transformation, street-scape visual features, travel-related carbon emissions, urban parks
Abstract_Text:
Promoting sustainable mobility has become an important component of low-carbon urban transformation. Existing studies have mainly examined the environmental characteristics of trip origins and destinations, while paying less attention to the built environment along travel routes. Taking Shenzhen, China, as a case study, this research investigates how street-scape visual features influence residents’ low-carbon travel to urban parks and evaluates the carbon-reduction potential of different urban transformation measures.
A questionnaire survey conducted among urban park visitors between March and May 2023 yielded 3,970 valid responses. Approximately 137,000 street-view images were analyzed to quantify visual features along respondents’ travel routes, including the green view index, sky openness index, sidewalk proportion, and wall coverage. These indicators were combined with visitors’ sociodemographic characteristics, park attributes, and other built-environment variables in a generalized ordered logistic regression model.
The results show that street greenery and sky openness are key factors associated with low-carbon travel (Std = −2.886, p < 0.001; Std = −2.249, p = 0.004). In 2023, the 176 urban parks included in the study received approximately 492 million visits, generating an estimated 41,300 tonnes of travel-related carbon emissions. Higher emissions were concentrated in coastal districts such as Nanshan and Futian, while emission intensity generally decreased from west to east.
Three transformation scenarios were evaluated: increasing the public transport modal share to 65%, increasing the proportion of new-energy vehicles to 40%, and increasing the green view index to 0.18. These scenarios could reduce emissions by 27%, 17%, and 4%, respectively. Although street-environment enhancement produces a smaller direct reduction, it remains a practical complementary measure for promoting sustainable mobility in high-density cities. The findings provide empirical support for integrating transportation, vehicle-energy, and street-environment measures into low-carbon urban planning.

Title: Nutritional Commitments of India: Challenges for Sustainable Development Goals and ‘Viksit Bharat Aspirations’
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Authors: Ansary, Rabiul; Sahoo, Amit kumar; Palta Singh, KR
Keywords: Nutrition, health, NFHS, SDG, Viksit Bharat
Abstract_Text: India carries one of the heaviest burdens of malnutrition in the world, with a double-edge sword situation. Child and adult undernutrition remain widespread even as adult overweight and obesity are on a steady rise , producing a double burden. Because this gets transmitted across the life course and between generations. This study assesses how far India and its major states have progressed toward the child nutrition targets under Sustainable Development Goal 2.2 and towards the ‘halt the rise’ benchmark for both 2030 and the Viksit Bharat 2047 horizon. We calculated prevalence rates, actual progress, and required time using NFHS-5 & 6 data. The results are sobering. Except for stunting, all other indicators experienced either very slow progress or deterioration. Most states are off target and may fail to achieve SDG 2.2 in 2030. Only two states have already met the children underweight target, and fifteen are unlikely to reach it even by 2047. Stunting is improving faster, wasting is effectively stalled, and maternal thinness is receding slowly. Adult obesity meanwhile rises unchecked in the absence of any binding reduction target. Better-performing states either recorded a little improvement or deterioration in child and maternal undernutrition. Closing these gaps by 2030 for SDG realisation and before 2047 for Viksit Bharat aspirations, requires effective intervention aimed simultaneously at both tails of the nutritional distribution.

Title: Are Southeast Asian Countries on Track to Reduce Household Air Pollution? A Regional Trend, Inequality, and Forecasting Analysis (1990–2030)
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Authors: Fitriangga, Agus; Alex, Alex; Fahdi, Faisal Kholid
Keywords: Household air pollution, Southeast Asia, Trend analysis, Forecasting, Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract_Text: Background: Household air pollution (HAP) remains a major environmental health risk in low- and middle-income countries, yet the extent to which progress has accelerated in the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) era is unclear. This study assessed long-term trends, HAP exposure projections by 2030, and shifts in trajectories before and after 2015 in Southeast Asia.Methods: An ecological longitudinal study was conducted using the Global Burden of Disease database for 1990-2023 in 11 Southeast Asian countries. Log-linear regression analysis was performed to obtain the annual percentage change (APC), autoregressive integrated moving average models were used to forecast HAP exposure up to 2030, and segmented regression was performed to assess changes before and after 2015. Regional estimates were population-weighted, and sensitivity, uncertainty, and panel mixed-effects analyses were done for robustness.Results: Exposure to HAP decreased in all countries, but to a different degree. Viet Nam and Thailand had the largest decreases, with projected 2030 exposures of 17.3% and 5.2%, against 96.4% in Lao PDR and 67.5% in Myanmar. Regionally, HAP exposure decreased from approximately 70% in 1990 to 40% in 2023 (p<0.001) and was projected to fall to 25-30% by 2030. However, there were several countries that remained off the desired trajectory. No significant regional shift in trend after 2015 was found, and large disparities between countries persisted.Conclusion: Exposure to HAP has decreased significantly in Southeast Asia, but it is uneven and insufficient in some countries. The lack of a significant change after 2015 suggests that the SDG era has not yet brought about a significant regional change in trajectory. More targeted and equitable interventions are needed to accelerate progress toward 2030.

Title: Artificial intelligence for urban sustainability synergies and spillovers across cities
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: FENG, Dr. RUNCHUAN | University of Groningen
Keywords: artificial intelligence, sustainable development, spillover effects, twin transition, urban governance
Abstract_Text: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to support climate adaptation, food security, energy transition, public health, and sustainable urban planning. Yet most urban AI applications remain city-centred: they evaluate how digital tools improve sustainability within one city, while paying less attention to how these interventions reshape sustainability outcomes elsewhere. This paper proposes an AI-assisted framework for understanding cross-city sustainability synergies and spillover effects in the context of the twin green and digital transition. The central argument is that AI can help cities move beyond isolated sustainability actions by detecting whether sustainable development progress in one urban system generate co-benefits or hidden burdens for other cities. The proposed framework integrates machine learning, natural language processing, and scenario modelling. It can be applied to identify how policies in climate governance, energy efficiency, food logistics, and health services influence other cities through resource and service demand, technology diffusion and migration, supply chains and policy learning. For example, AI-based traffic management may reduce local emissions while shifting logistics pressure to neighbouring cities; conversely, shared urban climate platforms may create positive spillovers by transferring knowledge, improving early warning systems, and coordinating regional adaptation. By linking local AI applications with inter-city sustainability interactions, this study updates artificial intelligence as more than a technical tool for optimizing individual cities. It becomes an auxiliary technology for identifying synergies, anticipating and decreasing unintended negative spillovers, and designing cooperative urban sustainability pathways. The framework contributes to post-2030 sustainable development by supporting cities that are not only smarter and greener internally, but also more responsible in their effects on other urban systems.

Title: From Hiti to Resilience: Lessons from Bhaktapur’s Traditional Urban Water System for Integrated Sustainable Transformation Beyond 2030
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: sustainable development; SDGs; post-2030; urban resilience; traditional water systems; hiti; ponds; indigenous knowledge; socio-ecological systems; Bhaktapur; Nepal
Abstract_Text:
As the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals approaches, sustainable urban transformation requires approaches that connect environmental systems with social institutions, cultural knowledge and everyday urban life. This paper examines Bhaktapur, Nepal, where traditional stone spouts (hiti), ponds, recharge areas, settlements, public spaces and community practices historically formed an interconnected urban water system. Rather than treating these elements solely as heritage assets, the study examines how their relationships can inform urban resilience and sustainable development beyond 2030.
Bhaktapur is examined as a qualitative case study using walking-based field observation, heritage and infrastructure documentation, community interaction, tourism observation, and analysis of relationships among hiti, ponds, neighbourhoods, public spaces and cultural institutions. The study conceptualises the traditional water system as socio-ecological infrastructure linking water management, settlement organisation, community stewardship, cultural practices, public space and local economic activity.
The findings indicate that Bhaktapur’s traditional water system extends beyond water provision. Its spatial organisation connects water infrastructure with neighbourhood life, public interaction, cultural practices and locally embedded knowledge. The hiti–pond network demonstrates how ecological functions and social institutions can operate as interconnected components of urban infrastructure. At the same time, its contemporary condition highlights challenges associated with urban transformation, changing environmental conditions and the continuity of traditional knowledge.
The paper argues that the post-2030 lesson is not to reproduce historical systems unchanged, but to recover their underlying principles of integration, community stewardship, local knowledge and multifunctional public infrastructure. Bhaktapur provides a locally grounded case for linking water resilience, cultural heritage, inclusive public space and community-based urban transformation. The study proposes greater recognition of locally evolved socio-ecological systems and community knowledge in post-2030 sustainability frameworks.

Title: Flood Exposure and Menstrual Health among Young Women in India: Implications for Climate-Resilient Health Systems
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Organisations: Health Systems Studies, Tata Institute of Social Sciences
Keywords: Menstrual hygiene management; Flood exposure; Disaster risk reduction; India; NFHS-5; SDG 3
Abstract_Text:
Floods have the potential to disrupt water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services, which are essential components of safe menstrual hygiene management (MHM). However, menstrual health remains insufficiently discussed in disaster preparedness and often receives limited attention in climate-resilient health planning. Our study assessed the association between residence in flood-prone districts and adequate MHM among young women in India.
The data were collected from two sources: the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21) and the Central Water Commission (CWC). NFHS-5 data
were linked with district-level flood classifications from the CWC. A total of 216,897 women aged 15–24 years were included. Adequate MHM was defined as hygienic absorbent use, improved access to water and sanitation, and the availability of a handwashing facility. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and multivariable logistic regression were used to examine the association between flood-prone residence and adequate MHM.
Overall, 35.1% of young women had adequate MHM. Prevalence was lower in flood-prone districts than in non-flood-prone districts (21.8% vs 36.2%). Women living in flood-prone districts had lower crude odds of adequate MHM (COR: 0.49; 95% CI: 0.47–0.52), and the association remained after adjustment for individual, household, and contextual characteristics (AOR: 0.83; 95% CI: 0.79–0.91).
The lower prevalence of adequate MHM in flood-prone districts brings menstrual hygiene into the climate–health nexus as a dimension that remains unheeded in disaster preparedness. Ensuring access to menstrual materials, safe water, sanitation, and handwashing facilities during floods connects reproductive health with the broader objectives of SDGs 3, 5 and 6. Future research should examine whether the duration and severity of flooding modify the relationship between flood exposure and MHM.

Title: Can Preference for Sons Lead to Health Penalty for Daughters? Evidence from Anaemia Among Young Girls in India
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Son preference, anaemia, gender, health penalty, gender discrimination, SDG
Abstract_Text:
This paper attempts to find out the causal impact of maternal son preference on childhood iron deficiency anaemia among female children in India. It uses microdata from the fifth round of National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21). We use a propensity score matching (PSM) framework and restrict our analytical sample to daughters aged 6–59 months. Treatment is defined as a mother's stated preference for sons (desiring more sons than daughters), compared against a control group of mothers with no stated son preference. Moreover, to isolate behavioural intra-household discrimination from intergenerational physiological transmission, we explicitly balance across mother’s anaemia status alongside demographic covariates, household wealth, and maternal land ownership as a proxy for empowerment. Our findings reveal a statistically significant "Daughter Penalty." In baseline specifications, daughters of mothers expressing son preference are 3.9 percentage points more likely to be anaemic relative to structurally identical counterparts. Controlling for maternal anaemia through matching marginally reduces this effect to 3.1 percentage points,
confirming a distinct behavioural channel beyond biological transmission of anaemia from mothers to daughters. Disaggregated age-group analyses demonstrate that this health penalty depends heavily on developmental stage: the penalty is statistically indistinguishable from zero during early infancy (6–23 months) where breastfeeding acts as a protective nutritional buffer but rises to 4.6 percentage points in the post-breastfeeding window (24–59 months).
This divergence indicates that intra-household gender discrimination manifests most acutely when young girls transition from breastfeeding to family-allocated solid diets where structural inequality persists. By demonstrating how entrenched gender bias actively exacerbates child malnutrition, this study highlights that achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, specifically SDG 2.2 (Ending All Forms of Malnutrition), SDG 3.2 (Ending Preventable Child Mortality), and SDG 5.1 (Ending All Forms of Discrimination Against Women and Girls) requires gender-transformative public health strategies that target intra-household allocation alongside clinical nutrition.

Title: Institutional mission as a missing link in sustainability beyond 2030: lessons from catholic universities
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Zitto Soria, Prof. Maria | Francisco de Vitoria University
Keywords: institutional and governance reforms, future sustainability priorities, sustainability beyond the Sustainable Development Goals, institutional mission, Catholic universities
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study examines whether environmental sustainability can be integrated into the core identity and mission of Catholic universities and considers how mission-based institutional cultures may contribute to sustainability priorities beyond 2030. It asks whether sustainability can move from peripheral initiatives or strategic commitments to a structural principle guiding university education, research, management, and social engagement.
Methodology: The study combines documentary and conceptual analysis. It reviews the social and ecclesial context of environmental sustainability, analyzes institutional websites, scientific literature, and official documents from sixteen Catholic universities across several continents, and examines Francisco de Vitoria University in Spain as an in-depth case. The analysis applies the Expanded Reason framework through four dimensions—anthropological, epistemological, ethical, and meaning—to assess the foundations and institutional implications of environmental commitment.
Key results: The comparative review identifies recurring forms of engagement, including references to Laudato Si’ and integral ecology, dedicated institutional structures, curricular integration, research, campus policies, and social action, but also differing levels of institutionalization. The case analysis shows progress in curriculum, sustainability research, and community engagement, alongside gaps in cross-curricular integration, interdisciplinary synthesis, and the visible coherence of campus practices. The framework indicates that sustainability can be grounded in institutional mission rather than treated as an external or temporary agenda.
Conclusions: For the post-2030 sustainability agenda, the findings suggest that institutional mission, culture, and value frameworks can function as drivers of long-term sustainability integration. Embedding sustainability in university identity can strengthen continuity across leadership cycles and connect governance, education, research, and operations. The study therefore identifies mission-based institutional culture as a potential missing link in sustainability agendas and as a contribution to institutional reform and future sustainability priorities.

Title: Localizing the Sustainable Development Goals without naming them: lessons from 4,875 municipal Instagram posts in Türkiye
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: SDG localization, monitoring progress, implementation gaps, Voluntary National and Local Reviews, municipal social media
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Local governments are central to localizing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet little is known about how the goals appear in their everyday public communication. This study examines what municipal social media communication reveals about SDG localization as 2030 approaches.
Methods: All 4,875 Instagram posts published by three municipalities in Türkiye's Bursa-Eskişehir-Bilecik region (two metropolitan, one provincial center) between April 2024 and April 2026 were analyzed. In a mixed-methods design, each post was coded in MAXQDA against the three pillars of the triple bottom line and all 17 goals, with pilot coding and an independent second coder, followed by thematic analysis.
Key results: Social sustainability dominated, appearing in 91% of posts, while economic (39%) and environmental (24%) content remained secondary. SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) appeared in 68% of posts, whereas clean energy (SDG 7) and life below water (SDG 14) were almost absent (14 and 28 codings). Crucially, posts did not frame their content in SDG terms: alignment was implicit, embedded in routine service and event announcements rather than presented as a shared agenda. Communication was event-driven rather than strategic, and the environmental gap was widest in the smaller municipality, whose environmental content per post was about half the metropolitan level.
Conclusions: Municipalities are localizing the goals in practice without naming them. This silent localization leaves local contributions largely unrecognized as part of the global agenda and keeps energy and water transitions at the margins of public communication. For sustainable development by and beyond 2030, the study draws two lessons: future agendas should support explicit, balanced, goal-linked communication at the local level, and municipal social media can serve as a low-cost, publicly available data source for Voluntary Local Reviews, using simple indicators of dimensional balance and goal coverage.

Title: Green Infrastructure as Climate Adaptation: A Cost-Benefit Analysis of Nature-Based Solutions in Vulnerable Cities
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Green Infrastructure, Climate Adaptation, Nature-Based Solutions, Urban Resilience, Environmental Economics
Abstract_Text: As climate change intensifies urban vulnerabilities—manifesting in severe heat island effects, flash flooding, and extreme stormwater runoff - municipalities worldwide face urgent demands to adapt infrastructure. Nature-Based Solutions (NbS), including urban wetlands, green roofs, permeable pavements, and biosphere corridors, have emerged as sustainable alternatives to traditional "grey" concrete infrastructure. This article provides a cost-benefit analysis (CBA) evaluating the economic, social, and environmental viability of green infrastructure in climate-vulnerable cities. While grey infrastructure offers single-purpose flood or heat control, it suffers from rapid capital depreciation and zero ecosystem co-benefits. In contrast, green infrastructure requires careful spatial integration and specialized ongoing upkeep, but delivers multi-functional value over its life cycle. On the cost side, this paper evaluates upfront capital expenditures, land opportunity costs, and maintenance budgets. On the benefit side, it quantifies direct financial savings - such as avoided flood damage repair, reduced stormwater management expenses, and lowered cooling energy demands - alongside broader co-benefits, including carbon sequestration, biodiversity conservation, and public health improvements. Through a comparative synthesis of municipal case studies, including Medellín’s Green Corridors and Copenhagen’s Cloudburst Management Plan, this study demonstrates that green infrastructure yields higher long-term net returns when co-benefits are factored into economic models. However, widespread adoption remains constrained by siloed municipal budgets, financing gaps, and short-term political horizons. The article concludes with key policy recommendations for urban planners and climate finance decision-makers to embed nature-based solutions into municipal capital budgeting frameworks.

Title: Global Trends in Ecosystem Disservices Research: A Systematic Literature Review
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Keywords: Ecosystem disservices, ecosystem services, human well-being, systematic review, adverse effects
Abstract_Text: The ecosystem services and disservices framework is a key approach for understanding complex human-nature interactions and the contributions of ecosystems to human well-being. Although ecosystem services research has expanded substantially across regions and disciplines, ecosystem disservices research remains an emerging field of inquiry, with limited synthesis of its geographic and thematic scope. This study, therefore, systematically examines the spatial extent, research patterns, and thematic evolution of global ecosystem disservices literature. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, a systematic search using relevant keywords was conducted in the Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus databases. A total of 13, 585 records were retrieved from the searches, of which 518 documents were retained following full-text screening for data analysis. Data were manually extracted and analyzed thematically. The findings indicate that agriculture and urban ecosystem management dominate ecosystem disservices research, with studies mostly concentrated in the Global North. Most studies adopt mixed-method approaches and focus on local and provincial scales. Health and economic impacts associated with ecosystem disservices are prominent themes in the literature. The systematic review further shows that ecosystem disservices are frequently examined alongside ecosystem services, highlighting the interconnected nature of beneficial and adverse effects of ecosystems on human well-being. At the same time, diverse terminology has been used to describe adverse effects of ecosystems on people, reinforcing conceptual ambiguity within the ecosystem disservices literature. Because ecosystem disservices can impede sustainable development, incorporating ecosystem disservice targets and indicators into post-2030 sustainability framework may be essential for effective environmental governance.

Title: Solutions for mitigating soil loss from a human-nature coupled perspective
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: food-land nexus, human-altered soil erosion modelling, human activities, socio-ecological coupled, MRIO
Abstract_Text: Soil erosion threatens agricultural productivity, ecosystem functioning, and sustainable development. Although erosion occurs locally, its drivers and consequences extend across regions through hydrological processes and socioeconomic connections. Understanding these interactions requires a coupled human–land systems perspective that connects biophysical dynamics with production, consumption, and governance. This study proposes an integrated framework linking the attribution of soil erosion, the transmission of its impacts, and collaborative governance across spatial scales. First, the framework combines soil erosion modelling with spatial analyses of environmental and socioeconomic drivers to distinguish the contributions of climatic variability, land-use change, agricultural practices, and conservation interventions, while examining their interactions. Second, it links hydrological connectivity with interregional supply-chain relationships to investigate two distinct transmission pathways: the downstream movement of sediment and associated environmental impacts, and the displacement of erosion pressures and propagation of erosion-related production risks through trade. This distinction enables an integrated assessment of where erosion originates, which regions drive erosion-intensive production through consumption, and where its consequences are experienced. Third, scenario analysis explores how coordinated soil and water conservation, adjustments in agricultural production, and interregional cooperation could reduce erosion while safeguarding food supply and avoiding the transfer of environmental burdens. Particular attention is given to trade-offs among conservation effectiveness, economic costs, and the distribution of responsibilities and benefits. The proposed framework provides a basis for connecting place-based conservation with shared responsibility across watersheds and supply chains, thereby supporting more equitable and coordinated responses to soil erosion.

Title: Parametric consequential life cycle assessment and global sensitivity analysis for sustainable food production systems
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Liu, Weier; Guo, Hui; Liao, Nanlin; Hamelin, Lorie
Keywords: agricultural system, life cycle assessment, uncertainty, food market, land use change
Abstract_Text: Sustainable agricultural management interventions not only alter inputs and outputs at farm level, but induce land use-related impacts and market driving feedback. Life cycle assessment (LCA) that omits these consequences or treat uncertain inventories deterministically may therefore misidentify environmental impacts and, therefore, mislead mitigation priorities. Here, we introduce a parametric, consequential LCA (cLCA) and global sensitivity analysis (GSA) workflow that emphasizes system expansion, uncertainty propagation and sensitivity for decision support. We model market-mediated product displacement and indirect land-use change (iLUC), while parameterized inventories preserve technical dependencies and propagate foreground and background uncertainties. We use GSA to identify key parameters governing result variances, and develop sensitivity-informed scenarios that convert influential, controllable parameters into robust mitigation thresholds and target-achievement probabilities. We demonstrate this methodological framework using vegetable soybean production and pond-based whiteleg shrimp farming systems in China. In the soybean case, our estimated benefits of improved management depended strongly on which foods the additional yield displaced. Substitution of plant-protein foods or meat produced substantially larger and more robust benefits than displacement of conventional soybean or vegetables, largely through avoided food production and iLUC. In the shrimp case, we combined one-at-a-time perturbation analysis of key control parameters and Monte Carlo simulations to show that lowering the feed conversion ratio to an threshold of approximately 1.30 established robust climate benefits and delivered consistent multi-impact improvements. Meanwhile solar substitution and electricity-efficiency scenarios produced favorable mean responses without a robust climate threshold over the tested ranges. Together, these cases show that the integration of parametric cLCA and GSA provides more nuanced LCA results that are explicit about substitution, LUC-impacts, uncertainty, trade-offs and the performance required for environmental improvement. Such information is critical for managers and practitioners in the decision-making processes.

Title: Towards a climate-adaptive governance framework for interconnected transboundary water infrastructure: the Lesotho Highlands Water Project and Integrated Vaal River System
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: Adaptive governance, transboundary water governance, climate adaptation, ESG, Southern Africa
Abstract_Text:
Climate change is exacerbating hydrological variability in Southern Africa; however, the governance of interconnected water infrastructure frequently lacks operational mechanisms that integrate climate-risk assessment, institutional accountability, and investment decision-making. This doctoral research endeavors to develop an evidence-based adaptive governance framework for climate adaptation planning in transboundary water infrastructure and to investigate whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) principles can serve as a complementary tool within this framework.
A comparative qualitative case study will examine the Lesotho Highlands Water Project and the Integrated Vaal River System, which are interconnected through water transfers into South Africa yet governed under distinct institutional frameworks: a bilateral treaty and national water governance. Document analysis of treaties, policies, strategies, and environmental and social management records will be complemented by semi-structured interviews with officials, operators, regulators, and practitioners. Hybrid deductive-inductive thematic analysis and cross-case comparison will identify implementation gaps, and a preliminary framework will be refined through expert review.
As the study is currently at the proposal stage, empirical findings are not yet available. The study is expected to generate comparative evidence on how climate risk and hydrological variability are incorporated into planning and governance; examine the potential complementarities, contributions and limitations of ESG in relation to established approaches such as adaptive governance and integrated water resources management; and contribute to the development of a context-specific governance framework for climate-adaptive interconnected transboundary water infrastructure.
The research is anticipated to provide policymakers and infrastructure operators with practical pathways for climate-resilient decision-making within shared water systems. Its significance extends beyond 2030, addressing Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 6 and 13 by examining how governance can transform adaptation principles into operational, accountable, and equitable practices across interconnected transboundary systems.

Title: Energy Storage as Shared Resilience Infrastructure under Climate-Driven Power Outages
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Yuan, Dr. Pengfei | University of Hamburg
Keywords: climate extremes; power outages; energy system resilience; cascading risk
Abstract_Text: Growing climate extremes are increasing power-outage risks worldwide, positioning energy storage as a critical adaptation strategy for enhancing power system resilience. Yet storage is often valued within the boundaries of the power system—through the flexibility and reliability it provides—while its contribution to the wider economy across locations and deployment scales in mitigating climate-driven supply chain disruptions remains poorly understood. Here we develop an integrated climate–energy–economic framework that links machine-learning projections of weather-induced outages at 4,353 primary substations under UKCP18 climate scenarios with an adaptive multi-regional input–output model spanning 32 regions and 61 sectors, using Great Britain as a case study. We find that future climate conditions intensify outage risk, while supply-chain propagation creates a marked spatial mismatch between physical outage exposure and economic losses. Storage in weather-exposed, supply-chain-critical regions can generate substantial economy-wide gains, averaging €129 million yr⁻¹. Accounting for cross-regional supply-chain spillovers increases the estimated resilience value of the same storage investment by 2–8-fold relative to a local-only valuation. These findings identify a previously missing value stream for storage in energy-system planning and provide a quantitative foundation for beneficiary-based cost allocation, regional coordination, and climate-risk-aware deployment of decentralized energy resources.

Title: Uneven attention and shifting narratives across the Sustainable Development Goals in national reviews
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Guan, Ting; Zhou, Xuan; Wu, Shaolin; Pradhan, Prajal; Gou, Ziwei
Organisations: Guan, Dr. Ting | Beijing Normal University
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals, voluntary national reviews, SDG prioritization, policy narratives, sentiment analysis, global sustainability governance
Abstract_Text: Voluntary National Reviews (VNRs) are a central means through which countries communicate progress on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet less is known about how the goals are prioritized and portrayed within these reports. We map SDG mentions and the sentiment of associated text in VNRs submitted between 2016 and 2025, examining variation across goals, income levels and regions, as well as changes between countries' first and most recent reviews. SDG 17 is the most frequently mentioned goal, followed by SDGs 1 and 8, while attention to individual goals varies substantially across national contexts. Higher national income is associated with more frequent mentions of sustainable consumption (SDG 12) and clean energy (SDG 7), and with a greater share of positive language about several well-being goals. Across repeated reviews, mentions of poverty (SDG 1) decline and its associated language becomes less positive; climate action (SDG 13) shows the opposite pattern on both measures. Considering attention and sentiment together reveals distinct reporting profiles, including frequently mentioned goals described in less positive terms. These findings show that VNRs do more than record coverage of the SDGs: they reveal how countries select and frame development priorities. Interpreting these patterns alongside outcome indicators could help distinguish changes in reporting from changes in sustainable development performance.

Title: Circular economy of clean energy technologies
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Organisations: Sun, Dr. Xin | University of Groningen
Keywords: Circular economy, Energy technologies, Critical raw materials, Life cycle assessment, Resource recovery
Abstract_Text:
The transition to low carbon energy systems requires the deployment of solar photovoltaics, wind turbines, batteries, electrolysers, and other technologies at unprecedented scale. Alongside their climate benefits, these technologies create demand for materials, infrastructure, and manufacturing capacity, while generating waste streams. Circular economy strategies offer opportunities to reduce primary resource demand, retain material and functional value, and strengthen supply security. Realizing these opportunities requires understanding when, where, and under what conditions circular approaches deliver environmental and societal benefits.
This panel examines the circular economy of energy technologies across their life cycles, from material sourcing and product design to operation, reuse, remanufacturing, and recycling. It brings together perspectives from industrial ecology, engineering, economics, and governance to explore how circular strategies can support a sustainable and resilient energy transition. Particular attention will be given to interactions between technology deployment, material availability, product lifetimes, and the timing and quality of secondary resource supplies.
The discussion will address three connected questions. How can circular design, lifetime extension, and improved utilization reduce material requirements while maintaining energy system performance? What technical, economic, and institutional barriers constrain collection, reuse, and recycling, and how can they be overcome? How should policies and business models account for tradeoffs among resource efficiency, emissions reduction, affordability, and equitable access to materials and technologies?
Drawing on material flow analysis, life cycle assessment, technoeconomic assessment, and system modeling, the panel will examine approaches for evaluating circular interventions across technologies, regions, and time horizons. It will also consider data gaps, uncertainty, international trade, and the distribution of costs and benefits along global supply chains. By connecting analytical evidence with practical implementation, the panel aims to identify research priorities and policy directions that move circularity beyond recycling targets toward measurable reductions in resource use and environmental burdens, while supporting energy security and social equity.
Global installed capacity of wind power reached 1,136 GW in 2024 (representing 8.1% of total electricity generation), and continued installation of new capacity is needed to provide renewable energy. Effective end-of-life (EOL) management strategies are, therefore, needed to recover materials from wind turbines. This work assesses current and emerging EOL practices, comparing the environmental and economic trade-offs across mechanical, thermal and chemical recycling technologies. Wind turbines are built from a range of materials, including structural metals, concrete, composites and magnetic materials, which have distinct recovery pathways and barriers. Structural metal recycling is well developed and used commercially, but concrete recycling is more nascent and not competitive. Near-term scalable composite recycling technologies - including mechanical recycling and cement kiln co-processing - cannot recover the structural strengths of the original composite, but more advanced technologies - such as thermal fibre recovery and solvolysis - face energy and economic barriers to wide-scale deployment. Magnet recycling can either preserve material in its intact form through shorter loop processes or recover valuable rare-earth elements through longer loop processes. The size of the magnets could enable direct reuse of magnets, but it is complicated by changing designs. Further development of recycling and reuse pathways should be complemented by design that enables EOL management and materials circularity.
Battery swapping has emerged as a commercially deployed charging paradigm for electric vehicles in
China, with dedicated station networks now operating at scale. Unlike conventional plug-in charging,swapping enables battery conditioning in a controlled thermal and electrical environment, attenuatingdegradation during the charging phase relative to uncontrolled fast-charging scenarios. The degradationstate accumulated over the first service life directly governs the residual performance available forcascade utilization and the environmental burden of end-of-life recycling, yet this full-chain linkageremains uncharacterized across China's climatically heterogeneous provinces, leaving critical evidence
gaps for infrastructure design, retirement policy, and cascade utilization planning.
This study develops an integrated framework using a semi-empirical aging model for lithium iron
ohosphate (LFP), nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC), and nickel-cobalt-aluminium (NCA) batteries, driven bynourly provincial temperature data across 30+ Chinese provinces and real-world vehicle SOC profiles.Both first-life and second-life aging are simulated continuously. Retired batteries are evaluated in twosecond-life scenarios exploiting regional peak-valley tariff differentials: industrial park load managementand 5G base station backup supply. The resulting degradation profiles feed into a cradle-to-grave LCA,
with sensitivity analysis on battery pack size.
Swapping mode extends first-life service and yields lower per-kWh lifecycle environmental burden relative
to conventional charging, with the benefit most pronounced for NMC and NCA in thermally demandingprovincial conditions, while LFP exhibits more uniform performance across China's climate gradient. Thetwo second-life scenarios produce divergent utilization-recycling trade-offs: the 5G base station profileextends service duration at the cost of lower energy throughput, whereas the industrial park profileachieves higher throughput with shorter second-life service, creating chemistry-specific and regionallydifferentiated LCA outcomes. Battery pack size introduces a nonlinear optimum in lifecycle
environmental performance, with the optimal range shifting by chemistry and provincial climate.
The EU Battery Regulation stipulates that, beginning in 2031, all electric vehicle (EV) batteries placed on the EU market must contain certain shares of recycled materials. However, the involvement of non-EU battery producers and recyclers makes that such requirements may not effectively stimulate domestic recycling due to cross-border trade flows. To examine this issue, this study develops a dynamic material flow analysis to project global demand and end-of-life volumes of lithium, cobalt, and nickel from EV batteries. Based on these projections, recycled material flows are traced across six stages from retirement to reuse, distinguishing whether processes occur within or outside the EU. The effectiveness of the regulation is then assessed using the minimum battery collection rate required for compliance. Results indicate that under the business as usual (BAU) scenario, EU demand for lithium, nickel, and cobalt will increase from 17.0 kt, 86.8 kt, and 13.0 kt in 2031 to 25.8 kt, 131.3 kt, and 19.7 kt in 2040. If the EU is considered a self-sufficient market, meeting the requirements would require collection rates for lithium, cobalt, and nickel of 42.5%, 44.2%, and 124.9% in 2031–2035, and 31.3%, 40.5%, and 72.7% in 2036–2040. Building sufficient cathode material production capacity within the EU is crucial for achieving the recycling targets, as it represents the key link for utilizing recovered materials. We argue that more flexible mechanisms should be adopted in the Battery Regulation that reflect evolving chemistries, shifting retirement volumes, and self-sufficiency of cathode production and transboundary material flows.
The upcoming terawatt-hours of retired batteries from electric vehicles are expected to drive substantial greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from waste treatments across cities. Using China, the world’s largest generator of retired batteries, as a case, we optimize the national recycling network under multiple emission and cost targets, integrating heterogeneities in battery retirements, energy mixes, and factor costs across 337 prefecture-level cities with 113,569 logistics paths. We reveal a trade-off between GHG emissions and costs of battery recycling across 59% of cities, while the remaining cities exhibit synergistic outcomes. As decarbonization goals tighten, the recycling capacity increasingly concentrate in southwestern cities, with five cities handling half of national retirement volume. This shift amplifies long-distance, interprovincial transport, accounting for 85% of total battery flows. Our findings provide actionable insights for leveraging the unique characteristics of various cities to accelerate cost-effective, low-carbon battery recycling network.

Title: Urbanisation’s Untapped Potential to Curb Livestock Antibiotic Use in China
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Keywords: Urbanisation, livestock antibiotic use; dietary change; pork consumption; China
Abstract_Text: Urbanisation is a multifaceted process that encompasses population migration and shifts in food consumption, particularly demand for livestock meat, whose production relies heavily on antibiotics. Yet the effects of urbanisation on livestock antibiotic use remain poorly understood. Focusing on China, the world’s largest antibiotic consumer amid rapid urbanisation, we combine a multi-regional input–output (MRIO) model with household-level expenditure data to estimate the dietary antibiotic footprint of rural and urban residents separately and identify drivers of temporal trends and disparities between population groups. We found that China’s overall dietary antibiotic footprint declined by roughly half, from 33.3 kilotons to 17.1 kilotons, between 2012 and 2019. This decline was driven primarily by reductions in antibiotic-use intensity and declining pork consumption among affluent urban residents, but was partially offset by rising incomes across the population. We also found contrasting effects of income growth in rural and urban settings: it increased the antibiotic footprint among rural residents through increased pork consumption, but reduced it among urban residents through declining pork consumption. Notably, income was associated with an inverted U-shaped relationship with per capita dietary antibiotic footprint among urban residents. Counterfactual scenario analyses suggest that China’s urbanisation-induced dietary shifts could reduce aggregate livestock antibiotic use by approximately 15% (3.7–4.3 kilotons) in 2050 relative to a non-urbanisation benchmark, primarily owning to declining pork demand among affluent urban residents. These findings collectively indicate that urbanisation in China can contribute to reductions in terrestrial livestock antibiotic use through shifts in meat demand. Although projections rely on modelled consumption data and entail uncertainty, our findings suggest that exposure to urban food environments and greater dietary diversity may provide an additional pathway for reducing livestock antibiotic use alongside measures targeting antibiotic-use intensity.

Title: Central and West African Child Health Outcomes: Why Efficient Spending and Strong Institutional Quality Matter
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Organisations: Balogun, Dr. Olaide | Tai Solarin Federal University of Education
Keywords: Child health, Public health expenditure, Institutional quality, Health-system efficiency, Central and West Africa, SDG 3
Abstract_Text: Child survival is a major challenge to sustainability in Central and West Africa (CWA) where high infant and under-five mortality rates coexist with limited health resources and unstable health system performance. Public health expenditure has increased, but evidence on how efficiently resources are converted into health services and how institutional quality influences child health outcomes is still limited. This study examines the impact of health system efficiency and institutional quality on child survival in CWA. The study investigates 24 countries between 2002 and 2024, covering the post-Abuja declaration, COVID-19 shock and recovery. Inputs are government health expenditure per capita and doctors per 1,000 population and outputs are infant and under-five survival rates to measure technical efficiency using Slack-Based Data Envelopment Analysis (SBM-DEA). The efficiency scores from SBM-DEA are then used in two-step dynamic system Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) models of infant and under-five mortality, along with institutional quality index and GDP per capita. The results of the SBM-DEA show that none of the considered country in the study reached efficiency frontier but Togo achieved the highest relative efficiency and Nigeria was among the least efficient. Slacks associated with major expenditure, workforce and mortality suggest that availability of resources does not necessarily translate into better child survival. In the baseline GMM models, better health system efficiency is significantly associated with lower infant and under-five mortality, while good institutional quality consistently reduces both infant and under-five mortality . The findings support a shift from expenditure centered health policy to efficient resource allocation and better institutions approach. The findings have direct relevance to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and the broader SDGs agenda.

Title: Group Inequality as the Systemic Constraint Hypothesis to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals: Evidence from Mexican regional gender data
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Charles, Dr. Aurelie | University of Bath
Keywords: systemic constraint; gender inequality; regional disparities; Mexico
Abstract_Text: This study examines how group inequality operates as a systemic constraint on achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Using regional data from thirty-two Mexican states between 2016 and 2022, gender-disaggregated indicators were constructed across nine SDGs to explore cross-goal interlinkages. Panel Generalized Least Squares regressions reveal that disparities in education, labour income, and governance participation are strongly interconnected, indicating that inequality functions as a structural bottleneck within the SDG network. Gender gaps reduce the transmission of progress across domains, slowing collective advancement toward sustainable development. The findings support the systemic constraint hypothesis, emphasizing that equity is not only a moral imperative but also a functional condition for achieving integrated and inclusive sustainability.

Title: Climate Change, Climate Action, and Human Security in Nigeria: A Comparative Analysis of Rural and Urban Vulnerability
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Authors: M Ahmed, Asmau; U Dikko, Maryam
Organisations: M Ahmed, Dr. Asmau | Kaduna State University
Keywords: Resource conflicts, geopolitical instability, transboundary climate risks, climate induced migration
Abstract_Text: Climate change has become one of the most pressing threats to human security in Nigeria, intersecting with resource scarcity, weak governance and pre-existing social vulnerabilities to produce compounding risks for livelihoods, safety and mobility. Framed within the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) - particularly SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), this study examines how climate change and climate action shape human security outcomes across Nigeria's rural and urban settings. The study employs a qualitative, comparative desk based methodology, synthesising peer reviewed literature, institutional reports and national policy documents on desertification and shrinking water bodies in the north, farmer herder resource conflicts, transboundary risks in the Lake Chad Basin, and urban flooding and heat stress in cities such as Lagos and Port Harcourt. Results show that rural human insecurity is driven primarily by resource based conflict and agrarian livelihood collapse, while urban human insecurity is driven by infrastructural deficits, informal settlement exposure and service overload, and that both dynamics are linked by accelerating climate induced migration and human mobility. The findings further reveal pronounced equity and justice gaps in Nigeria's climate governance architecture, with adaptation finance, planning and infrastructure investment favoured toward already better served urban and coastal areas, leaving rural and peri-urban populations structurally disadvantaged. Drawing lessons from Nigeria's SDG implementation record, the study concludes with policy recommendations for an integrated, justice centred human security framework that connects rural resilience building with urban adaptation planning and regional (transboundary) cooperation.

Title: An Inconvenient Legal Truth
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Organisations: Squintani, Prof. Lorenzo | University of Groningen
Keywords: climate law, effectiveness, ecology based approach
Abstract_Text: Current Climate Law suffers from systemic legal designs flaws that prevent it from achieving genuine achievement of climate goals, both in terms of mitigation and adaptation, and a fair energy transition, even when technical compliance is fully met. This institutional failure stems from a widening gap between rigid legal frameworks and dynamic ecological realities, equity imbalances in public participation that disadvantage vulnerable groups, and policy conflicts that prioritize short-term economic goals over long-term sustainability. This contribution postulates that, ultimately, relying on stagnant political limits rather than adaptive, science-based ecological standards undermines regulatory effectiveness and drives a global surge in climate litigation.

Title: Heatwave Adaptation in South Asia, Rooted in Cultural Inheritance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: National Institution for Transforming India [NITI Aayog]
Keywords: Adaptation, Cultural inheritance, Heatwaves, South Asia
Abstract_Text:
Rising global temperatures and the increasing frequency of heatwaves worldwide have drawn growing attention from academicians, policymakers, and practitioners. Adaptation is essential to building resilience at both the individual and community levels. While numerous studies have examined the explicit knowledge that informs people's understanding of heatwaves, one important source of knowledge production remains undercommunicated: lived experience. Individuals' direct experiences contribute to the formation of heatwave-related knowledge, which is then passed down across generations through cultural inheritance.
This article reviews behavioural adaptation practices at the individual level and examines how these practices are rooted in culturally inherited knowledge. South Asia, home to nearly one-fifth of the world's population, has a substantial proportion of climate-vulnerable communities. Existing heatwave research in the region, however, has largely focused on climate projections, health impacts, vulnerability mapping, and policy analysis. A systematic review examining heatwave adaptation behaviour through a cultural lens has yet to be undertaken for South Asia.
Using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology, this article draws on qualitative data from 32 studies spanning eight South Asian countries, analysed through a cultural adaptation knowledge framework. The intent is not to diminish the significance of government policies and initiatives, but to position culturally rooted practices as complementary to formal heat adaptation strategies and technologies. In a region where technocratic solutions remain limited in reach, and where dedicated healthcare systems and occupational safety standards for heatwaves are still emerging, behaviourally embedded, culturally inherited practices play a significant adaptive role.
Specifically, the article explores culturally embedded dietary practices and building designs and their effectiveness, how gender differences in adaptation stem from cultural norms, and how modern adaptive measures are shaping cultural adaptive practices.

Title: Whose priorities count? Local participation in protected areas of Morocco’s Intercontinental Biosphere Reserve
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Biosphere reserve; local participation; environmental governance; equity; Morocco
Abstract_Text:
International biosphere reserve designations encourage the reconciliation of biodiversity conservation and sustainable development. Yet their local relevance depends in part on whether residents can express their priorities and take part in decisions. This paper examines that question across protected areas on the Moroccan side of the Intercontinental Biosphere Reserve of the Mediterranean (RBIM).
Drawing on 37 interviews conducted with residents and local actors, the study explores how people describe environmental pressures, everyday needs and opportunities to participate in conservation.
