Strengthening community ownership, institutional capacity, sustainable financing, operation and maintenance systems, and accountability is essential for sustaining investments. Integrating WASH with public health, environmental protection, watershed management, and climate adaptation, alongside gender-responsive and disability-inclusive approaches, is equally important.
Beyond 2030, Ethiopia's rural WASH agenda should prioritize equitable access to safely managed, reliable, and climate-resilient services through evidence-based planning, innovative financing, renewable energy, digital monitoring, and strengthened governance. The paper emphasizes that sustainable WASH development requires moving beyond infrastructure coverage toward functional, accessible, and accountable services that address rural communities' needs, strengthen resilience, and ensure long-term sustainability.
Keywords: SDG 6, WASH, rural Ethiopia, water supply, sanitation, hygiene, climate resilience, sustainability, operation and maintenance, post-2030 development.

Title: Yahoo Plus, Ritual Anxiety, and Reproductive Health in the Era of Climate Change, Evidence from a Selected Community in Southwestern Nigeria
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Akinrinde, Dr. Olawale | Osun State University
Keywords: Climate change, Sexual and reproductive health and rights, Yahoo Plus, Reproductive precarity, Gendered vulnerability, Nigeria
Abstract_Text:
Climate change poses significant threats to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) across Africa. Yet, scholarship has largely emphasised direct pathways involving food insecurity, displacement, disease, and weakened healthcare systems. Less attention has been paid to the indirect socioeconomic mechanisms through which climate-induced livelihood disruptions reshape gender relations and reproductive vulnerabilities. This paper addresses this gap by examining the intersection of climate change, the cybercrime economy popularly known as Yahoo Plus, and women’s SRHR in a selected community in Osogbo, Southwestern Nigeria.
The study argues that livelihood insecurity associated with climate variability, declining agricultural productivity, and shrinking economic opportunities can encourage alternative income-generating strategies, including illicit ones, among urban youth. Within this context, narratives surrounding Yahoo Plus include allegations of ritual practices, transactional sexual relationships, reproductive exploitation, psychological coercion, and symbolic violence against women. Although such claims remain contested, their social consequences may shape perceptions of risk, bodily autonomy, intimate relationships, and reproductive decision-making.
The paper develops Climate-Induced Reproductive Precarity Theory (CIRPT), proposing that climate-related economic stress can expand informal and illicit survival economies that generate reproductive vulnerabilities. Through reproductive survival chains, climate stressors become indirectly connected to SRHR risks through economic desperation, gendered power asymmetries, and the commodification of intimate relationships.
Using a qualitative case-study design, the study draws on semi-structured interviews, focus groups, key informant interviews, and media discourse analysis involving women, youth, community leaders, health practitioners, and civil society actors. The study contributes to climate justice and SRHR scholarship by showing how climate vulnerability, digital informal economies, and gendered reproductive risks intersect in contemporary African societies.

Title: Enabling or Defining? AI, Digital Infrastructures and the Epistemic Politics of Sustainability in an Age of Emerging Security Technologies
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Trustworthy AI, information integrity, data autonomy, and sustainability impacts of AI
Authors: Qurat ul ain, Qurat ul ain
Presenter: Qurat ul ain, Qurat ul ain
Keywords: Epistemic agency; artificial intelligence; sustainable development; epistemic justice; peace and security
Abstract_Text:
If artificial intelligence, big data and digitalisation are to enable sustainable development, we must ask who determines what "sustainable development" means once these systems help define it. Dominant accounts treat such technologies as neutral instruments for delivering the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This conceptual paper argues instead that they are epistemic infrastructures: systems that shape what counts as knowledge, which risks become visible, and whose priorities inform policy.
The opportunities are considerable. Advanced analytics, satellite observation and decision-support systems can strengthen evidence-based policymaking, improve monitoring of progress, enable earlier identification of environmental, humanitarian and security risks, and open new possibilities for conflict prevention and peacebuilding. Yet the same systems can reproduce unequal data infrastructures, embed algorithmic bias, marginalise situated and community-based knowledge, amplify disinformation, obscure accountability through opacity, and concentrate technological power. Growing reliance on AI-generated knowledge risks eroding the epistemic agency of the people and institutions expected to interpret and act on it.
Drawing on feminist theory, epistemic justice and critical security studies, the paper develops epistemic agency as its analytical lens. It asks whether development can be inclusive when the tools that generate evidence and guide decisions also determine whose knowledge is recognised as legitimate. The emerging AI–space–nuclear nexus serves as an illustrative case rather than a primary focus. It shows how the convergence of AI, satellite data and strategic systems can enhance analytical capacity while complicating human responsibility, blurring civilian and military applications.
Looking beyond 2030, the paper argues that future sustainability agendas must treat data governance, algorithmic accountability and epistemic pluralism as core conditions of sustainable development, not technical add-ons. It contributes to debates on AI, digitalisation, peace and security by reframing digital enablement as a question of epistemic justice and human agency, offering a critical framework for assessing whose knowledge and decisions shape sustainability futures.

Title: Understanding Causal Chains of Land Use Change: A Systematic Review Based on the DPSIR Framework
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Authors: Xu, Xiaochun; Dahal, Kshitij; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: land use change, DPSIR framework, causal chains, systematic review
Abstract_Text: Land use change is a key driver of environmental change, yet its drivers and impacts are interlinked through feedback that studies rarely capture within a unified framework. We systematically reviewed 383 studies through the Driver-Pressure-State-Impact-Response (DPSIR) framework adapted to land use, providing the first synthesis that links fragmented causal chains of land use and locates where evidence is concentrated or missing. The evidence shows that urbanization and cropland expansion reduced forest and grassland, causing ecological loss and intensifying natural hazards. Human activities act in both directions: anthropogenic pressure degrades forest and grassland, whereas land use policy promotes their recovery. Beyond changes in area, land use intensity changes with both land conversion and land use management, and the resulting ecological impacts are nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous. However, the evidence is dominated by short causal chains that link land conversion under single pressures to ecological impacts. Compound pressures, land use intensity, socioeconomic impacts and feedback from land use change to natural hazards remain underexplored, and anthropogenic pressure and policy responses are rarely assessed together. As a result, it remains unclear whether land use change forms vicious or virtuous cycles. We argue that future research should extend short causal chains into complete causal loops by quantifying how far responses offset the ecological damage caused by anthropogenic pressure, tracing how land use change feeds back to natural hazards and evaluating the combined impacts of changes in land use quantity and quality.

Title: Quest for a Sustainable African Renaissance: Sectoral Determinants and Synergies for Climate-Resilient Development
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Aberu, Dr. Felix | Tai Solarin Federal University of Education, Ijagun, Ogun State, Nigeria
Keywords: Africa, Climate-Resilient, carbon cycle modeling, Sustainable Renaissance, Sectoral
Abstract_Text: Africa’s push for sustainable development beyond 2030 will increasingly rely on mainstreaming economic, social and environmental agenda within a shared development paradigm. However, evidence on the joint drivers of these sustainability objectives is scanty. Based on the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) theory, which suggests that sustainability is a process of moving towards achieving economic, social, and environmental goals concurrently, this research adds to the discussion on the trajectory of development in Africa by examining whether electricity, education, agriculture, and industrial performance lead to environmental sustainability in five African countries (2000-2025). The dynamic panel Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) was estimated to address issues of persistence and endogeneity. Results indicate significant persistence in environmental performance (EP), evidenced by a lagged coefficient of 1.02 (p<0.01). Electricity and education performance have positive and significant coefficients of (0.46; p=0.05) and (0.48; p=0.01) respectively. Marginal effects suggest that a 1% improvement in electricity and education is associated with approximately 0.46% and 0.48% increase in EP, respectively. Improvements in carbon emissions are associated with declines in EP (-0.07; p<0.01). One percent increase in carbon emissions will reduce EP by 0.07%. Similarly, industrial performance crowds out EP by approximately 0.01% (-0.01; p=0.01). The agriculture coefficient is negative but insignificant (-0.05; p=0.22). Hence, the results corroborate the TBL hypothesis, as environmental sustainability is closely related to the energy system, human capital, and economic activities. The results underscore the implementation of coherent policies that involve economic transformation and social development in combination with the environment, if Africa's inclusive, resilient and sustainable development agenda after 2030 is to be strengthened.

Title: Policy Uncertainty and Market Resilience in Carbon and Clean Energy Markets: A Regime-Switching Perspective
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Aboluwodi, Damilola; Mccullough, Kerry; Muzindutsi, Paul-Francois
Organisations: Aboluwodi, Dr. Damilola | University of KwaZulu-Natal
Keywords: Policy uncertainty, carbon markets, clean energy, MS-MIDAS, sustainable finance.
Abstract_Text:
Carbon and clean energy markets support the low-carbon transition, yet their responses to policy uncertainty may differ across stable and stressed conditions. Understanding these differences is relevant to financing climate action and sustaining progress towards SDGs 7 and 13. This study examines regime-dependent relationships between policy uncertainty and returns in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and the S&P Global Clean Energy Index (SPGCEI).
Using Bloomberg data, a Markov-switching mixed-data sampling (MS-MIDAS) framework combines daily market returns with monthly measures of Climate Policy Uncertainty, Global Economic Policy Uncertainty, and Energy-Related Uncertainty. The model preserves the original data frequencies while estimating latent market states, regime-specific uncertainty effects, and time-varying volatility.
The findings reveal pronounced differences in market dynamics. Clean energy returns exhibit a persistent low-volatility bull regime, with a continuation probability of approximately 98.7% and an expected duration of 77 trading days, compared with 16 trading days for the high-volatility bear regime. The EU ETS displays greater asymmetry, characterised by persistent low-volatility conditions interrupted by brief but more intense high-volatility episodes. Policy uncertainty coefficients vary in direction and magnitude across regimes, but their generally insignificant estimates provide limited evidence of a systematic direct effect on returns.
These results highlight distinct risk profiles within the low-carbon investment universe and caution against treating carbon and clean energy assets as interchangeable. The study contributes to discussions on sustainable transformation by showing how market instability differs across instruments supporting decarbonisation. Its findings inform portfolio diversification and carbon risk management, while providing a basis for further research on how policy credibility can support resilient transition finance beyond 2030.

Title: Connecting the missing links: how business model innovation integrates capabilities, legitimacy, and adaptation for post-2030 corporate sustainability
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Keywords: business models, strategic sustainability management, stakeholder legitimacy, value chains, post-2030 agenda
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Corporate contributions to the Sustainable Development Goals often stall because firms pursue sustainability through fragmented initiatives: capabilities that fail to earn stakeholder legitimacy, stakeholder engagement without operational substance, or adaptation to systemic change without the capabilities to sustain it. Management theory mirrors this fragmentation by treating resource-based, stakeholder, and systems perspectives as separate lenses. This paper asks how the three perspectives reinforce one another and which organizational mechanism activates their integration.
Methods: The study follows a conceptual framework development approach. It combines a structured review of the three theoretical traditions, a comparative analysis of prior integration efforts, and logical derivation of causal mechanisms, illustrated through four organizational configurations using public sustainability disclosures.
Results: The resulting Dynamic Integration Framework treats capability development, legitimacy building, and adaptive integration as interdependent dimensions linked by three reinforcing dynamics. Early adaptation to systemic change builds legitimacy through credible commitment signals; legitimacy supports capability development through resource access and protection from imitation; and capability development funds and informs further adaptation through slack resources and learning. Business model innovation, through value proposition reconfiguration, operational redesign, multi-stream value capture, and ecosystem governance, activates all three dynamics at once. The illustrative configurations show that emphasis on a single dimension produces characteristic failures, including greenwashing risk when legitimacy claims outpace operational change.
Conclusions: For a post-2030 agenda, the framework shifts attention from strengthening individual sustainability capabilities to governing the connections among capability development, stakeholder legitimacy, and systemic adaptation, with business model innovation as the organizational vehicle. Policy can support this by strengthening the links between dimensions: transparency requirements, including double materiality reporting, connect capabilities to legitimacy; preferential procurement connects legitimacy to capability; and collaborative research connects capability to adaptation. Because these mechanisms operate differently where formal verification is weak, integration strategies must be adapted to institutional context.

Title: Climate-Sensitive and Environmental Threats to Male Reproductive Health in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: Implications for Sustainable and Climate-Resilient Health Systems
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Authors: Arhin, Samuel Kofi; Arhin, Isaiah Kofi
Organisations: Arhin, Dr. Samuel Kofi | University of Cape Coast School of Medical Sciences, Ghana
Keywords: Climate change, male reproductive health, semen quality, environmental exposure, sustainability
Abstract_Text:
Background: Climate change and environmental deterioration are increasingly acknowledged as threats to human health; however, their impacts on male reproductive health have not been sufficiently integrated into discussions on sustainability and climate-related health concerns. Rising temperatures, heat exposure, air pollution, pesticides, heavy metals, and other environmental stressors may negatively influence spermatogenesis, semen quality, and male fertility potential.
Methods: A systematic scoping review was carried out following the JBI framework for scoping reviews and the PRISMA-ScR reporting standards. Studies published from 2000 to August 2026 were identified through major electronic databases and other pertinent sources. Eligible studies involved males aged 18–70 years in LMICs and examined associations between climate-related or environmental exposures and reproductive outcomes.
Results: The collected evidence highlights a wide range of environmental and climate-dependent threats to male reproductive health. Notably, increased ambient temperatures and occupational heat exposure are major concerns, linked to decreased sperm concentration, motility, count, and other semen quality indicators. Additional findings point to air pollution, pesticides, heavy metals, and various environmental pollutants as contributors to adverse reproductive effects. Agricultural, industrial, and outdoor workers may face significant exposure burdens. Nevertheless, the data is uneven geographically, with significant gaps particularly in African nations and other LMIC regions.
Conclusion: It is crucial to explicitly incorporate male reproductive health within the framework of sustainability and climate resilience initiatives. Preventive actions may involve reducing occupational heat exposure, controlling environmental pollution, implementing climate-adaptive occupational health policies, enhancing reproductive health surveillance, and integrating environmental risk assessments into fertility and reproductive services. Strengthening research infrastructure and monitoring systems in LMICs, especially in Africa, is vital for identifying at-risk populations and developing tailored interventions. Overall, these findings indicate that male reproductive health is an underrecognized aspect of climate-related vulnerabilities.

Title: Global progress in social foundations remains uneven over time and across dimensions
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: Li, Jing; Warchold, Anne; Hubacek, Klaus; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: well-being; sustainable development; SDG; social foundation
Abstract_Text: Achieving and sustaining human well-being requires progress across multiple dimensions of social foundations, yet existing measures provide limited evidence on whether such progress has been broadly shared across countries, balanced across dimensions, and sustained over time. We developed a Social Foundation Index (SFI), which combines four themes including self-identity, societal interaction, social provision, and macro-level measurement, based on a systematic literature review that integrates 31 indicators across 19 dimensions for 171 countries from 2000 to 2022. By grouping countries according to their average attainment in 2000-2005, we tracked how social foundation attainment evolved across national trajectories and its association with environmental and peace-related boundary conditions. Results show that despite improvements in social foundations in 155 countries, national trajectories varied substantially, even among countries with similar initial levels. Average annual progress has clearly slowed down after 2015. Improvements were concentrated in basic provision and infrastructure, whereas relational and institutional dimensions changed more modestly. Moreover, the pattern is asymmetric if accounting for environmental and peace boundaries over time. Countries with lower SFI generally had higher climate vulnerability and conflict exposure, while exerting much less ecological pressure. Our findings suggest that ensuring social foundations for long-term sustainability therefore requires differentiated policies to close remaining provision gaps, strengthen relational and institutional capacities, and respond to different climate and conflict vulnerabilities across countries.

Title: Defending Our Future : Using Football to Mitigate and Adapt to Climate Change
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Keywords: Football, Resilience, Education, Adaptation, Community
Abstract_Text:
This project examines the effectiveness and feasibility of using football as a medium for climate communication, with a particular focus on the role of trusted non-expert messengers such as professional football players. The original research design aimed to explore the use of Swansea City AFC players as climate communicators to engage audiences who are typically less responsive to traditional scientific messaging. However, due to limited engagement from the club despite extensive outreach, the study evolved to instead investigate the institutional barriers influencing football clubs’ willingness to engage with climate communication initiatives.
The revised research therefore combines two strands of inquiry: first, an analysis of football club engagement with sustainability and climate-related communication across multiple league levels in the United Kingdom; and second, an assessment of football fans’ perceptions of using the sport as a vehicle for climate messaging. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with football clubs that agreed to participate, focusing on their existing sustainability practices, communication strategies, and perceived constraints in engaging with climate change communication. In parallel, a questionnaire was distributed to football supporters to evaluate levels of climate awareness, attitudes towards climate messaging within football, and demographic differences in responses.
The study highlights the tension between the potential of football as a trusted communication platform and the institutional barriers that limit its use for climate messaging. It contributes to broader debates on climate communication, trusted messengers, and informational vulnerability by assessing both organisational willingness and public receptiveness within a major cultural institution.

Title: Understanding the water-energy-food nexus in an era of increasing resource competition
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Yi, Dr. Junjie | Chinese Academy of Sciences
Keywords: Water-energy-food nexus, water footprints, food-system transformation, energy transition, nexus governance
Abstract_Text: Water, energy and food systems are deeply interconnected, yet they are often assessed and governed separately. Agriculture is the largest global user of freshwater, energy production depends increasingly on water availability, and food production and consumption place substantial pressure on both water quantity and quality. Climate change, groundwater depletion, extreme weather, geopolitical conflicts and growing resource competition further intensify trade-offs among water, food and energy objectives. This session addresses Conference Theme 2.1 by moving beyond sector-specific assessments towards integrated water–energy–food (WEF) nexus approaches. It focuses on how nexus thinking can be translated into quantitative evidence, practical interventions and policy action. The session is organised around four sub-themes: (1) water, energy and carbon footprints in agriculture; (2) water use and greenhouse gas trade-offs in the energy transition; (3) water quality, food consumption and food-system transformation; and (4) nexus methods, data and policy, including industrial water use and circular water management. The 120-minute interactive session will feature five invited talks, a moderated panel and breakout discussions, and can be adapted to 90 minutes if required. By bringing together speakers from different disciplines and regions, the session aims to identify synergies, manage unintended trade-offs and inform resilient water, energy and food security strategies for the post-2030 agenda and the 2027 SDG Summit.

Title: Strengthening the Water-Energy-Food-Ecosystem Nexus through Participatory Planning of Renewable Energy Systems in Rural Communities.
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Akowuge Dugasseh, Frank; Pius Kyauke, Lucy; Mengu, Moses; Gyimah, Richard; Sanderson, Hans
Organisations: Akowuge Dugasseh, Dr. Frank | Aarhus University
Keywords: Nexus approaches, sustainable resource management; food system transformation, energy transition; smart grids
Abstract_Text:
Achieving food, water, and energy security requires integrated approaches that recognize the interdependencies among natural resources, local institutions, and community priorities.
Objective
This study presents a participatory framework to assess and enhance the sustainability of renewable energy interventions within the water-energy-food-ecosystem nexus in rural Ghana.
Methods
Drawing on conceptual underpinnings and principles of Community-Based Natural Resource Management, Social Life Cycle Assessment, and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the framework was applied to evaluate a renewable energy initiative comprising a solar microgrid, solar-powered irrigation, and a biomass combined heat and power system. Stakeholder consultations involving community members, local authorities, value chain actors, and technical experts were used to identify, prioritize, and benchmark needs and preferences against localized SDG indicators.
Key Results
Results reveal strong linkages between renewable energy access, poverty reduction, food security, livelihood diversification, and institutional strengthening. Stakeholders ranked SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) as top priorities, while food production, irrigation services, and productive use of energy emerged as critical pathways to improve resilience and socio-economic well-being. The framework further identified trade-offs and social hotspots, including farmer-herder conflicts and inequitable access to resources, highlighting the importance of inclusive governance in nexus planning.
Conclusion
The findings demonstrate that integrating renewable energy systems with water management, food production, and community-led governance can enhance resource efficiency, strengthen local economies, and accelerate progress toward multiple SDGs simultaneously.
By and Beyond
The study offers a practical nexus-based approach to sustainable resource management and insights for policymakers, planners, and practitioners seeking to support food system transformation, energy transition, and fragile ecosystems in vulnerable rural contexts for and beyond 2030.

Title: Demand-Side Decarbonisation and a Just Transition in Ireland: Regional and Gendered Employment Impacts
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Zhao, Tianning; Andreoni, Valeria; Daly, Hanah; Eakins, John
Keywords: Demand-side mitigation, Just transition, Input-output linear programming, Regional employment, Gender equity
Abstract_Text:
Climate mitigation can generate uneven employment impacts across regions and social groups. This study examines how sectoral final demand in Ireland can be restructured to achieve emissions reductions while prioritising regional and gender employment equity.
We combine an environmentally extended input-output model with vulnerability-weighted, two-stage linear programming. Ireland’s 2022 domestic input-output table, emissions accounts, and employment data covering 20 sectors and 26 regions are used to trace direct and indirect employment effects. The first stage minimises the maximum weighted relative employment loss, giving additional protection to structurally vulnerable regions and female employment. The second minimises net final-demand contraction while preserving the optimal equity outcome.
Three counterfactual scenarios apply production-side emissions reduction targets of 13.9%, 28.9%, and 48.8% relative to 2022. The first two take reduction rates derived from emissions projections under existing and additional measures as benchmarks; the third converts Ireland’s statutory 2030 target to a 2022 baseline. Rather than simulating those policy measures, we examine how equivalent reductions could be achieved entirely through final-demand adjustment under fixed technical, emissions, and employment coefficients.
Results show that the least stringent target can coexist with aggregate employment gains through sectoral reallocation, whereas tighter targets entail broader contraction and larger employment losses. Regional industrial dependence, gendered employment structures, and supply-chain linkages shape the distribution of these impacts. Gains in selected service sectors and construction coexist with losses elsewhere, demonstrating why aggregate employment outcomes alone cannot establish transition fairness.
The framework embeds distributional priorities in demand-side mitigation planning and identifies needs for regionally targeted and gender-sensitive transition support. It provides normative adjustment scenarios rather than forecasts of realised unemployment, connecting climate mitigation with decent work and reduced inequalities.

Title: Reimagining Sustainable Development After 2030: Emerging Priorities, Governance Reforms and Future Directions
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: post-2030 agenda, lessons learned, environmental governance, SDGs
Abstract_Text:
As the 2030 deadline approaches, attention is increasingly turning to the future of global sustainable development governance. While the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) have provided an unprecedented common framework for action, implementation has revealed persistent challenges related to policy coherence, financing, accountability, and the ability to address rapidly evolving global risks. At the same time, emerging issues such as climate resilience, biodiversity loss, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, social cohesion, geopolitical instability, and intergenerational justice raise important questions about whether the current framework remains fully fit for purpose.
This interactive session contributes to the discussion on a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030 by focusing on missing links and potential reforms. Rather than conducting another assessment of SDG performance, the session seeks to generate forward-looking insights on what should be retained, strengthened, reformed, or added in a future global agenda. It will explore how lessons from a decade of implementation can inform more effective, science-based, inclusive, and action-oriented approaches to sustainable development.
The session consists of a plenary round of short statements by representatives from government, municipalities, academia, business, and civil society, followed by a participatory World Café. Invited speakers will each address the question:What is the most important missing link that should be addressed in a post-2030 agenda?This will serve as input for four discussion tables focusing on: 1) emerging sustainability priorities, 2) governance and institutional reform, 3) measuring success beyond current indicators and 4) guiding principles for a future agenda.
By bringing together stakeholders from different discplines and sectors, the session aims to identify shared priorities, areas of divergence, and practical recommendations for future agenda design. The outputs will contribute to ongoing international discussions on how a post-2030 framework can better address interconnected sustainability challenges while remaining actionable, inclusive and responsive to changing global agenda.

Title: Building a Resilience Monitoring Framework: From Theory to Application
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: resilience, monitoring and evaluation, development, humanitarian
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
Resilience is at the same time both a straightforward and intuitive concept and an incredibly illusive concept, and key to the 2030 Agenda. Building resilience to climate change requires a multipronged approach, yet development actors often only focus on a single aspect. Development actors who take a more holistic approach to resilience face challenges in understanding what their interventions add up to, and how to use Monitoring and Evaluation data to adaptively manage their portfolio because it can feel like comparing apples to oranges.
In this presentation I discuss a custom-built Resilience Monitoring Framework centred around three themes: the Resilience of People, Services, and Institutions. The framework was designed for a large bilateral donor to Nepal and applied to monitor a multimillion-dollar portfolio spanning covering both development and humanitarian interventions.
Methods:
Systematic literature reviews underpinned the identification of relevant dimensions within each of the three resilience themes. Once the framework was developed, project implementers provided regular reporting on their contributions to the Resilience of People, Services, and Institutions after which the author and his team further broke this down across the different dimensions.
Key results:
As a result of the framework, the donor gained better insight into how its overall portfolio contributed to resilience and where there were blind spots in its programming. These insights facilitated accountability, but they also stimulated further discussion within programme teams and between programmes teams and delivery partners.
Conclusions:
The presentation gives the audience insight into the development of a theory-based resilience framework and its subsequent practical application in a Nepal covering a development and humanitarian portfolio. People will leave with a fuller appreciation of the challenges involved in understanding stakeholders’ contributions to building resilience to climate change in a complex and dynamic environment.

Title: Locally-Led Adaptation in Nepal: Principles and Practice
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: locally-led adaptation, climate action, climate finance, inclusion, governance.
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
Locally-Led Adaption (LLA) is a key approach to dealing with the ongoing climate crisis. International development actors such as bi- and multilateral donors and climate funds spent $23 billion on adaptation in 2023 (UNEP, 2025), of which a significant portion goes to LLA. However, we should question whether this finance reaches its objectives and ask ourselves how much more resilient LLA makes communities?
Methods:
This presentation draws on extensive fieldwork in Nepal between 2020-2025 across dozens of LLA projects. Data were collected through interviews and focus group discussions with beneficiaries, local politicians, project implementers, and other key stakeholders. While the analytical framework differed across fieldwork periods, the nine Principles for Locally-Led Adaptation play a key role in understanding how LLA is implemented in practice.
Key results:
Findings show that while the Government of Nepal and key development partners have officially endorsed the LLA Principles, their implementation is – at best – varied. This has direct implications for how inclusive LLA projects are as well as their long-term sustainability. The researched LLA projects often provided valuable short-term support to community members as they were delivered using a cash-for-work modality. At the same time, project selection rarely addressed the systemic climate risks communities faced, and the climate finance to maintain or scale these adaptation actions remains lacking.
Conclusions:
Local politicians rarely prioritise climate adaptation interventions. They are happy to endorse external donor-funded projects which bring resources into the community but are loath to structurally commit (local) government resources to them in practice. The inclusion and consultation aspects of the LLA principles are also rarely implemented effectively, let alone mainstreamed. As a result, while LLA in Nepal offered short-term benefits, it failed to address the structural risks and processes that leave people vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

Title: Does unit economics work for Profitable Resale of clothes at scale? Can EPR and ESPR Succeed Without Profitable Resale?
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: Physical AI, Circular Economy, Clothing Resale, EPR, ESPR
Abstract_Text:
Since July 2026 the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (ESPR) bans the destruction of unsold textiles. The textile EPR Directive makes producers pay for what happens to their clothing after sale, and the Dutch UPV Textiel sets rising reuse targets. These rules assume that a garment kept out of the bin can find a second life.
Most used, unsold and returned garments are processed by hand. Manual handling takes eight people, eight steps and about 19 minutes per item, at around €11. A garment must sell for roughly €49 to break even, and only about 4.5% of secondhand clothing clears that bar. For the rest, reuse costs more than it earns. A ban on destruction does not change that arithmetic. And therefore industry finds it cheaper option of burn or dump clothes rather than resale.
The session draws on the experience of VNYX, an Amsterdam-based startup founded in 2025 that builds physical AI robotic systems for resale processing. Robotic handling of soft, deformable textiles is an open problem in robotics. VNYX combines a robotic E-Mannequin, AI item assessment and automated listing to process a garment in under a minute for €2.50 to €3, lowering the break-even price to about €17.
We argue that EPR and ESPR can only succeed if resale becomes profitable at item level. Policy creates the obligation. Automation creates the margin that makes reuse the cheaper choice than burning or dumping.

Title: Linking Indonesia’s social forestry characteristics to climate mitigation outcomes
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: social forestry, Indonesia, socioeconomic, climate mitigation
Abstract_Text: Social forestry has become an Indonesia’s climate strategy in the forestry and land use (FOLU) sector. However, the extent to which socioeconomic characteristics may affect climate mitigation outcomes remains unclear. This study examines the spatial distribution of social forestry at the village level and assesses the characteristics of villages containing social forestry areas and their associations with aboveground biomass. We find that indicative social forestry areas occur in 18,654 villages, representing approximately 22% of all villages in Indonesia, and are distributed across 37 provinces. Land cover within these areas consists of forest (59 %), cropland (22 %), grassland (15 %), and other land cover types (4 %). Population density shows a consistent negative correlation with aboveground biomass across the years. Meanwhile, main livelihood, distance to forests, and community dependence on forests are significantly associated with aboveground biomass, although the magnitude of the associations is small. Agriculture and forestry sectors are the main sources of livelihood in most villages. Villages with greater dependence on forests also tend to have higher aboveground biomass. Farmer groups are present in most villages, indicating potential institutional capacity to support climate mitigation actions. Panel regression analysis will be conducted to examine the association between changes in village characteristics and forest biomass over time. This study can inform more context-specific social forestry policies by identifying socioeconomic conditions that may support or constrain climate mitigation. In addition, it contributes to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No poverty), SDG 10 (Reduced inequality), SDG 13 (Climate action) and SDG 15 (Life on land).

Title: Sustainable Governance: Exploring the Integration of Corporate Governance Practices with Sustainable Development Goals
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Keywords: Corporate Governance, Sustainable Development Goals, Sustainability
Abstract_Text: The Role of corporate governance in achieving sustainability has gained the attention of allstakeholders such as investors, customers and policy makers during the current era that is marked byheightened public expectations, social inequalities and increasing environmental challenges. At thisera, stakeholders do not only evaluate organizations based on their financial performance, but theyalso evaluate them on their contribution to sustainable development and social responsibility. It isargued that corporate governance should integrate sustainability into its business practices in orderto achieve the UN SDGs. These goals aim to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality, and protect theplanet. The literature states that a small number of firms (28%) of Eurostoxx 50 companies reportedSDGs in their annual reports. Previous studies have focused on corporate governance and earningmanagement, CEO remuneration, financial performance etc. There is still a research gap to explorethe impact of internal corporate governance strength on a firm’s tendency to address SDGs in itssustainability report. This is significant research that will address the current gap through the lens ofstakeholder and sustainable development theory to investigate how corporate governance practicescan be evolved to meet both tradition businesses objectives and to achieve the UN SDGs. Thisresearch will use both qualitative and quantitative data to address the current gap and provide deepinsights into the challenges and opportunities for improving a corporate governance model that willhelp achieve both financial goals and sustainable development goals. This research potentially hassignificant implications beyond finance, with the potential interdisciplinary impacts for managementand organizational studies research as well as policy and sustainability implications. Moreover, thisresearch also has significant implications for responsible leadership within a corporation byexploring how corporate governance can play a critical role in promoting responsible leadership andadvocating for sustainable business practices to achieve sustainability.

Title: Effect of Green Industrialization on Inclusive Growth in Sub Saharan Africa
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: BOUDA, RAYANGUENEWENDE ABDOUL KADER; ZOUNGRANA, TIBI DIDIER
Organisations: BOUDA, Dr. RAYANGUENEWENDE ABDOUL KADER | Université Thomas SANKARA
Keywords: Green industrialisation, Inclusive growth, Instrumental variable methods, Sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract_Text: This research analyses the effect of green industrialization on inclusive growth in 27 sub-Saharan African countries. The research covers the period from 2002 to 2021 and uses fixed effect IV regression, double least squares, and Lewbel's approach as its main methods. It concludes that green industrialization has a positive influence on inclusive growth in the 27 countries studied. A one percentage point increase in green industrialisation leads to an increase in inclusive growth of 0.00482 points at the 1% threshold. Green industrialization significantly contributes to the achievement of sustainable development goals, particularly economic growth and the reduction of inequalities. The main result of this research is in line with the theory of weak sustainability and structural transformation of the economy, which postulates green growth if appropriate mechanisms are employed. We suggest that the authorities in sub-Saharan African countries promote the development of green industrialization by applying taxes to polluters and granting tax breaks and subsidies to green industries. They can also invest in renewable energies to encourage a transition to clean energy use. It is also necessary to raise awareness among businesses about the need to protect the environment and encourage consumers to favor products from green businesses.

Title: Green industrialisation and sustainable development in sub-Saharan Africa: role of institutions
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: BOUDA, RAYANGUENEWENDE ABDOUL KADER; ZOUNGRANA, TIBI DIDIER
Organisations: BOUDA, Dr. RAYANGUENEWENDE ABDOUL KADER | Université Thomas SANKARA
Keywords: Green industrialisation; Sustainable development; Institutions; Two-step system GMM; Sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract_Text: Sustainable development has become a key factor for countries seeking continued growth. It is in this context that this study analysed the effects of green industrialisation on sustainable development in Sub-Saharan Africa. Particular emphasis was placed on the role of institutional quality. The study covered 40 countries in Sub-Saharan Africa over the period from 2000 to 2024 and employed the two-step system GMM estimation method. Our findings indicate that green industrialisation makes a positive and significant contribution to sustainable development in sub-Saharan Africa. The results suggest that this positive effect is amplified more than fivefold in an environment characterised by higher-quality institutions. These findings suggest that the authorities in sub-Saharan African countries should promote green industrialisation by investing in green technologies and reducing taxes on green investments in order to facilitate the transition. They should also improve the quality of institutions by enhancing their credibility through the fight against corruption, as well as by strictly enforcing property rights and contracts.

Title: From technology adoption to development outcomes: A systematic review of artificial intelligence’s contribution to sustainable development in Africa
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: responsible innovation, emerging governance frameworks, barriers, opportunities, risks
Abstract_Text:
Objective
This review will examine whether, how and under what conditions artificial intelligence contributes to sustainable development in Africa. It will distinguish technology adoption and technical performance from demonstrated social, economic and environmental outcomes, addressing the gap between technological promise and development impact.
Methods
Following PRISMA 2020 reporting guidance, the review will systematically search Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by targeted Google Scholar searches and citation tracking. Eligible empirical studies will examine artificial intelligence applications in African environments and report development-related outcomes. Study quality will be assessed using design-appropriate appraisal criteria. A structured narrative synthesis will compare sectors, countries, beneficiaries and outcome measures, examining how institutional capacity, infrastructure, data governance and stakeholder participation shape reported outcomes. Particular attention will be given to causal attribution, distributional effects and environmental trade-offs.
Key results
The planned outputs are an evidence map distinguishing adoption indicators, service and organisational improvements, and demonstrated development outcomes; an assessment of evidence strength and geographical coverage; and a framework explaining the conditions under which artificial intelligence produces inclusive and sustained benefits. The synthesis will also identify adverse effects, uneven access and gaps between reported efficiency gains and population-level impact.
Conclusions
The review will inform decisions about where artificial intelligence warrants investment, which safeguards are necessary and how development impact should be evaluated. Its relevance to sustainable development by and beyond 2030 lies in connecting technological interventions to measurable outcomes, equitable benefit distribution and institutional accountability. The resulting framework will support responsible innovation and help policymakers, universities, industry and civil society distinguish promising applications from interventions supported by credible evidence.

Title: A roadmap for target-oriented urban forest management models in warming cities
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Organisations: Broitman, Prof. Dani | Technion - Israel Institute of Technology
Keywords: Urban forest management, target-oriented models, warming cities
Abstract_Text:
The transformation of urban areas into sustainable cities and communities (SDG11) in a threatening climate change era is a key challenge. The development of a high-performance Urban Green Infrastructure (UGI) and its integration within a densely built urban environment is a central tenet of this challenge.
Good practices and principles for developing high-quality UGI in cities are well established. However, urban UGI guidelines usually focus on a combination of two intertwined approaches: On one hand, local interventions based on demonstrated microclimate assessments, such as green facades or tree planting recommendations. On the other hand, highly stylized guidelines at the neighborhood or city level suggest what can be achieved with a systematic application of these local interventions. However, such guidelines sometimes fall short when dealing with questions such as what the (measurable) objectives of the UGI development are, whether (or not) these objectives are realistic in the specific urban setting, and, finally, the cost and benefits of concrete implementations of UGI in specific sites. We suggest that this results from a lack of scientific models supporting target-oriented urban forest management.
The proposed model begins with a defined target required from UGI in the future, in terms of ecosystem services provision. For example, a certain level of thermal comfort for a share of the people moving daily on the city’s streets, considering local warming forecasts. Starting from the current urban setting, population, and green infrastructure status, the model will run forward suggesting a small set of economically feasible, physically possible, and timely manageable UGI alternative plans towards the required target. The main challenges of the model would be dealing with a vast universe of implementation possibilities, accounting for economic externalities, and managing UGI as a living stock that evolves over time. We will present a model development roadmap and initial results.

Title: Whose Future? Innovative workshop for Co-Designing Desirable Decarbonised Futures
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Net-zero pathways, just transition, stakeholder co-design, desirable futures, integrated assessment modelling
Abstract_Text:
Reaching net zero is not only a question of identifying technically feasible pathways, but also of asking what desirable goals these pathways should serve, what kind of post-decarbonised societies they should help create, and what trade-offs they generate. This innovative session will function as a Knowledge Arena of Horizon Europe project PANTHEON, which develops decarbonisation scenarios together with the stakeholders, using the WILIAM integrated assessment model and complementary CGE/MRIO modelling. This session brings together researchers, policymakers, NGOs, civil society organisations, industry and business representatives to critically engage with these scenarios.
After a short, non-technical presentation of the forecasting and backcasting pathways, participants disuses them in facilitated groups, asking which desirable goals they reflect, which remain missing, what assumptions shape the results, and what social, economic, environmental or political consequences are underrepresented. Particular attention will be paid to goals beyond emissions reduction, including social justice, wellbeing, affordability, health, employment, environmental protection and resilience. They identify trade-offs, inequalities and unintended effects, and consider how goals, assumptions and scenarios could be revised.
The reflections will inform the policy roadmaps and recommendations that PANTHEON will deliver for the European Union and the People’s Republic of China. The session therefore moves beyond asking how to reach net zero and creates a science-policy-society dialogue around the questions of net zero for what, for whom, and through which pathways, which are central to sustainable development beyond 2030.

Title: Using the iSDG model to explore sustainable policy pathways for the Netherlands
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Authors: Kluck, Teun; Pedercini, Matteo; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: System dynamics modeling, emission reductions, environmental policies
Abstract_Text:
The Netherlands’ economic trajectory is unsustainable, with existing policies falling short of addressing environmental degradation. This study evaluates whether drastic structural changes are necessary to achieve EU and national environmental targets.
We use the iSDG model, a national-level system dynamics model, to analyse the effects of policies across environmental and socio-economic sectors. Our study is the first to consider indicators across all 17 SDGs for the Netherlands. We explore policies that change economic incentives, such as a carbon tax and investments in green energy, as well as a policy pathway involving direct emission reductions through structural interventions, such as limiting livestock numbers, reducing pesticide and chemical fertiliser use, and phasing out machinery dependent on fossil fuels.
Preliminary findings suggest that drastic transformations are needed for the Netherlands to limit its contribution to environmental degradation. Public investments in green practices, while aligned with the values of the Green Deal and the Dutch National Recovery and Resilience Plan, are insufficient and require substantial scaling up. Alternatively, enforcing emission reductions to the required levels results in limited trade-offs with socio-economic indicators.
Combined with social reforms, direct emission reductions could lead to a truly sustainable society. This research highlights the urgency of structural economic and environmental reforms to meet sustainable development goals by and beyond 2030.

Title: From River Burial to Daylighting in Brussels: Renewed Human-River Interactions for Just Urban Adaptation
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: CAO, Yixin; van Griensven, Ann; Sadowski, Piotr
Organisations: CAO, Dr. Yixin | Vrije Universiteit Brussel
Keywords: social-ecological system, Nature-based Solutions, urban rivers, water governance
Abstract_Text:
Historically, cities developed within river floodplains. With industrialization, stream burial, i.e., the enclosure of watercourses in pipes and culverts, became a widespread strategy in European cities to address flooding, sanitary crises, and demand for buildable land. While enabling urban expansion, it disrupted hydrological connectivity and weakened socio-cultural relationships with rivers. As climate change intensifies flood and drought risks, river restoration has expanded since the 1980s; more recently, stream daylighting has emerged as a nature-based solution (NbS) that restores freshwater ecological functions, moderates urban microclimates, and reconnects people with water heritage.
Brussels illustrates how successive transformations of its river system have reshaped human–nature interactions. The city expanded within the flood-prone Senne valley, where the river was covered between 1867 and 1871 in response to recurrent flooding and public-health crises, its tributaries were diverted into the sewer network, and two constructed canals facilitated navigation and trade. These historical interventions still shape today’s hydrology, concentrating stormwater along former valley floors and increasing sewer overload and pluvial flood risk. Their effects are also unevenly distributed. Densely built, lower-income neighbourhoods face greater exposure to overheating and flooding, while combined sewer overflows contaminate the Senne, and canal-zone regeneration intersects with migration, social exclusion, and green gentrification.
Since the mid-2010s, Brussels has increasingly reframed its waterways as natural assets, with stream daylighting efforts underway, e.g., the reopening of 200m of the Senne near Buda Bridge in 2021 and a 650m planned under the ongoing Max-sur-Zenne project. In this context, our project explores river restoration as a coupled social–ecological intervention that reshapes land use policy, redistributes diverse riverine ecosystem services, and strengthens climate-adaptive capacity within civil society. Supported by digital citizen science, the project seeks to engage structurally under-represented residents along the Senne and canal. Ultimately, we ask how restored urban rivers can foster just urban transitions.

Title: Urban-Rural Healthcare Disparities in Ghana: Strategies for Promoting Sustainable Rural Healthcare.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Aikins, Prof. Eric Kojo Wu | University of Cape Coast
Keywords: Healthcare Disparities; Sustainable Rural Healthcare, Urban-Rural Disparity; Sustainable Developement; Health Insurance Coverage
Abstract_Text:
In most developing countries, including Ghana, urban–rural health disparities persist. Although Ghana has made significant progress toward achieving Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3) (Government of Ghana VNR, 2025; United Nations, 2025), substantial urban–rural disparities remain in the provision of healthcare facilities and healthcare professionals, the prevalence of non-communicable diseases, and access to health insurance (Government of Ghana VNR, 2025; WHO Country Profile, 2026).
The progress Ghana has made so far toward achieving Sustainable Development Goal 3 (SDG 3) in the areas of primary healthcare delivery, maternal and child healthcare, immunization, and infectious disease control has primarily benefited the urban population. For instance, the urban–rural doctor-to-patient ratios—0.57 doctors per 1,000 population in the Greater Accra Region (predominantly urban) and 0.03 doctors per 1,000 population in the North East Region (predominantly rural)—demonstrate this disparity (Government of Ghana, 2025; Ministry of Health, 2024; Ghana’s Healthcare Sector Report, 2022).
The study employed a systematic review methodology, involving a review of global, Government of Ghana, and local private health institution reports, to assess the extent of regional disparities in healthcare delivery in Ghana. Also, it provides strategies for fostering sustainable healthcare delivery in Ghana.
In all, the study proposed four main strategies to reduce urban–rural disparities in healthcare delivery in Ghana:
1. Encourage private investment in the provision of healthcare facilities.
2. Encourage community initiatives to provide scholarships for qualified and competitive individuals pursuing medical and nursing education.
3. Encourage private investment in the provision of pharmaceutical services.
4. Expand the scope of the National Health Insurance Scheme to cover vulnerable persons who can make weekly premium payments.

Title: Comparative Analysis of Data Balancing Techniques for Small Deep Learning Models on Low-Powered Devices Using the YawDD Dataset for Driver Drowsiness Detection.
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: Driver drowsiness detection  Edge AI, Low-powered devices, Data balancing techniques, YawDD dataset, Small deep learning models
Abstract_Text:
Driver drowsiness detection is critical to preventing road crashes and improving traffic
safety, yet real-world implementation of deep learning paradigms is hindered by dataset
class imbalance and automotive system embedded computational limitations. This
study undertakes a systematic comparative investigation of diverse data balancing
schemes comprising data augmentation, automatic/manual class weighting, focal loss,
and their hybrid settings in the context of lightweight MobileNetV2 framework on the
YawDD driver yawning dataset. Experimental results suggest that, if sensitivity to
minority yawning incidents is drastically improved by class weighting in any form, it
culminates in a balance between recalling such incidents and false positives through
manual tuning. Data augmentation by itself does not improve recognition of the minority
class sufficiently, whereas focal loss pays off to some extent only when aligned with
class weighting. A combination of focal loss with manually weighted classes offers the
best balanced performance significantly reducing false negatives with tolerable false
alarm rates. These findings are invaluable for developing effective, sensitive, and
deployable driver drowsiness detection architectures running on battery-powered
devices, with implications for both theoretical research and practical deployment in
vehicles.

Title: Localising Subjective Well-Being and Inner Development Among Settlements in the Mining Heartland of India
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Sustainability, labour well-being, mining health, inner development, inequalities.
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study analyses how mining settlement residents living on the edge conceptualise subjective well-being and inner development while battling everyday societal, economic, and environmental injustices.
Methods: This research was conducted across three different settlements in the proximity of mines in Raniganj, West Bengal, applying a mixed-methods approach, where qualitative ethnographic methods were employed to gather information about life history, narratives regarding livelihood precarity, occupational health hazards, and coping mechanisms. To complement this, stratified random sampling was used to obtain quantitative data regarding demographic profiles, household economic conditions, and family health information. This combination provided a rich ground-level perspective on the lived realities in resource extractive regions.
Key results: Findings reveal a complex psychological normalisation of severe environmental and occupational hazards among the labourers. Tuberculosis, fungal infections, anaemia, cataracts, heart issues, breathing issues, and hypertension are a few key issues found. Dealing with these, they treat physical morbidity as an inevitable sacrifice made to secure household survival, instead of looking at it as a mere health deficit. A solidified community network to tackle societal deficiencies is visible; so is how the women in the families had to deal with the dual burden of managing the household and daily impacts of toxicity.
Conclusions: acknowledgement and integration of certain ground-zero survival strategies are required to achieve true sustainable development. Marginalised perspectives of well-being and inner development, if incorporated with the broader spectrum of sustainability frameworks, can be vital in looking beyond theoretical models of equity and development. Prioritising the subjective realities of vulnerable workforces and anchoring justice and transition policies in the lived experiences of those most impacted by resource extraction environments will ensure equitable progress by and beyond 2030.

Title: Empowering Children as Environmental Stewards: Lessons from a Community Based Environmental Education Approach to Water Pollution and Environmental Sustainability in Ghana
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: Environmental Education, Environmental Stewardship, Water Pollution, Community Participation, Sustainable Development Goals.
Abstract_Text:
Ghana faces significant environmental challenges, including illegal small-scale mining pollution of rivers and coastal environments, improper waste disposal, plastic pollution and degradation of natural ecosystems. While regulation, enforcement and technological interventions remain essential, long-term environmental sustainability also requires changes in environmental knowledge, attitudes and behavior. Earth Stewards Foundation (ESF) believes that environmental education, particularly among children and young people, can contribute significantly to this transformation.
This practitioner-based presentation shares lessons from the emerging work of ESF, a Ghanaian environmental non-governmental organisation promoting environmental stewardship through child-centred education, community engagement and practical environmental action. ESF views children not only as beneficiaries of environmental protection but also as potential agents of behavioral change within their schools, families and communities.
The presentation draws on ESF's school and community activities, including environmental awareness programmes, community clean-up exercises and household education on waste segregation. A practical example is ESF's engagement in the coastal community of Asemko in Ghana's Western Region, where community clean-up activities have been combined with household education on separating organic waste for potential use in backyard gardens and plastics for recycling.
Drawing on these experiences, the presentation examines opportunities and challenges in translating environmental awareness into community-level action and highlights lessons concerning environmental education, community participation and local partnerships. It also considers how international knowledge exchange can strengthen locally appropriate environmental education.
The presentation argues that progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals and the post-2030 sustainability agenda requires greater recognition of children, schools and community-based civil-society organisations as partners in environmental transformation, behavioral change and intergenerational environmental responsibility.

Title: Examine the Environmental Determinants of Lung Cancer Risk - A Spatiotemporal Study in Bagmati Province
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Authors: Kumar Neupane, Basanta; Xu, Min; Cao, Chunxiang; Joshi, Pramod
Organisations: Kumar Neupane, Dr. Basanta | Nepal Health Research Council
Keywords: Environmental exposureair; pollution; lung cancer risk; spatial analysis.
Abstract_Text: Lung cancer, primarily driven by environmental pollutants, is a growing public health concern in Bagmati Province, Nepal. While numerous studies have linked environmental toxins to lung cancer, their spatial associations at the local level remain underexplored. This study investigates the municipal-level relationship between lung cancer incidence and environmental determinants using spatiotemporal analysis. We analyzed 2,184 lung cancer cases recorded between 2017 and 2021 across 119 municipalities, integrating 25 geographic, environmental, and socioeconomic variables. Spatial clustering was assessed using Moran's I Index, and associations were modelled using Ordinary Least Squares and Spatial Log Models. Our results reveal that air pollution (particularly SO2 and kerosene use) is significantly associated with increased lung cancer risk, whereas NDVI and soil organic matter show protective associations. High-risk clusters were identified in the eastern and central hilly districts, including Kabhrepalanchok, Ramechhap, and Sindhupalchok, while low-risk areas were concentrated in the southern plains. These findings highlight the importance of spatial epidemiology in identifying environmental risk zones and informing targeted interventions. This study offers evidence to guide resource allocation, risk mitigation, and prevention strategies for lung cancer in Nepal.

Title: What does it take to ensure well-being for all? Eliminating subjective well-being poverty in the EU using WILIAM
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: integrated assessment model; beyond GDP; subjective well-being
Abstract_Text:
The transition to a sustainable and low-carbon economy requires 1) new policies that decrease emissions, provide minimum standards of living, and reduce inequalities, and 2) the use of appropriate indicators to ensure that these goals are met. Most models currently used in policy evaluation only take into account traditional economic indicators such as income and consumption as proxies of people’s well-being, and policy goals are set using these indicators. However, these purely economic metrics may fail capture well-being accurately and should be complemented with subjective measures of well-being (life satisfaction, happiness) to provide more comprehensive insights into the distributional impacts of these policies. We introduce a newly incorporated subjective well-being indicator measuring life satisfaction in WILIAM (Within Limits Integrated Assessment Model), representing a beyond-GDP measure of well-being.
We assess the changes in income needed to eliminate subjective well-being poverty in Europe by 2050, using the macroeconomic multi-regional input-output model WILIAM. With the objective of ensuring high levels of well-being for all 27 EU member states by 2050, we model the effects of a progressive redistribution of income through wealth/income taxes and transfers to analyze the changes in income needed to reach this objective. Subjective well-being poverty is defined as a response of 6.5 or lower on the 11-point life satisfaction scale (0 = Not at all satisfied, 10 = Completely Satisfied), as recorded in the 2025 EU-SILC survey. We compare the redistribution scenario to a redistribution + carbon tax scenario and to a business as usual scenario, and evaluate the effects on subjective well-being, economic indicators, inequality, and carbon emissions. We additionally introduce an analysis of the GINI of subjective well-being to explore inequalities in well-being in the EU, and explore further integration within the WILIAM model, connecting life satisfaction to health, education, and employment.

Title: Power to the people, or power for the state? Energy communities and the geopolitics of the energy transition in the EMMENA region
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Authors: Kalemis, Marios; Upham, Paul; Nyborg, Sophie
Keywords: Energy communities; energy security; geopolitics of energy transition; EMMENA; policy translation
Abstract_Text: Energy communities are the European Union's flagship instrument for a decentralised, citizen-owned energy transition. In the Eastern Mediterranean, Middle East and North Africa (EMMENA) region, however, the transition is being made under conditions the instrument was not designed for: contested maritime boundaries, offshore gas discoveries, planned interconnectors with Europe, islanded or state-dominated grids, and an EU energy diplomacy driven since 2022 by the search for alternatives to Russian supply. These conditions favour large, centralised, export-oriented projects and cast energy as an attribute of sovereignty rather than a sector of the economy. This article asks what space such a geopolitical environment leaves for energy communities, and whether they can be made to serve, rather than compete with, the security agendas that dominate it. Drawing on a comparative analysis of energy strategies, regulatory frameworks and EU policy instruments in selected EU and non-EU states of the region, complemented by expert interviews with policymakers, regulators, utilities and civil-society actors, we trace how the EU energy community template is translated, adapted or set aside as it meets national imaginaries of energy security. We conceptualise energy communities as potential instruments of resilience and sovereignty rather than solely as market innovations, and examine how they interact with rentier and utility-dominated models, with EU conditionality and funding, and with regional rivalry over resources and infrastructure. The article offers recommendations for national governments and the EU, and contributes to debates on the geopolitics of decentralised renewable energy.

Title: From national commitments to provincial regulations: How Indonesia's climate policy mix integrates stakeholder engagement into nature-based solutions
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Hadiprasetya, Yoga; Warchold, Anne; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: multi-stakeholder engagement, nature-based solutions, multi-level governance, policy instruments, Indonesia
Abstract_Text: Our earlier review of 840 studies from 170 countries found that research on Indonesia gives climate governance twice the usual attention and engagement processes half. No study has examined which actors Indonesian climate policies name in nature-based solutions (NbS), what roles they assign, or what depth of participation they grant. Any post-2030 agenda that expects ecosystems to deliver mitigation, adaptation, and equity needs those answers, and the literature does not supply them. We read the policies instead, analyzing instrument composition, NbS conceptualization, and engagement structures across both tiers of government. We compiled more than 200 climate-related policies issued between 1990 and 2026 from legal databases, the portals of six national agencies and 38 provinces, and international repositories, then traced each one onward through the legal bases it cites. Documents qualify when they address climate mitigation or adaptation and reference NbS, explicitly or implicitly. We code engagement within them rather than searching for it. We apply a five-branch codebook in ATLAS.ti, scoring instrument type, ecosystem coverage against a 16-type classification, and engagement depth on the International Association for Public Participation (IAP2) Spectrum, which grades a stakeholder's role from being informed to holding delegated decision rights. Across Indonesia's five Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) submissions, the phrase "nature-based solutions" never appears. Policymakers write about landscape approaches and the forestry and other land-use sector. We report how each instrument conceptualizes NbS, which actors it names, what role it assigns them, and at what depth on the IAP2 Spectrum.
