The study addresses SDG 13 on climate action; SDG 6, 14, and 15 on freshwater, marine, and terrestrial ecosystems; SDG 16 on inclusive decision-making; and SDG 17 on multi-stakeholder partnerships. Mapping where engagement obligations sit and where they are missing shows national and provincial governments which instruments to amend before the next NDC cycle.

Title: Participatory indicators for inclusive Sustainable Development Goals
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Co-design of future agendas, indicator development, multi-stakeholder participatory processes, negotiation, institutional innovation
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals are perhaps the most prominent example of governance by goal-setting. As part of this strategy, indicators are used as a policy tool to support earth system governance from local to global scales. Indicators are assumed to offer objective decision-making input across all dimensions of sustainable development while Leaving No One Behind.
Yet research shows that indicators are heavily influenced by who develops them and how, risking existing exclusion mechanisms to become exacerbated if existing power asymmetries remain unchallenged in negotiations about indicators. Several scholars have therefore called for multi-stakeholder participatory processes of indicator development. Such studies tend to rely on deliberative notions of direct engagement. However, this may be difficult to achieve in highly contentious settings where structural barriers to direct deliberation exist.
In this article, we therefore developed and tested a multi-stakeholder participatory indicator development method which facilitates participation in highly contentious settings. We applied and tested this method in developing indicators for gender equality under the SDGs in the district of Faridabad in India through a series of workshops. Gender is a highly contentious issue in this area, with controversies surrounding gender equality leading to mass protests in the weeks prior to the workshops. We collected and analyzed data of eight workshop sessions, interviews with all 20 participants prior to and after the sessions, six expert interviews, facilitator meeting notes, and workshop outputs.
Our results show that our method that combines geographically and temporally dispersed participation with reflexive co-design, enables different groups that otherwise do not see eye to eye to deliberate about gender equality and develop indicators, thereby facilitating more inclusive development of sustainability indicators. In doing so, we contribute to the development of a methodology to democratize earth system governance, in order to foster the building of just and sustainable futures.

Title: Barriers and opportunities in local implementation of the SDGs
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: SDG localization, national and subnational strategies, monitoring progress, implementation gaps, enabling conditions
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are the most prominent example of sustainable development governance, including a set of SDG indicators that are supposed to be localized from global to subnational and local levels. Indicators are believed to be an effective monitoring tool to objectively inform policy decisions across sectors, scales and decision-making arenas. Yet in developing indicators, choices are made about what and how to measure, and how to display this. This influences what issues are deemed legitimate and what not, making indicator development inherently political. These politics of indicators has received little attention in governance of the SDGs. We argue this is problematic in contexts of growing diversities, power disparities among agents, and a growing importance of indicators.
We have developed and applied a framework for understanding the politics of indicators. The framework captures the socio-material nature of indicator politics along indicator design, collection, and presentation. We applied the framework to uncover the indicator politics of national and subnational SDG localization strategies in India. We specifically focus on the development of SDG indicators for gender equality. We collected and analyzed 33 in-depth interviews, participant observations, and 57 (policy) documents as part of two months in-depth fieldwork in Tamil Nadu and Haryana states.
Our findings show that in both states, indicator politics are socio-materially shaped by ideas embedded in governance (data infra)structures that severely lack gender-sensitivity. This resulted in indicators that are especially challenging for marginalized genders and local contexts. We argue that these often-overlooked issues of representation need to be made visible in order to make indicators more inclusive. We suggest that (sub)national governments actively seek ways to capture locally-specific inequalities by critically interrogating how and why issues are understood, framed and interpreted, and what and how is revealed and obscured.

Title: A Critical Analysis of Civil Society’s Engagement in South Africa’s Just Energy Transition: Dynamics and Debates
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: equity and justice
Abstract_Text: South Africa is currently undergoing a Just Energy Transition (JET) that seeks to design and create a clean and just energy industry in South Africa. This process is underpinned by a rapid revision of energy sector policies, regulatory frameworks and debates around energy reform. The aim of the study is to critically analyse the debates and dynamics underpinning Civil Society Organisations’ (CSOs) participation as key stakeholders in the JET process taking place within South Africa: How is civil society engaging in the energy reform process in general and specifically with regards to debates around JET in South Africa? Currently, civil society engages in state-sanctioned and self-created platforms around JET, however the extent to which it participates, the challenges it faces, and the dynamics of this civil space are not well understood. The research is based on a qualitative research design and involved in-depth interviews with representatives from several CSOs involved in JET debates, as well as desktop research. Strategic and purposive sampling was used as a method for choosing respondents best suited to provide answers for the research question. The research found that CSOs actively participate in energy transition debates in South Africa using a variety of strategies and tactics. These include litigation, public participation platforms, media, resistance campaigns and grassroots community activism. Whilst there have been considerable victories - including advocating for energy access, justice and broader consultation - CSOs face resource related challenges, threats and power dynamics whilst engaging in JET processes. There is also a disconnect between local and international CSOs working in this space. Recommendations are made for more funding and collaboration opportunities to increase the scope, depth and participation of civil society in the JET discourse. The research may assist policy makers, CSOs and researchers to better understand the current participation of civil society

Title: Artificial Intelligence and the Water-Energy-Carbon Nexus: A Time-Varying Connectedness Analysis
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Organisations: Musa, Dr. DASAUKI Caleb | University Of South Africa
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, Sustainable development, Twin transition, Water–energy–carbon nexus, Energy transition
Abstract_Text: Artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalisation are increasingly recognised as enabling technologies for sustainable development and the twin transition towards digitalisation and environmental sustainability. Beyond their direct technological applications, AI-related developments can provide new opportunities for understanding interactions across interconnected resource and environmental systems. This study examines the role of AI within the water–energy–carbon (WEC) nexus and explores how AI-related developments interact with the broader transition towards cleaner and more sustainable resource systems. Using daily data over a decade, the study applies a time-varying multivariate connectedness framework to examine the transmission and direction of shocks among AI, water, energy-transition, and carbon-related indicators, while decomposing connectedness across different investment horizons. The results show that AI has a measurable but structurally modest footprint within the WEC system. In contrast, the clean-energy transition emerges as the dominant transmitter of shocks, while water represents the principal net receiver of spillovers, particularly during the post-2020 period. Approximately 88.7% of total connectedness occurs at short-run frequencies corresponding to one-to-five-day horizons, highlighting the rapid and information-driven nature of interactions within the system. The findings demonstrate how AI-enabled analytical approaches can contribute to a more integrated understanding of the interdependencies underlying sustainable development and the twin transition. They also highlight the importance of considering digital, energy, water, and carbon systems jointly when assessing the opportunities and emerging sustainability pressures associated with AI-driven transformation.

Title: Layered, Relational Vulnerability in Coastal Khulna’s Water Crises: A Conceptual Synthesis Toward a Politicized Climate-Development-Health Nexus
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Climate-development-health nexus; Commercial determinants of health; Global South; Planetary health; Social determinants of health; Vulnerability; Water crises.
Abstract_Text: Despite growing recognition that the climate crisis is a health crisis, climate-health scholarship has yet to adequately account for how development processes shape the co-production of these crises. Addressing this gap, this paper draws together interdisciplinary scholarship to develop a three-layered, relational framework of vulnerability spanning macro-structural political economy, meso socio-ecological transformations, and micro embodied inequalities. Integrating commercial determinants of health (CDOH) – the profit-driven entities and practices that restructure environments – with social determinants of health (SDOH) – the structural positionalities that dictate daily exposure – the framework traces how global market paradigms and institutional arrangements, such as export-oriented aquaculture and depoliticized adaptation and water governance, redistribute environmental risks. Building further on this interdisciplinary foundation and informed by nexus scholarship, the paper then advances a politicized Climate-Development-Health (CDH) nexus that connects these processes across scales through three interrelated dynamics: (i) global-local connections driven by export-led commercial aquaculture and transboundary hydropolitics, (ii) the depoliticization of adaptation and water governance, and (iii) the structural inscription of intersecting inequalities onto marginalized bodies. The coastal Khulna case illustrates how salinized and degraded water landscapes are not merely environmental consequences of climate change but material expressions of historically uneven commercial relations whose effects become socially and biologically embedded in marginalized bodies. By situating these localized water crises within the broader production of structural vulnerability across scales, the synthesis highlights their implications for planetary health.

Title: Digitalising Public Investment Appraisal, Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) for Climate Resilience: Lessons from Pakistan
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV), digital appraisal, public investment planning, climate risk screening, evidence-based adaptation
Abstract_Text:
Climate change is increasingly challenging governments to ensure that public investments are resilient, sustainable and responsive to evolving climate risks. However, climate considerations are often addressed separately from mainstream public investment planning, appraisal and monitoring. This study explores how digitalising public investment appraisal and Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) can provide an institutional mechanism for mainstreaming climate resilience into development decision-making. Drawing on Pakistan as a case study, the study examines opportunities to integrate climate-risk screening, resilience measures and climate-related performance indicators throughout the public investment cycle.
The study reviews existing federal and provincial digital appraisal processes and identifies key institutional, technical, data and capacity requirements for systematically incorporating climate considerations into investment decisions. It proposes a phased approach that integrates Climate and Hazard Initial Risk Assessment (CHIRA), climate-resilient project requirements, climate-risk information and MRV into digital appraisal platforms. This approach can enable decision-makers to identify climate risks at an early stage, assess appropriate adaptation measures, track implementation and generate evidence on resilience outcomes.
The Pakistan experience demonstrates that digitalisation can move climate adaptation from a largely policy-level commitment towards a more systematic, transparent and measurable component of public investment management. At the same time, successful implementation requires interoperable data systems, reliable climate information, institutional coordination, clear responsibilities, strengthened technical capacities and common indicators for monitoring adaptation outcomes. The study also highlights the importance of considering gender equality, social inclusion and the needs of vulnerable populations in climate-informed investment decisions.
The findings offer lessons for other climate-vulnerable developing countries seeking to align public investment with climate-resilient and sustainable development pathways. The study argues that integrating climate risk, digital appraisal and MRV can strengthen the quality, accountability and long-term resilience of public investments while supporting evidence-based adaptation planning and more effective use of public and climate finance. https://www.giz.de/de/downloads/giz2025-en-digital-appraisal-system-study-2025.pdf.

Title: Cocoa Farmer Co-operatives as Social and Economic Institutions: Perceived Effectiveness under Illegal Mining in Ghana.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Organisations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Kumasi
Keywords: Cocoa farmer co-operatives, ICA Principles, Perceived effectiveness, Illegal Mining, Co-operative Governance
Abstract_Text: The study assessed the perceived effectiveness of the International Co-operative Alliance (ICA) principles among cocoa farmer co-operatives in the Amansie South District of Ghana. Specifically, it described the nature of the co-operatives, assessed members’ perceptions of the effectiveness of the ICA principles, examined factors influencing these perceptions, and identified and ranked the main challenges facing members. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data were collected from all 33 cocoa farmer co-operatives and 371 farmers selected from a population of 2,039. Descriptive statistics, multiple linear regression and Kendall’s Coefficient of Concordance were used for the quantitative analysis. Qualitative data from six Focus Group Discussions and three Key Informant Interviews were analysed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis. The results showed that the co-operatives were formally established but weak in several areas, including enforcement of by-laws, accountability, transparency, member participation, financial management and service delivery. The overall mean index for perceived effectiveness of the ICA principles was 2.19, indicating general ineffectiveness. Voluntary and open membership was the only principle rated as moderately effective, while the other six were rated ineffective. Age, sex, education, household size, landownership, availability of training resources and whether a farmer’s cocoa farm had been affected by illegal mining significantly influenced perceived effectiveness. Major challenges included declining cocoa production, forceful takeover of cocoa lands, reduced interest in cocoa farming, fewer extension visits, leasing of land for illegal mining and preference for mining because of its immediate financial returns. The qualitative findings supported the quantitative results and confirmed generally weak co-operative effectiveness among members. The study concludes that improving co-operative governance alone may not be enough unless cocoa lands and farmers’ livelihoods are also protected. It recommends regular training on ICA principles and stronger support for the protection and rehabilitation of cocoa farms.

Title: Public Assets in the Energy Transition: Evidence from Indonesia’s Upstream Oil and Gas Sector
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Ministry of Finance of The Republic of Indonesia
Keywords: Public asset management, legacy wells, carbon capture and storage
Abstract_Text: The energy transition raises questions about how governments manage existing fossil-fuel infrastructure and its associated obligations. In Indonesia, upstream oil and gas operations use a substantial portfolio of state-owned assets, including wells, platforms, pipelines and land. As fields mature and decarbonisation progresses, these assets face changing uses and potential retirement costs, while some may support carbon capture and storage (CCS). This study examines the institutional conditions for repurposing Indonesia’s state-owned upstream assets, particularly legacy wells, for CO₂ storage. It combines publicly reported government financial data and sector statistics with a structured review of asset-management and decommissioning regulations and Presidential Regulation No. 14/2024 on CCS. The analysis focuses on ownership, access to existing assets, funding arrangements and post-closure responsibilities. The regulatory framework provides a route for converting existing wells into CO₂ injectors, but implementation requires coordination between energy regulation and public asset management. The analysis identifies issues requiring clarification: access to state-owned wells by storage operators, the sequencing of abandonment and reuse assessments, valuation and revenue arrangements for repurposed assets, and the implications of continued government oversight after operator responsibilities end. Lifecycle framework covering asset recording, recovery, repurposing and retirement are proposed. It recommends assessing storage suitability and well integrity before abandonment decisions, clarifying asset-use arrangements, and coordinating funding across successive uses. These proposals offer an Indonesian perspective on the institutional requirements of net-zero pathways. Their relevance to other resource-producing developing countries depends on comparable ownership and governance arrangements. Integrating public asset stewardship into transition planning could help preserve reuse options while making long-term obligations and distributional concerns more transparent.

Title: Ambient Temperature and Emergency Department Visits: Association and Short-Term Prediction
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: System perspective for addressing one health nexus within ecological ceilings
Authors: Ghazanfar, Syed; Osama, Muhammad; Ali, Saima; Ayub, Rakhshanda; Charlton, Paul; Fahim, Ammad
Keywords: ambient temperature, emergency department, meteorological exposure, distributed lag non-linear model, time-series forecasting
Abstract_Text: Extreme and changing environmental conditions can influence emergency healthcare demand, making the ability to understand and anticipate ED utilization a global public health priority. However, evidence on temperature-related ED utilization and short-term forecasting remains limited in low- and middle-income settings, particularly in South Asia. We examined the association between ambient temperature and daily adult emergency department (ED) visits and evaluated meteorological and historical demand variables for short-term ED forecasting in Karachi, Pakistan. We conducted a retrospective time-series study of 1,322,537 adult ED visits recorded at Indus Hospital and Health Network over a 10-year period (2016–2025). Lagged Pearson correlations were used to assess associations between meteorological variables and ED visits, followed by a quasi-Poisson distributed lag non-linear model (DLNM) to characterize nonlinear and delayed temperature effects. SARIMA, SARIMAX, XGBoost, and LightGBM were trained using temporally ordered data and evaluated on an unseen test period. Temperature showed the strongest correlation with ED visits among the evaluated meteorological variables. Using 28.3°C as the reference, cumulative RR was 0.839 (95% CI 0.792–0.889) at 18.5°C and 1.062 (95% CI 1.034–1.091) at 31.7°C, demonstrating a nonlinear temperature-associated pattern. For forecasting, models incorporated meteorological conditions, calendar variables, and historical ED demand. LightGBM achieved an MAPE of 6.55% and R² of 0.56, followed by XGBoost (6.63%; R² 0.54). SHAP analysis showed that recent ED demand, particularly the seven-day rolling mean and recent lags, contributed most to predictions. This large, decade-long dataset provides evidence from a resource-constrained setting and demonstrates the potential of integrating environmental and demand signals to support short-term emergency healthcare planning under changing climatic conditions.

Title: Sustainable Entrepreneurship for Transformative Development: From the SDGs to 2030 and Beyond
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Organisations: Upham, Prof. Paul | University of Groningen
Keywords: Sustainable entrepreneurship; entrepreneurial ecosystems; sustainability transitions; sustainable business models; social innovation
Abstract_Text:
Entrepreneurship has increasingly been recognised as a potential contributor to addressing environmental, social and economic challenges. Yet, as the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals approaches, important questions remain about when, how and under what conditions entrepreneurial activity contributes to meaningful sustainability transformations.
We invite conceptual, empirical, methodological and interdisciplinary contributions that critically examine the role of entrepreneurship in advancing sustainable development during the remaining years of the SDGs and in shaping post-2030 sustainability agendas. We also welcome contributions that move beyond the assumption that entrepreneurship is inherently beneficial for sustainability and examine the conditions, tensions, trade-offs and unintended consequences associated with entrepreneurial approaches to sustainable development.
This track invites conceptual, empirical, methodological and interdisciplinary contributions that critically examine the role of entrepreneurship in advancing sustainable development during the remaining years of the SDGs and in shaping post-2030 sustainability agendas. The track aims to connects entrepreneurial agency with the wider institutional, societal and ecological systems in which entrepreneurship takes place.
A central question for the track is not simply whether entrepreneurship can contribute to sustainable development, but how, for whom, under what conditions and with what consequences. We invite academic researchers, corporate professionals, startup founders, government officials to take this as an opportunity to talk about their work, to explore the challenges and provide reflections on practical solutions. Contributions are particularly welcome that generate lessons from the SDG era and offer insights into the role sustainable entrepreneurship may play in shaping more inclusive, resilient and sustainable futures beyond 2030.
Climate change is accelerating, yet business and management education still largely reproduces epistemic regimes built around profit maximisation. This paper argues that business schools could instead become catalysts for societal transformation, but only if education moves beyond knowing (Head) and doing (Hands) to include being (Heart). Drawing on transformational learning theory, in particular Freire's critical pedagogy, and on Sipos et al.'s Head, Hands and Heart framework, we examine how Arts-based Learning (ABL) and contemplative methods inspired by kundalini yoga can foster the Heart dimension of a sustainability mindset in educational leaders.
The empirical case is a workshop for educators at a German higher education institution. Participants took part in a mindfulness exercise, an out-of-the-box thinking task and a sensorial activity that linked nature connectedness to climate change education. Eight educational leaders from German and Danish institutions, all with sustainability or climate education responsibilities, were later interviewed in semi-structured interviews. The data were analysed inductively.
The findings point to four themes: multi-level connections between university and society; transformational education that is practice-oriented and impactful; a "reset" of the educator's profile and personal journey, involving courage, openness and self-reflection; and obstacles at both structural and individual levels. Participants valued the sensorial and contemplative exercises as memorable "eye openers" that interrupt routine and invite critical reflection. They also warned that novelty can wear off, that mindset change cannot be achieved in a single session, and that fear of losing students' respect can deter educators from using such methods.
The study contributes by showing that ABL and contemplative methods are complementary tools for epistemic change, by documenting educators' reactions to them, and by identifying institutional tensions that hinder change. We conclude that these pedagogies can empower educators to reshape curricula and teaching practice, and we call for further research on their use beyond higher education.
This article examines sustainable entrepreneurship in international contexts. It draws on Freire's concept of conscientisation and John Shotter's withness thinking as its theoretical foundations. It aims to deepen understanding of the lived experiences of sustainability entrepreneurs in both developed and developing countries. Two research questions guide the study. What drives entrepreneurs to pursue sustainability through the economic, social and environmental innovations in their business models? What barriers do they face, and what solutions do they find?
Methodologically, the study elicits and analyses in-depth personal narratives from entrepreneurs seeking to make social and/or sustainability contributions. Following Shotter's phenomenological approach, the narratives are generated dialogically, so that entrepreneurs' experiences are understood in their own terms. The study makes no claims of wider generalisability, although structural commonalities may be shared by similar individuals.
The article makes four contributions. It identifies the factors motivating the pursuit of social innovation in sustainability-oriented enterprises. It explores the role of conscientisation in those motivations. It examines the barriers entrepreneurs experience and the solutions they develop. Finally, it advocates a methodological approach based on withness thinking, which moves away from treating marginalised subjects as research objects towards co-created meaning-making between entrepreneurs and researchers.

Participants took part in a mindfulness exercise, an out-of-the-box thinking task and a sensorial activity that linked nature connectedness to climate change education. Eight educational leaders from German and Danish institutions, all with sustainability or climate education responsibilities, were later interviewed in semi-structured interviews. The data were analysed inductively.
The proliferation of digital technology in the world is shifting how individuals, organisations and communities access information, acquire knowledge, collaborate, mobilise resources and respond to social and environmental challenges. Advancement in technology creates new opportunities for inclusive development, however, its meaningful and sustainable contributions depend on how effectively the technology is integrated with community participation, human values and sense of community.
When technological access is coupled with a culture of giving back, and shared responsibility, individuals can contribute their time, expertise, knowledge and resources to address community challenges. This study investigates how expanding availability and adoption of digital technologies can enhance social innovation and sustainable community development, provided they are underpinned by a strong social foundation rooted in a mindset of giving back to society. It aims to contribute to discussion on digital transformation and sustainable development by positioning the relationship between digital proliferation and human willingness.
The proliferation of digital technology can be a catalyst for social innovation when guided by empathy, community ownership, collective responsibility, and sustained commitment to giving back.

Title: Digitalizing Dryland Conservation: A Machine and Deep Learning Framework for High-Precision LULC Mapping of the Moroccan Argan Forest
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Authors: Benazun, Hoda; El Wahidi, Farid; Youssef, Lassiane; Ait Naceur, Hassan; Najem, Mohamed Reda
Keywords: Argania spinosa; LULC; Object-Based Image Analysis; Deep Learning; Digitalization.
Abstract_Text: The Moroccan argan forest (Argania spinosa) is a vital biosphere reserve, severely threatened by climate change and anthropogenic pressure. Until now, its spatial representation has been limited to rough, small-scale botanical sketches due to the complex challenges of dryland forest mapping, such as low canopy density, strong soil background reflectance, and extreme structural heterogeneity. To bridge this critical gap, this study presents the first-ever high-resolution, detailed land use land cover (LULC) map of the argan ecosystem, leveraging the synergy of remote sensing and artificial intelligence. We developed a novel two-step hierarchical mapping workflow. First, an Object-Based Image Analysis (OBIA) approach coupled with the Random Forest algorithm was deployed to distinguish forest ecosystems from all other classes identified and classified as non-forest. Second, a parallel classification was applied to the core argan ecosystem, comparing machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost) against a deep learning architecture (CNN). The comparative analysis reveals that the CNN (OA = 95%) significantly outperformed Random Forest (91%) and XGBoost (87%). Specifically, the pixel patch-based CNN effectively resolved the radiometric confusion caused by dense vegetation structures, dominating complex classes like Pure Thuya and Mixed Argan. By merging the highly accurate non-forest matrix with the best-performing CNN ecosystem classification, we produced an unprecedented final map. This first-of-its-kind mapping of the entire argan spatial distribution provides a crucial, highly accurate decision-making tool to support the conservation and sustainable management of this endemic forest.

Title: Banking on Her Resilience: Integrating Gender into Climate-Related Financial Risk Management in Ghana's Rural and Community Banks
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Frimpong Mensah, Dr. Thelma | ARB Apex Bank PLC
Keywords: climate finance; multilevel governance; community-based climate action; maladaptation; gender-responsive finance; rural banking; Ghana
Abstract_Text:
Climate change and gender inequality meet at the point of rural finance. In Ghana, women make up the majority of smallholder farmers, market traders and micro-entrepreneurs, and are the primary clients of Rural and Community Banks (RCBs). They are among the most exposed to climate shocks, yet land-title collateral rules, spousal guarantees and thin credit histories limit their access to adaptation finance. As the Bank of Ghana's Climate-Related Financial Risk Directive extends to RCBs from January 2027, will climate risk management reinforce women's exclusion or support a just transformation?
This paper presents a conceptual framework drawn from the ARB Apex Bank Gender Policy (2026), which sets standards for more than 144 RCBs, treating this apex-to-RCB structure as multilevel climate governance. It argues that climate risk and gender-based financial exclusion should be assessed together, through three components: gender-responsive climate risk screening in credit decisions; products that turn adaptation needs into bankable demand, including climate-smart agricultural loans, crop insurance, collateral beyond land title and community-based Susu group finance; and gender-disaggregated loan data reported alongside climate returns, so supervisors can see whether climate-driven credit tightening falls disproportionately on women.
The paper argues that SDG 5 and SDG 13, largely pursued in parallel, can be joined up in climate finance beyond 2030, and sets out unresolved tensions, including maladaptation through de-risking and the limited capacity of small rural banks.

Title: A Multi-regional Physical Input-Output Table Framework for Gallium and Indium
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Do, Thi Thu Huong; Grebel, Thomas
Keywords: value chains, material efficiency, production and consumption, physical input-output table, critical raw materials
Abstract_Text: Objective: Resource-efficiency targets under the SDG rely on aggregate material indicators that are blind to by-product critical metals: where they originate, how they are transformed, and where they are lost. We develop a physical input-output table (PIOT), in kilograms, tracing gallium and indium from extraction to final use. Both are by-products of aluminum and zinc production, indispensable for photovoltaics, light-emitting diodes and electronics. Methods: The table is built from observed physical data, not derived from a monetary table. Geological survey statistics anchor extraction and refining across 15 regions for 2000-2022. Stoichiometric closure with partner elements (nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) generates compound flows. Customs trade statistics and balancing synthetic flows link refineries, and final demand shares from a multi-regional monetary database allocate devices to consuming regions. Because by-product supply is fixed by host-metal output, the system is solved with a supply-driven (Ghosh) model closed by a terminal loss node. Key results: Mass is conserved at every refining and synthesis node in every year, with residuals below one microgram, and total extraction equals total loss for each element-year. Supply concentration is traceable with visualizations, especially for by-products with routes and in physical units, a distinction a monetary model with one coefficient per sector cannot separate. Conclusions: The framework is transferable to other metals and delivers what expert-based criticality frameworks cannot: measured supply concentration, losses, scenario-conditioned extraction requirements and substitutability. For sustainable development by and beyond 2030, this could complement material footprint indicators under the responsible consumption and production goal and inform secure metal supply for the energy transition. Further research could be extended to secondary production of by-products, taken into account of lifetime of final products and recycling rates for new and old scraps.

Title: Evaluating the Efficacy of Ascophyllum nodosum-Mediated Priming of Tomato Seedlings Under Waterlogging: Physiological, Biochemical, and Metabolic Responses
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Tanni, Sadia Tabassum; Zhang, Dr. Leilei; Lucini, Dr. Luigi
Organisations: TANNI, SADIA TABASSUM | Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore
Keywords: Ascophyllum nodosum, biostimulants, waterlogging, tomato, metabolomics
Abstract_Text:
Background: Waterlogging (WL) is an increasingly important abiotic stress that limits crop productivity by inducing soil hypoxia, disrupting root development, and promoting oxidative stress. Seaweed extracts are widely used as plant biostimulants, but their efficacy against WL stress remains poorly understood. Ascophyllum nodosum (AN) contains diverse bioactive compounds, including polysaccharides, minerals, and hormone-like compounds, which may enhance plant stress resilience.
Methods: This study evaluated the effects of AN application on cherry tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L. cv. Heinz 1301) seedlings exposed to 72 h of WL followed by an 11-day recovery period. Plants were primed twice with AN at 7-day intervals through soil drenching before WL stress initiation. Physiological, biochemical, and root architectural responses were evaluated. Untargeted metabolomic profiling using UHPLC-QTOF is currently underway to further investigate metabolic responses to AN priming under WL.
Results: WL induced pronounced oxidative and membrane damage in untreated plants, with H₂O₂ and malondialdehyde (MDA) levels increasing 1.5- and 1.7-fold, respectively, compared with untreated controls. Although photosynthetic responses did not differ significantly between untreated and AN-treated WL plants after 72 h, AN-treated plants exhibited improved protection during the recovery period. WL also markedly altered root architecture, significantly reducing primary root length by 34.48% and increasing average root diameter by 50.5% compared with CK; AN treatment reduced this WL-induced increase, with root diameter 9.38% lower than in untreated WL plants. Adventitious root formation was also prominent under WL. Interestingly, AN-treated plants showed partial protection against these WL-induced root alterations.
Conclusion: AN priming appears to enhance tomato resilience to WL, particularly during post-stress recovery. Ongoing UHPLC-QTOF metabolomic analysis will provide further insight into the primary and secondary metabolic pathways underlying AN-mediated stress tolerance. These findings highlight the potential of AN-based biostimulation as a sustainable approach for improving crop resilience to WL under changing climatic conditions.

Title: Does stress timing matter? Biochemical and metabolomic insights into stage-dependent tomato responses to waterlogging, salinity and their combination
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Authors: Tanni, Sadia Tabassum; Zhang, Dr. Leilei; Salehi, Dr. Hajar; Lucini, Dr. Luigi
Organisations: TANNI, SADIA TABASSUM | Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore
Keywords: Salinity, waterlogging, combined stress, metabolomics, tomato
Abstract_Text: Salinity (S) and waterlogging (WL) frequently co-occur in agricultural systems, yet their combined (WL+S) effects across early reproductive developmental stages remain poorly understood. This study investigated stage-dependent physiological, biochemical, photosynthetic, and metabolomic responses of cherry tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L. cv. Ciliegino a Terra) under S, WL and WL+S. The plants were exposed to 36 hours of stress in controlled environmental conditions during early flowering and early fruiting stages. Combined stress reduced shoot growth at both developmental stages, whereas photosynthetic responses were relatively similar across stages. In contrast, oxidative and antioxidant responses differed between stages. Lipid peroxidation showed antagonistic effects under combined stress at early flowering but synergistic increases at early fruiting. At final harvest, WL+S induced coordinated upregulation of catalase (CAT), superoxide dismutase (SOD), and ascorbate peroxidase (APX) activities in early flowering, whereas no significant antioxidant enzyme response was observed at early fruiting. Importantly, untargeted metabolomic profiling (UHPLC-QTOF) further revealed stage- and treatment-dependent metabolic reprogramming. At early flowering, only two metabolites were shared among the stress treatments, while combined stress produced the highest number of unique metabolites. In contrast, 41 metabolites were shared among the stress treatments at early fruiting, indicating greater metabolic convergence at this developmental stage. Consistently, AMOPLS analysis identified developmental stage as the primary source of metabolic variation. Overall, the integrated responses highlighted the complexity of combined stress alongside contrasting biochemical and metabolic adjustments, demonstrating that developmental stage is a key factor influencing tomato growth and yield, particularly under changing climate.

Title: Nature Relationship Index: An Aspirational Approach to Planetary Futures
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Zhang, Dr. Junze | Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences
All_Countries: China, Netherlands, New Zealand, United States
Keywords: Nature Relationship Index, Sustainable Development, Aspirational Approach, Transformation
Abstract_Text:
How can we measure progress toward a future in which people and the rest of nature thrive together? Existing global metrics, from GDP to the Human Development Index, capture human wellbeing but say little about the health of our relationship with the living world. To address this gap, Ellis et al. (2025) proposed an aspirational approach to planetary futures based on the Nature Relationship Index framework. It argues that metrics should not merely track ecological decline, but measure human agency, i.e., what societies are doing right, in shaping mutually beneficial relationships with nature. This framework underpins the NRI as a new metric of national progress along three dimensions: nature that is thriving and accessible, nature used with care, and nature safeguarded through governance and investment.
This session brings together contributors to the NRI's international development to showcase its latest advances. This includes indicator design, global data integration, and early applications across diverse social-ecological contexts. The session comprises presentations on the NRI and its derivatives, elaborating its conceptual foundations and demonstrating its potential to shift policy narratives from ecological crisis to positive, achievable action.
The session will also seek to stimulate discussion on the post-2030 global development agenda: how can aspirational, nature-centred metrics inform the next generation of global goals? It will conclude with an interactive discussion, inviting the GSC participants to explore these metrics as tools for inspiring and steering planetary transformation beyond 2030.

Title: Inclusive wealth convergence in Africa: the role of institutional quality and foreign direct investment
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Organisations: Baloyi, Dr. Nxalati | University of Stellenbosch Business School
Keywords: Inclusive wealth convergence, institutional quality, foreign direct investment, sustainable development, beyond GDP
Abstract_Text: The increasing recognition of the inadequacy of per capita GDP convergence in capturing the environmental sustainability of economic growth and societal aspects of well-being, necessitates convergence metrics that extend beyond GDP. This paper examines how institutional quality and foreign direct investment (FDI), along their interactive effects, influence convergence beyond GDP (inclusive wealth) in 40 African countries. Employing the two-stage system generalised method of moments (2SGMM) to a panel data ranging from 1995 to 2020, the empirical results reveal persistent unconditional and conditional divergence in inclusive wealth among numerous African countries. This divergence is attributed to many nations being ensnared in suboptimal institutional environments, along pronounced regional and sectoral disparities associated with FDI flows to Africa. Further, the reported results posit that FDI can effectively synergise with institutional quality to promote inclusive wealth convergence in Africa. Achieving inclusive wealth convergence is crucial for enhancing sustainable development in Africa. Enhanced levels of sustainable development break persistent cycles of low-growth and alleviate conditions of extreme poverty and inequality. Evidence of inclusive wealth convergence signifies progress towards an inclusive and sustainable development pathway, consistent with the Sustainable Development Goals and the African Union’s Agenda 2063. The findings emphasise that inclusive wealth convergence in Africa is conditional rather than absolute, necessitating robust governance structures that align external capital investment with sustainability and development objectives.

Title: From Human Rights Evidence to Responsible AI for Sustainable Development: Lessons from Conflict-Affected Yemen for the Post-2030 Agenda
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: Responsible AI, Human rights evidence, Data governance, Conflict-affected settings, Sustainable development beyond 2030
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals have demonstrated that progress towards sustainable development depends not only on the availability of data, but also on the quality, inclusiveness, governance and usability of evidence. This challenge is particularly acute in conflict-affected and fragile settings, where institutional disruption, information gaps and unequal access to digital technologies can undermine evidence-based decision-making. At the same time, the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) creates new opportunities to analyse complex evidence while introducing significant risks related to bias, information integrity, privacy, accountability and exclusion.
This contribution examines the potential of responsible AI and evidence governance to support sustainable development beyond 2030, drawing on lessons from human rights documentation and information management in conflict-affected Yemen. It explores how systematically collected and verified human rights evidence can contribute to more effective data-driven analysis and decision-making, while identifying the safeguards required to prevent AI from amplifying weaknesses in source data or reproducing existing inequalities.
The paper proposes an evidence-to-AI framework linking data quality and verification, responsible data governance, contextual analysis, human oversight, accountability and sustainable development outcomes. It argues that the post-2030 agenda should move beyond a narrow focus on producing more data towards building trustworthy, contextualised and actionable evidence ecosystems. In conflict-affected settings, this requires treating affected communities not merely as data sources, but as participants in responsible data governance and the interpretation and use of evidence.
The contribution concludes with practical lessons for designing inclusive, rights-respecting and accountable AI-enabled approaches to sustainable development beyond 2030.

Title: A Novel Framework for Codesigning Nature-based Solutions for Climate-resilient and Sustainable Communities across Africa
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Climate Change, Mitigation, Nature-based solutions, Community resilience, Codesign
Abstract_Text:
Africa faces accelerated convergence of climate change, biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, and socioeconomic vulnerability, placing unprecedented pressure on communities, livelihoods, food and water security, and human well-being. Nature-based Solutions (NbS) provide a promising pathway for addressing these interconnected challenges by harnessing ecosystems to deliver climate adaptation and mitigation, biodiversity conservation, disaster-risk reduction, and societal benefits. However, NbS implementation across Africa remains constrained by fragmented planning, limited integration of Indigenous and local knowledge, inadequate stakeholder participation, weak science–policy linkages, and insufficient consideration of diverse ecological, cultural, socioeconomic, and institutional contexts. This study proposes a novel transdisciplinary framework for codesigning NbS with African communities, positioning communities, knowledge holders, scientists, practitioners, policymakers, and other stakeholders as co-creators of solutions.
The framework integrates climate-risk and vulnerability assessment, ecosystem and biodiversity diagnostics, socioeconomic analysis, Indigenous and local knowledge, participatory geospatial approaches, scenario modelling, multicriteria decision analysis, and stakeholder engagement within an iterative decision-support architecture. It guides NbS development from risk and ecosystem assessment through opportunity-identification, collaborative design, spatial prioritisation, feasibility and trade-off analysis, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and adaptive learning. NbS interventions were evaluated against interconnected dimensions of climate resilience, biodiversity, ecosystem services, livelihoods, social equity, cultural relevance, economic viability, governance feasibility, and long-term sustainability.
By connecting scientific evidence with Indigenous and local knowledge and strengthening collaboration among communities, researchers, policymakers, practitioners, and financing institutions, the framework seeks to transform NbS from fragmented interventions into locally owned, evidence-based, scalable, and adaptive strategies for sustainable development. This transferable methodological framework and decision-support approach capable of supporting context-specific NbS planning across diverse African landscapes. Ultimately, it will demonstrate how integrating ecological science, local knowledge, participatory governance, and spatial decision-making can unlock the transformative potential of NbS to strengthen climate resilience, conserve biodiversity, enhance livelihoods and well-being, and advance inclusive, equitable, and sustainable Africa communities.

Title: Beyond 2030: From Sustainable Development Goals to Individual Development Goals through Local Action and Regional Cooperation
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: The Central Asia Pakistan Afghanistan Sustainable Development Initiative
Keywords: SDG localization, youth leadership, multilevel governance, sustainable development, regional cooperation
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals have provided an unprecedented global framework for sustainable development, but their implementation has often been constrained by limited local ownership, institutional capacity, fragmented interventions and insufficient political will. As the international community considers sustainable development beyond 2030, this contribution proposes a more targeted, people-centred and locally grounded approach.
Drawing on practical experience from Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), Pakistan and regional cooperation initiatives, the presentation explores how SDG implementation can become more effective by prioritizing selected goals according to local needs, defining specific and measurable objectives, and concentrating resources on achievable outcomes rather than attempting to address all goals simultaneously. Particular attention is given to people with fewer opportunities, including marginalized and underserved communities, whose participation is essential to meaningful development.
The presentation further introduces the complementary perspective of Individual Development Goals (IDGs): recognizing that sustainable societies depend not only on institutional and environmental progress, but also on the development of individuals’ capacities, agency, skills, resilience and ability to participate in development processes. Linking SDGs with IDGs can help connect global targets with individual and community-level transformation.
The contribution argues that effective implementation beyond 2030 requires stronger political will, accountable multilevel governance, meaningful youth participation and locally designed solutions. It also emphasizes that local approaches should be connected through regional cooperation, allowing neighbouring countries and communities to exchange knowledge, mobilize resources and address shared challenges.
The Central Asia–Afghanistan–Pakistan Sustainable Development Initiative (CAPSDI) is presented as an emerging regional platform for translating these principles into dialogue, partnerships, knowledge exchange and sustainable investment, connecting local priorities with regional cooperation.
The presentation concludes by proposing a targeted SDG–IDG approach in which global goals provide direction, local communities define priorities, individuals become agents of change, and regional cooperation enables scale and continuity beyond 2030.

Title: AI-Enabled SDG Intelligence: From Global Indicators to Micro-Level Monitoring, Local Action and Regional Data Cooperation
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Organisations: The Central Asia Pakistan Afghanistan Sustainable Development Initiative
Keywords: Artificial intelligence, SDG monitoring, big data, digitalization, regional data cooperation
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence, big data and digitalization can fundamentally change how progress toward the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is understood, measured and acted upon. This contribution proposes an AI-enabled SDG intelligence framework that moves beyond aggregated national statistics toward granular, real-time and actionable monitoring of individual targets, indicators, initiatives, gaps, impacts and time-bound objectives.
The proposed approach uses AI modelling to assess each SDG target and indicator, identify implementation gaps, track progress and impact, estimate emerging risks, and recommend areas for improvement. It seeks to narrow monitoring to the micro level—from individual communities and development projects to snow and glaciers on mountains, rivers and water systems, forests and plants, climate conditions, public health, education, human rights, governance, peace and livelihoods. Such granular intelligence can reveal changes and inequalities that conventional aggregate datasets may overlook.
A central component is an accessible digital dashboard that presents progress against selected goals and specific objectives over defined timeframes. The platform would enable governments, researchers, organizations, communities and individuals to access information and contribute observations, evidence and local data, creating a participatory model of sustainable-development monitoring.
The framework also proposes regional data-sharing mechanisms among countries, regions and organizations, particularly for shared challenges such as climate change, water, migration, biodiversity and peace. Special attention is given to developing countries, underprivileged communities and conflict-affected regions, where data gaps and limited institutional capacity can constrain evidence-based policymaking.
The Central Asia–Afghanistan–Pakistan Sustainable Development Initiative (CAPSDI) is proposed as a potential regional cooperation platform for piloting such approaches, connecting local data and AI-enabled monitoring with cross-border knowledge exchange, policy dialogue and sustainable investment.
The presentation argues for a transition from data collection to data intelligence, from national averages to micro-level realities, and from passive reporting to participatory, AI-driven sustainable development.

Title: Advancing Sustainable Development and Inclusion Using AI in Low-Resource Language Contexts
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Keywords: Small Languge Model, Inclusion, Explainable AI (xAI), Data Soverignty, Superintelligence
Abstract_Text:
Objective: AI is trained where data is abundant, not where the need is greatest. The "Geography of AI for Peacebuilding" dataset (Harvard Dataverse, 2026) indicates that 90% of AI training data originates in Europe and North America, while 83% of conflicts occur in the Global South. This study critically examines four roles of AI, big data, and digitalisation (analytical method, implementation tool, decision aid, and agenda-setter) through voice-first, sector-specific AI for Nigeria's low-resource languages, weighing opportunities against challenges.
Methods: We assemble an open developer stack from N-ATLaS, Nigeria's Llama-3-based multilingual model; Meta's NLLB-200 for translation; and Google's WAXAL corpus for speech-to-text and text-to-speech. Each component is audited for language coverage, licensing, compute, energy and data costs. The stack is mapped onto services in healthcare, digital democracy, financial literacy, agriculture, information integrity, peacebuilding and education. SHAP and LIME attributions are generated in English, translated and voiced, then tested for whether explanations remain faithful across languages.
Key Results: Each role carries an opportunity and a constraint. As method, explainable AI exposes bias, yet attributions computed on English proxies may not hold for Hausa, Igbo or Yoruba. As implementation, voice lowers literacy barriers, yet WAXAL offers text-to-speech but no transcribed speech for these languages. As decision aid, spoken explanations make outputs contestable, yet NLLB-200's non-commercial licence limits local enterprise. As agenda-setter, digitalisation competes with poverty hindering affordability of mobile data prices, poor internet penetration, and grid electricity averages 456 gCO₂/kWh before diesel back-up.
Conclusions: Beyond 2030, and as capabilities approach superintelligence, trustworthy AI depends on who owns language data, who can audit explanations and who bears the energy cost. We propose data autonomy commons, permissive licensing, multilingual explainability standards and privacy-preserving, carbon-aware deployment as practical levers for SDGs 2, 3, 4, 5, 13, 16 and 17.

Title: Kumayam: Reviving Traditional Shell-Lime Mortar for Coastal Ecosystem Resilience and Sustainable Landscapes along India’s Malabar Coast
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: Sal, Prof. Hasna | LMSAI Harvard University
Keywords: Coastal ecosystem services; Kumayam; shell-lime mortar; nature-based resource management; circular material systems; traditional ecological knowledge; coastal resilience.
Abstract_Text:
Along India’s Malabar Coast, Kumayam, a traditional shell-lime mortar derived from calcium-rich mollusk shells, represents an enduring relationship between coastal ecosystems, vernacular architecture, and local ecological knowledge. Historically employed in Kerala’s built environment, Kumayam embodies a resource-based construction practice connecting aquatic biodiversity, artisanal livelihoods, and regional material traditions. However, industrial cement production, changing coastal economies, and declining intergenerational knowledge have contributed to its gradual disappearance.
This research investigates Kumayam as a potential model for regenerative material practices within sustainable coastal landscape and seascape management. Focusing on Kerala’s Vembanad Lake ecosystem, the study examines the historical interdependence of shell resources, aquatic habitats, traditional lime production, and vernacular construction. It explores how locally sourced biological materials have shaped architectural practices while supporting coastal communities and their cultural identities.
Employing an interdisciplinary methodology integrating field documentation, oral histories, traditional production techniques, and comparative material analysis, the research evaluates Kumayam’s ecological significance and its potential contribution to circular construction economies. Particular attention is directed toward responsible shell sourcing, the reuse of discarded shells, biodiversity conservation, and the environmental implications of lime calcination compared with conventional cement production.
The study further considers how reviving traditional material knowledge can strengthen community resilience, preserve artisanal livelihoods, and encourage environmentally responsive architectural practices. Rather than treating coastal ecosystems solely as extractive resources, it proposes a reciprocal framework linking ecological stewardship with sustainable material production.
By positioning Kumayam within the discourse of nature’s contributions to people, this research demonstrates how traditional construction knowledge can inform contemporary sustainability strategies. It advocates integrating cultural heritage, aquatic ecosystem protection, and circular material innovation to advance regenerative coastal landscapes, strengthen human–nature relationships, and support resilient communities confronting ecological degradation and accelerating environmental change across vulnerable coastal regions.
