Title: Repairing What, for Whom? A Conceptual Framework for Re-imagining Power, Justice, and Care in Contaminated Sites Remediation Projects in Indonesia
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Ministry of Environment, Republic of Indonesia
Keywords: hazardous waste contaminated sites, remediation, health equity, political ecology, environmental justice
Abstract_Text:
Remediation of hazardous sites is increasingly recognised not only as an environmental governance challenge but also as an issue of health equity, community well-being, and environmental justice. In Indonesia, government policies and programmes have sought to address contamination associated with community-based economic activities, including artisanal and small-scale gold mining, metal smelting, e-waste, and used lead-acid battery recycling. Yet remediation is often approached primarily as a technical intervention, with limited attention to the historical, social, economic, cultural, and institutional conditions that shape both exposure to environmental harms and access to the benefits of remediation.
This study develops a conceptual framework for rethinking remediation as a process concerned with justice, care, and collective well-being. It asks: (1) How do political, historical, and socio-environmental factors shape remediation processes and their outcomes? (2) To what extent do technical approaches align with or diverge from environmental justice concerns? And (3) How can remediation be reimagined to better recognise local knowledge, lived experiences, and community well-being? The study examines four remediation projects in Tegal, Jombang, Bogor, and Lebak, Indonesia, using thematic analysis of government reports, feasibility studies, engineering design, and media sources.
The analysis demonstrates that remediation has largely been framed and implemented as a technical exercise, while insufficient attention has been given to the complex interplay of non-technical aspects. This can contribute to an uneven distribution of environmental burdens, health risks, and the benefits of remediation, while limiting opportunities for affected communities to participate meaningfully in decisions that shape their well-being. In response, the study proposes a conceptual framework that positions remediation as an ongoing and relational process of care and collective healing. By integrating environmental justice, local knowledge, lived experience, and attention to community well-being, the framework offers a pathway towards more equitable and context-sensitive forms of environmental governance.

Title: Community Perceptions of Cultural Ecosystem Services in Restoring Degraded Urban Forests: Evidence from Aboabo Forest, Ghana
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Cultural Ecosystem Services; Community Perceptions; Urban Forest; Urban Forest Restoration; Open Defecation; Aboabo Forest
Abstract_Text: Cultural ecosystem services (CES), including aesthetic, educational, recreational, spiritual, and social values - provided by urban forests, are critical to the well-being of urban communities. However, the Aboabo Forest in Tamale, Ghana, a 138.64-hectare gazetted reserve, is severely affected by persistent open defecation (OD) by surrounding community members. While prior studies have established the prevalence and behavioural determinants of OD in this forest and its institutional management arrangements, the impact of OD on the CES of the forest and the community's preferred strategies for their restoration remain unexamined. This study addresses this gap using data drawn from a cross-sectional mixed-methods research design: a structured survey of 110 households and ten key-informant interviews with community and institutional leaders. Findings reveal that aesthetic value (91.8%), educational value (90.0%), recreational and ecotourism value (80.9%), and spiritual and religious value (76.4%) are the CES most severely degraded by OD. The degradation manifests largely through deterrence - residents avoid the forest for fear of stigmatisation and due to the foul environment - and through the desacralisation of sacred shrines. Paradoxically, OD appears to strengthen social relations among practitioners (56.4%), thus depicting a complex social facet of the practice. Community members prioritise the restoration of aesthetic (94.5%), educational (87.3%), and spiritual/religious (71.8%) CES and propose four pathways: public education campaigns, promotion of religious and cultural activities in the forest, multi-stakeholder collaboration, and integration of recreational infrastructure.

Title: AI enhanced geospatial assessment of climate, conflict, ecosystem resilience and sustainability in the Blue Nile Region
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Organisations: Nori, Dr. Wafa | University of Bahri
Keywords: AI, ecosystem resilience, sustainability, geospatial analysis
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study investigates how climate variability, armed conflict, and governance fragility interact to shape land-cover and land-use dynamics in Sudan’s Blue Nile Region. The objective is to quantify environmental change, assess ecosystem resilience, and identify compound-risk hotspots where climatic stress, conflict intensity, and institutional weakness converge. The project aims to generate actionable evidence that supports sustainable landscape management and long-term recovery in fragile environments, contributing to regional and global sustainability goals beyond 2030.
Methods: The research applies an integrated geospatial workflow that combines multi-temporal satellite imagery, climate records, conflict data, displacement information, and governance indicators. Landsat, Sentinel-2, and MODIS datasets are harmonized to derive land-cover maps and vegetation indices. Random Forest classification provides baseline land-cover outputs, while a CNN-LSTM deep-learning model captures spatial patterns and temporal transitions in vegetation dynamics and forest degradation. Climate anomalies, conflict events, and governance conditions are spatially aligned to evaluate their combined influence on land-system change. Additional spatial analyses, including Geographically Weighted Regression, examine local relationships among environmental and socio-political drivers.
Key Results: The project produces high-resolution land-cover maps, vegetation productivity trends, climate anomaly profiles, conflict intensity surfaces, and governance fragility layers. The CNN-LSTM model identifies areas with reduced ecosystem resilience and predicts the likelihood of forest degradation under interacting stressors. Compound-risk hotspots emerge where drought, conflict, and weak institutions overlap, revealing zones of heightened environmental vulnerability and limited capacity for recovery.
Conclusions: The integrated AI-enabled framework demonstrates how climate variability, conflict dynamics, and governance fragility jointly influence land-system change in the Blue Nile Region. The results provide a transferable approach for environmental monitoring in conflict-affected landscapes and support evidence-based planning for sustainable development. By linking environmental resilience with socio-political conditions, the study contributes to achieving and extending sustainability objectives beyond 2030, particularly in regions facing compound risks and institutional fragility.

Title: Bio-Composite Retrofit Panels: Upcycling Agricultural Residues with Mycelium for Climate-Resilient Building Insulation
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Baloch, Nosheen; Ali, Muhammad Maaz; Danish, Muhammad
Keywords: Mycelium-based insulation, Bio-composite materials, Agricultural waste upcycling, Circular bioeconomy, Thermal performance
Abstract_Text:
Rapid urbanization and expanding building footprints have heightened operational energy consumption, driving reliance on carbon-intensive synthetic insulation materials. Concurrently, open field burning of agricultural residues severely degrades air quality and ecosystem stability in developing regions. To address these interconnected challenges, this research develops and experimentally evaluates low-carbon, bio-composite building thermal insulation panels fabricated from upcycled agricultural waste (wheat straw, sawdust, and luffa fibers) bound by fungal mycelium.
The bio-composite formulations were optimized through physical and thermal testing. Experimental characterization demonstrated an optimized dry density of 132.2 kg/m³ and thermal conductivity values ranging between 0.040 and 0.055 W/mK, positioning the material competitively against conventional expanded polystyrene (EPS) and mineral wool. Water-repellent calcium stearate treatments were introduced to mitigate moisture absorption, preserving structural integrity and hygrothermal behavior. Fire reaction testing revealed promising self-extinguishing behavior forming a protective char layer.
By transforming localized agricultural waste streams into high-performance insulation, this bio-composite panel reduces building heating and cooling loads while mitigating agricultural residue burning. The proposed solution offers a scalable, circular framework for resilient construction, aligning natural ecological cycles with human architectural systems to drive regional climate action.

Title: Demand-side control saves least where people live: functional and seasonal inequality in a mixed-use building
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: just transitions, social equity, demand-side management, residential heating, building energy
Abstract_Text:
Objective. Demand-side control is widely promoted as a low-cost route to building decarbonisation, and is almost always reported as a single building-level percentage. That average conceals who carries the constraint. This study disaggregates demand-side savings by function and season, rather than reporting one aggregate value, for a mixed-use building.
Methods. A rule-based energy management model was developed for a 10,000 square metre mixed-use redevelopment in Amsterdam, covering four functions sharing one structure: a museum, a restaurant, an office and housing. A two-tier rule set screens outdoor conditions, then indoor temperature, humidity, occupancy and time of day, modulating heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting. Demand is computed hourly, not assumed. Mean, coldest and hottest weather profiles were built from three years of local measurements, and compared against uncontrolled operation.
Key results. Aggregate savings ranged from 81% in summer to 26% in winter. Disaggregated, the spread is far wider. Under mean conditions restaurant demand fell by 87% and office demand by 86%, both empty most of the week; museum demand by 71%; housing by only 40%, continuously occupied with little to switch off. Housing saves least under both mean and summer conditions, and in winter savings for every function fall to between 15% and 34%. The two effects compound: housing in winter saved 16%, against 94% for the restaurant in summer, a nearly sixfold difference. Control is weakest where people live and when they need heat.
Conclusions. Building-level averages overstate the savings achievable in continuously occupied residential space. The functions saving most stand empty; the one saving least shelters people, and its weakest performance coincides with the coldest months. Efficiency-first strategies therefore deliver uneven benefits across functions unless residential heating is addressed separately. Beyond 2030, a single aggregate percentage is the wrong unit for reporting demand-side potential in mixed-use buildings.

Title: Wavelet-Coupled Boosting Algorithms for Daily Multi-Reservoir Outflow Simulation in the Rufiji River Basin, Tanzania
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Keywords: Boosting Algorithms, Multi-Reservoir; Outflow Simulation; Rufiji River Basin; Wavelet Transform
Abstract_Text: Effective simulation of reservoir outflow is imperative for early warning systems, sustainable water resource management, economic development, and the extended lifespan of hydraulic structures. This study juxtaposed five boosting algorithms, subsuming Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost), Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), Light Gradient Boosting (LightGBM), Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (Boost), for simulating daily outflow from the multi-reservoir with diverse characteristics and climatic conditions in the Rufiji River Basin, Tanzania. Addressing the limitations of previous studies that relied on restricted input variables, this study incorporated comprehensive hydroclimatic datasets and assessed the influence of variable combinations across various scenarios. Additionally, the study explored the potential of Wavelet denoising within the boosting algorithms framework for simulating reservoir outflow. Historical daily reservoir, hydrological, and meteorological data (January 1990 to December 2024) were employed for training and validation. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) was employed to refine the variables' time series, and both wavelet-coupled and traditional boosting algorithms were compared using the Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) and Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) metrics. Results demonstrated that DWT-preprocessed models consistently outperformed their traditional counterparts, with improvements in NSE of 1.9% for the Mtera and 3.0% for the Kidatu reservoir. Among the models, WA-LightGBM emerged as the highest robustness across reservoirs, particularly in scenarios that integrated observed and satellite data. These findings offer actionable insights to optimize reservoir operations and enhance flood mitigation and water management strategies.

Title: Science is Essential to Address Global Humanity Questions
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Science, technology, research, partnership
Abstract_Text:
Science is Essential to Address Global Humanity Questions
Keywords: SDG localization, science-policy interface, global research cooperation, sustainable development, post-2030 agenda
A decade after the adoption of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), global progress remains insufficient to achieve the ambitions of the 2030 Agenda. Recent United Nations assessments indicate that only a minority of SDG targets are on track, while many are progressing too slowly or have regressed. Persistent financing gaps, weak policy coherence, limited local implementation capacity, fragmented governance systems, and increasingly complex global challenges continue to hinder sustainable development. Developing countries face an estimated annual financing gap of approximately US$4 trillion.
These realities raise a critical question for the post-2030 development agenda: what must be done differently to accelerate progress toward sustainable development? This paper examines key lessons from the implementation of the SDGs and explores how these lessons can inform a more action-oriented framework beyond 2030. Particular emphasis is placed on the role of science, technology, and research, which should move from a supporting function to a central pillar of development planning and implementation.
We need stronger integration of scientific evidence into policy processes for enhanced global research cooperation as a foundation for addressing shared development challenges. It explores the potential establishment of a dedicated goal focused on science and research, together with an international platform linking researchers, research funding organizations, and the United Nations.
The post-2030 agenda should prioritize knowledge exchange, equitable access to science and technology, and stronger science-policy dialogue. It should also support integrated assessment of SDG synergies and trade-offs, strengthen national and local implementation, and address emerging priorities.Ultimately, sustainable development beyond 2030 will require institutional mechanisms that enable scientific knowledge to move more effectively from research into policy and practice, ensuring that evidence-based solutions contribute to transformative and lasting change

Title: From mercury pathways to just transitions: closing the execution gap in African artisanal gold mining
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Just transition, Decarbonization, Equity and justice, Nationally Determined Contributions, Community-based climate action.
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
Africa’s artisanal and small-scale gold mining (ASGM) sector sits at the centre of the climate–development nexus. It supports millions of livelihoods, yet mercury use and weak governance undermine both environmental integrity and the equity of mineral-linked climate transitions. This paper examines why mercury phase-down and formalisation commitments repeatedly fail at the point of implementation, and what execution conditions would make mercury-free pathways compatible with decent work and just transitions beyond 2030.
Methods:
The analysis draws on applied policy research and practice-based evidence from ASGM settings in Western Kenya, Tanzania and comparable African contexts. It combines review of National Action Plans under the Minamata Convention, responsible-sourcing and due-diligence frameworks, and field-level patterns of monitoring, enforcement and programme delivery. Particular attention is given to who captures formalisation benefits, how environmental monitoring gaps persist, and how gender, capital and location shape who is reached by “clean” mining interventions.
Key results:
Policy frameworks for mercury reduction and responsible minerals are comparatively advanced; execution is not. Monitoring and remedy remain thin, so contamination pathways stay largely invisible. Mercury-free technologies and formal licences tend to reach operators who already have capital, networks or association positions, while women in crushing, washing and processing, and poorer miners more broadly, remain outside the transition. Climate and critical-minerals narratives rarely treat ASGM livelihoods as a design constraint, producing a risk of exclusionary decarbonisation rather than a just one.
Conclusions:
Just climate transitions in mineral economies will not be secured by additional strategy documents alone. Beyond 2030, mercury phase-down and critical-minerals pathways need community-level monitoring, formalisation rules that do not presuppose capital, and accountability tied to field outcomes rather than association attendance. Closing this execution gap is a condition for resilient, equitable climate-development pathways in Africa’s resource economies.

Title: Rooted in Ubuntu: AmaBomvana Indigenous Healing Knowledge and Resilience Across Human and Natural Systems
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Stellenbosch University - Tygerberg Campus: Stellenbosch University Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences
Keywords: Ancestral calling; decolonial epistemology; Indigenous healing; resilience
Abstract_Text: This article examines how amaBomvana Indigenous healers of Elliotdale (Xhora), Eastern Cape, conceptualize resilience through the isiXhosa idiom ukunyamezela (endurance). Using critical ethnography informed by postcolonial and decolonial theory, data were generated through focus group discussions with healers (amagqirha, amaxhwele, abathandazeli, amatola, oonobumba) and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: endurance as ancestral mandate rather than personal trait; the "paper wall" of bureaucratic and clinical exclusion inherited from the Witchcraft Suppression Act of 1957; strategic pluralism that collaborates with biomedicine and the church without epistemic surrender; and illness categories exceeding biomedical recognition. Findings reposition resilience as a theological and ethical obligation rather than a Western psychological capacity. The article recommends that religious, cultural and policy institutions recognize ukunyamezela as a legitimate framework for healer wellbeing and calls for repeal of the Act's lived legacy.

Title: Mediating participation: The Role of Local Organizations in Sustainability-Oriented Citizen Science
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Riedl, Pia; Teufer, Birgit; Hartl, Barbara; Seebauer, Sebastian
Organisations: FERNFH - Distance Learning University of Applied Sciences
Keywords: community participation, citizen science, co-creation
Abstract_Text:
Objectives:Citizen Science increasingly seeks to involve communities in sustainability research and action. Existing local organizations provide access to established structures and networks that are not yet involved in sustainability issues, but they also shape and filter this access. Rather than simply serving as recruitment channels, organizations’ leaders mediate how research projects reach their members and how participation takes place. This contribution examines how local organizations actively mediate participation in sustainability-oriented Citizen Science.
Methods:The analysis is based on CoClimA, a Citizen Science project conducted with eleven local organizations in two regions of Lower Austria. Organization members participate as Citizen Scientists in the development and implementation of climate interventions. We analyze contact and conversation protocols, documentation of co-creation processes and climate interventions, feedback and reflection sessions with organization leaders, and observations from the research team’s ongoing collaboration with participating organizations. The collected materials are analyzed qualitatively, with a focus on their content and a cross-case comparison of the different organizations. This allows us to identify patterns in how organizations mediate access, communication, and participation between researchers and organizational leaders and members.
Key results:The findings show that organizations are not neutral recruitment channels but actively shape participation. While they provide established structures, translate project requirements into their organizational context, and extend access to members, leaders also select and filter who is reached and how participation takes place. Participation is often mediated through a small number of key individuals who act as gatekeepers and take responsibility for communication and engagement.
Conclusion:Collaboration with local organizations can both enable and constrain participatory sustainability initiatives. While organizations can extend the reach of sustainability-oriented Citizen Science, organizational access does not equal community engagement. Recognizing this distinction is key to effectively engaging local communities in sustainable development and sustaining participatory approaches over time.

Title: Beyond visitor counts: an alternative sustainability metric for viral community-based tourism villages in Indonesia
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Keywords: alternative metrics, business models, sustainable tourism, community-based tourism, algorithmic exposure
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Indonesian tourism villages (desa wisata) are promoted as engines of rural development, yet their performance is judged mainly by visitor arrivals and revenue, metrics that reproduce the growth-as-success logic of GDP. Viral social media exposure can multiply arrivals overnight, yet many viral villages lose visitors within years. This study examines why algorithmic exposure leads to sustainability in some villages but to decline in others, and proposes the Virality-Marketing Alignment (VMA) Gap as an alternative sustainability metric: the distance between the demand a destination generates and its readiness to absorb it.
Methods: An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design is applied in Magelang Regency, Central Java. Study 1 contrasts two pairs of neighbouring villages that went viral, one sustained and one declined in each pair (Nepal Van Java and Mangli; Punthuk Setumbu and Giritengah), through in-depth interviews with village managers. Study 2 tests the resulting model with an on-site tourist survey analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling and multi-group analysis, comparing visitors reached through algorithmic exposure with those who actively searched for the destination.
Key results: The framework identifies three dimensions of the gap. Temporal: demand peaks faster than infrastructure and governance can adjust. Image-reality: tourists' experience disconfirms the image promised by viral content. Agency: managers lose control over how their village is represented. Managers' adaptive capacity is expected to distinguish sustained from declining villages. Full results will be presented at the conference.
Conclusions: Arrival-based indicators reward exposure rather than resilience and push managers and policymakers to chase virality at the expense of long-term viability. Measuring alignment between exposure and readiness complements growth indicators for Sustainable Development Goal targets 8.9 and 12.b on sustainable tourism. Beyond 2030, local economies should be judged not by the activity they attract but by the value they retain for host communities.

Title: AI and Sustainable Development Beyond 2030: Evidence, Society and Security
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Bali Swain, Prof. Ranjula | SIR, Stockholm School of Economics
All_Countries: China, India, Japan, Sweden, United States
Keywords: AI governance frameworks, Sustainable development beyond 2030, sustainability analytics, responsible innovation
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) and big data offer new ways to monitor sustainable development and support decisions, while creating environmental pressures, social inequalities and security challenges. This innovative session examines the conditions under which these technologies can accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and contribute to a more effective and equitable agenda beyond 2030.
Convened and moderated by Bali Swain, the 90-minute science–policy dialogue combines five brief evidence contributions with moderated debate and an audience exercise. Erik Gråd presents Nordic evidence on public acceptance of data-centre establishments; Ashok Swain addresses AI and resource security; Lei Huang explores Big Data and AI based Post-2030 SDG ; Shyam Ranganathan examines AI’s impacts on social sustainability; and Xin Zhou considers a big-data- and AI-based post-2030 SDG indicator framework. Each contributor addresses the following shared questions:
• What can AI and Earth observation measure credibly, and where do data gaps, uncertainty or weak validation remain?
• Which decisions can this evidence improve, and what institutional conditions enable its use?
• Who gains from digital monitoring and AI deployment, and who bears their resource, economic, social and distributional costs?
•What principles should guide responsible use of AI and big data in the agenda beyond 2030?
The dialogue will identify where improved monitoring can inform practical action and where institutional capacity, unequal access, public acceptance or security concerns constrain its value. Participants will formulate two or three principles linking credible evidence and useful indicators with accountability, equitable access and assessment of AI’s resource and societal impacts.
Sustainable development requires evaluating both what AI enables and the consequences of its deployment. By connecting analytical advances with implementation and governance, the session will generate recommendations for responsible innovation and international cooperation by and beyond 2030.

Title: Nutritional consequences of maternal migration: Does duration matter?
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: school feeding; child nutrition; maternal migration; structural threshold effects; intrahousehold bargaining power
Abstract_Text: Children are usually left behind by migrating parents in Sub-Saharan Africa. However, empirical evidence on the net effects of maternal migration on child nutrition remains ambiguous. In this study, we analyse the nutritional consequences of maternal migration duration and examine whether school feeding programmes attenuate the adverse impact of migration. We develop a simple conceptual framework that links maternal migration to child nutrition through household income, intrahousehold bargaining and school feeding programmes. We analyse this using the Ghana Socioeconomic Panel Survey, employing a structural threshold model that addresses endogenous migration duration and allows its effect to vary discontinuously across migration-duration regimes. Our results reveal a pronounced nonlinear effect: short-term migration reduces child weight-for-age z-scores (WAZ), but increases WAZ once migration exceeds 6.4 months. We further find that school feeding is associated with improved nutritional outcomes among children left behind and attenuates the adverse nutritional effect of shorter-duration maternal migration. This reconciles mixed evidence on migration-child nutrition studies and identifies school feeding as a potential policy margin for protecting children in high-migration settings.

Title: An Explainable 3D CNN, CNN-LSTM Framework Integrating LADA-FAO Indicators for Spatio-Temporal Prediction and Early Warning of Land Degradation in Arid Oasis Ecosystems: Case Study of the Draa Oasis System, Morocco.
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Authors: LASSIANE, YOUSSEF; El Wahidi, Farid; Benazun, Hoda; Ait Naceur, Hassan; Najem, Mohamed Reda
Keywords: Deep Learning, Earth Observation, Land Degradation, Early Warning, Oasis Ecosystems.
Abstract_Text: Land degradation in arid oasis ecosystems results from complex interactions between climate variability, water scarcity, vegetation stress, soil degradation, and human pressures. This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence framework integrating Earth Observation data and LADA-FAO indicators for spatio-temporal prediction and early warning of land degradation in the Drâa Oasis System, Morocco. A hybrid 3D-CNN and CNN-LSTM architecture will capture spatial patterns and temporal dependencies from multi-source environmental indicators. Model performance will be evaluated using RMSE, MAE, and R². To enhance interpretability, SHAP will identify the importance and contribution of environmental factors, Grad-CAM will locate spatially influential areas, and an attention mechanism will identify critical temporal periods. The proposed framework aims to move beyond retrospective assessment toward predictive and interpretable early warning, supporting proactive land-management decisions and sustainable oasis resilience. This research demonstrates how AI, big Earth Observation data, and digitalization can contribute to SDG 15 (Life on Land), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and sustainable development in vulnerable arid environments.

Title: Country-specific Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) target prioritization using Machine learning
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Khot, Utkarsh; Pradhan, Prajal; Warchold, Anne
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals; SDG interactions; Explainable machine learning; policy prioritization
Abstract_Text: As we enter the final phase of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, it is imperative to unravel the interlinkages among the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). With only four years remaining, identifying which targets to prioritize has become vital. To date, these interlinkages have largely been quantified through statistical associations that capture only linear, pairwise relationships, overlooking the non-linear, multivariate dependencies that characterize how progress on one target reshapes others. While research is increasingly turning to machine learning, its potential remains underutilized, particularly its capacity to learn complex, interacting structures directly from data and to make them interpretable for policy. We use the unified SDG database, which integrates observations for all indicators from the UN, the World Bank, and the Sustainable Development Report across 192 countries. Using gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost), with random forests for robustness, we model each indicator as a function of all others and apply SHAP to quantify how each contributes positively (synergies) or negatively (trade-offs) to the rest. By aggregating these contributions to the target level, we derive a directed interlinkage network for each country. Because each indicator is modeled conditional on all others, the resulting contributions net out confounding within the indicator set and capture non-linear dependencies that pairwise correlation cannot capture beyond association, though short of identified effects. Ranking targets by their aggregate contribution distinguishes multipliers, whose progress propagates most widely across the system, from buffers, which chiefly prevent regression elsewhere, thereby yielding, for each country, a ranked set of candidate priorities for coordinated action. The approach enables country-specific prioritization and, by grouping results by income level, provides a scalable basis for comparing how priorities shift along the development spectrum, directing limited effort toward the targets where it matters most as the 2030 deadline nears.

Title: Artificial Intelligence for Sustainable Development: Bridging the Green and Digital Transitions
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Organisations: St. Joseph's Technical Institute for the Deaf-Nyang'oma
Keywords: Artificial intelligence; sustainable development; big data; digitalization; twin transition.
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence (AI), big data, and digitalization are increasingly shaping how societies understand sustainability challenges, formulate policies, and implement development strategies. As countries pursue the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) beyond 2030, these technologies offer opportunities to strengthen evidence-based decision-making and accelerate the twin transition: the interconnected transformation towards environmental sustainability and digital advancement. However, their contribution depends on how effectively technological innovation is aligned with social inclusion, environmental responsibility, and equitable development.
This paper examines the enabling role of AI in understanding sustainable development and advancing the green and digital transitions. It develops a conceptual framework for understanding how AI-driven analytics, big data, and digital technologies can integrate environmental, economic, and social indicators to identify sustainability trends, assess policy interventions, and support decision-making across sectors. Particular attention is given to applications in climate change mitigation, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, water resource management, smart cities, and education and skills development. The paper further explores how AI can facilitate predictive modelling, optimize resource utilization, improve service delivery, and strengthen the capacity of institutions to respond to emerging sustainability challenges.
Beyond technological opportunities, the paper critically considers the risks associated with algorithmic bias, data privacy, digital exclusion, energy-intensive computing, and unequal access to digital infrastructure. These challenges demonstrate that digitalization does not automatically produce sustainable outcomes and that AI systems must be governed through transparent, inclusive, and environmentally responsible approaches. The paper argues that realizing the potential of the twin transition requires integrating AI adoption with sustainability-oriented policies, digital literacy, appropriate governance frameworks, and investment in accessible digital infrastructure. It contributes a conceptual perspective on how AI can serve not merely as a technological tool but as an enabling mechanism for interpreting complex sustainability relationships and guiding transformative action towards the SDGs beyond 2030.

Title: Climate-Related Migration, WASH Conditions and Mental Health in Nairobi's Informal Settlements: A Desktop Review and Research Agenda for Mathare, Nairobi, Kenya
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Authors: Ntikabura, Asa Haki; Kalumbi, Zaina Divine
Keywords: climate migration, informal settlements, mental health, WASH, human security
Abstract_Text: Climate stress, rural-to-urban migration and poor water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) conditions are each linked to psychological distress, but they are rarely studied together. This desktop review synthesises peer-reviewed and institutional evidence on how these pressures converge for migrants in Mathare, one of Nairobi's oldest informal settlements. Kenya's drought frequency has risen, and an estimated 318,000 people were internally displaced in 2022, mostly by drought; most movement is rural-to-urban, led by young adults. More than 60 percent of Nairobi's residents live in informal settlements, where Mathare studies report shared toilets serving from 17 to over 230 people, depending on site and year, alongside documented sanitation-related violence against women. A systematic review of migration and mental health in low- and middle-income countries finds the evidence base dominated by cross-sectional designs and unvalidated instruments, limiting causal claims. Kenyan and East African studies link water insecurity and inadequate sanitation to anxiety, shame and distress, and Nairobi research on menstrual poverty documents embarrassment, stigma and reduced school participation among adolescent girls. The review identifies five gaps: no Mathare study applies validated mental-health instruments to migrants; migration status is not isolated in WASH-mental health research; longer-term psychosocial outcomes of menstrual poverty remain unexamined; internal migrant youth are not analysed as a distinct group; and designs remain largely cross-sectional. These gaps motivate Migration Lens, a youth-led mixed-methods project combining Swahili-validated screening tools, qualitative interviews, citizen science, podcasting and policy engagement through existing mechanisms such as settlement-upgrading programmes. The review argues that climate adaptation and human security in informal settlements require evidence that links environmental, sanitary and psychosocial conditions.

Title: Digital farmer registration and e-vouchers for sustainable agriculture: Lessons from Kenya for post-2030 development goals
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development
Keywords: Digital Governance, Sustainability Analytics, Transformation of Food Systems, Accountability, Responsible Innovation
Abstract_Text:
ABSTRACT
Objective: This paper looks at lessons learned from Kenya regarding digital farmer registration and e-voucher systems through its National Fertilizer Subsidy Programme and how digital public infrastructure improves the delivery of agricultural services, accountability of institutions and sustainability of the food system. It considers the role of digitalization in achieving SDG 2 “Zero Hunger”.
Methodology: This paper is based on practice-driven evidence from programme implementation and monitoring and evaluation at the Kenyan Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development. Farmer registration, data cleansing, verification of beneficiaries, use of electronic vouchers, and monitoring of fertilizer distribution are some aspects considered in the analysis. Implementation opportunities, institutional barriers, and lessons learned for improvement in digital agricultural governance are considered.
Results: Implementation experience underscores the benefits of integrated farmer databases and electronic vouchers for better beneficiary identification, traceability, and monitoring of subsidized fertilizer distribution. In addition, some implementation challenges, such as keeping proper records for farmers, lack of interoperability between various systems, issues of data quality, accountability among delivery partners, and equal access by farmers with poor digital connectivity or literacy skills are noted. Digital systems form an essential basis for informed decision-making; however, their role in sustainable governance requires robust governance, reliable data, and climate-smart agriculture extension services.
Conclusion: The Kenyan example highlights the possibilities inherent in digital agriculture systems in achieving the goals of SDG 2 while ensuring sustainable use of resources according to SDG 12 and climate change activities according to SDG 13. In the future, after 2030 and beyond, states must marry inclusive digital platforms with sound data protection, accountability mechanisms, collaboration and sustainability indicators. These experiences provide useful lessons for developing inclusive and farmer-friendly agricultural development systems in the post-2030 agenda.

Title: Transitioning towards regenerative agricultural systems in the Netherlands: lessons from the ReGeNL program
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Authors: Posthumus, Helena; Wauben, Noortje; Galama, Naomi; Besijn, Joost; van der Bij, Hillie; Gelao, Yuri; van Huizen, Ingrid
Keywords: regenerative agriculture, food system transition, farmer engagement
Abstract_Text:
Objective: The Dutch agricultural sector faces urgent challenges, including environmental pressures (soil degradation, biodiversity loss, water pollution, and greenhouse gas emissions) while farmers struggle (volatile prices, rising costs and public scrutiny over environmental impacts). Regenerative agriculture offers a solution to close nutrient cycles and reduce dependency on external inputs, aligning food production with soil health, nature restoration and profitability. ReGeNL, a national program, drives this transition by supporting up to 1,000 Dutch farmers in adopting regenerative business models and practices.
Methods: ReGeNL supports farmers in developing their business models to regenerative principles in nine dimensions: soil health, crops, animals, air and water, biodiversity, footprint, economics, social wellbeing, and healthy diets. ReGeNL unites 54+ partners, including knowledge institutions, farmer networks, businesses, and financial organizations, to share expertise and resources. Since late 2025, 200+ farmers have joined, with about 150 farmers completing onboarding and business development plans. Based on initial data and documents, insights have been collected about motivations, objectives but also constraints that farmers face.
Key results: Many farmers are willing to adopt regenerative practices, motivated by economic savings, environmental concerns, or interest in knowledge and skill development. All farmers are looking for strategies to make their farming businesses futureproof for next generations. The business development plans, however, remain cautious. When farmers have access to additional funding to cover financial risks, they are encouraged to make bolder changes. But their willingness to change also depends on their licenses, off-taker contracts, environmental laws, land ownership and practical knowledge on regenerative practices.
Conclusions: Dutch farmers adapt to evolving market and societal demands. However, multiple actors define the “room of manoeuvre” farmers have to experiment and adapt their farm business that align with both economic viability and environmental goals. Multi-stakeholder collaboration across value chains and public sectors is essential to enable regenerative transitions.

Title: Sustainable Destination Governance in Cambridge, UK: Small Business Participation, Local Power and Institutional Influence
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Organisations: Lemos Pimenta, Dr. Ricardo | Anglia Ruskin University
Keywords: collaborative governance, multi-level governance, stakeholder co-creation, institutional arrangements, accountability
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study examines how small businesses are positioned within sustainable destination governance and whether their recognised contribution to local distinctiveness, everyday vitality and visitor experience is translated into meaningful institutional influence. Using Cambridge, UK, as a theoretically revealing context, the paper addresses a wider governance problem relevant to sustainable development beyond 2030: the gap between stakeholder participation and substantive influence.
Methods: The study adopts a qualitative, interpretive and review-based approach, combining a critical literature review with secondary academic and documentary material. The analysis integrates sustainable tourism governance, destination management organisations, stakeholder participation, local power, local development and small-business embeddedness.
Key results: The findings suggest that small businesses are widely acknowledged as important to place experience and local vitality, yet are less securely positioned within the institutional arrangements through which destination priorities are defined. Their participation appears more frequently advisory than decision-shaping. The analysis therefore distinguishes between stakeholder recognition, voice and institutional influence, and introduces developmental responsiveness as an important dimension of governance quality.
Conclusions: The paper argues that sustainable destination governance should not be assessed simply by whether stakeholders are present or consulted. More inclusive and effective governance requires institutional arrangements capable of translating locally embedded knowledge into meaningful influence. This has wider relevance for post-2030 sustainability agendas, particularly in relation to collaborative governance, multi-stakeholder partnerships and the design of more accountable local decision-making systems.

Title: Youth-Led Carbon Stewardship for Climate Change Mitigation and a Just Transition: Evidence from a School-Based Intervention in Urban Bangladesh
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Deb, Biplob Kumer; Rozario, Hemanto Pius; Muhaimen, Al; Rayat Taj, Tahsin; Bin Nasir, Munif
Keywords: Climate Change, Youth Stewardship, Mitigation, Carbon Footprint
Abstract_Text: Climate change mitigation and the transition toward net-zero emissions require inclusive, behavior-oriented approaches that empower young people to adopt sustainable practices. This study examines the potential of school-based carbon stewardship to strengthen youth participation in climate mitigation and support an equitable transition toward a low-carbon future. A mixed-methods approach was employed among 487 students in Grades 9–12 from six educational institutions in Dhaka, Bangladesh. The intervention comprised interactive workshops, facilitated discussions, educational resources, and videos focusing on carbon footprints, greenhouse gas emissions, carbon footprint calculation, and practical emission reduction strategies. Students were encouraged to develop carbon reduction models at individual, household, and institutional levels. Quantitative responses and qualitative feedback were analyzed to assess carbon literacy, awareness of everyday emission sources, reported reduction practices, and perceptions of the model’s potential to promote inclusive climate action. Findings revealed that 86% of respondents encountered the concepts of carbon footprints and their calculation for the first time through the intervention, while 78% recognized their previously unacknowledged contributions to carbon emissions. Furthermore, 82% believed the framework could help reduce their carbon footprints. At the household level, 77% reported at least a 10% reduction in their family’s carbon footprint, while 92% reported a 16% reduction in school carbon footprints. Additionally, 84% perceived school-based initiatives as effective in encouraging greater youth participation, and 85% of teachers and administrators expressed appreciation for the model. These findings suggest that school-based carbon stewardship may offer a promising and potentially replicable framework for connecting climate education with individual and collective mitigation practices. By fostering awareness, behavioral responsibility, and institutional engagement, the approach could support broader net-zero ambitions and more inclusive climate participation. However, independently verified emission measurements and longitudinal assessments are necessary to establish the magnitude, attribution, and durability of the reported reductions.

Title: The Contemporary Socio-Behavioural Dynamics of Health and Well-being in Enhancing Women's Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience in Zimbabwe
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Climate Change, Behavioural Dynamics, Food Security, Mitigation, Adaptation
Abstract_Text:
Introduction:
The world is grappling with climate-related challenges that pose a serious threat to agricultural development. Food security is one of the most pressing issues worldwide. Zimbabwe’s economy is agriculture-based, and it is affected by factors such as droughts, rising temperatures, cyclones, and extreme weather conditions. The factors that drive behavioural changes that enhance individual and community capacity to adapt to and mitigate the effects of climate change stem from agricultural activities through which health and well-being shape women's capacity to adapt, cope, and build resilience in the face of climatic disruptions.
Research problem:
Communities in Zimbabwe are vulnerable due to the impact of climate change. There are so many strategies to consider when mitigating climate change. If climate change is not given serious attention, communities might face serious challenges to food security. It is prudent for this study to examine strategies to mitigate and adapt to climate change.
Objective:
To investigate the socio-behavioural factors influencing health and well-being and their role in enhancing women's climate change adaptation and resilience.
Methodology:
The study employed a descriptive case study of selected communities successfully implementing adaptation strategies to climate change. The study gathered primary data through an interview guide and focus group discussions. Data were collected from captive farmers and indigenous leaders through convenience and purposive sampling. Thematic analysis was used to analyze data.
Results/Findings:
The anticipated findings are expected to contribute to theoretical advancements in climate adaptation and resilience scholarship by integrating health, well-being, and socio-behavioural perspectives into existing climate resilience frameworks.
Recommendations:
The research will inform the design of gender-responsive climate policies, public health interventions, and community-based adaptation strategies that strengthen women's resilience while advancing sustainable development, social justice, and inclusive climate governance.

Title: Field Study of Development and Agronomic Evaluation of a Fortified Blended Organic Fertilizer from Municipal Waste Resources for Maize Production in Malaw
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Valaro, Arnold; Nalivata, Patson; Njolomole, Joyce; Khudze, Sarah
Keywords: : fortified blended fertilizer, waste valorisation, circular agriculture, soil fertility, food security
Abstract_Text: Malawi’s agricultural sector faces a dual challenge: smallholder farmers cannot afford imported synthetic fertilizers, while urban centres struggle with mounting organic waste. This field study developed and evaluated a low-cost fortified blended fertilizer (FBF) produced from locally available waste streams sanitized sewage sludge, wood ash, agricultural lime, and processed human urine supplemented with small amounts of commercial NPK and urea. A randomized complete block design with three replications was established at two contrasting sites in Malawi (Chitipa and Zomba) during the 2024-2025 cropping season. Three treatments were compared: T1 (unfertilized control), T2 (FBF basal plus top-dressing), and T3 (standard inorganic fertilizer at 100 kg/ha NPK + 50 kg/ha urea). Post-application soil analysis showed that FBF substantially raised nutrient levels (N: 308-359 mg/kg; P: 432-503 mg/kg; K: 988-1150 mg/kg), with a composite fertility index of 3397–3953 mg/kg. Maize grown with FBF showed vigorous growth without deficiency or toxicity symptoms, producing an average yield of 3.2 t/ha a 78% improvement over the control (1.8 t/ha) and 82% of the yield obtained with conventional inorganic fertilizer (4.0 t/ha). Soil pH remained slightly acidic (5.7-6.1), and electrical conductivity was elevated. These findings suggest that waste-derived fortified fertilizers offer a viable, sustainable, and affordable alternative to imported synthetic inputs, supporting circular economy principles and improving food security in Malawi.

Title: Environmental Determinants and Forecasting of Paediatric Emergency Department Visits
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: System perspective for addressing one health nexus within ecological ceilings
Authors: Ghazanfar, Syed; Osama, Muhammad; Jamshaid, Anila; Ayub, Rakhshanda; Fahim, Ammad
Keywords: ambient temperature, paeds emergency department, meteorological exposure, distributed lag non-linear model, time-series forecasting
Abstract_Text: Climate change challenges healthcare systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where resources are constrained and capacity to anticipate climate-related health risks is limited. Understanding environmental influences on healthcare demand can support climate adaptation and strengthen health-system resilience. This study examined the association between ambient temperature and paediatric emergency department (ED) utilization and evaluated meteorological data for short-term demand forecasting in Karachi, Pakistan. We analysed 765,249 paediatric ED visits recorded at Indus Hospital and Health Network between 2016 and 2025. Pearson correlations assessed associations between meteorological variables and daily attendance across lags of 0–3 days. A quasi-Poisson distributed lag nonlinear model examined nonlinear and delayed temperature associations. SARIMA, SARIMAX, XGBoost, and LightGBM models were evaluated on a temporally held-out test period. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) quantified predictor contributions. Temperature showed weak linear correlations with daily ED attendance across lags 0–3 days (r = 0.10, 0.10, 0.09, and 0.09, respectively). However, nonlinear modelling identified a minimum-risk temperature of 13.6°C, with a cumulative relative risk of 0.687 (95% CI 0.540–0.875) relative to the 28.3°C reference temperature. The highest cumulative relative risk was 1.099. LightGBM achieved the best forecasting performance (RMSE 34.85, MAE 21.15, MAPE 8.06%, R² = 0.602). Recent attendance patterns were the strongest predictors, particularly the seven-day rolling mean and visits one and two days earlier, while meteorological variables provided additional predictive information. These findings demonstrate that weak linear correlations can obscure nonlinear temperature-associated patterns in paediatric emergency care. Integrating environmental monitoring with routine hospital attendance data could improve demand anticipation, staffing, and resource allocation. This approach supports climate-resilient healthcare planning and contributes to the ambitions of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3 (Good Health and Well-being), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action). Locally generated evidence and data-driven forecasting can help translate sustainability commitments into practical healthcare preparedness in resource-constrained urban settings.

Title: Advances in integrated assessment modeling for decarbonization pathways: reflections on an EU-China project, PART 1
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Organisations: Prell, Dr. Christina | Cultural Geography, Faculty of Spatial Sciences, University of Groningen
Keywords: IAMs, decarbonization, EU-China, socio-environmental impacts, stakeholder participation
Abstract_Text:
PANTHEON is 4 year international research project funded in 2024 by the EU Horizon Europe programme and the Chinese Ministry of Science and Technology. The project aims to develop an integrated assessment modelling framework and decarbonisation roadmaps for the EU and China, combining technological, regulatory, social, health and environmental dimensions within an overarching, participatory stakeholder approach. Working with a heterogeneous range of stakeholders and experts, PANTHEON combines technical and modeling expertise from both regions to explore alternative pathways toward carbon neutrality, and in doing so, assess their wider socio-economic and environmental impacts.
This panel uses recent findings from across the PANTHEON consortium to highlight work addressing technological change, emissions, socio-economic impacts, policy architectures, stakeholder perspectives and participatory modelling. As such, one aim of the panel is to present recent methodological and empirical advances from PANTHEON. A second aim, however, is to reflect on challenges that have arisen in our project, for example, how to include diverse forms of knowledge and values from our mapped stakeholders with the goals of EU and China policy actors; the trade-offs between model complexity and transparency; and the challenges of incorporating knowledge across different scales. We invite audience members to join our panel participants for what we hope will be a lively discussion on the challenges and trade-offs of participatory integrated assessment models for decarbonization pathways.
The Paris Agreement has established nationally determined contributions (NDCs) as the cornerstone of global climate mitigation, yet carbon sequestration and cooling (CSC) responses during successive phases of NDC implementation remain poorly constrained. Land-use policies are important to national commitments; however, their implementation rarely accounts for spatial heterogeneity in carbon sequestration potential. Here, using satellite observations combined with model simulations, we assess global CSC dynamics and land-use change-induced carbon emissions (ELUC) over the period 2010–2024 and evaluate an optimized land-use allocation strategy that prioritizes carbon sequestration potential. We find that the global area characterized by CSC increased across the first two NDC phases, reaching 17.8% in 2020–2024 relative to 2010–2015. Although global ELUC remained a net carbon source during 2010–2024, emissions declined at an average rate of 0.04 PgC yr⁻¹. Moreover, the optimized land-use allocation strategy enhances mitigation efficiency while maintaining a similar global CSC proportion, delivering an additional −0.12 ± 0.29 °C of avoided warming by 2100, with benefits concentrated in low- and middle-income countries. Our results highlight the importance of post–Paris Agreement mitigation efforts and the integration of spatially optimized land-use strategies into future NDCs to better align climate ambition with effective implementation.
Technological development and diffusion of cleaner technologies are
fundamental to achieving decarbonisation and mitigating the impacts of
climate change. This work presents an integrated modelling approach to assess technologies’ decarbonization contribution and anticipates economic, social and
environmental outcomes of this dynamic and complex process. The main
objective is threefold: i) to examine the evolution of a set of
technological indicators from 1990 to 2023. Using counterfactual
scenarios, we estimate the potential effects on global emissions if developing
economies were to operate with the technology’s capabilities of more advanced
economies; ii) to understand the socioeconomic and environmental implications of decarbonization efforts across a range of sectors; iii) to evaluate the socioeconomic and environmental impacts of changes in the lifestyles of EU and Chinese households towards a low-carbon economy, with an in-depth analysis of household characteristics (gender, income). To address this, we integrate dynamic input-output and Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) approaches, using a Multi-Regional Input-Output model (MRIO) with high country and sector detail, with extensions on i) the final demand side for households with differing income groups and gender; ii) the production side via employment data on gender, sector and occupation; and iii) environmentally, via regional data on local to global impacts. The adoption of new technologies is simulated, and we evaluate the long-term effects in a context of economic growth as well as the implications of technological changes.
