Title: The Architecture of Just Resilience: Navigating the Intersections of Climate Disruption, Economic Vulnerability, and Transformative Global Governance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Climate-Development Nexus, Just Transitions, Climate Justice, Real Resilience, Systems Change, Structural Equity, Community Governance
Abstract_Text:
The dual crises of accelerating climate disruption and deepening economic inequality are not separate, parallel problems; they are fundamentally entangled. For decades, global policy has treated climate action and human development as isolated agendas on a checklist. This siloes approach has yielded top-down, technocratic adjustments—such as localized engineering fixes or carbon offset markets—that consistently fail because they ignore the political and economic systems driving vulnerability in the first place. This paper provides a comprehensive evaluation of the climate change–development nexus, arguing that we cannot build a physically resilient world on a foundation of structural injustice.
Drawing on the intersections of political ecology and development economics, we analyze how climate shocks act as a severe crisis multiplier. These disruptions follow historical fault lines, disproportionately harming marginalized communities across both the Global South and North who possess the least resources to adapt but bear the heaviest burdens of historical carbon debts. We contend that true, lasting resilience requires moving far beyond incremental survival strategies. Instead, a dual framework of climate justice and equitable development must be operationalized to actively dismantle systemic exclusion, unfair resource distribution, and top-down institutional mandates.
By evaluating emerging pathways—specifically community-led adaptation metrics, just energy transitions, and regenerative economic models—this paper outlines actionable mechanisms to align urgent decarbonization targets with foundational human rights and poverty alleviation. Ultimately, we demonstrate that a sustainable planet is entirely impossible without an equitable society. Successfully navigating this nexus demands a profound transformation in global governance, shifting power and funding away from distant boardrooms and handing them directly to frontline communities to guarantee procedural, distributional, and recognitional justice.

Title: From passion of the youth to progress in societies: Lessons and critical reflections on youth participation, climate governance and Sustainable Development in Kenya
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Dinda, Gabriel; Turhan, Ethemcan; Adaawen, Stephen; Zuidema, Chris
Keywords: Youth participation, Climate governance, Kenya, Sustainable Development Goals, Tokenism, Resource mobilisation.
Abstract_Text: Kenya’s demographic structure has been described as a “youth quake”, with roughly a third of the population aged between 18 and 35. Article 10 of the Constitution of Kenya requires public participation in governance and young Kenyans have used that opening to press into sustainable development and climate policy at local, national and international levels. Kenya’s climate commitments make this participation consequential. Under its Second Nationally Determined Contribution (NDCs), submitted in April 2025, Kenya undertakes to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 35% by 2035 relative to a business-as-usual scenario, superseding the 32% by 2030 target of the updated first NDC. Meeting a commitment of this scale requiresall hands-on decksince economic losses from weather and climate-related disasters are estimated at 3–5% of GDP annually. This chapter asks how youth participation in Kenyan climate governance is enabled and constrained and what that reveals about the relationship between climate action and the wider development agenda. Drawing on documentary analysis of scholarly, policy, civil-society and media sources published between 2020 and 2025, and on two illustrative cases, the Ondiri Wetland Botanical Garden in Kiambu County and the One Million Trees for Kilifi project, we construct a critical narrative synthesis of resource mobilisation, policy engagement and public outreach. We argue that constraints on youth climate participation are not specific to sectors but compound. Deficits in climate education, employment, institutional inclusion and regional equity reinforce one another and jointly suppress the capacity for climate action. We name this the compound-deficit model and use it to show why interventions framed around a single Sustainable Development Goal reliably underperform.

Title: Does board sustainability expertise make governance work? Environmental, social, and governance disclosure in Saudi Arabia's energy sector
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Mousa, Hassan; Sharawi, Hussam; AlQurashi, Shatha
Organisations: Mousa, Dr. Hassan | Jeddah International College
Keywords: SDG implementation, corporate governance, sustainability reporting, board expertise, Saudi Arabia
Abstract_Text:
Objective:Energy companies in resource-dependent economies are pivotal to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet it remains unclear which board mechanisms produce credible environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure rather than symbolic reporting. This study examines how board size, independence, gender diversity, ESG committees, and government ownership affect ESG disclosure quality in Saudi Arabia's listed energy sector under Vision 2030. It also tests whether board ESG expertise is the boundary condition that determines when these governance structures become effective.
Methods:Grounded in stakeholder, agency, and resource dependence theories, a cross-sectional survey collected primary data from 378 finance directors, chief sustainability officers, board members, and senior executives across the population of energy companies listed on the Saudi Exchange. Partial least squares structural equation modeling estimates direct and moderating effects, controlling for firm size, profitability, leverage, age, ownership concentration, and international exposure. Procedural and statistical remedies address common method bias.
Key results: Hypotheses predict that ESG committees and gender diversity improve disclosure quality, while larger boards reduce it through coordination costs. Board ESG expertise is expected to amplify the effects of independence, diversity, and committees and to offset the costs of board size, indicating that board capability, not composition alone, drives disclosure quality.
Conclusions:Governance reforms that mandate board structures without building sustainability competence risk producing compliance-driven rather than substantive disclosure. The study offers regulators and energy companies evidence for linking board appointment, training and committee design to disclosure outcomes. Beyond 2030, credible disclosure by hydrocarbon producers is a precondition for tracking progress on clean energy, responsible production, climate action and strong institutions (SDGs 7, 12, 13 and 16) and for holding resource-dependent economies accountable in post-2030 sustainability frameworks. Lessons extend to other Gulf and emerging energy economies.

Title: Towards Decolonizing Medicine and Healthcare: The Place of African Health and Healing Traditions
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Organisations: Nwaka, Prof. Geoffrey | Abia State University, Uturu
Keywords: Traditional medicine, Africa, medical pluralism, comparative medicine
Abstract_Text:
Global health science today needs to integrate the health and healing traditions of local communities in Africa. To achieve the ideal of Universal Health Coverage in Africa, we need to promote comparative medicine, and synergy between the practice of traditional and modern medicine.
Traditional medicine and therapeutic techniques have a long history of treating a wide range of human and animal health conditions in Africa. . This rich body of knowledge has been undervalued because of the dominance of Eurocentric mindsets and practices. But current research confirms that many of today’s medicines are derived from tropical African medicinal plants, and that traditional medicine can provide a lead to scientific breakthrough in modern medicine and drug discovery. With colonialism, traditional medicine has been discredited because it does not always appear to conform with the scientific principles of modern medicine, least of all the spiritual and cultural aspects of healing that sometimes involve divination and traditional rituals. Many doctors, scientists and government officials distrust traditional medicine, and hesitate to provide the regulatory and legislative framework for integrating traditional medicine into the national healthcare system until it is possible to validate, codify and standardize its practice to ensure greater safety and efficacy. Unfortunately, modern medicine, with all its obvious merits, is not readily accessible and affordable to a large percentage of the populations, especially in the rural areas; and even in cities, most people combine traditional and modern medicines, especially in response to epidemics and ailments like HIV/AIDS EBOLA, insanity, and COVID19, for which orthodox medicine has not provided ready cure. We argue that global health science today needs to integrate the healing traditions and innovations of local communities in Africa. But the medical pluralism and synergy we desire need to be regulated in order to avoid the indiscriminate mixture of traditional and modern medicine.

Title: Gender and Climate change mitigation in transport: A Just transition Perspective on Policy and Practice in India
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Baruah, Nirmali; Barua, Anamika; Mallikarjuna, C.
Keywords: Climate Mitigation, Policy, Gender, Transport, Just transition
Abstract_Text:
Reducing carbon dioxide emissions is increasingly urgent in the context of climate change, with the transport sector being a major contributor to greenhouse gas emissions. However, mitigating transport emissions is complex and challenging, involving various interests and complexities such as mobility, access, gender, age among others particularly in emerging economies facing dual challenges of economic growth and climate change impacts. Although transport systems are essential for enabling mobility and access to opportunities, it remains unevenly distributed across gender, raising concerns about equity in climate mitigation efforts. This complexity demands holistic policies that reduce emissions while ensuring equitable mobility access and addressing diverse stakeholders' needs.
Focusing on India as a key emerging economy in the Global South, this paper, therefore, critically examines how gender is incorporated within transport-related climate mitigation policies. Employing a qualitative approach from a just transition lens- analyzing existing 35 policy documents of related Ministries of India and by conducting 20 interviews with government officials and civil society, the study aims to analyze the national level policies and challenges in addressing the gender concerns and identifying practical solutions.
The findings reveal a lack of meaningful gender inclusive participation from pre-policy phase onward, limiting integration of women’s experiences, mobility needs, and perspectives into policy formulation and implementation. Integration of gender perspectives into transport decarbonization is largely missing from transport policy landscape. Furthermore, assumptions that low-carbon transitions benefits are equally distributed risk overlooking structural barriers women face in accessing mobility or participating in climate action. The paper argues that without embedding gender-sensitive perspectives, climate mitigation policies may inadvertently reproduce structural inequities, underscoring the need for more inclusive and justice-oriented policy frameworks.

Title: Building Climate-Resilient Livelihoods Beyond 2030: Evidence from Nigeria’s Great Green Wall Initiative
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Balogun, Dr. Cecy Edijala | University of Johannesburg, Centre on the Study of Race, Gender and Class
Keywords: Sustainable interventions, Climate action, Great Green Wall Initiatives, Climate resilience, Rural adaptation
Abstract_Text: Climate change intensifies livelihood vulnerability across rural communities in Nigeria, undermining resilience and progress towards sustainable development, especially in the northern states where desert encroachment and land degradation are evident. Although adaptation often prioritises environmental restoration, livelihood-centred interventions are equally important for strengthening households’ capacity to withstand climate shocks. This study examines how livelihood interventions implemented under Nigeria’s Great Green Wall initiative improve livelihood capitals and identifies the interventions most capable of supporting Sustainable Development Goal achievement by and beyond 2030. Primary survey data were collected from 262 beneficiaries and non-beneficiaries in Gombe, Kebbi and Sokoto States in Northern Nigeria. Analysed interventions included capacity-building programmes, community development initiatives, household support and distributed starter packs to enhance livelihood diversification in farm and non-farm livelihood activities. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to assess changes in livelihood capitals and determine which interventions produced the strongest improvements to guide interventions beyond 2030. Results show an overall improvement in respondents’ livelihood capitals, with significant changes in physical and human capital. Among capacity-building interventions, poultry and goat rearing, lubricant production and perfume making significantly improved livelihood capital. Community interventions including solar street lighting, water tanks and food seedling orchards also contributed to improvement. Household-targeted support, particularly energy-efficient cookstoves, gas cylinders and fruit seedlings, further strengthened livelihood capitals. Starter packs, including tailoring machines and kits, veterinary drugs, and soap and lubricant-making kits, similarly generated significant gains. This evidence demonstrates that climate adaptation is more sustainable when ecological restoration is integrated with locally relevant livelihood support. The study concludes that targeted livelihood interventions can reduce vulnerability, expand productive opportunities and reinforce the human, social and material foundations of resilience. Prioritising scalable, inclusive and context-sensitive interventions within climate programmes can accelerate progress towards climate action, poverty reduction, clean energy and resilient communities by 2030 and beyond.

Title: Beyond Sustainable Development Goal 6: Scaling Inclusive Water Innovations for Climate-Resilient Communities in Sub-Saharan Africa
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Balogun, Dr. Cecy Edijala | University of Johannesburg, Centre on the Study of Race, Gender and Class
Keywords: Climate resilient water innovations, Household water security, Inclusive water access, fog harvesting direct water reuse
Abstract_Text: Achieving universal and equitable access to safe drinking water remains a major sustainable development challenge in sub-Saharan Africa as climate change, population growth, urbanisation, pollution and infrastructure deficits intensify household water insecurity. This paper examines progress towards Sustainable Development Goal 6 and identifies climate-resilient water innovations capable of accelerating inclusive water access by 2030 and sustaining progress beyond the current framework. Specifically, it compares household access to improved drinking water in Ethiopia, Kenya, Namibia, Nigeria and South Africa and assesses innovative responses to persistent water scarcity. The study employs descriptive and comparative case-study designs, drawing on secondary data from the World Bank and the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme for 2013–2022, supplemented by institutional reports and academic literature on water innovations. Indicators include access to basic drinking water, water availability on premises and when needed, freedom from contamination, and piped and non-piped provision across urban and rural areas. The findings reveal progress in basic water coverage but substantial inequalities in service quality and location. Namibia and South Africa record comparatively higher household access, including piped water, while Ethiopia, Kenya and Nigeria continue to experience limited on-premises provision and pronounced rural–urban disparities. Nigeria demonstrates particularly low piped-water access in both urban and rural areas. Fog harvesting, renewable-energy-powered desalination, community water kiosks and direct potable reuse offer viable pathways for diversifying water supplies and strengthening climate resilience. However, high costs, weak regulation, maintenance failures, uneven infrastructure and urban-centred implementation constrain their transformative potential. The paper concludes that progress beyond 2030 requires location-sensitive combinations of water technologies, public investment, quality regulation, community participation and deliberate rural inclusion. Scaling proven innovations while safeguarding affordability and water quality can advance the Sustainable Development Goals SDGs 6, 3, 5, 10, 11 and 13 and support a more equitable post-2030 sustainability agenda.

Title: Skills for the Green and Digital Transition: A Comparison of Major Labour Markets
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Organisations: UCAL, Prof. Meltem | Kadir Has University
Keywords: Green and digital transition; occupational skills; labour markets; artificial intelligence; comparative analysis.
Abstract_Text:
Renewable energy employment reached 16.6 million worldwide in 2024. China accounted for approximately 7.3 million jobs, compared with 1.8 million in the European Union, 1.4 million in Brazil, 1.3 million in India and 1.1 million in the United States (IRENA and ILO, 2026). This uneven distribution raises questions about how training priorities differ across labour markets.
This study proposes a comparative analysis of occupational skill requirements and employment structures, focusing on these five markets where comparable data are available. It asks which occupational groups combine green and digital skill requirements and how their employment shares differ across economies.
The analysis will use ESCO and O*NET occupational descriptions, the published correspondence between these systems, and employment statistics classified by ISCO. Selected occupations in renewable energy, manufacturing and technical services will be examined to identify shared skills and potential pathways between related occupations. Employment shares will indicate their relative importance in each market. Comparisons will use a common reference period and compatible levels of occupational aggregation.
The study will distinguish occupational requirements from workers’ actual skills. It will examine the limitations of applying European and US occupational descriptions to economies with different technologies, production practices and employment conditions. Alternative mappings will be tested to assess robustness.
The intended contribution is a transparent basis for identifying potential training priorities and informing AI-supported skills matching. Particular attention will be paid to which occupational relationships can be transferred across national contexts and which require local evidence.
This work is supported by the European Union’s Horizon Europe programme through the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Staff Exchanges project AI4SUSTAIN, under Grant Agreement No. 101296730.

Title: Student Perspectives on Environmental Pollution and Sustainability Priorities: Lessons from an International Educational Initiative
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Diédhiou, Idrissa; Alcalá Jáuregui, Jorge Alonso; Flavia Filippini, María; Cónsoli, Daniela; Venier, Matias; Martínez Carretero, Eduardo; Rojas Velázquez, Ángel...
Keywords: Sustainability education, Sustainable Development Goals, Environmental pollution, Student perceptions, International collaboration
Abstract_Text:
Objective:Understanding how university students perceive environmental challenges and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) is essential for strengthening sustainability education and identifying priorities beyond 2030. This study examined students’ perceptions of environmental pollution, SDG priorities, environmental data management, and preferred learning approaches within an international educational initiative.
Methods:A virtual workshop on environmental pollution data management was organized in June 2025 through collaboration among universities in Costa Rica, Mexico, and Argentina. A structured, anonymous online questionnaire was administered to 155 undergraduate and postgraduate students from more than 15 countries. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics to identify priorities related to the SDGs, environmental information systems, professional training, and educational strategies.
Results:Responsible consumption and production (SDG 12, 15%) and climate action (SDG 13, 11%) emerged as leading sustainability priorities. Students identified agricultural production systems (21%), climate change (17%), and environmental engineering technologies (14%) as important professional training areas. Environmental impact assessment (17%) was the most frequently highlighted application of pollution data management. Students also expressed interest in remediation technologies (21%) and environmental impact assessment (19%) as specialized educational topics. Collaborative teamwork (11%) and statistical and digital tools (8% each) featured among preferred learning approaches.
Conclusions:The findings identify student-defined priorities for strengthening practice-oriented sustainability education. International university collaboration provides a promising framework for integrating environmental data literacy, applied learning, and interdisciplinary perspectives. These insights can inform educational approaches that support SDG implementation and contribute to a more inclusive sustainability agenda beyond 2030.

Title: Soil carbon and nutrient cycling in cocoa rehabilitation scheme in low latitude environment
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Adu Adjei, Francis; Logah, Vincent; Abisah, Joshua
Organisations: Ghana Cocobod/ Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology
Keywords: Cocoa rehabilitation; particulate organic carbon; mineral-associated organic carbon; carbon sequestration; soil fertility
Abstract_Text:
Cocoa (Theobroma cacao L.) production is vital to the economies of many tropical countries but faces persistent challenges, including long-term soil fertility decline and swollen shoot virus disease. These challenges are usually addressed through complete removal of infected trees and replanting with hybrid cocoa varieties and shade trees, often with minimal soil management. Although rehabilitation is expected to alter litter and root inputs that stabilise soil organic carbon (SOC) and consequently nutrient cycling, its impact in low-latitude environments remains poorly quantified.
Consequently, this exploratory paired-plot study in the Bia West District of Ghana compared rehabilitated and non-rehabilitated farms at fixed depths of 0–15, 15–30, and 30–45 cm. In both farms, we sampled four 20 m × 20 m sub-plots and evaluated partitioning of bulk or total SOC into mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) and particulate organic carbon (POC) pools. We also assessed the extent to which rehabilitation influences soil nutrient stocks.
At 0–15 cm, bulk SOC and nitrogen stocks were respectively 19% (p<0.01; 42.44 Mg C ha−1) and 15% (p=0.05) greater in rehabilitated plots. Cumulative total SOC stock to 45 cm, determined by the equivalent soil mass (ESM) approach, was 82.89 Mg C ha−1 in rehabilitated plots, compared with 83.31 Mg C ha−1 calculated through the fixed-depth method. At 0–15 cm, MAOC increased by 17% (p=0.01) in the rehabilitated farm, suggesting a shift towards long-term carbon stabilisation in topsoil, but this effect appeared compounded by greater clay content. At 15–30 cm, the rehabilitated farm exhibited a significant decrease of 33.3% in POC (p=0.02) relative to the non-rehabilitated farm type. Topsoil available phosphorus (p=0.03) and effective cation exchange capacity (p=0.001) increased significantly under rehabilitation. Although the study was limited to one site, it provides valuable information on carbon and nutrient cycling in cocoa rehabilitation schemes.

Title: A Waqf Framework for Financing Recurrent Costs of Primary Healthcare During Donor Transition in Nigeria
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Muhammad, Aishatu Usman; Yusoff, Murni; Mohammed, Nura
Organisations: Muhammad, Dr. Aishatu Usman | Gombe State University
Keywords: waqf, donor transition, primary healthcare, Nigeria
Abstract_Text:
The primary healthcare system in Nigeria depends mostly on funding from foreign donors. As uncertainty about donor support continues, it becomes difficult to pay staff salaries, medicines, supplies, utilities, and general routine maintenance. Funding capital projects can improve health facilities, but to keep them running requires regular and sustainable funding. This paper examines how waqf (Islamic endowment) could help cover these recurrent costs during and after donor transition.
Waqf could help meet these costs because the endowed asset is kept intact while the income it generates provides continued funding instead of one-off grants. A recent study in Gombe State found that waqf institutions build health facilities, equip clinics, and support staff. However, reliance on one-off donations, poor asset management, and limited coordination with the government make it difficult to keep paying salaries and buying supplies (Muhammad et al., 2025). Building from this problem, the paper examines how income from waqf could be used to pay for the regular costs of running primary healthcare facilities.
Using a conceptual analysis and policy review, the paper groups the recurrent costs of primary healthcare and examines how income from property, cash, and productive waqf could help cover them. The proposed framework has three parts, which include clear rules on which regular costs the waqf income will cover, professional management with open financial reporting, and formal arrangements with the state authorities to include waqf funding in health budgets and plans.
The paper argues that waqf can provide additional funding alongside government and donor support. It suggests practical steps that policymakers and waqf institutions can take to help primary healthcare services run beyond 20230.

Title: Beyond licence renewal: Eye-care seeking among commercial drivers in Cape Coast, Ghana, and implications for sustainable development
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Agyare, Eunice; Boadi-Kusi, Samuel Bert; Morny, Enyam; Ampiah, Emmanuel Ekow
Organisations: Ampiah, Dr. Emmanuel Ekow | University of Cape Coast
Keywords: governance, occupational eye health, commercial drivers, eye-care seeking, sustainable development
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
To distinguish licensing-related from non-licensing eye-care attendance among commercial drivers in Cape Coast, Ghana, and examine associated occupational and health-belief factors, with implications for licensing governance and the integration of eye care into sustainable development.
Methods:
An analytical cross-sectional study recruited 239 male commercial drivers aged 25–60 years through convenience sampling at five purposively selected transport stations. A structured questionnaire assessed examination history, attendance reasons, occupational characteristics, ocular symptoms and Health Belief Model constructs. Presenting visual acuity was measured. Logistic regression examined factors associated with self-reported eye examination within the preceding 24 months.
Key results:
Overall, 130 drivers (54.4%) reported a recent eye examination. Of these, 100 (76.9%) attended solely for licence renewal; 30 (12.6% of the full sample) attended for routine checks, eye pain or visual problems. Ocular symptoms were reported by 62.8%, while 99.2% had presenting visual acuity of 6/12 or better in the better eye. Auto-rickshaw drivers had lower adjusted odds of recent examination than taxi drivers (adjusted odds ratio 0.36; 95% confidence interval 0.15–0.89), although the overall regression model was not statistically significant. The overall Health Belief Model was also not significant. Exploratory analysis identified higher cues to action among non-licensing attenders.
Conclusions:
Recent eye-care attendance was predominantly licensing-related, highlighting the importance of distinguishing regulatory contact from attendance for other health-related reasons when interpreting service coverage. Licence-renewal encounters could provide entry points for comprehensive assessment, referral and follow-up. Linking licensing authorities, transport unions and eye-care providers offers a practical governance approach to integrating eye health into occupational health and transport systems, with potential relevance to worker well-being and sustainable development by and beyond 2030. Non-probability sampling and the cross-sectional design limit generalisability and causal interpretation.

Title: Digital eye strain and sustainable working lives: A biopsychosocial framework for occupational eye health
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Ampiah, Dr. Emmanuel Ekow | University of Cape Coast
Keywords: digital eye strain, occupational eye health, well-being, governance, sustainable development.
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
To synthesise evidence on digital eye strain within a biopsychosocial framework and identify implications for occupational eye health, worker well-being and sustainable development as workplaces become increasingly digital.
Methods:
A narrative review used structured searches of MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science and African Journals OnLine, supplemented by Google Scholar and citation searching. The latest search was conducted in June 2026. Primary studies and reviews were synthesised thematically across biological, psychological and social or occupational domains. Engel’s biopsychosocial model, Karasek’s job demand–control model and Andersen’s model of health-services use informed conceptual integration. No new meta-analysis was undertaken.
Key results:
Published meta-analytic evidence reported a pooled digital eye strain prevalence of 69% across 103 studies, although definitions, instruments and populations varied. Biological vulnerability included tear-film instability, incomplete blinking and accommodative or binocular-vision demands. Occupational factors included prolonged screen exposure, glare, workstation design, work–rest schedules and job demands. Psychological factors included perceived stress, cognitive load, anxiety and disturbed sleep. The proposed framework links these domains with symptom burden, functional consequences and access to eye care. Evidence was predominantly observational, limiting causal interpretation, and integrated occupational studies from African settings remained scarce.
Conclusions:
Sustainable digitalisation should incorporate workers’ ocular health into workplace design and occupational health provision. The framework supports evaluating coordinated approaches combining appropriate eye care, ergonomic improvements, scheduled breaks and attention to psychosocial working conditions. Employer-supported access and clear referral pathways could help embed eye health within healthier working lives. These proposals require prospective testing, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Positioning ocular health within the health and governance dimensions of sustainable development offers a research and policy agenda extending beyond individual screen-use advice.

Title: Deconstructing Epistemological and Eurocentric Biases in AI-driven Education: An Afrognosis Counter-perspective AI for Sustainable Development
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Trustworthy AI, information integrity, data autonomy, and sustainability impacts of AI
Authors: Kola-Olusanya, Anthony; ADEWALE, Peter; Braimoh, Victor
Organisations: ADEWALE, Dr. PETER | Osun State University
Keywords: Afrognosis, AI-driven education, Eurocentric biases, Culturally responsive AI, Sustainable Development, Decolonisation
Abstract_Text: This study aims to identify and critique the perceived dominant Eurocentric AI-driven educational frameworks and community leaders and develop an Afrongnosis (African culturally responsive) counter-perspective that centres on African Indigenous knowledge and cultural values for environmental education. A mixed methods approach was used for the study. Questionnaire and interviews were used to draw data from educators, learners and community leaders from diverse backgrounds and analyse AI-driven educational platforms and tools used in different regions and contexts. Eurocentric biases in AI-driven educational platforms revealing limitations in representing diverse cultural perspectives were identified. The result channelled dominant epistemologies and promote Afrognosis as a viable alternative. Culturally responsive AI frameworks for environmental education can empower African communities through inclusive knowledge representation. Therefore, to promote inclusive and equitable quality education in Africa, we recommend adopting an Afrognosis counter-perspective that centres African Indigenous knowledge and cultural values in the development of culturally responsive AI solutions for sustainable development education.

Title: Health as Foundation, Not Footnote: Evidence for Equitable, Self-Reliant Health Systems in Africa
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Authors: Ohanyido, Francis; Gushe, Seyilnan; Adoyi, Thomas; Ohanyido, Chioma
Organisations: Ohanyido, Dr. Francis | Africa Future of Health Commission
Keywords: Africa health systems, health financing, air pollution, health workforce, equity and post-2030 agenda
Abstract_Text:
Africa's health gaps are development challenges. Healthy people make sustainable development possible, yet health is still funded as an afterthought once growth arrives. The Africa Future of Health Commission follows the Theme 4 pathway, from systems to risks to solutions to equity, using the best available public evidence.
Foundations are thin. The WHO African Region has about 1.55 physicians, nurses and midwives per 1,000 people against a threshold of 4.45, and faces a projected shortfall of 6.1 million health workers by 2030 (WHO, 2022). Only South Africa sustained the Abuja target of 15% of government spending on health between 2014 and 2020 (WHO AFRO, 2023). Africa CDC reports that development assistance fell 70% between 2021 and 2025, while public health emergencies rose from 152 to 213 between 2022 and 2024 (Africa CDC, 2025).
Many risks sit outside the clinic. Air pollution contributed to an estimated 1.1 million deaths in Africa in 2019, 63% from household air pollution (Health Effects Institute, 2022). Africa imports about 99% of its vaccines, against a continental target of producing 60% by 2040 (Africa CDC; Gavi).
African experience shows what works. Rwanda's community-based insurance and community health workers took coverage from 43% in 2005 to 87% in 2020 (Exemplars in Global Health), as life expectancy rose from about 50 years in 2001 to about 70 in 2022 (Think Global Health). Nigeria's National Health Act (2014) ring-fenced at least 1% of federal revenue for primary care; in April 2026 the Senate passed an amendment to double that share.
The Commission's central argument is that equitable outcomes require health within energy, climate, urban, education and fiscal policy, not only health ministries. We offer this evidence to help shape a post-2030 agenda in which African institutions lead the solutions.

Title: Strengthening Climate Resilience Through Domestic Law: Assessing Zimbabwe's Path Toward Paris Agreement Alignment and SDG 13.
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Climate change, climate finance, Sustainable Development Goals
Abstract_Text: This paper investigates the legal and institutional readiness of Zimbabwe in implementing its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement and Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13). Specifically, it examines how the historical lack of a dedicated statutory framework has constrained cross-sectoral coordination, climate finance mobilisation, and domestic climate resilience in a highly vulnerable developing economy. Employing a doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, the research evaluates international climate change instruments including the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement alongside Zimbabwe’s national policy documents. It critically reviews contemporary legislative proposals, including the emerging Climate Change Management Bill, to identify institutional bottlenecks and enforcement gaps across public and private sectors. The study reveals that while Zimbabwe demonstrates international commitments through voluntary policy frameworks and set emission reduction targets, the absence of a binding, overarching legislative architecture creates severe implementation hurdles. Key obstacles include sector fragmentation across agriculture, mining, and finance ministries, inadequate Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) systems, and legal barriers to scaling up domestic and international climate finance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that existing policies insufficiently mandate public participation and climate justice for marginalised rural communities. Achieving SDG 13 in Zimbabwe requires a transition from voluntary policy guidelines to a binding domestic legislative framework anchored by a specialised Climate Change Act. Enacting strong legal mandates with clear enforcement mechanisms, transparent accountability frameworks, and decentralized institutional structures is critical for bridging the climate finance gap and ensuring legal alignment with international commitments. Looking beyond 2030, a formalised legal framework ensures long-term regulatory certainty, de-risking green investments in renewable energy and sustainable land-use practices. This institutionalised approach lays the groundwork for intergenerational climate justice and sustainable economic transformation well into the future, aligning national growth with a low-carbon, climate-resilient trajectory.

Title: Beyond Outcome Indicators: A Capabilities-Based Approach to Measuring Sustainable Development for the Post-2030 Agenda.
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Perdomo, Dr. Jhoner | Central University of Venezuela
Keywords: Administrative Data; Capabilities Approach; SDG Indicators; Sustainable Development Measurement; Well-being; Post-2030 Agenda
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) rely on official statistical systems, including administrative records, to monitor progress through indicators largely designed to measure observable outcomes. Although these data provide essential information for policy evaluation, their coverage and measurement frameworks may limit our understanding of the conditions required to sustain progress over time. This research examines how a capabilities perspective can complement existing approaches to measuring sustainable development.
The study compares a selection of official UN SDG indicators with alternative indicators developed from a capabilities perspective, using Spain as a case study. Drawing on available official statistics, including administrative data where applicable, the analysis examines how both approaches represent the same dimensions of sustainable development. Particular attention is paid to differences in the information captured by outcome-based indicators and by alternatives designed to reflect the capabilities and conditions underlying people's opportunities to sustain and improve their well-being.
The comparison explores how the choice of indicators and underlying data sources shapes the interpretation of social progress. While conventional indicators describe achieved outcomes, capability-oriented alternatives seek to identify conditions and opportunities that may remain less visible in existing measurement systems. The Spanish case provides an empirical basis for examining the potential contribution of this complementary approach.
The research argues that improving sustainable development measurement requires not only reviewing indicator values and data coverage, but also reconsidering what official statistical systems are designed to capture. Integrating a capabilities perspective into the use and interpretation of administrative and other official data could help inform the development of a post-2030 indicator framework better suited to assessing the conditions required to sustain well-being over time.

Title: Affordable Housing at Risk: The Geography of Heat and Flood Vulnerability in New York City
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: affordable housing; climate justice; extreme heat; flood vulnerability; spatial analysis; New York City
Abstract_Text: New York City has financed about 290,000 affordable homes since 2024, but few studies ask what climate hazards those investments face. The study joined 6,886 geocoded buildings supported by the Department of Housing Preservation and Development to the city's Heat Vulnerability Index, tract level Flood Vulnerability Index, and stormwater flood maps. About 69% of affordable units sit in neighborhoods with high heat vulnerability. The share units in tracts with high coastal flood vulnerability rises from 14.1 to 25.8 by the 2080s, and 40.1% units lie within 50 feet of projected extreme rainfall flooding. Preserved and homeownership units were more coastal flood vulnerability than new construction and rentals. Buildings with deeper affordability were not more exposed once borough and project size were held constant. Tracts with high heat vulnerability contained 2.3 times more affordable units per square kilometer. The study recommends that climate risk should be treated as a condition of housing affordability in both sitting and preservation decision.

Title: Measuring the Dynamics of Structural Change in India: An MLI and NAV Approach
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Structural Transformation, MLI, NAV
Abstract_Text: India has witnessed a complex interplay between economic expansion and employment opportunities over the past four decades. Despite high economic growth, India's labour market has struggled to absorb the surplus workforce, raising concerns about employment growth and a weak process of structural transformation. This study examines the magnitude of structural transformation in output and employment using the Modified Linen Index (MLI), Norms of Absolute Value Index (NAV). The study further employs a time series analysis to examine the relationship between economic growth and structural transformation at the aggregate level. This study utilize the NSSO-Employment and Unemployment Survey and Periodic Labour Force Survey employment datasets from 1993-94 to 2023-24. The findings of the study reflects that despite the high output growth, the rate of employment is very low, indicating that the growth has not been absorbing the labour entering the market. It also suggests that the variation in employment allocation is much more higher compared to the output allocation. The regression results further indicates that HDI, social sector expenditure, Money supply and the urban population are the majore drivers of structural transformation in India. This study indicates that the process of structural transformation remains weak in India, which underscores the need for targeted policy for the provision of decent work and economic growth.

Title: Same Dilemma, Different Reasoning: Making Hidden Assumptions Visible in Sustainability Decisions
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Procedural justice; Sustainable transformation; Stakeholder inclusion; Decision-making; Diagnostic challenges.
Abstract_Text:
Sustainable transformation is not only a question of choosing solutions, but also of examining whose interests, assumptions and perspectives shape those choices. Participants may support the same sustainability objective while overlooking different consequences for affected communities. How can these differences in reasoning be identified and constructively challenged?
This presentation introduces a practice-informed, four-stage diagnostic-challenge framework for examining reasoning in complex sustainability decisions, with particular attention to stakeholder inclusion and procedural justice.
The framework is informed by exploratory educational sessions involving approximately 40 students in Warsaw, organized into four groups addressing two dilemmas, with each dilemma assigned to two groups. Informal facilitator observations suggested variations in participants' interpretations and priorities. These observations informed the framework's development but did not constitute an evaluation of its complete mechanism.
The proposed process begins with an evidence-based decision, followed by identification of its most consequential reasoning weakness. A challenge is then selected to test that specific weakness, such as an overlooked stakeholder interest, an unsupported assumption or an unequally distributed impact. Participants subsequently defend, qualify or revise their decision, with the reasoning behind their response documented.
The framework's contribution lies in explicitly connecting initial reasoning, diagnostic interpretation, targeted challenges and subsequent justification. It does not assume that changing one's position necessarily indicates better reasoning or greater justice.
Using an illustrative renewable-energy dilemma, the presentation will demonstrate the framework and propose criteria for assessing its feasibility, diagnostic consistency and relevance of matched challenges. It will also identify priorities for evaluating reasoning quality and stakeholder consideration in future empirical research.
The central question is not simply which sustainability decision participants make, but what they recognize, overlook and reconsider in reaching it.

Title: Digital Labor Opportunities and (Im)Mobility: Technological promise and legal paradoxes of digital remote for migrants and refugees
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Martin-Shields, Dr. Charles | German Institute Of Development And Sustainability (IDOS)
Keywords: Digitalization, Labor mobility, Regulation, Migration
Abstract_Text: Countries need workers and workers need jobs, however it is often the case that these two needs are not spatially matched. This paper will explore the current conditions that limit the ability of employers and workers to match remotely across borders, and lays out a research agenda focused on making digital remote labor a viable solution for including those who cannot, or prefer not to, move across border for jobs that can be done remotely. In migration policy the increased use of bilateral labor agreements (BLAs) between countries is evidence that innovative approaches to growing the global labor pool are needed. However, the success or failure of BLAs remains contingent on the coherence of the employment country’s immigration policies and the country providing labor having a large pool of people who are willing and able to relocate to the country where the employer is incorporated. There are cases where people have made digital remote work possible, but the reasons it has worked are often very idiosyncratic. This paper will focus on the experience of an urban refugee who was able to work digitally from Malaysia, while being subject to social security, taxation, and insurance in the United States. The idiosyncrasies of his case help point to spaces for reforming social security, tax, and insurance rules to reduce their ‘bordered-ness’, potentially making digital remote work more systemically viable for migrants and refugees.

Title: When sustainability meets existing organizational systems: Pathways to integration and disconnection
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Keywords: Institutional arrangements, coordination mechanisms, accountability, collaborative governance, stakeholder co-creation
Abstract_Text:
As sustainability becomes increasingly embedded in institutional policies, standards, and governance frameworks, an important question is what happens when new sustainability requirements encounter existing organizational systems. While formal requirements can create opportunities for strengthening sustainability within organizations, their implications depend on how they interact with established structures, responsibilities, and expertise. Understanding these interactions is particularly relevant to discussions about effective sustainability governance beyond 2030.
This study examines how sustainability and quality assurance (QA) interact within higher education institutions under a common external accreditation requirement. Drawing on institutional documents and 32 interviews with university leaders, sustainability officers, QA professionals, and student representatives across 13 Swiss public higher education institutions, the analysis explores how two organizational domains with distinct expertise and responsibilities engage with one another. QA, combining accountability and continuous improvement with stakeholder participation, provides an established organizational system through which sustainability requirements are addressed.
The findings identify four recurring organizational dynamics. First, QA can strengthen the organizational position of sustainability by increasing its formalization, visibility, and institutional leverage. Second, where sustainability is already established, QA may draw on existing sustainability expertise, goals, and monitoring practices without determining their substantive direction. Third, QA and sustainability can mutually reinforce one another through processes adaptation. Fourth, the two domains may remain organizationally disconnected, interacting primarily around formal review requirements while developing in parallel.
These findings show that incorporating sustainability requirements into existing organizational systems does not necessarily produce integration. Instead, interactions depend on existing organizational arrangements, capacities, and expertise. For sustainability governance beyond 2030, the study highlights the importance of recognizing different organizational starting points and enabling governance and improvement systems to engage with sustainability expertise without prescribing a single organizational model.

Title: From Participation to Agency: Children's Capabilities and the Right to the City in Sustainable Urban Development
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Ataol, Dr. Özlemnur | University Of Groningen
Keywords: children's participation, capability approach, right to the city, participatory urban planning, SDG 11.
Abstract_Text: SDG 11 and the New Urban Agenda recognize inclusive and participatory urban development as essential to sustainable cities. Yet, translating participation into meaningful influence remains a challenge, particularly for young people. This study examines how participatory approaches can advance children's agency and right to the city, contributing to a more inclusive sustainability agenda beyond 2030. It brings together insights from participatory work with young people in urban planning, climate adaptation, everyday mobility, and circular urban development. Participatory work includes co-design, photovoice, participatory mapping, and artwork elicitation. The Lundy model, capability approach, and right to the city provide complementary theoretical lenses for examining substantive opportunities to participate in and influence urban development. As a result, first, child-centered participatory approaches reveal valuable situated knowledge, spatial experiences, and capacities for addressing urban challenges that conventional adult-centered planning and design may overlook. However, recognizing environmental problems or possessing relevant knowledge does not necessarily translate into collective agency. Second, meaningful participation depends on enabling conditions extending beyond participatory methods, including educational opportunities, supportive policies, and institutional responsiveness. Advancing SDG 11 beyond 2030 requires shifting attention from participation as procedural inclusion toward participation as an expansion of substantive capabilities and shared decision-making power. In alignment with the New Urban Agenda's vision for sustainable urban development toward 2036, this study argues for institutionalizing children's participation in urban decision-making and recognizing children as present urban citizens and agents of sustainable transformation, rather than postponing the recognition of their citizenship until adulthood.

Title: Beyond Solar Lamps: Women’s Pathways to Economic Empowerment and Intrahousehold Bargaining Power
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: social equity, just transitions, social vulnerability, leave no one behind
Abstract_Text:
Objective: To investigate how clean energy entrepreneurship empowers women economically and impacts their agency and intrahousehold bargaining power, addressing the critical roles of social equity and just transitions within sustainable energy interventions.
Methods: This research employs a mixed-methods approach, utilizing an anonymized secondary dataset from 60 Decibels encompassing surveys of women clean energy entrepreneurs in Kenya. Quantitative analysis of self-reported impact metrics is triangulated with qualitative key informant interviews to systematically assess shifts in household decision-making, financial independence, and social vulnerability while maintaining strict analytical independence from programme stakeholders.
Key Results: The analysis demonstrates that women's active participation in clean energy micro-enterprises significantly enhances their agency and intrahousehold bargaining power. Increased economic agency directly correlates with greater influence over household expenditures, resource allocation, and strategic life choices. However, findings also reveal that while economic empowerment is a critical catalyst, entrenched socio-cultural norms remain persistent barriers to achieving full social equity within the home, illustrating the localized complexities of ensuring we leave no one behind.
Conclusions: Measuring intrahousehold power dynamics is essential for designing genuinely gender-transformative climate action and interventions. To advance sustainable development by and beyond 2030, global energy policies must transcend technical implementation to actively address and mitigate localized social vulnerabilities. Integrating intersectional feminist frameworks and rigorous monitoring and evaluation metrics into environmental programming ensures that just transitions actively dismantle existing inequalities rather than merely equipping women with clean technologies.

Title: FLOOD HAZARD MAPPING AND ANALYSIS USING HYDRODYNAMIC MODEL HEC-RAS IN BHARATPUR METROPOLITAN CITY, CHITWAN: CHURE CONSERVATION AREA OF NEPAL
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Keywords: Flood inundation, Flood management, HEC-RAS, Flood Risk, Climate Change
Abstract_Text: Flood is the most common natural disaster in Nepal. Climate Change and the fragile geology of Nepal to be the main contributing factor of increasing frequency and severity. This study was carried out in Bharatpur Metropolitan City within the confines of the Chitwan district, adjacent to left bank of the snow-fed Narayani River encompassing an expanse of 418.8 square kilometers. Out of 28 wards of Bharatpur Metropolitan City, 8 wards namely 3, 4, 16, 17, 18, 26, 27, 28 were studied in this research and involved systematic process of preparation of 2D flood plain maps using HEC-RAS and QGIS. This study aimed to assess the flood inundation area and to access the flood risk associated with different return period such as 2, 5, 10, 50, 100 years respectively. The HEC-RAS river flow model of the Narayani River was calibrated against measured water depth for the year 2016. The produced inundation map indicates direct relationship between the inundation area increases significantly with flood discharge of various return periods. The discharges predicted by Gumbel’s distribution were 10212.68 m 3 /s, 11495.5m 3 /s, 12726.02 m 3 /s, and 14318.8 m 3 /s, 15512.36 m 3 /s for the 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 YRPs, respectively. The context of spatial impact analysis, Ward 28 emerges as a focal point, consistently reflecting substantial repercussions of the identified phenomenon across diverse return periods. In 10-year return period (10YRP), the ward experiences impact, covering 9.61 km² and constituting 75.64% of its total area. This heightened impact persists into the 50-year return period (50YRP), with an extent of 10.23 km², representing a substantial 80.48% of Ward total area. Even in the 100-year return period (100YRP), the impact remains remarkably high at 10.56 km², covering an impressive 83.11% of the ward total area.

Title: Sustainable AI starts with the network: cutting the energy cost of data-center interconnect
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Adhikari Joshi, Dr. Susmita | Credo Semiconductor Inc.
Keywords: artificial intelligence, data-center energy efficiency, co-packaged optics, sustainable digitalization
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence is now basic infrastructure of daily life, and that ubiquity carries a fast-growing infrastructure footprint: data centers consume 1-2% of global electricity, with AI training and inference the fastest-growing load. When the SDGs were conceived in 2015, neither this technology nor its energy demands existed; the post-2030 agenda must explicitly account for the cohabitation of humanity and AI. Yet policy debate still focuses on compute hardware, while a growing share of power goes to moving data, not processing it. Network equipment draws roughly 5-10% of data-center electricity, but inside the machines most energy metered as compute is spent moving data between processors and memory: over 60% of total system energy in profiled large-scale workloads. As AI clusters scale to hundreds of thousands of accelerators, interconnect becomes a first-order sustainability problem.
This talk traces the industry's answer from copper through pluggable optics to near-packaged optics (NPO) and co-packaged optics (CPO). Each step moves optics closer to the switch silicon, shortening the energy-intensive electrical link: NPO designs, which eliminate the pluggable module's DSP, are reported at around 50-60% lower power, and CPO platforms now entering volume production at 51.2 terabits at up to 70% below pluggable transceivers. The second half turns to governance: energy-per-bit metrics and disclosure, efficiency criteria in procurement, coordinated roadmapping. It closes by proposing that industry and policymakers jointly set the first targets for the AI era, beginning with the energy per bit of AI data-center interconnect: reduce it by 2035 against a 2025 baseline, under standardized public disclosure.

Title: From Poverty Reduction to Poverty Durability: Global Lessons from SDG 1 for the Post-2030 Agenda
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Joshi, Dr. Sushobhan | University of Groningen
Keywords: SDG 1; poverty durability; post-2030 agenda; means of implementation; global assessment; sustainable development goals
Abstract_Text:
A decade of SDG 1 implementation yields a striking lesson for the post-2030 agenda: reducing poverty and keeping it reduced are different achievements. Analyzing 37,926 SDG 1 indicator records across all seven targets for 2000-2024, we find poverty outcomes near the observed performance frontier; 98.6% of robust Target 1.1 trajectories improving; while the systems meant to sustain those gains lag badly: financing and implementation targets sit farthest from the frontier, with 38.2% of trajectories worsening. Organized into outcome, intermediate, and enabling layers, the asymmetry is stark: enabling systems worsen at 7.6 times the rate of outcome systems. Country contrasts sharpen the point: Indonesia, Costa Rica, Bangladesh, Cabo Verde, and Liberia show durable broad-based progress, while Honduras, Equatorial Guinea, Côte d'Ivoire, Kenya, and Jordan regress across multiple dimensions, with trajectories diverging from current levels and income alike.
We propose a poverty durability perspective: the post-2030 framework should treat durability of gains as an explicit objective, strengthen financing, institutional, and resilience systems alongside outcome targets, and monitor the direction of enabling systems, not just outcome levels.

Title: RegionsAdapt: a global initiative supporting subnational governments in adapting to climate change
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Rei, Prof. Fernando | Catholic University of Santos
Keywords: RegionsAdapt, Climate Change Adaptation, Subnational Governments, Multilevel Climate Governance, Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13).
Abstract_Text: Launched in 2015 at COP21 in Paris by the Governments of Catalonia and Rio de Janeiro, RegionsAdapt celebrates ten years of promoting climate change adaptation through subnational governments. Coordinated by Regions4, the initiative strengthens regional capacities, fosters knowledge exchange, and encourages concrete adaptation measures, connecting governments across five continents. RegionsAdapt contributes directly to Sustainable Development Goal 13 (SDG 13) of the 2030 Agenda, which calls for urgent action to combat climate change and its impacts. By promoting climate resilience, integrating adaptation into public policies, and strengthening institutional capacities, the initiative helps translate the objectives of the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda into practical territorial action. Its distinctive contribution lies in its method of subnational implementation, which connects global climate commitments with regional priorities and local realities. This approach can be understood through five interconnected steps: (1) political commitment and institutional engagement; (2) assessment of climate risks and vulnerabilities; (3) integration of adaptation into regional planning and public policies; (4) implementation of measures, supported by technical expertise and financial resources; and (5) monitoring, reporting, and knowledge-sharing to assess progress and improve performance.This collaborative framework recognises that subnational governments are strategically positioned to address climate risks through land-use planning, infrastructure, public services, and ecosystem protection. Peer-to-peer learning and the exchange of methodologies and good practices help transform political commitments into institutionalised and measurable adaptation policies. After ten years, RegionsAdapt illustrates the importance of multilevel and polycentric climate governance. Its experience demonstrates that achieving SDG 13 requires more than international agreements: it depends on institutional capacity, territorial knowledge, cooperation, and sustained political engagement. Regional governments are not merely implementers of global agendas; they are active agents in building climate resilience and advancing sustainable development.

Title: Global sustainable development trajectories did not improve with the adoption of the SDGs
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Authors: Luo, Xu; Wu, Xutong; Wang, Shuai; Guan, Ting; Liu, Jianguo; Fu, Bojie
Keywords: sustainable development goals (SDGs), regression discontinuity design (RDD), evenness, network analysis
Abstract_Text: The world remains alarmingly off track to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by 2030, highlighting the urgency and necessity of reflecting on implementation outcomes and identifying specific accelerating actions. Here, using global SDG data for 2000–2024 covering 167 countries, we show that trajectories of SDG performance, evenness, and interactions did not improve overall with the adoption of the SDGs; instead, post-2015 progress largely reflects a continuation of pre-existing trends. Nevertheless, countries with greater attention to the 2030 Agenda and stronger economies tend to exhibit a larger number of SDGs with improved performance trajectories. By distinguishing lagging and leading goals and their systemic influences, we identify country-specific SDGs requiring prioritized advancement or structural reform to catch up or maintain progress, and reveal that current implementation is rarely transformative. These findings indicate that the SDGs have fallen far short of the ambition of “transforming our world”, and provide critical evidence to guide SDG acceleration and the design of post-2030 sustainability initiatives.

Title: The Ubuntu Alignment Index: survival governance to safeguard humanity from autonomous weapons and technocratic artificial intelligence dominance
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: emerging governance frameworks, responsible innovation, international cooperation, risks, Ubuntu
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is being embedded in lethal autonomous weapons, mass surveillance and state decision systems faster than binding governance can follow. Leading scientists warn of catastrophic, potentially extinction-level risk from loss of human control, while technocratic states and corporations race for AI dominance. Sustainable development is impossible without human survival. This contribution proposes Ubuntu, operationalised as the Ubuntu Alignment Index (UAI), as a survival governance mechanism.
The methodological approach is conceptual and comparative policy analysis. The UAI assesses AI systems and their deploying institutions on ukuthembana (relational trust), ukubambisana (participatory consensus) and ubuntu bokuphila (communal wellbeing), across five pillars (People and Culture; Fairness and Justice; Privacy and Security; Technical Rigour; Environmental Stewardship). It is contrasted with technical audit tools and with state-centred, security-led AI governance, and illustrated with South African cases in financial inclusion and marketing.
It is propounded that prevailing tools measure statistical fairness, not who holds power over life-critical decisions. Three governance failures potentially emerge: absent consent from affected communities, decision authority concentrated in technocratic elites, and no measure of communal harm. The UAI aims to convert these into auditable thresholds: no deployment without participatory consensus, accountable human authority over life-and-death decisions, and demonstrable communal benefit.
The UAI is designed to be a testable proposition, not a proven safeguard. Validation against high-risk systems is the next step. The argument is nonetheless forceful, governance placing relational accountability above technical capability and state power is a precondition for a post-2030 agenda in which humanity stays in command of its tools. Ubuntu, "a person is a person through other persons", offers the Global South a leading voice in international AI cooperation.

Title: Water-energy-food nexus solutions for climate-resilient and sustainable irrigated agriculture in Pakistan
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Siyal, Abdul Wahab; Thomas, Swarts; Gerbens-Leenes, P. Winnie
Organisations: Siyal, Dr. Abdul Wahab | Pakistan Agricultural Research Council (PARC)
Keywords: water-energy footprints, Pakistan, Irrigation, groundwater pumping
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Ensuring food security while reducing pressure on scarce water and energy resources is a major sustainability challenge in irrigated agriculture. This study examines water-energy-food nexus interactions in Pakistan’s Indus Basin Irrigation System and explores how spatially informed crop redistribution can reduce water use, energy demand and associated carbon emissions while maintaining food production.
Methods: The analysis builds on spatial assessment of irrigation water supply, energy requirements and carbon emissions for four major crops: wheat, rice, cotton and sugarcane. Irrigation hotspots were identified based on crop water requirements, surface and groundwater use, groundwater depth and pumping energy sources. A multi-objective optimization model was subsequently applied to redistribute these crops across 170 sub-canal command regions in Punjab and Sindh while maintaining crop production. Water, energy and carbon outcomes were evaluated under average conditions and an extreme-weather scenario representing the 2022 floods.
Key results: Irrigation energy use is highly spatially concentrated, with ten hotspot districts accounting for 42% of the four crops' energy footprint. Under average conditions, optimized crop redistribution reduces the agricultural blue water footprint by 6.3%, energy footprint by 10.9% and carbon footprint by about 9.3%. Energy-focused optimization achieves about 75% of the potential water savings while producing substantially greater energy and carbon reductions than water-focused optimization. Under extreme flood conditions, however, reducing the blue water footprint can increase energy use and carbon emissions, revealing important nexus trade-offs.
Conclusions: Sustainable food, water and energy security requires integrated planning rather than optimizing individual resources independently. Beyond 2030, climate-resilient cropping patterns, combined with efficient irrigation and carefully managed clean-energy transitions, can help avoid shifting environmental burdens between water, energy, food and climate goals while strengthening the long-term resilience of irrigated agriculture.

Title: Decoding Mechanism and Inequity of Biodiversity Loss and Socioeconomic Benefits Along Global Value Chains
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Huang, Yiqing; Liu, Ludi; Kang, Ailin; Pradhan, Prajal; Tian, Xin
Keywords: Global Value Chains, Biodiversity, Environmentally Extended Multi-region Input-output Analysis, Value Added, Employment
Abstract_Text:
Biodiversity is facing an unprecedented loss crisis. The expansion of global value chains (GVCs) and vertical specialization has obscured the sources of biodiversity loss, complicating conservation and creating an inequal distribution of biodiversity impacts and socio-economic benefits. Few studies have traced biodiversity impacts across different production stages from a value chain perspective, while inequalities between biodiversity impacts and socio-economic benefits across countries remain insufficiently understood, limiting the development of pathways that jointly advance biodiversity conservation and sustainable development.
This study applies an environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model and GVCs analysis to quantify biodiversity and socio-economic impacts and examine their inequalities. The results show that GVCs are important drivers of biodiversity impacts and contribute to a systematic mismatch between biodiversity impacts, social benefits, and economic gains. Specifically, 78.3% of GVC-related biodiversity impacts are concentrated in ecologically sensitive regions, including Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia, while 71.6% of the associated value added accrues to developed economies, particularly North America and Europe. Employment is relatively concentrated in populous developing countries. Biodiversity-sensitive regions bear 33.5% of GVC-embedded biodiversity impacts through upstream primary production, with intermediate production accounting for more than three-quarters of these impacts, whereas downstream-oriented regions capture substantial employment and value added. Spatially, final demand from developed regions drives 55.3% of biodiversity impacts toward developing regions, while the associated value added is mainly retained within developed economies. This creates a pronounced separation between ecological pressures and economic benefits, placing developing regions at a structural disadvantage in many bilateral trade relationships, with the imbalance intensifying along the value chain.
These findings highlight the need to consider GVCs contribution when allocating conservation responsibilities. Restructuring production, promoting industrial upgrading, and establishing multidimensional responsibility-sharing mechanisms could help reduce the inequality and better align global biodiversity conservation with sustainable development.

Title: Emission trading, financial frictions, and transition risks
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research
Keywords: Financial frictions, macroprudential policy, transition risk, permit trading, intensity target
Abstract_Text: I examine how a carbon permit market affects financial stability by using a two-sector Environmental Dynamic General Equilibrium model with emission intensity target and financial frictions. The Ramsey-optimal environmental target and macroprudential policy (taxes or subsidies on bank assets) are contingent on initial permit allocation method and financial frictions. I find that the asymmetric effect of permit trading between firms due to their differing policy compliance propagates from firms’ profit maximization to banks’ portfolio composition. Permit trading and macroprudential policy shift lending toward permit sellers. When policy is implemented without prior announcement, bank net worth falls. Auctioning generates larger losses and a recession, while free allocation entails smaller losses and avoids recession under optimal targets but can be recessionary under stringent targets.
