However, macroprudential policy limits these losses. Advance policy announcements mitigate transition risk by reducing net worth losses under auctioning and increasing bank net worth under free allocation.

Title: Macroeconomic Implications of Permit Market: Evidence from India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Kumar, Saurav; Ghosh, Taniya; Banerjee, Shesadri
Organisations: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research
Keywords: E-DSGE, Permit market, Intensity target, Business cycle, Energy transition
Abstract_Text: We study how a carbon permit market shapes firm-level emission reduction incentives and aggregate environmental and macroeconomic outcomes. We develop a novel and tractable microeconomic framework in which firms endogenously decide whether to become a permit seller. We find that a higher previous period abatement or current green energy adoption increases a firm's probability of becoming a permit seller but reduces equilibrium share of permit sellers as overall compliance improves, revealing a distinction between individual and aggregate participation. We embed this mechanism in an Environmental-Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium model of India's emission intensity target policy. We find that it achieves energy transition at lower economic costs than a carbon tax. A stricter target and cheaper green energy can accelerate this transition. Finally, endogenous permit price adjustment accommodates shocks that increase fossil-fuel dependence from translating into higher fossil-fuel use, providing a novel stabilization mechanism for permit markets.

Title: Comparative Evaluation of APSIM and AquaCrop for Multiplier Onion Yield Simulation and Irrigation Strategy Assessment under Climate Variability in Ilocos Norte, Philippines
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: AquaCrop, APSIM, multiplier onion, Ilocos Norte, irrigation interval, net irrigation requirements, crop-water stress, climatic variability, scenario analysis, sustainability assessment.
Abstract_Text: Efficient irrigation management is essential for sustaining crop productivity and conserving water under climate variability. This study compared APSIM and AquaCrop for simulating multiplier onion yield in Ilocos Norte, Philippines, and applied the model with better validation metrics to assess irrigation strategies across ten historical growing seasons (2015–16 to 2024–25). Both models were calibrated and independently validated using field datasets from Batac, Pasuquin, and Badoc under varying management conditions. AquaCrop achieved lower root mean square error than APSIM (1.066 versus 2.090 t ha⁻¹), higher R² (0.916 versus 0.678), and greater agreement with observed yields. The models also differed in simulated crop–water dynamics, with AquaCrop producing higher mean relative transpiration and fewer transpiration-limited days. Historical simulations identified reference evapotranspiration and climatic water deficit as climatic variables consistently associated with simulated yield under farmers’ irrigation practices. Irrigation scenarios combined 100%, 80%, and 60% of net irrigation requirement (NIR) with 10-, 15-, and 20-day application intervals. Applying 100% NIR at 10- and 15-day intervals produced the highest mean simulated yields (39.77 and 39.60 t ha⁻¹, respectively). However, 80% NIR at these intervals offered a favorable balance among yield, water conservation, irrigation water productivity, and interannual reliability. Relative to farmers’ practices, these strategies reduced simulated irrigation requirements by approximately 67% while increasing mean simulated yield by approximately 11–13%. Although 60% NIR achieved the greatest irrigation-water savings and highest irrigation water productivity, it increased crop water stress, reduced yield, and weakened reliability across seasons. These findings support AquaCrop as a decision-support tool for evaluating irrigation trade-offs and highlight the importance of balancing irrigation amount and timing to sustain agricultural productivity and water-use efficiency under historical climate variability.

Title: Keeping Cities Moving During Extreme Heat: Built Environment and Cycling–Metro Resilience in Shanghai
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Dammag, Abdulkarem Qasem Abdo Derhem; Zhang, Yongping; Zhou, Jiali; Zhou, Xingang
Organisations: Dammag, Dr. Abdulkarem Qasem Abdo Derhem | Tongji University
Keywords: Extreme Heat, Urban Mobility Resilience, Built Environment, Bike-sharing, Metro
Abstract_Text:
Extreme heat is becoming a critical challenge for sustainable urban mobility, yet the ability of cycling and metro systems to maintain travel activity under thermal stress remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates how built-environment characteristics relate to the heat-related resilience of bike-sharing and metro travel within 282 metro-station areas in Shanghai, China.
Using approximately 4.9 million bike-sharing trips and 32.5 million metro trips, we compared travel activity during a sustained heatwave with thermally normal conditions, separately for weekdays and weekends. Resilience was expressed as the ratio of heatwave to normal trip activity. Building enclosure and greenery ratio were derived from street-view imagery, and geographically weighted regression was applied to examine associations with resilience while accounting for other station-area characteristics.
Bike-sharing activity declined by 16.7% overall, with greater reductions during off-peak and weekend periods. Metro activity remained relatively stable on weekdays but decreased by 7.1% on weekends. Building enclosure and greenery ratio were positively associated with bike-sharing resilience across the study areas, while greenery ratio also showed consistently positive associations with metro resilience. Distance to the city centre was negatively associated with cycling resilience.
These findings highlight the relevance of station-area environments to climate-resilient urban mobility. Integrating human-scale streetscape characteristics into sustainable transport planning may help identify priorities for adaptation to extreme heat. However, the observed associations do not establish causal effects or directly demonstrate the effectiveness of specific interventions.

Title: From environmental pressures to economic damages in European food trade
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Contor, Henri; Kasaw, Molla Tigabu; Mathijs, Erik
Keywords: European food trade, food system, externalities, FABIO, true cost accounting
Abstract_Text:
Objective. European food trade separates consumption from the environmental pressures and prospective economic losses associated with production across global value chains. This study examines where these pressures and damages occur, whose demand drives them, and whether monetary damage valuation changes the hotspots identified from physical pressures alone.
Methods. We link FABIO, a product-resolved physical input-output model of global food supply chains, with SPIQ-FS, which provides country-, pathway-, scenario- and uncertainty-specific marginal damage costs. Producer-commodity-consumer tracing attributes environmental pressures generated along food supply chains to European and non-European final demand. By connecting physical pressures with prospective economic damages, the approach develops an alternative metric for assessing production and consumption beyond conventional measures of economic activity. We distinguish domestic, intra-EU, import and export channels and estimate distributions of prospective economic losses across SSPs. Robustness tests assess uncertainty and alternative allocation assumptions. We additionally compare damage-cost exposure with value added associated with the same demand.
Key results. Preliminary results use FABIO’s environmental extensions to map the physical pressures embodied in European food production, consumption and trade. We compare non-EU production serving EU demand, EU production serving foreign demand, and intra-EU trade, identifying the producer countries, commodities and bilateral links that dominate environmental pressures. Further analysis will examine their resulting economic damages using SPIQ-FS. At this point, results will only reveal how the geography and composition of environmental pressures differ across European food-trade relationships.
Conclusions. By connecting the geography of food production to the demand that ultimately drives environmental pressures, the study will make visible economic damages that conventional physical footprint accounts do not capture. It contributes to economic approaches beyond GDP by complementing value-added measures with indicators of environmental pressure and prospective economic loss across food value chains. This integrated perspective can inform more accountable and resilient food-system strategies beyond 2030.

Title: Partisan control drove United States state carbon farming legislation, 2009 to 2025: lessons for subnational climate governance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: regional climate action, multilevel governance, carbon farming, agricultural policy, state legislation
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This study evaluated how United States state legislatures used law to promote agricultural carbon sequestration and which state characteristics predicted legislative activity.
Methods: A systematic review of all 50 states used LegiScan to identify enacted carbon farming legislation from 2009 through 2025. Each bill was coded as a substantive statute or a non-binding resolution and scored against five policy design criteria. A negative binomial regression fit by maximum likelihood tested state-level predictors of enacted bill counts.
Key results: The review identified 193 relevant enacted bills: 163 substantive statutes and 30 non-binding resolutions. Only 24 states enacted any relevant legislation. Eleven bills in seven states (California, Colorado, Hawaii, Maryland, Minnesota, Oregon and Washington) met all five design criteria. Democratic trifecta control was the sole significant predictor of legislative activity, with an incidence rate ratio of 10.82.
Conclusions: State carbon farming policy remained concentrated in a small group of states and tracked partisan control more than any other tested factor. Comprehensive frameworks were rare even where legislation existed. For sustainable development by and beyond 2030, these results showed that voluntary subnational leadership produced an uneven patchwork rather than a national floor. Durable agricultural mitigation will likely require multilevel governance arrangements that pay farmers for verified sequestration without depending on single-party control of state government.

Title: Beyond conventional farm performance: integrating True Cost Accounting and business-model heterogeneity in farming systems
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Kasaw, Molla Tigabu; Contor, Henri; Bourgeois, Liselot; Mathijs, Erik
Organisations: ILVO-Institute for Agricultural, Fisheries & Food Research
Keywords: life-cycle assessment, business models, alternative metrics, dairy farming, environmental valuation
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Sector-level averages can obscure farm-system heterogeneity and weaken the policy relevance of environmental sustainability metrics. This study develops a comparative farm-level True Cost Accounting approach to assess how environmental impacts and external costs vary across dairy-farm business-model (BM) configurations, which impact categories and processes drive these differences, and whether conclusions depend on expressing performance per unit of milk or per farm.
Methods: Environmental inventory data from Flemish dairy farms that completed a Klimrek climate scan are matched to four previously identified dairy BM profiles using structural and managerial characteristics. The farm remains the analytical unit, while the profiles provide a comparative interpretive lens. We conduct a cradle-to-farm-gate life-cycle assessment using different functional units. ReCiPe 2016 midpoint indicators characterise environmental pressures, while endpoint indicators estimate damage to human health, ecosystems and resource scarcity. These damages will be monetised using documented valuation factors and harmonised to a common price year; midpoint, endpoint, and monetary results remain separate. Sensitivity analyses examine allocation, system boundaries, profile matching and valuation.
Key results: Preliminary results show that across 114 farms, each represented by one annual inventory, the median climate-change impact was 902 t CO₂-eq per farm (IQR: 647–1,309). For the included pathways, median modelled endpoint damage was 2.81 DALYs (IQR: 1.95–3.87) for human health and 9.97 × 10⁻³ species·yr (IQR: 7.18 × 10⁻³–1.42 × 10⁻²) for terrestrial and freshwater ecosystems combined. When endpoint damages were pooled across farms, fine particulate matter contributed 70% of human-health damage, land use 47% of terrestrial-ecosystem damage, and freshwater eutrophication 90% of freshwater-ecosystem damage.
Conclusions: By linking farm heterogeneity to physical impacts, endpoint damages and monetised environmental costs, the study moves beyond sector-average and carbon-only assessments. It provides a transparent basis for differentiated farm transition strategies and environmental policy within agricultural and natural-resource economics.

Title: Navigating barriers and pathways to climate-smart agriculture in high-mountain areas: Farm-level evidence from Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Ali, Dr. Iftikhar | Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF), Germany
Keywords: Barriers; Pathways; Climate Smart Agriculture; Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan
Abstract_Text: Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices such as adopting disease-tolerant crop varieties and shifting from traditional cropping to diversified horticulture and extensive livestock herding have been widely promoted to ensure sustainable agriculture in climate-sensitive regions. However, the adoption of CSA remains limited in Pakistan’s high mountain regions, restrained by diverse underlying barriers. This study examines the barriers and pathways to CSA adoption in Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan, employing a mixed method approach. Quantitative data were collected using a structured household survey, involving 388 randomly selected farm households, while qualitative data were obtained via face-to-face key informant interviews and focus group discussions. Descriptive statistics, non-parametric tests, and thematic analysis were used to analyze the collected data. The study findings show that the adoption of climate smart agriculture is restrained by diverse socio-economic, institutional and technological barriers. Poverty and limited financial resources emerged as the most severe socio-economic barriers, reported by 73.4% of farmers, followed by a lack of awareness about climate change (64.2%). In addition, 59.4% identified limited access to credit services as a major institutional barrier, while 39.9% reported lack of technical know-how about CSA as a key barrier. The results further reveal several pathways to improve CSA adoption suggested by farmers, including farmer awareness programs (90.3%), monetary subsidies to offset adoption costs (87.9%), and farmer training programs (71%). The findings underscore the urgent need to mainstream locally adapted CSA frameworks into regional and local development planning to ensure sustainable agricultural development in the high mountain region of Gilgit-Baltistan in Pakistan.

Title: Strategic Resource Dependencies and the Governance of Infrastructure Connectivity: A Global South Perspective
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: Resource security, infrastructure governance, political economy, institutional coordination, sustainable development
Abstract_Text:
Objective: This paper examines how strategic dependencies involving energy, water, transport and urban infrastructure shape the governance of sustainable development in Global South metropolitan systems. It asks how resource interdependence becomes a source of vulnerability or resilience, and under what institutional conditions infrastructure connectivity can support progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals beyond 2030.
Methods: The paper develops a conceptual framework linking resource dependencies, infrastructure interdependence, political economy and institutional coordination. Karachi, Pakistan, serves as an illustrative metropolitan case through a proposed qualitative analysis of relevant policy documents, publicly available institutional materials and secondary literature. The analysis distinguishes material interdependence from the governance arrangements through which dependencies are managed.
Key results: The framework identifies three analytical mechanisms: resource dependence can transmit external and domestic disruptions across interconnected systems; fragmented institutional mandates can impede coordinated responses; and effective coordination can improve the capacity to manage trade-offs between resource security, infrastructure investment and equitable development. These are conceptual propositions to be examined through the case analysis, rather than assumed empirical findings.
Conclusions: Sustainable development requires more than expanding infrastructure or diversifying resource supplies. It also depends on institutions capable of coordinating interdependent systems across administrative and territorial boundaries. By connecting resource security with metropolitan governance and political economy, the paper offers a framework for examining how Global South cities can strengthen resilience and inform integrated sustainability policies beyond 2030.

Title: AI’s Potential to Facilitate More Agile Development Cooperation: Introducing a New Database
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Sinanoglu, Dr. Semuhi | German Institute of Development and Sustainability
Keywords: database, organizational learning, development cooperation, adaptive cooperation
Abstract_Text: How does development cooperation use artificial intelligence (AI), and does this use help the sector learn? While AI can free up capacity for the local, political work at the heart of development, it also risks crowding that work out. To assess who deploys AI in the development cooperation sector, and for what purposes, we built an original primary-source database of AI deployments by donor ministries, implementing agencies, development banks, and international and humanitarian organizations. Our database shows that program delivery, such as using AI for more efficient forecasting and targeting, and internal operations, such as staff chatbots, make up more than half of existing AI deployments in the sector. By contrast, the functions closest to organizational learning, such as monitoring, evaluation, coordination and governance, account for less than 1/5th. In addition, maturity remains modest: 23 percent operate at scale, and 17 percent are still pilots. Our results suggest that the sector uses AI to do its existing work faster, not to change how it works and learns. We call this “plug-and-play efficiency.” In response, we propose a framework that turns information into institutional change. For sustainable development by and beyond 2030, AI adoption must be paired with reforms toward iterative, adaptive cooperation so freed capacity flows to local political work.

Title: Cognitive autonomy and responsible artificial intelligence use in higher education: lessons from NeuroIA in Uruguay
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Trustworthy AI, information integrity, data autonomy, and sustainability impacts of AI
Keywords: responsible AI; cognitive autonomy; AI literacy; higher education; social sustainability.
Abstract_Text:
Objective: To describe NeuroIA, an interdisciplinary higher education course in Uruguay, and examine participants’ perceptions of its contribution to critical and responsible artificial intelligence (AI) use. Cognitive autonomy is considered in relation to socially sustainable digitalization.
Methods: NeuroIA was delivered in 2026 as a 30-hour, primarily self-paced course integrating cognitive psychology, neuroscience and ethics. This descriptive case study examined 165 voluntary end-of-course questionnaires, including 132 open-ended responses, and records of 214 final-project submissions. Open responses underwent preliminary thematic interpretation, compared with a non-random exploratory sample of projects across three assignment formats. The datasets could not be linked at participant level.
Key results: Among valid questionnaire responses, 94.5% (154/163) rated the course positively, 95.7% (156/163) reported that it connected neuroscience and AI, and 90.8% (148/163) perceived that they achieved its learning objectives. Additionally, 66.9% (109/163) rated its perceived influence on their interaction with AI highly. Open responses emphasized cognitive delegation, critical judgment and attention management. Sampled projects proposed verifying AI outputs, protecting focused attention and maintaining human oversight. Some projects also contained unsupported claims about neurological harm.
Conclusions: NeuroIA offers an educational example for discussing cognitive autonomy, accountability and digital well-being within socially sustainable digitalization. Findings concern self-reported perceptions and proposed practices, not observed behavioral change, objectively measured cognitive improvement or causal course effects.

Title: Collective Threats and Fiscal Demands in Fragile States: Experimental Evidence from Haiti
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Lopez Garcia, Ana Isabel; Berens, Sarah
Organisations: Lopez Garcia, Dr. Ana Isabel | Maastricht University
Keywords: natural disasters, taxation, fragile states, Haiti, climate finance
Abstract_Text: Existing research associates wars, disasters, and pandemics with greater solidarity, stronger demand for protection, and increased willingness to pay taxes. Most evidence however comes from contexts in which the state is seen as a credible provider of protection. Focusing on fragile states, we ask whether, and under what conditions, collective threats can generate support for taxation. We argue that the fiscal effects of collective threats depend on whether citizens understand them as exogenous or endogeneous to government action. We test this using a survey experiment fielded in autumn 2026 (N = 2,000) in Haiti. Respondents are randomly exposed to a neutral prompt, a natural-disaster prompt, or a gang-violence prompt. We then examine effects on the ranking of competing local spending priorities and support for both higher and more progressive property taxation. We expect the disaster prime to increase support for spending on preparedness and security, as well as the taxation required to finance it. The gang-violence prime should have the opposite effects because armed violence in Haiti is closely associated with political collusion.

Title: Financing Climate Resilience: Evidence from a Survey Experiment in Haiti
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Lopez Garcia, Ana Isabel; Berens, Sarah
Organisations: Lopez Garcia, Dr. Ana Isabel | Maastricht University
Keywords: Haiti, climate resilience, disaster preparedness, taxation, nonstate provision, foreign aid.
Abstract_Text: In fragile states, public services are often financed and delivered by non-state actors, including communities, migrants, and international donors. This paper asks whether governments can nonetheless build support for taxation by performing visible administrative roles in such projects (e.g. by issuing permits, monitoring implementation, and ensuring compliance with agreed rules). It also explores whether the effects of government involvement vary with project transparency and the identity of the external funder. We address this using a vignette experiment embedded in an online survey in Haiti in autumn 2026 (N = 2,000). Participants are randomly assigned presented a community-led disaster-preparedness project that varies in whether the local government helps regulate and oversee the project, whether funding comes from the Haitian diaspora or international donors, and whether information about project spending and implementation is made publicly available. Respondents are then asked about their willingness to pay higher local taxes for funding similar disaster-preparedness projects. We test whether government involvement changes willingness to contribute because citizens give local authorities more credit for the project or because they expect the project to be more effective.

Title: Diaspora Finance for Climate Resilience in Fragile, Conflict-Afflicted States
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Lopez Garcia, Dr. Ana Isabel | Maastricht University
Keywords: diaspora finance; remittances; climate adaptation; disaster resilience; public goods; foreign aid; fragile states; conflict-affected states
Abstract_Text: As foreign aid contracts, migrant remittances and diaspora finance are increasingly viewed as potential sources of funding for climate resilience. However, diaspora resources are not politically neutral. By substituting for public provision, diaspora finance may loosen the fiscal relationship between citizens and governments. Diaspora contributions often respond to community obligation, and, where armed actors hold territory, are subject to extraction and licensing by them. This project asks whether the way climate-resilience projects are designed can turn diaspora contributions into a force for state-building rather than -erosion. It makes use of a conjoint experiment embedded in parallel online surveys of diaspora members resident in Canada. Respondents are presented hypothetical climate-resilience projects in their country of origin. Projects vary the role of public authorities and the degree of armed control over access to the project site, alongside other attributes such as who selects the project, who monitors implementation, how expenditure is reported, whether diaspora contributions are matched by an external funder and the project site’s exposure or not to a severe climate-related hazard. The outcomes of interest are: (i) project choice and (ii) willingness to contribute to the chosen project. The focus is on diaspora members from Haiti and Somalia, both extremely fragile countries featuring heavy aid dependence, recurrent climate risks and fragmented public authority but differing in the types of hazards they face and in the character of armed authority. Results will shed light on: (i) what combinations of institutional features practitioners could use to attract diaspora investment in climate finance while simultaneously keeping a role of state institutions in contested areas and (ii) whether arrangements preferred in one setting can travel to another. By producing experimental evidence on what drives diasporas to finance public goods in conflict-afflicted states, the study expands research on diaspora finance, informal taxation, hybrid governance and environmental politics.

Title: Data-driven process simulation and techno-economic evaluation of microalgae hydrothermal liquefaction
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: XU, Dr. Yongdong | National university of Singapore
Keywords: machine learning; renewable energy; waste management; hydrothermal liquefaction
Abstract_Text:
Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) is a promising route for converting wet microalgae into biocrude oil, but its process evaluation can be strongly affected by the yield and higher heating value (HHV) values selected from individual experiments. This study developed a data-driven workflow integrating literature-scale machine learning (ML), laboratory validation, and Aspen Plus-based gate-to-gate energy, cost, and carbon assessment. A
dataset containing 406 microalgae HTL records was used to predict biocrude yield and HHV, screen feedstockcondition-specific candidate scenarios, and identify key influencing factors. The optimized models achieved testing R2 values of 0.7313 for HHV and 0.7909 for yield. The ML-screened conditions were then experimentally validated using Spirulina and Chlorella, with prediction errors ranging from 1.98% to 15.0%. The process assessment showed that the scenario with the highest feedstock-based energy recovery efficiency (ERE) did not provide the highest overall energy conversion efficiency (OECE). Chlorella treated at 270 ◦C, 30% solid concentration, and 60 min achieved an ERE of 63.71%, an OECE of 58.00%, a gate-to-gate process-energy-derived cost of $85.03 per barrel equivalent, and direct process-energy-derived CO2 emissions of 57.03 kg per barrel equivalent. These results indicate that yield or HHV alone is not sufficient for HTL condition selection. A feedstock-specific energy-yield screening step, followed by experimental validation and process-boundary-aware simulation, provides a clearer basis for comparing microalgae HTL scenarios under a defined gate-to-gate boundary

Title: Water management regulates vegetation recovery in photovoltaic farms across China
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Organisations: Hu, Dr. Yueran | Chinese Academy of Sciences
Keywords: Evapotranspiration, Geographic contexts, Water management, Photovoltaic farms, Vegetation recovery
Abstract_Text:
Expanding photovoltaic (PV) energy is central to climate change mitigation, but its ecological benefits depend on how solar farms are managed. In particular, vegetation restoration may require additional water, creating trade-offs between renewable energy development, ecosystem recovery and water conservation. Yet the role of water management in shaping vegetation responses remains poorly understood.
We assessed vegetation changes in PV farms across China using satellite observations and an integrated modelling framework. We adjusted the normalized difference vegetation index to account for PV panels and their shadows, and estimated human-induced evapotranspiration change as a proxy for water management intensity, separating it from natural and microclimatic contributions. Machine learning and dose-response modelling were used to examine vegetation responses and compare observed, no-management and optimized-management scenarios.
Vegetation responses to water management were nonlinear and varied across climatic conditions. The estimated optimal human-induced evapotranspiration change increased from 92 mm per year in humid regions to 200 mm per year in arid regions. Under the optimized scenario, the improvement in vegetation greenness was 2.3 times that under observed management, while total water consumption decreased by 21.5%. These modelled benefits indicate that better water allocation, rather than uniformly increasing water inputs, could improve ecological outcomes. Estimated optima should be interpreted as indicative ranges rather than precise prescriptions.
Our findings support incorporating climate-specific water management into PV planning and operation. This approach could help reconcile renewable energy expansion with ecological restoration and sustainable water use, contributing to more environmentally sustainable low-carbon transitions.

Title: Interactive Effects of Natural and Human Factors on LST in China’s Urban Boundary Areas
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: Huang, Dr. Rui | Nanjing Normal University
Keywords: urban boundary areas; land surface temperature, natural factors, human factors, interaction effects
Abstract_Text: Urban boundary areas in China are thermally sensitive zones shaped by urban expansion and jobs–housing separation, where land surface temperature (LST) is jointly influenced by complex interactions between natural and human factors. Based on MODIS LST products from 2003 to 2023, combined with multi-source data including DEM, meteorological data, nighttime lights, population density, road network density, land use composition, two-dimensional landscape metrics, and three-dimensional building morphology, this study constructs a natural–human factor system and employs Geodetector, interaction detector, random forest, and SHAP to analyze the spatiotemporal differentiation of LST and its driving mechanisms in China’s urban boundary areas. The results show that: (1) LST in urban boundary areas exhibits significant diurnal and seasonal differences; daytime LST is strongly affected by natural factors and two-dimensional landscape patterns, while nighttime LST is dominated by human factors, with notable nighttime warming in winter. (2) Nighttime lights, impervious surface proportion, building density, and road network density are the main warming factors, whereas DEM, NDVI, water body proportion, and wind speed have significant cooling effects. (3) Natural and human factors show significant interaction enhancement effects; the q-statistics of interaction terms such as nighttime lights ∩ DEM, building morphology ∩ vegetation cover, and road network density ∩ water bodies are generally higher than those of single factors, indicating that the thermal environment in boundary areas is a coupled result of natural background and human activities. (4) The direction and strength of factor effects vary by season; natural factors contribute more in summer, while human factors become more influential in winter. This study suggests that thermal environment governance in China’s urban boundary areas should integrate natural background protection with human morphology optimization and implement diurnal- and seasonal-specific spatial regulation strategies to mitigate thermal risks and support sustainable urban planning.

Title: Can sustainability afford to overlook culture? Evidence for the post-2030 agenda
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Authors: Gaitán, Mar; Ramírez, Indra; Gandía, Alba; Leon, Arabella; Alba, Ester
Keywords: Culture & language, Sustainability indicators, Education for sustainable development, Civic participation, Post-2030 agenda.
Abstract_Text:
If museums can help young people understand environmental challenges and imagine different futures, how should their contribution count towards sustainable development? As debates on the post-2030 agenda gather momentum, the place of cultural institutions in sustainability education deserves closer examination.
This paper draws on TOWCHED, a Horizon Europe project coordinated by the Universitat de València, to investigate what museum-based education can contribute to future sustainability priorities. It presents findings from nine educational pilots in Spain and Latvia, evaluated through retrospective self-assessments from 159 children and young people, a survey of 36 museum professionals and educators, and 12 interviews.
Participants reported statistically significant improvements in sustainability-related competencies (r = 0.78), with the strongest results in environmental sustainability. Yet outcomes varied considerably across museums. The evaluation identified a recurring condition for effective learning: the relationship between the museum collection, the sustainability issue being explored and the participants' own experiences. Qualitative findings also revealed forms of civic engagement and attachment to place that the original assessment framework captured only partially. Meanwhile, collaboration between museums and schools emerged as an important contribution to the continuity of educational activities.
These findings raise a question for the post-2030 agenda: how can cultural contributions to sustainability be recognised without overlooking the conditions that make them meaningful? The paper proposes two directions for future policy: explicitly recognising cultural institutions within sustainability education frameworks and developing evaluation indicators that capture locally situated learning and civic participation. It also considers the need to assess whether educational partnerships can endure beyond individual interventions.
Although the evaluation cannot establish long-term or causal effects, its findings provide empirical grounds for reconsidering how cultural learning is represented in future sustainability priorities.

Title: Financial Development, Transition Risk and Decarbonization Policy in Oil and Gas Producing Economies: Evidence from Egypt
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Ibrahim, Mohamed; Harraz, Asmaa; Mandouh, Rasha
Organisations: Ibrahim, Dr. Mohamed | Faculty of Graduate Studies for Statistical Research ,Cairo University
Keywords: energy transition risk; financial development; financial inclusion; renewable electricity; oil and gas producing economies
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Oil and gas producing developing economies must decarbonize while their fiscal revenues, banks and industry remain built around hydrocarbons. This study asks whether financial development accelerates their transition to renewable electricity, and introduces a new tool for measuring the risks that can derail that transition.
Methods: A balanced panel of Egypt, Indonesia, Kazakhstan and Malaysia (2015–2024) links the renewable share of electricity to banking depth, stock market size and financial inclusion, using pooled, fixed-effects and random-effects estimators selected by Hsiao and Hausman tests. A Bayesian network maps Egypt’s systemic transition risks, and these feed an original Energy Transition Risk Index (ETRI) covering policy, economic-financial, technological and geopolitical risk.
Key results: Once country heterogeneity is controlled for, domestic credit and market capitalization have no significant effect on the renewable share. Financial inclusion has a significant negative effect (β = −0.27, p < 0.01), a “Financial Inclusion Paradox”: where fossil fuels are subsidized, new access to finance funds energy-intensive consumption supplied by fossil generation. GDP growth and FDI show no association. The Bayesian network classifies five risks as unacceptable, including debt arrears, gas field depletion and energy security crisis. The ETRI scores Egypt at 72.3, in the high-risk band.
Conclusions: In hydrocarbon economies, finance follows policy. General financial deepening will not shift the power mix; targeted green finance, sequenced fossil fuel subsidy reform and risk-informed policy will. The ETRI offers governments and lenders a transparent way to diagnose transition risk and decide where to act first.

Title: Modular, Integrated, Sustainable Data Centers
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Bruntink, Magiel; van der Waaij, Bram
Keywords: datacenters, sustainability, measurement, heat reuse, flexibility
Abstract_Text:
How can we build the next generation of data centers that are not only sustainable and secure; but also modular, decentralized, and deeply integrated with our energy systems?
The MISD (Modular, Integrated, Sustainable Data Centers) project is a national flagship initiative supported by the Dutch government under the IPCEI-CIS program, which was instated by the EU. With a target of deploying 10,000 highly secure and climate neutral edge nodes by 2030, the EU’s focus is on creating a sovereign cloud and data infrastructure for Europe’s digital independence. Under the umbrella of the IPCEI-CIS program, MISD is developing a new concept for edge data centers that are close to users, sustainable, energy-flexible, and secure-by-design.
From orchestration algorithms to liquid cooling, from cybersecurity frameworks to field labs, MISD is laying the foundation for a new ecosystem.
We will share a first look at the distributed network of data centers of the future and invite you to co-develop it.
Whether you’re driving energy innovation, shaping policy, building tech, or using data services, MISD offers a platform for strategic collaboration and co-creation with:
- Utility providers and grid operators to optimize integration with the grid
- Policymakers and governments to align climate and sovereignty goals
- Vendors and suppliers to co-develop modular and scalable solutions
- Consultants, operators, and developers to share their own expertise and views
- Users who benefit from modular, sustainable, and secure-by-design data center solutions
Join us to shape the future of green data centers in Europe and be part of shaping it!

Title: Mapping Cascading Risks in Egypt’s Energy Transition: A Bayesian Network and Energy Transition Risk Index
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Ibrahim, Mohamed; Harraz, Asmaa; Mandouh, Rasha
Organisations: Ibrahim, Dr. Mohamed | Faculty of Graduate Studies for Statistical Research ,Cairo University
Keywords: systemic risk; Bayesian network; energy transition risk index; resilience; Egypt
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Energy transitions in fossil-fuel-dependent developing economies rarely fail because of one risk. They fail because financial, operational, geopolitical and policy risks interact and amplify each other. Using Egypt’s oil and gas sector as a case, this study maps how these risks cascade and proposes a practical way to measure and act on them.
Methods: A qualitative Bayesian network links 14 risk sources, 5 initiating events and 5 consequences. Each element is assessed for probability, severity and strength of knowledge, and evaluated against ISO 31000-based tolerance criteria. The results feed a new Energy Transition Risk Index (ETRI) that scores country-level transition risk from 0 to 100 across policy, economic-financial, technological-infrastructure and geopolitical-security dimensions.
Key results: Five risks are classified as Unacceptable: high debt burden and payment arrears, natural field depletion, failure to maintain export capacity, energy security crisis, and economic and fiscal crisis. Four critical pathways drive the system, the most immediate being a production-decline cascade from field depletion to energy-security and fiscal crisis. Three feedback loops (economic, investment-deterrent and production-constraint) turn sector shocks into self-reinforcing decline. The ETRI scores Egypt at 72.3 (high risk), driven by economic-financial (76.7) and geopolitical-security (76.3) risk.
Conclusions: Building resilience in such systems requires breaking feedback loops, not treating risks one by one. We propose a Diagnose–Map–Target framework: diagnose the dominant risk dimension with the ETRI, map its causal pathways with a Bayesian network, then target precise interventions such as arrears resolution, investment guarantees and binding renewable targets. The approach is transferable to other resource-dependent economies.

Title: PERCEPTIONS OF ECOSYSTEM SERVICES IN RELATION TO CLIMATE CHANGE AND LIVELIHOOD ADAPTATION AMONG LOCAL COMMUNITIES IN THE NUI CHUA BIOSPHERE RESERVE, VIETNAM
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Ecosystem services, Local perceptions, Livelihood dependence, Environmental pressures, Núi Chúa Biosphere Reserve
Abstract_Text:
Climate change and increasing human pressures are intensifying ecosystem degradation, with severe consequences for communities that depend on natural resources for their livelihoods. Understanding how these communities value ecosystem services and perceive environmental change is essential for effective conservation and climate adaptation. The Núi Chúa Biosphere Reserve in south-central Vietnam provides a relevant case study, where high biodiversity coincides with substantial climate stress and environmental degradation. This study investigates local perceptions and valuations of ecosystem services, differences across livelihood groups and socio-demographic backgrounds, and perceived environmental changes and adaptation strategies. Structured household surveys were conducted at five coastal sites in the Reserve’s buffer zone (N = 107).
All ecosystem service categories were rated highly, with provisioning and regulating services valued slightly more than cultural services. Among households with calculable natural resource dependence index (NRDI) scores (N = 44), resource dependence was high and significantly greater among older respondents. However, NRDI scores were not significantly associated with ecosystem service valuation. Agricultural and forestry households showed somewhat stronger preferences for terrestrial ecosystem services, whereas fishing households placed greater emphasis on marine ecosystem services. Reported environmental problems, including poor waste management, water pollution and declining fish stocks, were associated with lower ecosystem service valuations, suggesting a potential link between perceived ecological degradation and the value attributed to natural resources. Most respondents reported changes in weather patterns, particularly increasing drought frequency and severity. Despite widespread climate awareness, few respondents had received climate adaptation training, and reported adaptation strategies were largely reactive rather than preventive. These findings highlight a gap between awareness of climate change and access to practical adaptation support. Effective management of UNESCO Biosphere Reserves should therefore integrate ecosystem protection with livelihood support and targeted climate adaptation training.

Title: Mapping Food Security Drivers through Resilience Capacities: An Integrated Resilience Framework for European Food Systems
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Kandel, Giri; Dettenhofer, Markus; Vasiljevic, Marjana; Manikas, Ioannis
Organisations: Kandel, Dr. Giri | Czech University of Life Sciences
Keywords: Food system vulnerabilities; climate change; biodiversity loss; resilience assessment; adaptive capacity; policy pathways; systematic risk mapping
Abstract_Text: Food security is a complex and evolving challenge shaped by climate change, biodiversity loss, and the nexus among biophysical, technological, economic, political, supply chain, and socio-demographic drivers. Addressing these challenges requires system-level approaches that go beyond analysing individual sectors. This study aims to develop and apply a structured, resilience-oriented framework to systematically classify and analyse food security drivers across European food systems. The analysis is based on a structured integrative literature review, complemented by participatory insights from ten EU Living Labs, to categorise food system risks into six thematic domains. Using the four Global Food Security Index pillars as outcome dimensions, the framework qualitatively maps drivers across availability, affordability, quality and safety, and sustainability and adaptation, linking them to absorptive, adaptive, and transformative resilience capacities. The results indicate that biophysical and environmental, economic and market, and food supply chain drivers are prominent across the European contexts examined. In contrast, institutional, technological, and socio-cultural drivers vary across contexts. The findings further indicate that availability and sustainability may be particularly affected where climate-induced shocks, biodiversity loss, and market volatility interact. Mapping drivers through resilience capacities identifies potential intervention points that require further empirical validation, including governance coordination, supply-chain diversification, and investments that enhance adaptive and transformative capacity to manage trade-offs within food systems. By integrating food security drivers, resilience capacities, and GFSI pillars within a single analytical framework, this study offers an analytically grounded, conceptually derived tool intended to support, rather than replace, context-specific policy design, collaborative problem-solving by food-system practitioners, and future research on systemic food-security risks.

Title: The role of digitalisation in supporting farmers and strategic policies for food security and sustainability in Europe
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Kandel, Giri; Poláková, Jana; Hamouz, Pavel; Hruška, Adam; Varvaris, Ioannis; Manikas, Ioannis
Organisations: Kandel, Dr. Giri | Czech University of Life Sciences
Keywords: Digital solutions, agrochemical independence, one-stop-shop, Common Agricultural Policy, precision agriculture, EU strategies
Abstract_Text: Ensuring food security while reducing dependency on agrochemical inputs has become a strategic priority for European agriculture amid climate change, geopolitical instability and environmental degradation. This paper examines the role of digitalisation in supporting sustainable and resilient agri-food systems across the European Union. Drawing on an extensive literature review, we analyse the current state of agricultural digitalisation, the systemic barriers constraining its uptake, and the effectiveness of key EU policy instruments, primarily the Common Agricultural Policy. Our study shows that several digital technologies, such as precision agriculture, sensor-based monitoring, and decision-support systems, have reached high technological readiness levels, yet adoption remains uneven. In terms of precision agriculture, several technologies exist, including variable-rate technology for crops, which can increase wheat production by 1% to 10% and offer savings in nitrogen fertilisation ranging from 4% to 37%. However, there are trade-offs to consider, such as power asymmetries, rebound effects, and a digital divide stemming from uneven digital literacy among farmers. The paper explores three detailed implementation pathways, including mechanisms, resources, feasibility and time horizon. The pathways include 1) EU framework for agrochemical independence and agricultural data digitalisation; 2) CAP Eco-schemes for low-input digitalisation; and 3) Cooperative digital inclusion for small and medium farms. Overall, the findings underscore that digitalisation alone is not a panacea, but its contribution to food security depends on governance, inclusive policy design and long-term investment in enabling conditions.

Title: ating the Climate Change–Development Nexus for Resilient, just and Equitable Transformations in Subnational Entities: A Study of Kano State
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Abdulkadir, Dr. Abdulkadir Inuwa | Federal University Dutsinma Katsina State
Keywords: climate change; development nexus; climate justice; transformative adaptation; subnational governance; Kano State; Nigeria
Abstract_Text:
Abstract
Subnational governments are where global climate commitments meet everyday development outcomes. In Nigeria, however, state-level climate action remains thinly theorised and unevenly resourced, even though the effects of a warming climate are felt most directly in farms, neighbourhoods, markets and households. This paper examines how the climate change–development nexus is playing out in Kano State, northern Nigeria’s most populous state and a major commercial, agricultural and industrial centre, and asks what would make its response resilient, just and equitable. Drawing on qualitative document analysis of national and state policy instruments, multilateral and project documents (including the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes, ACReSAL, programme) and the recent peer-reviewed literature, and read through the lenses of climate justice and transformative adaptation, the paper advances three findings. First, climate stressors in Kano (erratic rainfall, heat, flooding, land degradation and water stress) compound pre-existing development deficits in agriculture, urban services, waste management, energy access and livelihoods rather than operating as a separate environmental problem. Second, the institutional response is fragmented, project-driven and heavily dependent on external finance, which limits its capacity to deliver transformation rather than incremental coping. Third, the distribution of risk and benefit is uneven: smallholders, women, peri-urban poor households and displaced people carry disproportionate burdens yet have limited voice in planning. The paper proposes a five-pillar framework (integrated planning, locally led adaptation finance, inclusive governance, nature-based and circular-economy investment, and data and learning systems) for moving Kano from reactive coping towards resilient, just and equitable transformation, and draws lessons for other Nigerian states and subnational entities in comparable drylands.
Keywords: climate change; development nexus; climate justice; transformative adaptation; subnational governance; Kano State; Nigeria

Title: Climate-risk analytics for nature-based solutions: assessing resilience, risk reduction and adaptive management in Portugal's marine Natura 2000 network
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: University of Lisbon and NOVA University Lisbon
Keywords: nature-based solutions, ecosystem services, marine management, biodiversity, limits to adaptation
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Salt marshes, seagrass meadows, dunes and intertidal flats are promoted as natural coastal defences, yet their protective effect is conditional and the habitats are themselves exposed to the hazards they buffer. Area-based targets such as SDG 14.5 measure protected coverage, not whether protected habitats keep functioning as the climate changes. In Portugal, many such habitats lie in EU Natura 2000 sites whose conservation objectives are rarely climate-informed. This doctoral research asks where and under what conditions these habitats reduce coastal hazards, whether that role will persist, and how evidence can guide site management.
Methods: The study couples two risk perspectives usually assessed separately: climate risk to habitats, and habitats' role in reducing risk to people and assets behind them. A systematic evidence map will yield graded rules on when habitats reduce hazards, feeding a spatial risk assessment to 2100 under three climate scenarios, using satellite, climate-projection and census data. All mainland coastal sites will be screened, with Ria Formosa, the Tagus estuary and Ria de Aveiro analysed in detail. Policy analysis, interviews and workshops will test translation into management.
Key results: So far, this ongoing research has built a framework adjusting each habitat's protective contribution for its likelihood of persisting. Review of 2026 European Commission guidance on Natura 2000 and climate change shows it leaves site-level vulnerability methods to Member States and habitats' risk-reduction role to case-by-case assessment. Expected outputs are maps of where protection is durable, at risk or overstated, and who lives behind it, plus draft climate-informed objectives and monitoring triggers.
Conclusions: Linking risk evidence to measurable site objectives offers a transferable route to keeping nature's contributions to people durable, helping protected areas serve biodiversity and adaptation goals by 2030 and informing post-2030 targets that track ecological function, not just coverage.

Title: Nutrition profile, sugar disclosure, and marketing practices of sugar-sweetened beverages in Nepal: A cross-sectional package analysis
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Authors: Subedi, Ranjeeta; Gautam, Ghanshyam; Sapkota, Sujan; Dulal, Bishnu; Aryal, Tara; Shah, Shalabh; Baral, Sushil
Keywords: Sugar, Nepal, Sugar Sweetened Beverages
Abstract_Text:
Background: Sugar sweetened beverages (SSBs) are the major contributors of excessive sugar intake resulting in increased obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs), including diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and dental caries. Despite the increasing consumption of SSBs in Nepal, evidence on their nutritional composition, labelling practices, and regulatory environment remains limited.
Methods: A cross sectional Package label analysis of 449 unique SSB products available across Kathmandu valley, Lumbini and Madesh province was done
Findings: The study found high compliance with basic mandatory labelling requirements given by Food Hygiene and Quality Act, 2024. However, nutrition information of public health importance was inadequately disclosed. While approximately three-quarters of products reported total sugar content, only 37·6% disclosed added sugar information, limiting consumer’s ability to make informed dietary choices.
The sugar levels in beverages available in Nepal was substantial. The median total sugar content was 11 g/100 ml. Most products exceeded the WHO South-East Asia Region nutrient profile thresholds for restricting marketing to children. Products with higher sugar content were also found to be relatively less expensive, potentially increasing their accessibility among lower-income populations.
Approximately one in seven products employed child-appealing marketing techniques, and nearly two-thirds of these products exceeded WHO nutrient thresholds. Furthermore, only around 16% of products displayed any form of warning label, while sugar-specific warnings and front-of-pack labels were virtually absent. Existing excise taxes appeared insufficient to meaningfully discourage consumption of high-sugar beverages.
Interpretation: These findings highlight the need for comprehensive policy reforms in Nepal, including mandatory disclosure of total and added sugars, implementation of interpretive front-of-pack warning labels, restrictions on child-directed marketing of high-sugar products, and adoption of sugar-tiered taxation. Strengthening market surveillance and public awareness initiatives would further support healthier dietary environments and contribute to reducing consumption of SSBs and the growing burden of non-communicable diseases in Nepal.

Title: Shaping Decisions Before They Are Made: Intermediary Influence and Democratic Legitimacy in Energy Transition Governance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: intermediaries, legitimacy, democracy, pre-decisional influence, municipal planning
Abstract_Text:
Intermediaries in sustainability transitions can shape the conditions under which collective decisions are prepared. Brokerage may structure access to governance arenas and resources; translation may affect which forms of knowledge become accessible and relevant; mediation may shape how conflicting interests are articulated and processed; and sense-making may influence problem definitions and the range of options considered. These forms of pre-decisional influence are democratically consequential because political influence can operate through the structuring of agendas and alternatives before formal decisions are taken (Bachrach & Baratz, 1962).
Existing research has examined how intermediaries obtain and maintain legitimate positions within transition processes (van Lente et al., 2020) and has raised questions about the democratic nature and legitimacy of place-based intermediation (Loeber & Kok, 2024). What remains less systematically developed are normative democratic criteria for evaluating the influence exercised through intermediary practices. This paper asks: How do intermediary roles shape the pre-decisional conditions of energy transition governance, and what are the democratic implications of such influence? Under what conditions can such pre-decisional influence be democratically justified?
The paper distinguishes the democratic relevance of intermediary influence from its democratic justification. It draws on democratic theory to examine how intermediary practices may structure access, knowledge, conflict, problem definitions, resources, and the range of available options before formal decisions are made, and why influence over these conditions matters democratically. It then takes Beetham’s (1991) account of legitimacy as a starting point and combines it with democratic accounts of accountability, contestation, and public justification. These considerations inform an evaluative framework that is applied to and further specified through cases of municipal energy transition planning in Germany. We argue that intermediary influence generates distinct legitimacy requirements when it shapes politically consequential conditions of decision-making without being directly subject to the authorisation and accountability mechanisms associated with formal decision-making authority.

Title: Socio-economic factors and policy incentives for household biogas adoption in Gulu City, Uganda
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Keywords: Biogas adoption; Policy incentives; Clean cooking; Household energy transition; SDG 7.
Abstract_Text: The study investigates the determinants of biogas technology adoption among households in Gulu City, Uganda, emphasizing the importance of decentralised renewable energy for achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7. The research utilised a mixed-methods approach, surveying 88 households and conducting interviews with key informants. Findings revealed high awareness of biogas benefits, such as cost savings and improved air quality, but low actual adoption. Economic barriers, notably high installation costs and limited financing, were significant obstacles, while social factors had minimal impact. Policy incentives, including subsidies and training, enhanced the positive effects of socio-economic factors on adoption. The study concludes that successful biogas adoption requires affordable technology, accessible financing, reliable support services, and strong policy frameworks, urging local stakeholders to implement targeted strategies for fostering sustainable energy transitions in urban settings.

Title: Sugar-Sweetened Beverage Consumption in Nepal: Evidence, Policy Gaps, and Governance Challenges
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Developing solutions and innovations for healthier societies
Authors: Subedi, Ranjeeta; Gautam, Ghanshyam; Baral, Sushil
Keywords: Sugar Sweetened Beverage, Taxation, Labelling, regulation
Abstract_Text:
Changing global food environment marked by rapid rise of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) consumption, particularly sugar-sweetened beverages (SSBs), reflects broader governance and market challenges. SSB consumption is strongly associated with obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and other non-communicable diseases (NCDs). In Nepal, NCDs account for 71% of total mortality, with dietary risks playing a major role.
This study used a mixed evidence-synthesis approach combining: scoping review of national and global literature; secondary analysis of nationally representative datasets, and review of national policies, laws, and regulations shaping food environment.
In Nepal, 68% of the population consumed SSBs. Consumption is higher in urban and among wealthier households. Furthermore, 86.8% of commercially available food and beverage products commonly consumed by children exceed at least one threshold, indicating early exposure to excessive sugar intake. SSBs are widely available, with low unit prices and small package sizes encouraging frequent purchases. Marketing exposure remains substantial, over 70% of food advertisements aired during children’s television programming promote products high in sugar, fat, and/or salt.
Nepal has established a legal and policy foundation for regulating SSBs through food safety legislation, consumer protection provisions, advertising regulation, and commitments under MSNP III. However, current excise taxes remain low and volume based. Mandatory front-of-pack warning labels, standardized nutrient thresholds, and systematic enforcement mechanisms are not fully operational. Policy ambiguity and competing economic interests further limit decisive action, reflecting broader governance challenges in regulating commercial determinants of health.
Rising SSB consumption represents a critical yet under-addressed public health challenge in Nepal. While policy commitments exist, weak implementation, limited financing, and insufficient regulatory capacity constrain their impact. Strengthening fiscal measures, enhancing regulatory enforcement, and improving policy coherence across sectors are essential. Addressing SSB consumption requires navigating complex governance and power dynamics, and leveraging coordinated, multisectoral responses to advance health equity in an era of polycrises.

Title: Accelerating SDG 6 and Related Goals through Open Data
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
All_Countries: Netherlands, Palestine, United Kingdom, United States
Keywords: SDG 6; open data governance; open ML models; AI; digital twins; Multi-agent simulations
Abstract_Text:
Progress on SDG 6 depends on using evidence to improve water services, allocate resources and protect ecosystems. Yet fragmented data, limited access and uneven institutional capacity often prevent available knowledge from informing decisions. Climate pressures and competing demands make these gaps more consequential. Addressing these gaps requires multistakeholder cooperation and a shift towards managing water as a finite, shared resource through reliable evidence and collective responsibility.
Open data, open solutions and open machine learning models can widen access to knowledge and analytical tools. Artificial intelligence can support analysis, while digital twins can integrate observations and models to visualize changing conditions and test alternative responses. Multi-agent simulations can explore interactions among water users and institutions, helping assess policy choices and their consequences.
These opportunities depend on five domains of open data practice: leadership and commitment; open data governance and management; resources and institutional capacity; risk management and trust; and implementation and demonstrated results. Together, these domains connect political support and clear responsibilities with reliable, interoperable data, sustained financing and skills. They also require safeguards for privacy and security, transparency about uncertainty and bias, and evidence that applications improve decisions.
The session will use these five domains to structure a panel discussion on how openness and digital approaches can accelerate SDG 6 and advance related goals. It will examine government understanding of openness, readiness to share and use data, and barriers to implementation. Discussion will connect data governance with practical decisions on water services, resource allocation and long-term water security and sustainability. It will also consider how public participation and accessible evidence can strengthen responsible water use. The panel will identify capacity-building needs and draw lessons across health, food, energy and climate priorities, providing insights for the 2028 United Nations World Water Development Report and preparedness beyond 2030.
This presentation will introduce UNESCO’s Open Solutions approach, which connects open educational resources, open access to scientific information, open data, and free and open-source software. It will examine how these components can support SDG 6 by making water knowledge and tools easier to access, adapt and reuse. Discussion will address the policies, licensing arrangements, institutional capacity and partnerships needed to sustain their use. The presentation will connect openness with practical water decisions, highlighting its contribution to education, innovation, equitable access to knowledge and cooperation across the SDGs.
Water policies affect users and institutions with different needs, priorities and capacities to respond. This presentation will explore how AI, digital twins and multi-agent simulations can help examine these interactions and compare policy options for advancing SDG 6. It will consider how simulated responses to allocation rules, conservation measures and service disruptions can inform decisions and reveal potential trade-offs. Emphasis will be placed on transparent assumptions, uncertainty and stakeholder participation, connecting water management with reduced inequalities, effective institutions and climate resilience.
Open machine learning models can expand access to analytical tools for advancing SDG 6 and related sustainability goals. This presentation will examine their potential to assess water availability, identify water-quality risks and inform resource allocation. It will consider how model sharing, transparent documentation and local adaptation can support use across different institutional settings. Particular attention will be given to data quality, validation, technical capacity and the resources needed to maintain models. The discussion will connect these requirements with practical decisions linking water security, sustainable agriculture and climate resilience.
Digital twins can connect observations and models to represent changing water conditions and test management responses. This presentation will examine their practical use in advancing SDG 6, with attention to urban water systems, resource availability and climate-related risks. It will explore how scenario testing can inform infrastructure planning, service continuity and ecosystem protection. The discussion will address monitoring requirements, interoperability, model validation and institutional ownership, including when a digital twin adds value. Applications will be considered through their contribution to water security, sustainable cities and climate adaptation.

Title: A policy-oriented monitoring system for regional sustainability transformation. Insights from a German case study
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: sustainable development; regional sustainability transformation; evidence-based decision-making; monitoring system; surveys
Abstract_Text: The UN Transformation Agenda 2030 including the global sustainable development goals (SDGs) are not on track and will likely fail to meet its ambitious targets till 2030. Given that un-sustainable developments keep on going and - in some areas - are worsening, policy-oriented research and support for evidence-based decision-making in politics, public and private sectors as well as society at large remain important. In particular indicator-based international and national sustainability monitoring systems are crucial for orienting sustainability policy and governance and need to be further developed within the Post-2030-Agenda, for example regarding data availability, cross-cutting indicators, impact-orientation and policy relevance. Even though improved indicator-based monitoring systems will be essential, they are not sufficient. In this presentation it is argued, that beyond "objective" data, insights on "subjective" assessments of sustainability transformation is needed, in order to secure social acceptance and allow for resonant, adaptive transformation governance. Based on a pilot project on the subnational regional level of Lower-Saxony in Germany, a monitoring system for surveying decisionmakers from public and private sector as well as citizens regarding their perceptions, attitudes and actions on sustainability transformations is presented. Finally it is discussed, how this monitoring information may complement indicator-based monitoring systems, support evidence-based decision-making for sustainable development, and what its implementation at the science-policy-interface would require.

Title: From Awareness to Action: Household Food Waste and the Behavioural Challenge of Circular Consumption in Oman
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Organisations: Saboori, Dr. Behnaz | Sultan Qaboos University
Keywords: Household food waste; food-waste awareness; awareness–action gap; circular economy; sustainable consumption; household behaviour; resource efficiency; Oman.
Abstract_Text:
Reducing household food waste is essential for advancing sustainable consumption, resource efficiency, and circular-economy transitions. However, increasing awareness does not necessarily translate into changes in actual household behaviour. This study examines the relationship between food-waste awareness and actual household food waste in Oman, focusing on how socioeconomic, demographic, educational, employment, housing, and geographic characteristics shape this relationship.
The empirical analysis uses survey data from 347 households. Actual household food waste is measured using household food-related expenditure and the reported proportion of food wasted, providing an outcome-oriented measure rather than relying exclusively on attitudes or perceptions. The analysis examines the association between awareness and actual food waste while accounting for differences in household circumstances.
The findings indicate that higher food-waste awareness is associated with lower actual household food waste. Nevertheless, this relationship is heterogeneous across educational groups, employment categories, residential locations, and housing conditions. Household income is also positively associated with actual food waste, suggesting that greater purchasing capacity may increase the volume of food available for consumption and the potential for unnecessary disposal. Differences in household composition further highlight the importance of demographic context in food purchasing, preparation, consumption, and leftover management.
These findings demonstrate that awareness alone is insufficient as a comprehensive food-waste reduction strategy. Effective interventions must translate knowledge into practical and sustained behavioural change. For Oman, this requires targeted communication, improved meal planning and storage practices, responsible purchasing, portion management, and locally adapted initiatives involving households, educational institutions, and municipalities. Integrating measurable food-waste outcomes into policy evaluation would also help distinguish improvements in awareness from actual reductions in waste.
The study contributes to the sustainable-consumption and circular-economy literature by highlighting the importance of household heterogeneity in the awareness–action relationship. Its policy message is that effective food-waste reduction requires moving beyond information provision towards context-sensitive interventions.

Title: SPATIO-TEMPORAL ANALYSIS OF GREENSPACE CHANGE AND ITS IMPACT ON URBAN FLOOD RISK IN KUMASI, THE MIDDLEBELT OF GHANA
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: Adarkwah, Dr. Francis | University of Ghana
