Keywords: Greenspace Change, Urban Flood Risk, Land Use/Land Cover, GIS, Remote Sensing
Abstract_Text: Rapid and largely unplanned urbanisation in Kumasi, Ghana, once celebrated as the "Garden City of West Africa," has progressively eroded the city's greenspace cover, weakened natural flood mitigation capacity and intensified urban flood risk. This study employed GIS and remote sensing techniques to investigate the spatio-temporal relationship between greenspace change and flood risk in the Greater Kumasi Metropolitan Area between 2015 and 2025. Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery were classified using a Random Forest algorithm, achieving overall accuracies of 84% and 86% for 2015 and 2025 respectively, while NDVI analysis and a DEM-derived hydrological model were used to assess vegetation health and flood susceptibility. Results showed that built-up land expanded from 63% to 82% of the study area, while total greenspace declined by over 33 km², with dense vegetation losing more than half its 2015 extent. Spatial overlay analysis revealed substantial coincidence between areas of high greenspace loss and zones of high to very high flood risk, particularly in Aboabo, Anloga, Moshie Zongo, Asawase, and parts of Bantama, with emerging flood risk also evident in peri-urban areas such as Ahinsan and Kentinkrono. The findings indicate that flooding in Kumasi is driven not only by climatic factors but substantially by land cover change, underscoring the need for stricter land use enforcement, greenspace restoration, and nature-based flood mitigation measures to support the city's long-term hydrological resilience.

Title: Operational ensemble forecasting of electricity demand and post-curtailment photovoltaic generation in Cyprus
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Authors: Herodotou, Panagiotis; Neofytos, Ilia; Davidian, Viken; Makrides, George; Georghiou, George
Keywords: Electricity demand forecasting, photovoltaic generation forecasting, ensemble learning, power-system operation, renewable energy integration
Abstract_Text:
Increasing photovoltaic (PV) penetration creates a growing need for reliable electricity-demand and generation forecasts to support power-system operation. This study presents machine-learning ensembles for forecasting aggregated demand and post-curtailment PV generation in Cyprus. The ensembles are deployed through the “Loadcaster” online platform for the Transmission System Operator of Cyprus, supporting scheduling, reserve planning, and PV-curtailment management.
Separate forecasting ensembles combine XGBoost, LightGBM, and ExtraTrees regressors through wighted averaging. Models are retrained daily using 360 days of historical data and generate forecasts at 15-minute resolution over a five-day window comprising the current day and four subsequent days. Inputs include lagged demand or generation, weather information from five regions of Cyprus, solar-position variables, and calendar features. These predictors capture meteorological influences and temporal patterns, including daily and weekly cycles and holidays. Operational performance is evaluated for the first 24 hours against measured data over approximately 45 days.
Demand forecasts achieved root mean squared errors (RMSEs) of 33.00 MW on weekdays and 35.10 MW on weekends, corresponding to normalized RMSEs of 2.70% and 3.26%, respectively. For post-curtailment PV generation, RMSEs were 41.24 MW on weekdays and 34.32 MW on weekends, with normalized RMSEs of 5.41% and 5.70%, respectively. Relative to the reference demand forecast, the ensemble reduced RMSE by 13.4% on weekdays and 39.2% on weekends.
The proposed ensemble provides an applied example of digital forecasting infrastructure supporting electricity-system operation during the energy transition. Anticipating demand and renewable generation can inform resource scheduling and reserve requirements while supporting curtailment management. Such capabilities are relevant to affordable and clean energy and climate action, supporting the integration of renewable electricity by 2030 and beyond. Longer evaluation periods are needed to establish performance across seasons and operating conditions.

Title: The Textile Ecosystem Living Lab: AI-assisted mapping of the sectoral activity in the Netherlands
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: ecosystem mapping, digitalization, circular infrastructure
Abstract_Text:
The Textile Ecosystem Living Lab (TELL) is a novel effort to improve visibility into local ecosystems in the Textile, Clothing, Leather, and Footwear (TCLF) sector, offering an open-source tool to different stakeholders (businesses, governments, research and network organizations, etc.) pursuing their sustainability and economic performance targets. Focusing on the Netherlands, this research aims to illustrate the challenges and opportunities for organizations engaging in the Twin Digital and Green Transition, providing a more complete picture of local and national actors in the textile sector.
The presented approach combines 1) a dataset (or business registry) of companies, 2) an interactive dashboard, 3) an AI data scraper, and 4) an interactive input form. Users of the TELL can locate organizations on a map and search for potential collaborators using the keywords obtained from companies' websites through the AI data scraper. Providing a semantic basis for business classification and identification, the tool works as a search engine specifically for the textile sector.
The key result of the TELL development is an accessible, regularly updated inventory enriched with keywords and supporting classification methods beyond standard industry classifications (i.e., NACE). Since the first version was launched, public institutions and subsidy providers have acknowledged the variety of textile activities and SMEs that can innovate and contribute to the circular transition.
In conclusion, ecosystem mapping is gaining prominence in shaping future generations of e-government applications and circular ecosystem orchestration, supporting the large-scale coordination of actors engaged in Climate Action, Innovation, and Infrastructure development (i.e., recycling). Beyond 2030, with the Digital Product Passports (DPP) and Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) fully rolled out across the EU, the quality of the sectoral mapping can support policymaking around sustainability and improve the effectiveness of (differentiated) incentive systems.

Title: Heat, Density, and Green Space as Indicators for Development Priorities in Dense Urban Area of Palembang, Indonesia
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Organisations: University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign
Keywords: social well-being, social equity, land surface temperature, NDVI, urban greenery, urban heat island
Abstract_Text: Dense neighborhoods in Palembang, Indonesia, face growing climate stress as the city expands. Green cover keeps shrinking, and land surface temperature (LST) rose by about 2°C between 2008 and 2018. Rising heat harms both physical and mental health, and the harm falls hardest on low-income residents of overly dense areas. These residents also have the least access to green space. Urban greenery is often proposed as a nature-based solution for heat and well-being. But green space is usually placed without first asking where social welfare is most at risk, and its health benefits are measured only after it is built. This study offers recommendations for where urban greenery would do the most for health equity. Using Landsat 8–9 imagery, the study derives the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) for vegetation cover, LST from the thermal band for heat exposure, and the Normalized Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) for building density. The result is validated against a kernel density map of census population. The three layers are scaled from 0 to 1 and combined at the sub-district level into a Social Wellbeing–Density Index (SWDI). The output index is tested with a sensitivity analysis. The results show that sub-districts with high SWDI tend to fall mostly within Palembang’s older, dense urban core, where urban heat island effects, high population density, and low vegetation overlap, making these places urgent targets for greening to support the equal health of the population. By treating social wellbeing as a planning input rather than a final outcome, this study links environmental exposure to health equity. The approach can be used in other fast-growing cities.

Title: Pain Inequity by Design? Administrative Gaps in Indonesia’s Universal Health Coverage and the Right to Pain Relief: Evidence from Knee Osteoarthritis
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: Yuniza, Mailinda Eka; Hisam, Muhammad Yusuf
Organisations: Yuniza, Prof. Mailinda | Universitas Gadjah Mada
Keywords: health inequalities, pain management, administrative law, right to health, universal  health coverage
Abstract_Text:
Chronic pain constitutes a major cause of disability and diminished well-being, yet access to effective pain management remains highly unequal. The Lancet Commission on Palliative Care and Pain Relief identifies an “access abyss” in which the majority of individuals in low- and middle-income countries lack basic pain relief. This inequity arises not only from clinical factors but also from legal and administrative structures. Pain equity should therefore be established as an explicit objective of universal health coverage (UHC) in the post-2030 agenda.
First, through doctrinal legal analysis, we examine how Indonesian law shapes access to pain care: constitutional and international right-to-health norms, the narcotics regime (Law 35/2009; Constitutional Court Decision 106/PUU-XVIII/2020), and the national health insurance (JKN/BPJS Kesehatan) benefit package, including formulary restrictions and case-based tariffs. Applying the general principles of good administration (Law 30/2014), we assess whether coverage exclusions are evidence-based, transparent and contestable, and what remedies exist.
Second, evidence is drawn from a doctoral clinical study at Universitas Gadjah Mada (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07355712) involving patients with knee osteoarthritis. Prolotherapy combined with personalized physical activity demonstrated superior outcomes compared to prolotherapy alone in reducing matrix metalloproteinase-3 (MMP-3) and improving WOMAC pain, stiffness, and function scores; both interventions reduced interleukin-1β (IL-1β). However, these low-cost, non-surgical pain interventions are not explicitly included in the JKN benefit package, resulting in cost burdens for older patients and exacerbating inequalities in healthy aging.
A pain equity framework is proposed: (1) transparent, health technology assessment (HTA)-based benefit decisions with published reasoning; (2) administrative appeal pathways for denied pain care; (3) inclusion of evidence-based chronic pain and palliative services in UHC packages; and (4) balanced narcotics regulation that safeguards medical access. Integrating pain relief into UHC governance links SDG 3.8 and SDG 16 to promoting healthy aging beyond 2030.

Title: Fostering Sustainable Science Education: Practical STEM Instruction and Low-Cost Pedagogical Strategies for Resource-Constrained Contexts.
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Use of ICT tools in teaching and learning of STEM education
Abstract_Text:
Quality STEM education is central to achieving Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) and equipping the next generation with problem-solving skills for sustainable development.
However, delivering practical physics and integrated science lessons in resource-constrained environments often presents significant challenges due to limited laboratory infrastructure and materials.
​This presentation explores actionable strategies for implementing hands-on, low-cost practical instruction in secondary science classrooms.
By integrating accessible experimental setups such as low-voltage solar kits, practical circuit mechanics, and visual instructional materials educators can effectively demystify abstract physical concepts while fostering environmental awareness and technical competence.
The session highlights practical approaches to activity-based learning, student engagement strategies, and the integration of digital tools to support science pedagogy. Ultimately, enhancing practical STEM literacy at the secondary level serves as a crucial driver for sustainable community development and capacity building.

Title: Agricultural land and food-system transitions for sustainability beyond 2030 (p1)
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Hu, Dr. Yuanchao | Guangdong University of Technology
Keywords: Agricultural sustainability, land-use change, carbon emissions, nutrient flows, human health
Abstract_Text:
Agricultural and food-system transitions reshape land use, resource flows, and ecological processes, with far-reaching implications for sustainability. Their consequences extend beyond production sites: policies promoting domestic food self-sufficiency can redistribute global land-use pressures, changes in vegetation cover can generate climate feedbacks, and food consumption can drive nutrient pollution in distant inland and coastal waters. As the international community looks beyond 2030, understanding these connections is essential for advancing sustainability while avoiding unintended consequences across regions and environmental systems.
Proposed by Yuanchao Xue, Zhen, and other colleagues, this session will examine how changes in agricultural production, food demand, and resource management interact with land-use dynamics to shape sustainability outcomes across local, regional, and global scales. From seasonal underutilization of farmland and long-term abandonment to shifts in crop production and aquatic food consumption, these changes link food security to climate regulation, biodiversity conservation, and nutrient cycling. This session brings together research on farmland underutilization and abandonment; agricultural policy, food self-sufficiency, and global land demand; vegetation–climate feedbacks; and opportunities to improve protected-area connectivity through food-system transformation and ecosystem stewardship. The session also explores the management of agricultural residues, nutrient surpluses and deficits, phosphorus depletion and conservation, and consumption-driven eutrophication. By linking these perspectives, we aim to identify how coordinated policies, spatially differentiated management, and integrated food-system strategies can reconcile productive land use with resource conservation, ecosystem protection, and environmental quality. We have invited eight speakers, and we welcome more relevant speakers to join our discussions.
Farmland underutilization has become an increasing challenge to global food security and sustainable agricultural development, with yearly and seasonal abandonment representing two important but distinct forms. However, their spatiotemporal dynamics, key drivers, and interrelationships remain insufficiently understood at the global scale, limiting comprehensive assessments of farmland underutilization and future abandonment risks. To address these gaps, we developed an integrated global assessment framework combining long-term high-resolution land-use and cropping-intensity datasets, a three-stage least squares (3SLS) model, and an XGBoost-SHAP framework to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of yearly and seasonal abandonment, disentangle their interactions and underlying drivers, and project future yearly abandonment risk under multiple SSP-RCP scenarios. The results indicate that: (1) Yearly and seasonal abandonment exhibited contrasting spatiotemporal dynamics during the study period. Seasonal abandonment generally declined across major agricultural regions, whereas yearly abandonment continued to expand globally. Despite these contrasting trends, both forms of abandonment displayed pronounced spatial clustering and significant spatial associations. (2) The two forms of abandonment were governed by distinct environmental and socioeconomic drivers. Seasonal abandonment was more responsive to climatic variability and extreme events, whereas yearly abandonment was primarily shaped by landscape fragmentation, accessibility, and broader socioeconomic conditions. (3) Both contemporaneous and lagged seasonal abandonment significantly shaped yearly abandonment across several regions, with these effects further modulated by landscape configuration and topographic constraints. (4) Under all SSP-RCP scenarios, the future risk of yearly abandonment is projected to increase by 2050, with high-risk areas becoming increasingly spatially clustered.
Growing demand for animal-sourced foods is intensifying global reliance on soybeans, with China, the largest consumer and a low self-sufficiency rate (SSR) country, driving global largest imports and associated environmental spillover. To improve its SSR, China has implemented policies including rehabilitating salt-affected land, approving genetically modified soybeans and promoting healthy dietary transition. Here we evaluated these interventions using a scenario-based framework benchmarked against a no-policy baseline reconstructed soybean demand. China’s SSR declined from full self-sufficiency in 1961 to 17% by 2022 and is projected to decline to 12% by 2050 without intervention. Each 10% implementation of salt-affected land and genetically modified soybeans alone could increase soybean SSR by 1.4% and 1.0%, whereas a 50% healthy dietary implementation alone could raise to 17%. Although individual policies yield modest improvements, their combined implementation could increase SSR to 74% by 2030 and 80% by 2050. This shift could free soybean sufficient to feed 1.89 billion additional people globally while avoiding cropland expansion in tropical frontiers, enabling reforestation and carbon sequestration.
Aquatic foods provide high-quality protein and essential micronutrients, with considerable potential to reduce global nutritional inequalities. Yet soaring aquatic food production stresses local environments through intensive nitrogen and phosphorus losses to aquatic ecosystems. Meanwhile, production and consumption of aquatic foods are unevenly distributed across regions. International trade moves aquatic foods and their nutritional benefits across borders, while nitrogen and phosphorus pollution from aquaculture remains largely in producing regions and can contribute to eutrophication. How additional demand driven by dietary and nutritional equity goals will reshape global supply chains and their environmental impacts remains unclear. Here, we build a spatially resolved aquaculture system model to quantify nitrogen and phosphorus burdens embodied in global aquatic food trade. We combined a novel dynamic trade network with region-specific material-flow and environmental-fate models to reveal local eutrophication driven by aquatic food demand from elsewhere. We then simulate changes in production and trade under dietary and nutritional equity scenarios, accounting for production capacity and existing trade relationships. We also assess the resulting eutrophication-related ecosystem damage in inland and coastal waters. This study is expected to identify key production regions supplying additional demand, shifts in nitrogen and phosphorus burdens, and potential hotspots of ecosystem damage. The findings could inform efforts to reconcile nutritional equity with aquatic ecosystem protection, advancing Sustainable Development Goals 2, 6 and 14 beyond 2030.
Food systems underpin human nutrition and livelihoods but are currently on unsustainable trajectories, failing to ensure global food security while exerting substantial environmental pressures. Transitioning towards sustainable food systems therefore requires robust, integrated modeling frameworks to assess impacts, pathways for change, and trade-offs. In this study, we conduct a systematic review of food system modeling studies and synthesize 850 sustainability indicators from 150 publications. We show that indicator use is highly fragmented across the reviewed literature: of the 850 indicators identified, 436 are unique, with limited convergence in definitions, metrics, or reporting practices. This lack of standardization substantially constrains comparability across models, scenarios, and regions, hindering cumulative knowledge building and cross-study synthesis. We further find that around one-third of studies apply model coupling or integrated assessment frameworks, yet such approaches remain unevenly adopted across spatial scales and transition strategies. Our findings highlight the need for harmonized, transparent, and policy-relevant indicator frameworks to enable systematic and comparable assessment of food system transition outcomes.
Land-use change driven by ecological restoration can substantially alter vegetation greenness and land–atmosphere interactions, yet the future climate feedbacks of vegetation greening under different restoration configurations remain poorly understood. Here, we coupled the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with the Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model to investigate the seasonal temperature responses to vegetation greening associated with the Grain for Green Program (GFGP) on the Loess Plateau and to assess future climate feedbacks under alternative land-use scenarios. The results showed pronounced seasonal differences in temperature responses, with the strongest cooling occurring in summer and weaker responses in other seasons. Summer cooling was associated with changes in surface energy partitioning and boundary-layer processes, and its magnitude increased along the precipitation gradient, indicating that background hydroclimatic conditions modulate the thermal effects of vegetation greening. Among the future land-use scenarios, Scenario III produced the strongest regional mean summer cooling, while the precipitation-based Scenario VI most closely reproduced this cooling among Scenarios IV–VI. These findings demonstrate that the future climate feedbacks of vegetation greening depend on both land-use configuration and regional precipitation conditions. Accounting for these interactions can improve the spatial allocation of ecological restoration and support climate-informed land-use planning on the Loess Plateau.
Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) has become a vital approach to adapting to and mitigating climate change while safeguarding food security. Future climate change is projected to shift suitable cropping areas northward in China. Guided by the CSA framework, this study establishes a refined spatial linear optimization model for multi-cropping at national and provincial scales to explore the potential of crop switching in synergizing climate change adaptation and mitigation under the RCP4.5 and RCP6.0 scenarios in the 2050s. Results indicate that under national planning compared to the future baseline scenario without spatial crop reallocation, an adaptation optimization strategy increases crop production by 24.1% to 24.6% and achieves staple crop self-sufficiency (wheat, maize, rice, and soybean) by the 2050s under RCP4.5 and RCP6.0, but at the cost of a 19.2% to 23.3% increase in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Alternatively, the mitigation optimization strategy can reduce direct cropland GHG emissions (CH4 and N2O) by 30.8% (86.0% from CH4)to 52.0% (79.9% from CH4) while maintaining crop production. While trade-offs exist, specific weighting regions of the Pareto front reveal co-benefits, including crop production (+4.0% to +21.4%), economic profits (+13% to +28.3%), reduced GHG emissions (−52% to −16.2%), and irrigation water savings (−12.8% to −0.7%). Acknowledging implementation constraints alongside modeling uncertainties, these optimal outcomes indicate that carefully designed crop-switching strategies such as expanding soybean cultivation in North China and replacing rice with wheat, maize, and soybean in the Yangtze River Plain could both enhance climate adaptation and mitigation and help meet China's food demand in the 2050s without cropland expansion.

Title: Agricultural land and food-system transitions for sustainability beyond 2030 (p2)
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: Hu, Dr. Yuanchao | Guangdong University of Technology
Keywords: Agricultural sustainability, land-use change, carbon emissions, nutrient flows, human health
Abstract_Text:
Agricultural and food-system transitions reshape land use, resource flows, and ecological processes, with far-reaching implications for sustainability. Their consequences extend beyond production sites: policies promoting domestic food self-sufficiency can redistribute global land-use pressures, changes in vegetation cover can generate climate feedbacks, and food consumption can drive nutrient pollution in distant inland and coastal waters. As the international community looks beyond 2030, understanding these connections is essential for advancing sustainability while avoiding unintended consequences across regions and environmental systems.
Proposed by Yuanchao Xue, Zhen, and other colleagues, this session will examine how changes in agricultural production, food demand, and resource management interact with land-use dynamics to shape sustainability outcomes across local, regional, and global scales. From seasonal underutilization of farmland and long-term abandonment to shifts in crop production and aquatic food consumption, these changes link food security to climate regulation, biodiversity conservation, and nutrient cycling. This session brings together research on farmland underutilization and abandonment; agricultural policy, food self-sufficiency, and global land demand; vegetation–climate feedbacks; and opportunities to improve protected-area connectivity through food-system transformation and ecosystem stewardship. The session also explores the management of agricultural residues, nutrient surpluses and deficits, phosphorus depletion and conservation, and consumption-driven eutrophication. By linking these perspectives, we aim to identify how coordinated policies, spatially differentiated management, and integrated food-system strategies can reconcile productive land use with resource conservation, ecosystem protection, and environmental quality. We have invited eight speakers, and we welcome more relevant speakers to join our discussions.
Functional connectivity of protected areas (PA) is critical to global biodiversity yet faces growing threats from land-use change. Using an integrated framework, we evaluate how future PA connectivity, measured by mammal movement probability (MMP) and protected area isolation (PAI), responds to food-system transformation and targeted ecosystem stewardship (EcoS) strategies through 2070. Without interventions, global PA connectivity is projected to decline from 2020 to 2070 (-2.0% in MMP and +3.7% in PAI), with substantial regional variability (e.g., PAI ranging from 8.49% decline in Europe to 16.9% increase in Africa). However, coupling food-system transformation with EcoS strategies can not only fully counteract these trends but restore connectivity to above 2020 levels. These integrated strategies also deliver great co-benefits for food security and human health. Our study underscores the necessity to align food-systems transformation with conservation policies to reconcile ecological connectivity with global food security and sustainability.
While household energy transitions are critical for climate mitigation and public health, reliance on macro-scale averages often obscures micro-scale trade-offs in health benefits, affordability, carbon footprints, and distributional equity. This study leverages rural household surveys from five Chinese provinces to evaluate electricity and natural-gas substitution scenarios against a 2022 baseline. Historical data confirm a clear shift toward non-solid fuels—rising from 12.2% in 2018 to 30.5% in 2022—which corresponded with a 33.0% drop in direct household PM2.5 emissions. Scenario modeling reveals that no single transition rate optimizes all policy objectives simultaneously. Electricity substitution minimizes household expenditure and the high-burden share at a 70% transition rate, while maximizing net benefits at 84% (CNY 749.52 per household). Conversely, natural-gas substitution reaches its maximum net benefit at 70% (CNY 537.31 per household). At full substitution, natural gas drives 15.92% of households into high-burden status and generates negative net benefits and elevated carbon footprints in 20 and 47 villages, respectively. Furthermore, although overall expenditure inequality decreases across both pathways, energy-burden inequality experiences a localized rebound effect at higher transition rates. These findings demonstrate that effective transition policies must move beyond broad regional targets to explicitly monitor threshold-crossing affordability risks and village-level carbon dynamics.
Potassium (K) is a crucial factor limiting global food security. However, K imbalance on a large spatial scale has received relatively little attention. Here, we developed a K material flow analysis framework integrating long-term farm survey data from more than 400,000 farms during 2003-2022 to quantify the evolution of K balance and K use efficiency (KUE, K absorption-to-input ratio) in China’s rice cultivation systems. We found that China underwent a substantial transition from widespread K deficit in 2003 towards K surplus in 2022. Spatial K imbalance remains severe. Potassium-supplementing regions have shifted from an extreme K deficit (KUE=2.14) in 2003 to a K balance in 2022, but potassium-stabilizing regions are experiencing K surpluses with a markedly aggravating trend. Scenario analyses showed that optimizing fertilizer nutrient composition provided the greatest potential to correct future K imbalances. These findings highlight the significance of spatially targeted strategies for sustainable K management.
Hidden costs of the agrifood system are damages to the environment, human health and livelihoods that are not reflected in market prices. Such costs are increasingly estimated at the national scale, but where they arise along the supply chain, and how they compare with the value captured at each stage, remain poorly understood. We traced global food consumption through a multi-regional input–output (MRIO) model and attributed environmental, health and social costs to six farm-to-fork stages across 163 regions. We estimate that the global agrifood system generated US$2.6 trillion in hidden costs in 2023, comprising $1.2 trillion in environmental damage, $1.1 trillion in health impacts and $0.3 trillion associated with poverty among food-system workers. Primary production accounts for more than three-quarters of total hidden costs, despite capturing a much smaller share of value added. These findings reveal a sharp divergence between cost generation and value capture along the food chain, with primary production being approximately nine times more cost-intensive per dollar of value added than downstream stages. pressure. Our findings suggest that stage-resolved true cost accounting can reveal where hidden costs accumulate relative to value creation, providing a basis for targeting investment, procurement and policy towards the largest sources of hidden costs.
Phosphorus is an irreplaceable nutrient essential for sustaining agricultural production and global food security. However, growing demand from agriculture and clean-energy technologies, the uneven distribution of phosphate rock resources, and concentrated trade expose countries to varying risks of phosphorus depletion and supply disruption. Meanwhile, phosphorus losses throughout production and consumption further intensify resource pressures and environmental pollution. This study will develop a country-level dynamic material flow model to project phosphorus demand from agriculture and batteries through 2050. By integrating phosphate rock reserves, extraction, international trade, and soil legacy phosphorus, the model will assess regional phosphorus depletion risks and supply vulnerabilities. Scenarios involving improved phosphorus-use efficiency, dietary shifts, reduced food loss and waste, and waste recovery will then be developed to quantify the phosphorus conservation potential, environmental benefits, and interactions among these pathways. The study will identify regions vulnerable to future phosphorus supply risks, reveal how global trade alleviates or amplifies regional scarcity, and determine combinations of strategies suited to different resource endowments and demand structures. The findings will inform efforts to secure food and energy supplies, reduce phosphorus releases to the environment, and advance the Sustainable Development Goals.
Cropland is critical to food security and agricultural development. As a result of adjustments in farmers’ livelihood strategies, their abandonment behavior is jointly influenced by the labor opportunity cost of farming (LOCF) and land fragmentation. However, existing research on the relationships among LOCF, land fragmentation, and cropland abandonment remains insufficient in terms of analyzing farmers’ behavioral decision-making mechanisms. To address this gap, this study developed a theoretical framework based on push–pull theory and cost–benefit analysis to explain the relationships between these, and employed multiple econometric models to estimate the effects using survey data from 2540 mountainous farmers. The findings reveal that both LOCF and land fragmentation could significantly promote farmland abandonment, although the significance of LOCF is relatively low, likely due to the influence of other factors. This suggests that, for mountainous areas, managing land fragmentation remains an important approach to addressing abandoned farmland. Furthermore, LOCF and land fragmentation affect cropland abandonment by promoting labor migration, and LOCF also plays a role by encouraging cropland transfer. The effects of LOCF and land fragmentation on abandonment vary by cropping system and location, with stronger and more pronounced impacts in multi-cropping regions and regions closer to county towns. Therefore, to effectively manage cropland abandonment, improving land markets, developing new agricultural business entities, and developing specialty agriculture in mountainous areas are important strategies for promoting sustainable agricultural development in mountainous areas.

Title: Decentralized Justice and Community Resilience: Nepal's Local Government as a Vehicle for Equitable Sustainable Transformation
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Decentralization, local government, equity, justice, community resilience, sustainable transformation, Nepal
Abstract_Text:
Background & Rationale: Nepal's transition to a federal democratic republic through the 2015 Constitution established three tiers of government—federal, provincial, and local—fundamentally reshaping governance structures and enabling localized approaches to sustainable development. With 753 local government units comprising rural municipalities, municipalities, and district assemblies, Nepal presents a critical case study of how constitutional decentralization can advance equity, social justice, and community resilience while addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Key Question: How can Nepal's local government institutions serve as instruments of just transition and equitable sustainable transformation, particularly in ensuring that vulnerable populations—including smallholder farmers, Indigenous Peoples, and marginalized communities—are not left behind in the implementation of sustainable development?
Focus & Approach: This paper examines the enabling potential and structural challenges of Nepal's three-tier governance system in fostering:
• Equity & Justice: How decentralized governance facilitates locally responsive, culturally appropriate solutions to sustainability challenges while addressing historical inequities and systemic vulnerabilities.
• Community Resilience: The role of local government in building adaptive capacity, social cohesion, and livelihood security in agricultural and rural communities facing climate variability and development pressures.
• Leave No One Behind: Mechanisms and gaps in inclusive participation and benefit-sharing at the local level, particularly for marginalized and Indigenous communities.
Evidence & Implications: Drawing on Nepal's experience implementing decentralized structures and initiatives linking research, extension, and education (REE) at local levels, the analysis identifies how grassroots governance can embed sustainability principles while advancing substantive justice. Insights from agricultural extension, market-led development, and community-based adaptation inform recommendations for strengthening the role of local institutions in resilient, equitable transformation aligned with national and provincial policy frameworks and SDG targets.

Title: A spatial framework for quantifying hail impacts on crop production in Germany
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Authors: Giri, Surendra; Palka, Marlene; Augenstein, Markus; Kunz, Michael; Merz, Bruno; Nendel, Claas
Organisations: Leibniz Centre for Agricultural Landscape Research (ZALF)
Keywords: Hailstorms, Potential Hail Track, Bayesian Beta Regression, MONICA, yield loss
Abstract_Text:
Hailstorms are among the most destructive convective hazards affecting agriculture, yet their high spatial and temporal variability makes it difficult to represent hail damage in crop models. This study developed a spatial framework to estimate hail-induced crop losses by combining radar-derived hail tracks, simulated crop maps and phenological stages, and insurance claims into crop-specific damage. Hail damage was expressed as a reduction factor representing the proportion of effective yield loss and estimated using Bayesian Beta Regression. The model accounted for hail severity, crop type, phenological stage, their interactions, and parameter uncertainty.
The model showed strong predictive performance, explaining 80% of the variation in the training dataset and 77% in an independent test dataset. Yield losses generally increased with hail severity, although crop responses varied across growth stages. Potatoes were particularly vulnerable to moderate and severe hail, while winter rye and spring barley showed greater susceptibility under the most severe hail conditions. The Bayesian approach also provided credible intervals to quantify uncertainty in predicted damage.
The framework was subsequently applied to eight crops, including four winter and four summer crops, across Germany under +2 K and +3 K global warming scenarios. Monthly downscaled hail-occurrence probabilities, regional hail-intensity distributions, and phenology-specific damage factors were combined with MONICA-simulated yields to estimate hail-related yield losses and damage percentages from April to September. When multiple growth stages occurred within a month, the highest stage-specific loss was retained. This approach allowed spatial and seasonal comparisons of projected hail impacts under different warming levels.
By linking observed crop damage relationships with future hail hazards and simulated crop development, the framework extends hail damage assessment from individual events to regional climate change applications. It offers a practical basis for incorporating hail-related losses into crop modelling and evaluating agricultural vulnerability under future climate conditions.

Title: Application of AI and Knowledge Graphs to Environmental Complaint Management for Sustainable Urban Governance
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Chuang, Yen Hsun; Wei, Shih Hsuan; Ho, Zi You
Keywords: Nature Language Processing, Sentiment analysis, Speech Recognition, Environmental pollution management, AI Inference
Abstract_Text: Environmental complaints provide important information on pollution impacts experienced by urban residents. However, complaints often contain ambiguous descriptions and overlapping pollution issues, making it difficult for local authorities to identify specific environmental problems and determine appropriate responses. This study aims to apply artificial intelligence (AI) and knowledge graphs to analyze citizen complaints and support environmental problem identification for sustainable urban governance. A total of 200 environmental complaint calls were collected and divided into 259 audio samples. Speech recognition and semantic analysis were applied to extract pollution-related information from citizen descriptions. Environmental complaints were classified into four major categories: water pollution, odor and air pollution, waste pollution, and noise pollution. Knowledge graphs were constructed to establish relationships among complaint descriptions, pollution characteristics, potential sources, and environmental impacts. The results showed that environmental complaints frequently involved multiple pollution characteristics, particularly those related to odor, waste, and noise. The developed knowledge graphs enabled the identification of relevant pollution categories and potential environmental problems from unstructured complaint descriptions, including cases involving overlapping pollution issues. Furthermore, incorporating environmental terminology improved the reported speech recognition accuracy from approximately 85% to 95%. These findings indicate that integrating AI with knowledge graphs can transform citizens' descriptions of pollution impacts into structured environmental information. This approach provides a basis for improving environmental complaint assessment and supporting local authorities in identifying potential environmental problems, thereby contributing to sustainable urban governance

Title: Ageing at the Margins: How SDG-Linked Deprivations Accumulate to Shape Health and Care-Seeking Among Older Adults
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Organisations: Oduro, Dr. Joseph Kojo | University of Cape Coast
Keywords: Healthy ageing; SDG interactions; health equity; care-seeking; post-2030 agenda; multilevel analysis
Abstract_Text:
Background: Population ageing is rapidly increasing in low- and middle-income countries, yet older adults remain largely invisible in SDG monitoring. This study examines how multiple SDG-linked deprivations accumulate to shape health and care-seeking among older adults, offering lessons for the post-2030 agenda.
Methods: We analysed nationally representative data on 4,753 adults aged 60+. Five SDG-linked indicators were constructed: SDG 1 (poverty), SDG 3 (recent illness), SDG 4 (no formal education), SDG 10 (rural residence), and SDG 13 (Savannah ecological zone). We quantified co-occurring deprivations through an accumulation matrix and composite deprivation score (0–5) and fitted multilevel logistic regressions with random intercepts for enumeration areas.
Results: Disadvantages were common, geographically concentrated, and accumulated additively. Only 14.5% had zero deprivations; 24.5% had four; 4.0% had five. Mean deprivation rose from 0.98 (Coastal) to 3.75 (Savannah), where 95.3% had high deprivation (score ≥3). Rural residence increased illness odds (OR=1.83, 95% CI [1.39, 2.42]) but reduced care-seeking by nearly half (OR=0.54, 95% CI [0.37, 0.79]); lack of education also reduced care-seeking (OR=0.65, 95% CI [0.47, 0.90]). Interaction terms were non-significant (poverty × education: β=0.27, p=.414; poverty × rural: β=0.06, p=.907), but a four-indicator deprivation score was strongly associated with reduced care-seeking (OR=0.79 per additional deprivation, 95% CI [0.70, 0.88], p<.001): each additional deprivation reduced care-seeking by approximately 21%. Intraclass correlations (0.18–0.29) confirmed strong community clustering.
Conclusions: Older adults experience SDG-linked deprivations as accumulating, geographically concentrated burdens. Because deprivations compound additively, every removal of a single deprivation yields a proportional improvement in care-seeking. Three lessons emerge: SDG monitoring must be age-inclusive; health systems must be reoriented toward communities and toward reducing specific barriers (education, rural access); and social protection must be integrated with health policy. As the post-2030 framework takes shape, older adults must move from the margins of sustainable development to its centre.

Title: Perspectives on circular and regenerative supply chains
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Organisations: Rosca, Dr. Eugenia | University of Groningen
Keywords: circular economy, circularity, regeneration, supply chains
Abstract_Text:
Circular supply chains are becoming a reality in many places, yet, many open questions remain about how to design, coordinate, and govern them. This special session brings together research on circular supply chains addressing themes such as governance of inter-organizational relationships needed for circularity, the role of orchestration and digital platforms as enablers, and best practices from several countries. These presentations of empirical insights from ongoing research present various tensions and trade-offs emerging in the implementation of circular economy. Participants will present new findings, exchange perspectives across methods and contexts, and help shape an agenda for the next generation of circular supply chain research.
The transition to circular and regenerative supply chains requires inter-organizational participation. This study uses an inductive, exploratory multiple case study approach to examine the supply chains of 12 award-winning B Corps to understand how they build collaborations to support regeneration within and outside their supply chains. Based on insights from extensive qualitative data, we then deploy collective action theory as an interpretive lens to generate theoretical propositions situated in the empirical data. The findings unpack mechanisms needed to activate stakeholders for regeneration and the use of generosity to reinforce collaborations for regeneration. Using metaphorical imagination, we propose a theoretical explanation for how positive deviants in the regenerative domain develop collaborations for regeneration within and beyond their supply chains. We theorize positive deviance for addressing societal challenges through inter-organizational collaboration by revisiting the B Corp practices through the lens of collective action theory.
Pressing ecological and social challenges demands a fundamental shift from a take-make-waste to a circular economy, where value creation is interconnected across value networks. However, promising circular business models often face structural lock-ins: their diffusion requires synchronized changes across supply systems, infrastructures, regulations, and adoption behaviours. This interdependence creates a systemic chicken-and-egg problem, stalling transformative innovations in pilot phases. Our study explores how a regional ecosystem in Friesland, Netherlands, overcame this lock-in through a value-chain-bootstrapping approach. In 2023–2024, over 30 organizations—farmers, processors, construction firms, municipalities, and provincial authorities—collectively committed to scaling a regenerative, biobased insulation value chain. Despite absent market demand or supportive frameworks, 110 farmers pledged to cultivate hemp on peatland, processors invested in new technologies, and adopters committed to integrating hemp insulation into 1,000 projects within three years. This synchronous alignment of diverse actors in the innovation ecosystem contradicts incremental niche development theories, warranting an in-depth case study. Using a qualitative, process-oriented design, we triangulate semi-structured interviews with actors across the value chain, archival materials (policy documents, reports, agreements), and internal consortium documents. Inductive coding, informed by grounded theory, surfaces mechanisms of coordination, issue framing, and trust-building. Theoretically, we introduce value-chain bootstrapping as a means to pre-construct market configurations, extending literature on circular entrepreneurship and ecosystem orchestration. Practically, we offer actionable insights for policymakers and entrepreneurs to design initiatives scaling circular solutions.
Circular economy transitions require supply chains to develop reverse flows, recovery processes
and open-loop material exchanges that involve a wider and more diverse set of actors than
traditional linear chains. Achieving collective circular outcomes requires these autonomous
actors to work together often across organizational and sectoral boundaries. Traditional supply
chain governance which focuses on vertical buyer-supplier relationships managed by a focal
firm, cannot address the governance challenges of multi-actor, cross-sectoral circular networks
where no single actor holds authority over the whole. However, there is limited empirical
research on network governance mechanisms in circular networks, with literature being
fragmented across sectors and contexts as most studies are often limited to single industries or
specific network types. This paper asks what network governance mechanisms are documented
in published empirical cases of circular networks, and what patterns emerge across different
network types and contexts.
To answer this, we conduct a two-phase study. In the first phase, we conduct a systematic literature study using the PRISMA framework to identify published empirical case studies of circular networks from Web of Science and Scopus. From a final sample of approximately 25 papers, we extract governance mechanisms, actor types, relationship types, network characteristics and governance challenges, wherever specified. We analyze the data through an iterative, abductive approach, moving between analytical constructs from network governance theory and emerging themes from data to identify recurring patterns and develop categories. In the second phase, we conduct 10-12 semi-structured interviews with practitioners and network orchestrators to complement and extend the literature findings to identify mechanisms under-reported in published cases and providing richer understanding of how governance operates in practice. Together, these phases produce an integrative framework of network governance mechanisms in multi-actor circular networks.
Due diligence regulations, carbon reporting and circular economy requirements are
increasing the need for information on suppliers and products. Digital platforms seek to meet this need by providing supplier ESG ratings, carbon footprints and traceability data. In this study, we examine how these platforms represent suppliers, products and material flows, and how buying firms use this information. We analyzed 22 cases, each involving a platform provider and a client firm, based on 44 interviews and public documents. We find that platforms produce sustainability
information in different ways. Supplier assessment platforms mainly use supplier declarations to generate ratings based on their own scoring methods. Carbon accounting platforms combine buyer data with emission factors and estimates when supplier data are unavailable. Traceability platforms record the movement of materials and products. Across these platforms, providers check documents, methods and records, but only partly verify the accuracy of the underlying data.
Buying firms therefore need to check, interpret and combine platform outputs with other information. These outputs are more likely to inform decisions when integrated into existing processes, such as supplier qualification, tenders and product design. Product-level data are particularly relevant for sourcing and design choices, while circularity applications remain largely at the pilot stage. Our findings show that the value of platform-based sustainability information depends not only on how platforms produce it, but also on how buying firms assess and use it.
Objective: The transition to a circular economy is central to Sustainable Development Goal 12
and the European Green Deal, yet evidence on how companies in emerging European capital
markets integrate circularity into corporate strategy remains limited. This study examines the
extent, evolution and quality of circular economy engagement among companies listed on the
Bucharest Stock Exchange between 2015 and 2025, a period covering the shift from voluntary
disclosure to the Non-Financial Reporting Directive and the Corporate Sustainability
Reporting Directive.
Methods: A content analysis was applied to sustainability, non-financial and integrated
reports published by companies listed on the regulated market. A disclosure index was
developed around circular economy principles (reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, redesign),
covering waste management, resource and material efficiency, eco-design, industrial
symbiosis, circular business models, targets and performance indicators. Disclosures were
scored by depth (narrative, quantitative, target-based) and compared across years, industries
and company size.
Results: Circular economy disclosure increased markedly after mandatory non-financial
reporting was introduced and again during preparation for the European Sustainability
Reporting Standards. However, reporting remains dominated by waste management and
recycling, while redesign, product life extension and circular business models are rarely
addressed. Energy, utilities and manufacturing companies report more extensively than
financial and service firms. Quantitative indicators and time-bound targets remain scarce,
suggesting a gap between symbolic commitment and substantive implementation.
Conclusions: Companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange are increasingly engaged in
circularity, but mainly through compliance-driven, end-of-pipe practices. Stronger regulatory
guidance, sector-specific metrics and investor pressure are needed to move toward
transformative circular strategies. The findings inform the sustainable development agenda by
and beyond 2030, showing that mandatory reporting is an enabler, but not a guarantee, of
corporate contributions to sustainable production and consumption in emerging markets.

Title: MicroBIS A novel AI/ML based platform for bacterial and antimicrobial resistance identification and prediction
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Authors: OTIENO, DAVID; OTIENO, BEATRICE; Martin, Evans
Keywords: AMR, antimicrobial resistance, identification and prediction
Abstract_Text:
Background
Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR), one of the top 10 global health threats, poses a critical public health challenge with a projected 10 million deaths annually by 2050 if left unchecked1,2. In 2019, 1.27 million deaths were attributed to AMR, with data gaps in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) impeding global efforts3,4. Fragmented databases limit the understanding of regional AMR burdens and hinder the development of data-driven interventions. Datasets like the Pfizer-ATLAS program are essential for real-time tracking of antibiotic resistance and for building predictive models to forecast AMR.
Methods
The microBIS platform combines a web server, AI/ML processing, and a user-friendly client interface. The MERN Stack workflow was used for web development and Python-based tools like Random Forest and PyBact for AI/ML modeling. Biochemical test results simulated and the Pfizer ATLAS datasets were used to train the platform's models to identify bacteria and predict AMR.
Results
The microBIS app offers intuitive interfaces for bacterial identification and AMR prediction. It uses biochemical test panels (8 or 20 tests) for bacteria identification, achieving a 79% accuracy with the 20-panel and 31% with the 8-panel. When predicting the top 5 bacterial species, accuracy increased to 99% for the 20-panel and 74% for the 8-panel. Certain tests, like citrate production, showed higher predictive value.
For AMR prediction, the Machine Learning (ML) model trained on the Pfizer ATLAS dataset achieved 56% accuracy in predicting antimicrobial susceptibility profiles . Key predictors included bacterial phenotypes and species.
Conclusions
microBIS bridges the gap between accessible biochemical assays and advanced ML tools, offering a cost-effective, scalable solution for bacterial identification and AMR prediction. It empowers healthcare providers and researchers in resource-limited settings with rapid diagnostic capabilities, enhancing clinical decision-making and AMR surveillance. By integrating AMR datasets and predictive analytics, microBIS enables
better care delivery and supports the global fight against AMR.

Title: Digitalisation in Global Climate Adaptation Governance
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: Digitalisation, AI, climate adaptation, climate policy
Abstract_Text: Digital technologies from early warning systems to artificial intelligence are increasingly presented as enablers of climate adaptation. However, systematic evidence on how governments plan to use them, which technologies are planned for different adaptation themes remain scarce. The study offers a near global text-as-data based assessment of digitalisation in national adaptation planning under the Paris Agreement. We analyse the main adaptation documents submitted to the UNFCCC namely the National Adaptation Plans (81 NAPs), Adaptation Communications (71 ACs), and Nationally Determined Contributions (167 NDCs and the EU) to extract 1622 distinct passages which we distinguish using a codebook on technology family, adaptation themes, climate hazards, implementation status, evidence strength, and intensity of digital climate links. Evidence was triangulated across all three documents, duplicate passages were counted once and false positives were removed by reassessing passages, unsure interpretations in documents submitted in Spanish, French, and Arabic. This approach gave us a holistic view on digitalisation in adaptation governance as reliying solely on one document set would have given a broad overview instead of an in-depth view needed to assess the extent to which digitalisation is included in climate adaptation planning. Our findings suggest that digital technology features in 89% of countries, 76% of countries link it a specific climate application. Data platforms and information systems are among the highest use cases (80%) followed by decision support systems (76%) and remote sensing (75%). AI appears in 19% of country submissions and is the most aspirational technology for adaptation. Countries mainly deploy or want to attain technologies for risk assessment and early warning systems specifically for floods (58%) and droughts (57%) with sea-level rise being the main theme in Small Island Developing States. Additionally most of the coded measures utilising technology are conditional goals while only 27% are operational.

Title: Failure of Translating Rights of Nature into French Water Governance? Insights from the Loire and Tavignanu Cases
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Organisations: CAO, Dr. Yixin | Vrije Universiteit Brussel
Keywords: rights of nature, water governance, Europe, France, multispecies justice
Abstract_Text:
The global water crisis has intensified calls to move beyond anthropocentric water governance. Inspired partly by Indigenous cosmologies that understand rivers/nonhumans as living beings, the Rights of Nature (RoN) movement has led to the legal recognition of rivers in countries including Colombia, New Zealand, Australia, etc. Yet translating RoN into Europe’s highly institutionalized and technocratic water-governance systems remains challenging. While some RoN initiatives strengthen stakeholder engagement and empower riverine communities (e.g., the Mar Menor lagoon in Spain), others remain largely symbolic, with limited effects on formal policy and implementation.
This study examines how RoN is translated into the French context through two pioneering initiatives: the Parlement de Loire (2019) and the Déclaration des Droits du Fleuve Tavignanu in Corsica (2021). The Parlement de Loire, the first major RoN initiative in France, reimagines the Loire as a subject and creates spaces for dialogue among scientists, stakeholders, artists, and citizens. In 2026, a bill proposing recognition of the Loire as a natural legal entity was submitted to the French National Assembly. In Corsica, the Tavignanu Declaration emerged from civil-society mobilization against a landfill project in 2015 and was subsequently endorsed by the Corsican Assembly, representing the first formal political recognition of river rights in France. After more than a decade of legal battles, the dispute culminated in a 2026 court ruling that halted the landfill project.
Drawing on 38 interviews conducted in 2025 and participant observation at meetings and events, the study analyses both the opportunities and limitations of RoN in France. It highlights persistent difficulties in translating river personhood into French institutional frameworks and in establishing legitimate forms of nonhuman representation. Although neither initiative has secured enforceable legal status, both cases create new socio-political spaces for renegotiating human–river relationships and advancing discussions on ecocentric transformations in water governance in France.

Title: Youth lead current dietary emissions while seniors increasingly drive total emission growth
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Li, Yanxian; Yan, Jin; He, Pan; Pradhan, Prajal; Fang, Shuai; Shan, Yuli; Ruzzenenti, Franco; Hubacek, Klaus
Keywords: Climate change, emission accounting, food consumption, age groups
Abstract_Text: Diets across age groups vary in both nutritional quality and greenhouse gas emissions, yet their relationship remains poorly understood in the context of population aging and evolving dietary patterns. We evaluated dietary emissions associated with 141 products across 22 age groups in 149 countries from 2000 to 2019, combining age-specific dietary intake from the Global Dietary Database with a consumption-based emission inventory derived from FAOSTAT. We quantified changes in emissions alongside shifts in nutritional quality and examined contributions of demographic and dietary factors. Adolescents and young adults generally had the highest per-capita dietary emissions, while seniors contributed most to global emission growth, particularly in high- and upper-middle-income countries. Increased meat intake was a leading contributor to rising emissions and frequently coincided with declining nutritional quality. These findings highlight the need for dietary-emission mitigation efforts across age groups that account for demographic shifts, nutritional needs, and national development contexts.

Title: Counting Care in Thailand's Smoky Season
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Keywords: equity and justice, transboundary climate risks, human mobility
Abstract_Text: Environmental governance under the SDGs relies on instruments such as air quality indices and hotspot maps that make harm visible and measurable. This study asks what those instruments leave out. Drawing on three months of fieldwork in Ban Pong, northern Thailand, I examine how the annual smoky season organises gendered care work and who pays for breathable air. I argue that unpaid reproductive labour during the season is what keeps households habitable through the atmospheric crisis, and that current governance instruments are designed in ways that systematically overlook this labour. I adopted a qualitative design informed by feminist political ecology. My study draws on eleven individual interviews, five of which are life-history depth, a focus group with eight elders, and three key informants from government and NGOs. Coding was abductive and done in MAXQDA. The analysis develops two concepts. Seasonal habitability describes the differentiated capacity to stay, work, care or leave during recurring environmental degradation. Institutional displacement refers to the shift in responsibility from state instruments onto households. Residents describe the season as pakati, or ordinary. Exposure becomes normal when livelihood and care obligations make leaving impossible. Women absorbed most of the additional domestic work, which included cleaning and sealing rooms. Men were also drawn into care, though disproportionately. Their public and technically organised work, such as fire patrol and monitoring, was recognised and equipped by state agencies. Intimate care, mostly carried out by women, remained invisible. None of the instruments I reviewed, from PM2.5 standards to clean-air rooms, treated households as reproductive units. This study argues that haze policy should count and support the reproductive labour that sustains lives during the smoky season. Sustainability metrics that ignore reproductive labour produce unjust outcomes. So, this paper calls for a post-2030 agenda that counts care as a precondition for equitable transformation.

Title: Towards Fire-informed Conservation Management in Wasur National Park: Integrating Human and Ecological Dimensions of Fire
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: national research and innovation agency, republic of Indonesia
Keywords: biodiversity, biosphere integrity, landscape management, indigenous people, conservation area
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Fire is an integral component of the landscapes of Wasur National Park (Wasur NP) and is closely connected with Indigenous livelihoods, ecological processes, and landscape management. This study aims to understand fire as a social-ecological process and develop implications for conservation management that integrate ecological dynamics with Indigenous knowledge, fire practices, and institutions.
Methods: The study was conducted in Wasur NP, South Papua, Indonesia. The park is a designated Ramsar Site and forms part of the Trans-Fly biogeographic region, a distinctive landscape characterized by extensive savannas, wetlands, and forests in southern New Guinea. A mixed-methods approach examined Indigenous fire practices and traditional ecological knowledge, fire regime dynamics and their relationships with climate and human activities, ecological changes associated with repeated burning, and institutions governing traditional fire use.
Key results: Fire was found to be embedded in Indigenous livelihood practices and landscape management rather than functioning solely as an ecological disturbance. Traditional fire practices are informed by knowledge of vegetation, landscape conditions, seasonality, and livelihood needs. Fire regime dynamics reflect interactions between human activities and environmental conditions, while repeated burning is associated with changes in ecological conditions across the landscape. Institutional arrangements governing fire use differ among situations, with variations in rules, actors, monitoring, compliance, and enforcement shaping institutional effectiveness. These findings indicate that uniform fire suppression may not adequately reflect the social-ecological complexity of fire in Wasur.
Conclusions: The study proposes fire-informed conservation management as a basis for integrating human and ecological dimensions of fire into protected-area governance. This approach can support context-sensitive conservation while recognizing Indigenous knowledge, livelihoods, and local institutions. Beyond 2030, integrating fire dynamics, biodiversity conservation, Indigenous knowledge, and institutional capacity can contribute to more resilient and equitable pathways for sustainable management of social-ecological systems.

Title: COMMUNITY-BASED ECOTOURISM FOR THE SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT GOALS: EVIDENCE FROM NINH BINH, VIETNAM
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Tran, Thi Thu Ha; Do, Thi Phuong
Organisations: Tran, Prof. Thi Thu Ha | Vietnam National University of Forestry (VNUF)
Keywords: Biodiversity conservation, community-based ecotourism, Sustainable Development Goals, participatory governance, local livelihoods
Abstract_Text:
This study examines the evidence on the contributions of community-based ecotourism (CBET) to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 1, 8, 12, 15, and 16 across three protected areas in Ninh Binh, Vietnam including Cuc Phương and Xuan Thuy National Parks, and Van Long Nature Reserve. The SDG 14 is considered specifically for Xuan Thuy where evidence relating to coastal ecosystems and aquatic resources is available.
The study combines secondary document analysis with a comparative case study approach. The documents are analysed across four dimensions: (i) livelihoods and employment; (ii) responsible tourism practices; (iii) ecosystem and biodiversity conservation; and (iv) governance, coordination, and community participation in decision-making. Each finding is classified into five evidence levels: potential, activities, outputs, outcomes, and impacts. This classification distinguishes between anticipated contributions, implemented actions, and verifiable changes.
The three cases exhibit different approaches to organising tourism activities. In Cuc Phuong, tourism services are linked to national park management and buffer-zone communities. In Van Long, boat-tour services are organised through a cooperative and a rotational system. In Xuan Thuy, tourism services are provided by local households within the context of coastal livelihoods. These arrangements indicate preliminary contributions to the SDGs by creating opportunities for community members to provide tourism services, supporting local livelihoods, and linking tourism activities with resource management. However, the extent of these contributions varies across the sites. Available evidence remains insufficient to establish actual outcomes and impacts in terms of increased household income, employment quality, equitable benefit distribution, responsible tourism practices, participation in decision-making, and conservation effectiveness.
CBET can contribute to advancing the SDGs, but the extent to which these contributions are realised needs to be assessed through verifiable socioeconomic and environmental outcomes. These dimensions warrant particular attention in monitoring progress towards the 2030 Agenda and in designing sustainable development programmes for the post-2030 period.

Title: Who pays for the cloud? Data centre expansion, water and energy trade-offs in Indonesia’s digital transition
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Trustworthy AI, information integrity, data autonomy, and sustainability impacts of AI
Organisations: Al Asyari, Dr. Haekal | Universitas Gadjah Mada
Keywords: AI spillover effects, data governance, water–energy nexus, data centres, Indonesia
Abstract_Text:
Indonesia is positioning itself as Southeast Asia’s next artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure hub. Data localisation rules, tax holidays and special economic zones attract record data centre investment, framed as progress towards Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 9. This paper asks who bears the costs of that expansion, and whether current governance distributes them in line with the SDGs.
The study combines doctrinal and policy analysis of Indonesia’s legal framework (Government Regulation 71/2019 on electronic systems, the Personal Data Protection Law, investment incentive and special economic zone rules) with the non-binding ASEAN Guide for Sustainable Data Centre Development (2025). Industry and market reports supply data on capacity, energy and water demand. A distributional lens maps benefits and burdens across SDGs 6, 7, 9 and 13.
Preliminary findings show a structural mismatch: legal instruments reward installed capacity, while environmental performance remains voluntary and largely undisclosed. Coal supplied two-thirds of national electricity in 2024, yet data centres alone could require about 19,000 GWh by 2030. Their projected water use more than doubles, from roughly 38 to 87 billion litres between 2025 and 2030, with capacity concentrated almost entirely in Greater Jakarta and Batam. Forecasts for 2030 range from under 1 GW to almost 12 GW, so grid, water and incentive planning rests on unverified projections. Burdens fall on grid users, local water users and public budgets; benefits accrue mainly to operators and foreign cloud demand, including load displaced from Singapore.
Data centres can enable sustainable development only if growth is conditional. The paper proposes linking incentives to efficiency and clean-energy thresholds, mandatory disclosure of energy, water and carbon performance, water-stress-sensitive siting, and local benefit-sharing. These measures offer a transferable model for governing digital infrastructure in a post-2030 agenda, ensuring the digital transition does not undermine the green one.

Title: Sovereign for whom? Digital sovereignty, the postcolonial state and the blind spots of Sustainable Development Goal 16
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Al Asyari, Dr. Haekal | Universitas Gadjah Mada
Keywords: emerging governance frameworks, data governance, digital sovereignty, Third World approaches to international law, Indonesia
Abstract_Text:
Digital sovereignty has become a rallying claim for Global South states resisting data extraction by foreign platforms. Yet sovereignty can be turned inward, against the very people it claims to protect. This paper asks how the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) shape this tension, using Indonesia as a case study.
Drawing on Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), the paper combines doctrinal analysis of Indonesia’s digital governance framework with a critical reading of the SDG targets and indicators that govern data and connectivity. It examines the 2019 internet shutdowns in Papua, later declared unlawful by the Jakarta Administrative Court, the 2022 platform blocking under the electronic systems operator registration regime, and state data integration through the One Data Indonesia policy.
The SDG framework strengthens the data-hungry state. Through the “data revolution” agenda and targets 17.18–17.19, it treats national governments as trusted custodians of data for development. The same sovereignty, exercised against citizens, undermines targets 9.c on universal internet access, 10.2 on inclusion and 16.10 on public access to information and fundamental freedoms. The burden falls hardest on marginalised regions such as Papua. These harms remain invisible: no SDG indicator measures shutdowns, blocking or surveillance, and indicator 16.10.2 records only whether access-to-information guarantees exist. A state can therefore report progress while cutting entire regions offline. This reproduces a pattern TWAIL has long identified, in which the postcolonial state accumulates power in the name of development and its people.
Digital sovereignty supports sustainable development only when it is anchored in people rather than the state alone. For the post-2030 agenda, the paper proposes a people-centred data sovereignty principle: a digital rights target with indicators on shutdowns and blocking, community data governance inspired by Indigenous data sovereignty, and independent monitoring beyond state self-reporting.

Title: Blueprinting Nigeria's Future: Sustainable Urbanization for Healthier, Equitable, and Resilient Cities
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Amadasun, Prof. Akongbowa Bramwell | Federal University Wukari, Wukari,  Taraba State, Nigeria
Keywords: Sustainable Urbanization, Public Health, Nigeria, Clean Sanitation, Affordable Housing.
