Abstract_Text: Nigeria's rapid demographic shift has triggered unprecedented urban growth, presenting a dual challenge: managing vast population influxes while safeguarding public health and ecological integrity. This paper explores the intersection of sustainable urbanization and public well-being in Nigeria, positioning healthy cities as the foundation for the nation's long-term sustainable development. Specifically, it examines the synergistic impacts of three core pillars within the Nigerian context: clean sanitation, integrated green spaces, and affordable housing. Employing a mixed-methods research design, this study synthesizes qualitative policy evaluations with quantitative infrastructure deficit data across three major Nigerian metropolitan hubs: Lagos, Kano, and Abuja. The methodology includes a systematic review of federal and state urban development frameworks alongside empirical field observations of sanitation distribution, urban canopy coverage, and housing affordability indices. Spatial analysis via GIS mapping is utilized to evaluate the accessibility of green spaces and sanitation facilities relative to population density and socioeconomic strata. The findings indicate that isolating these infrastructure components leads to fragmented, inefficient urban governance. Conversely, a holistic, health-centric planning paradigm yields compounding benefits across multiple United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities). Circular economy solutions in waste management can significantly mitigate endemic disease risks, while urban greening combats the sub-Saharan heat island effect. Ultimately, this paper provides Nigerian policymakers, urban planners, and public health advocates with an actionable framework to transition from speculative real estate growth toward human-centric, climate-adaptive urban ecosystems

Title: Establishing an EHS Wide Scope 3 Emissions Baseline: A Data-Driven Digital Platform for Healthcare Carbon Accounting
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Advances in AI methods, big data, and digital technologies for sustainability analytics
Authors: Alloghani, Nouf; Al ketbi, Yomna; Khoori, Maitha; Alattal, Zakaria
Keywords: Scope 3 emissions, healthcare sustainability, greenhouse-gas accounting, carbon accounting; automated emissions calculation, spend-based method, digital health innovation, hospital carbon footprint
Abstract_Text: Healthcare Scope 3 emissions arise across complex procurement and operational activities, making measurement difficult. At Emirates Health Services (EHS), fragmented data and no standardised process limited portfolio visibility. Costly commercial platforms offered limited healthcare customisation, creating the need for a practical, internally governed digital alternative. This project aimed to establish an EHS-wide Scope 3 baseline through a purpose-built, in-house digital platform that converts financial data into decision-ready greenhouse-gas (GHG) outputs. EHS developed a hospital-specific GHG platform with centralised data-quality review and benchmarking. The platform imports available financial data and automates calculations using both spend-based and activity-based methods. Calculations are aligned with the GHG Protocol Scope 3 framework and cover all 15 Scope 3 categories. The 2025 exercise included procurement, transport, waste, catering, professional services, and other expenditure categories across the EHS portfolio. The programme established the first EHS-wide Scope 3 baseline across all 17 hospitals. Total reported emissions for the 2025 reporting year were 154,297 tCO₂e. Medical devices represented 35% and pharmaceuticals 27% of the total footprint; together, these categories accounted for 62% of reported emissions, identifying procurement as the principal reduction opportunity. Al Qassimi Hospital recorded the highest footprint, at 43,697 tCO₂e or 28% of the EHS total. At this site, medical devices and pharmaceuticals accounted for 73% of reported emissions, guiding a targeted reduction roadmap. All 17 EHS hospitals were onboarded to the platform. The in-house model also indicated estimated annual savings exceeding USD 150,000 compared with equivalent commercial GHG software. The EHS platform demonstrates that an automated, governed Scope 3 accounting process can provide healthcare organisations with portfolio visibility and site-level priorities for action. The programme supports green procurement, supplier engagement, hospital reduction roadmaps, ESG reporting readiness, and alignment with UAE Net Zero 2050. Further work will finalise data-quality review and increase activity-based data for priority categories.

Title: Urban emergy metabolism of China’s cities
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: System perspective for addressing one health nexus within ecological ceilings
Keywords: Urban metabolism, Emergy analysis, Urban system, Sustainability, China
Abstract_Text: Unprecedented pace of urbanization and industrialization caused a massive increase in China’s urban metabolic pressure. The trend presents an urgent challenge for detailing the long-term changes and disparities in urban metabolic performances in a wide range of cities. Here, we present empirical evidence of 283 China’s cities from 2000 to 2020 based on emergy analysis indicating that China’s urban metabolic performance gradually becomes worse. For example, the environmental sustainability index decreased by 81.64% between 2000 and 2018. In addition, emergy-based performances among China’s cities show considerable differences. Agricultural cities and light manufacturing cities have better sustainability; energy production cities face high environmental pressure. Scenarios for 2030 show that total emergy use would experience slower growth; and most cities continue their decline in emergy metabolism. To ensure overall progress on urban metabolic performance, heavy manufacturing cities and energy production cities should give more attention in adjusting emergy structure.

Title: Listening before optimising: consultation and iterative modelling for integrating public and stakeholder opinion in energy and integrated assessment models
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Organisations: Velasco Herrejon, Dr. Paola | University of Oslo
Keywords: energy system modelling; integrated assessment; stakeholder participation; social acceptance; wind power; well-being
Abstract_Text:
Energy system models (ESMs) and integrated assessment models (IAMs) underpin decarbonisation pathways, yet they typically optimise for cost and technical feasibility. Local perspectives about fairness and well-being are usually treated as exogenous or omitted. As a result, pathways can look optimal but be contested in practice, as strong local opposition to onshore wind in Norway illustrates. Within the SAMVIND project, which combines stakeholder analysis, the capabilities approach and energy system modelling, we examine the challenges and options for representing stakeholder opinions, particularly at the community level in such models.
We identify four core challenges. First, qualitative, plural and place-specific values are hard to translate into model parameters without flattening them. Second, consulted groups may not be representative, and organised or vocal groups can dominate. Third, opinions can shift over time and in response to the very scenarios being modelled. Fourth, local concerns sit at a different scale from national or global model resolution. Available options range from survey-derived acceptance constraints and proxy indicators to spatial exclusion layers, multi-criteria approaches and well-being metrics.
We argue that no single static data source or quantitative method can resolve these tensions. Rather, public and stakeholder opinion is best captured and integrated through consultation and iterative modelling in participative processes. Stakeholders help frame questions, review assumptions and scenarios, and challenge model results. Model structures and parameters are then revised, and the cycle repeats. This treats opinion as dynamic and deliberative rather than as a fixed input. It makes value judgements explicit and builds legitimacy for, and ownership of, the results. The approach has costs: time, resources and facilitation skills, plus the need to manage power asymmetries and consultation fatigue. Drawing on the SAMVIND approach, we offer practical recommendations for modellers who wish to embed participation in ESM and IAM workflows.

Title: Perceived Impacts of Climate Variability on Human Health and Resilience: Evidence from a Mountain Community in Nepal
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Khanal, Sulav; Acharya, Apurba; Kafle, Bharat; Aryal, Umesh Raj
Organisations: ARYAL, Prof. Umesh Raj | Karnali Academy Of Health Sciences
Keywords: Climate variability, perceived health impacts, public health preparedness, and SDGs
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Climate change has already affected the global community and is a priority issue of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Therefore, this study aims to assess household heads’ perceptions of climate variability (PCV) and its association with perceived reported disease (PRD) occurrence in a mountain community of Nepal.
Methods: A mixed‑methods approach was used by integrating quantitative, qualitative, and meteorological data. A total of 244 household heads were interviewed face‑to‑face in Chandannath Municipality, Jumla, Nepal, during September & October 2026. Perceived climate variability index (PCVI) and perceived disease scores were computed using 107 binary response questions. Next, FGD and KII were conducted to triangulate with survey data. These findings were correlated with decadal meteorological data. Ethical Clearance was obtained from the IRC-KAHS.
Results: One-third of households reported high climate change variability, and more than nine-tenths of them reported PRD in the last 10 years. A higher percentage of them perceived an increase in temperature (94.7 %), followed by erratic rainfall (93.9%), and reduced snowfall (93%). The most common diseases reported were diarrhea, dysentery, common cold/fever, headache, and body pain. No significant relationship was found between total PCV score and PRD score (rs=0.043, p=0.509). Qualitative study explored increased temperature and changing patterns of rainfall & snowfall as accountable for the above-mentioned diseases in the community. Further, Meteorological data supported findings of increased temperature (τ=+0.511, P=0.040) and increased relative humidity (τ=+0.511, P=0.040), while seasonal rainfall patterns showed no statistically significant trends (τ=+0.333, P=0.180), and snowfall data were limited for the last 10 years.
Conclusion: The results highlight that local people are already having their health affected by changing patterns of climate variability. This suggests the need to strengthen public health preparedness for climate change in mountain areas, which will also contribute to achieving the SDGs.

Title: Assessing the socioeconomic impacts of cross-border power interconnection: evidence from Asia
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Mao, Hanjie; Gerasimenko, Daria; Zhang, Da; Su, Bin
Keywords: decarbonization, mitigation scenarios, cross-border power interconnection, net-zero transition pathways, socioeconomic impact assessment
Abstract_Text:
Cross-border power interconnection can support net-zero electricity transitions by enabling regional coordination of infrastructure investment and system operation. Its socioeconomic implications unfold over time as power systems respond to changing demand, technological options and decarbonisation requirements. This study examines how regional electricity cooperation shapes transition pathways and how the associated infrastructure and operating configurations relate to socioeconomic outcomes.
A pathway perspective links decisions across successive planning periods, connecting near-term infrastructure choices with longer-term system development. Infrastructure built in one period can remain in service for decades, influencing subsequent capacity needs, operating patterns and opportunities for regional exchange. The scale and composition of investment, together with changes in electricity supply, link decarbonisation pathways to their economic and social implications.
Focusing on regional power systems in Asia, the study examines cross-border interconnection pathways through 2050 using a spatially resolved, multi-period planning framework. It integrates power system planning with an assessment of associated socioeconomic impacts, including investment costs, employment and affordability. Comparable cooperation scenarios are used to examine how interconnection development influences the configuration and use of power infrastructure across the transition. The analysis follows these relationships across planning periods to assess how the socioeconomic implications of cooperation evolve alongside the electricity system.
By connecting infrastructure decisions with their implications over time, the study places regional electricity cooperation within the broader context of sustainable development. Its contribution is an integrated assessment of interconnection pathways that brings technical planning and socioeconomic considerations into the same analytical framework. This perspective informs regional cooperation strategies that address both decarbonisation objectives and the economic and social dimensions of the transition.

Title: Environmental Plans to (Re)distribute Scarce Environmental Utilisation Space: The Case of Pesticides
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Keywords: pesticides, environmental health, exposure pathways, regulatory responses, sustainable land use
Abstract_Text:
The use of pesticides raises concern regarding their effects on human health and environmental quality. In the Netherlands, municipalities are required to regulate the use of pesticides through their environmental (land-use) plan (omgevingsplan). Especially in the last years, Dutch municipalities aim to further reduce, or completely ban the use of pesticides through their environmental plans.
In this contribution, we hypothesize that regulating the use of pesticides in environmental plans can be understood not only as a response to environmental and health risks, but also as a means to (re)distribute scarce environmental utilisation space: the leeway within a specific area to authorise human and economic activities while staying within environmental quality standards. Agricultural activities indeed compete for scarce environmental utilisation space with other activities, such as housing development. This, in turn, raises questions about the legal framework that should govern this (re)distribution. Legal concepts and principles developed in other areas of law concerning scarce public rights, such as subsidies, may offer a useful point of reference for assessing the regulation of scarce environmental utilisation space.
Our contribution begins with an overview of the instruments municipalities use in practice to regulate the use of pesticides, which involves the application of the precautionary principle and the duty of care. Subsequently, we argue how the use of these competences can be understood not only as a response to environmental and health risks, but also as a means of (re)distributing scarce environmental utilisation space. Finally, we set out what we believe are the important (legal) ideas and safeguards that should be considered when regulating the use of pesticides in environmental plans.
A sufficient legal framework to redistribute scarce environmental utilisation space is key to pursue sustainable development towards and beyond 2030, where healthy living environments and land use must be pursued within the ecological limits.

Title: Waste, Water and Warming: How Indian Capital Markets Value Environmental Sustainability Performance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Tandon, Dr. Anjali | Institute for Studies in Industrial Development
Keywords: Environmental sustainability, Climate finance, Firm valuation, Capital markets, ESG performance
Abstract_Text:
The transition towards a low-carbon and resource-efficient economy depends critically on transforming production systems and mobilising investment in clean technologies. While climate finance has traditionally been viewed as a domain of public intervention, the scale of investment required increasingly places private investment at the centre of climate action. Financial markets play a critical role in transmitting the signals through firm evaluations of their environmental and sustainability-related actions. However, evidence on the link between firm valuation and sustainability is divided and suffers from the composite measurement, thus limiting our understanding of market response to individual dimensions.
This paper examines distinct operational dimensions: consumptive water use, resource recovery, residual waste management, and warming (direct emissions and renewable energy adoption) in firm-level sustainability and the response received from the capital market. By combining firm-level disclosures reported under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework with the corresponding financial and market information, the differential market valuations are studied across environmental.
Findings provide evidence in support of the heterogeneity hypothesis. First, environmental sustainability is not a homogeneous construct. Second, market valuation differs across the operational dimensions, with stronger response to dimensions where the environmental performance translates into immediate and tangible economic outcomes, such as cost reductions, revenue generation, or lower regulatory risks. Capital markets place a premium on waste recovery and discounts on direct greenhouse gas emissions. The end-of-pipe operations do not appear to receive investor recognition due to their limited economic or regulatory benefits for the firm. Renewable energy adoption is not yet recognised as an investment opportunity primarily due to delays in regulatory uncertainty and competition from conventional fossil-based alternatives.
Private investments are likely to occur in dimensions that generate valuation premiums or discounts. There remains scope for public interventions in the dimensions that are yet to be recognised in capital markets.

Title: Potential employment demand changes under the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism by gender and skill level
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM), Labor demand, Climate policy, Input-Output analysis
Abstract_Text: The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has raised considerable international concern regarding its potential disproportionate impacts on non-EU countries. In this research, we use a multi-regional input-output (MRIO) approach to evaluate short-term employment demand changes across 164 countries resulting from the implementation of the CBAM. We find that although the global net employment demand changes are modest, substantial disparities emerge across regions, countries, skill levels, and genders. EU member states primarily gain employment demand in medium- and high-skilled labor in energy sectors, with increased employment demand under the expanded CBAM that covers all sectors within the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). Conversely, employment demand losses are concentrated in low- and medium-skilled labor in developing countries. In addition, while absolute job losses are larger for men, the relative impacts on women are higher in East Asia and Latin America. These findings suggest that CBAM may reshape global employment demand in ways that reinforce existing international and labor-market inequalities, highlighting the need to incorporate equity considerations into the design of border carbon policies.

Title: Renter Status and Heat Adaptation: Evidence from India
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Climate change adaptation; Cooling technologies; Housing tenure; Inequality, India
Abstract_Text:
The ownership of effective cooling technologies, along with economic resources, climatic and housing conditions, influences the household adaptation to extreme heat. The paper examines the conditional association between active rent-paying status and the ownership of cooling technologies in India. By employing nationally representative data spanning 2014 to 2025, coupled with district-specific monthly climate metrics, it estimates a weighted linear probability model with fixed effects. The research reveals a conditional negative association between the two, notably pronounced for superior technology, i.e., air conditioners (AC). As compared to non-renters, rent-paying households are 4.6 percentage points less likely to own an AC and 3.5 percentage points less likely to own any
cooling appliance. The effect is heterogeneous, depending on income, social stratification, and urban residency. Urban residency plays a moderating role for AC ownership, while income and caste serve as moderators for ownership of any cooling technology. Findings highlight that other than climatic exposure, adaptation inequalities may be driven by socio-economic and structural constraints linked to renter status. Thus, alongside conventional factors that impact heat adaptation, housing-related
constraints should also be considered by the policymakers.

Title: Climate Change and Cropland Distribution: Scenario-based shifts in agro-ecological suitability and potential food-production capacity
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Modeling Earth system interactions, including climate impacts on development
Organisations: KC, Dr. Krishna | University of Guelph
Keywords: Climate change, agricultural frontiers, crop suitability, food security
Abstract_Text: Climate change is expected to reduce crop productivity in many regions while also shifting the geographic distribution of land that is biophysically suitable for agriculture. We examine whether newly suitable land could, under explicitly defined land-conversion and yield assumptions, provide potential production capacity that partly offsets losses where existing cropland becomes less suitable. Using a GIS-based framework built from FAO Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZ) suitability data, historical FAOSTAT yields, and RCP4.5 climate projections, we assess four staple crops (rice, maize, wheat, and potato) to 2100 across six continental regions. We emphasize that the production quantities are scenario-based potential changes rather than forecasts of realized production: cultivation, soil and terrain constraints, infrastructure, institutions, environmental safeguards, and farmer decisions will determine how much of this potential could actually be realized. The analysis indicates a strong geographic redistribution of agro-ecological opportunity, with larger potential gains in North America and Europe and important crop-specific losses in Asia, Africa, South America, and Oceania. The results therefore highlight both adaptation opportunities and major distributional, environmental, and social risks associated with any expansion of agriculture into emerging northern frontiers.

Title: Waste, Water and Warming: How Indian Capital Markets Value Environmental Sustainability Performance
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Tandon, Dr. Anjali | Institute for Studies in Industrial Development
Keywords: Environmental sustainability, Climate finance, Firm valuation, Capital markets, ESG performance
Abstract_Text:
The transition towards a low-carbon and resource-efficient economy depends critically on transforming production systems and mobilising investment in clean technologies. While climate finance has traditionally been viewed as a domain of public intervention, the scale of investment required increasingly places private investment at the centre of climate action. Financial markets play a critical role in transmitting the signals through firm evaluations of their environmental and sustainability-related actions. However, evidence on the link between firm valuation and sustainability is divided and suffers from the composite measurement, thus limiting our understanding of market response to individual dimensions.
This paper examines distinct operational dimensions: consumptive water use, resource recovery, residual waste management, and warming (direct emissions and renewable energy adoption) in firm-level sustainability and the response received from the capital market. By combining firm-level disclosures reported under the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) framework with the corresponding financial and market information, the differential market valuations are studied across environmental.
Findings provide evidence in support of the heterogeneity hypothesis. First, environmental sustainability is not a homogeneous construct. Second, market valuation differs across the operational dimensions, with stronger response to dimensions where the environmental performance translates into immediate and tangible economic outcomes, such as cost reductions, revenue generation, or lower regulatory risks. Capital markets place a premium on waste recovery and discounts on direct greenhouse gas emissions. The end-of-pipe operations do not appear to receive investor recognition due to their limited economic or regulatory benefits for the firm. Renewable energy adoption is not yet recognised as an investment opportunity primarily due to delays in regulatory uncertainty and competition from conventional fossil-based alternatives.
Private investments are likely to occur in dimensions that generate valuation premiums or discounts. There remains scope for public interventions in the dimensions that are yet to be recognised in capital markets.

Title: How Cascading Impacts Framing on Disasters Foreclose Public Dissent: Lessons for Post-2030 Agenda
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: development indicator, disaster governance, governance process, inclusive participation
Abstract_Text:
Objective: The SDG Report 2026 shows 15% of targets on track and 21% on moderate progress. Goals 11 (sustainable cities) and 13 (climate action) score highest, with about 60% or more of assessed targets on track and no regression, despite the report cited insufficient trend data. Their disaster indicators stay ambiguous on slow coastal hazards such as tidal flooding and land subsidence. This paper examines how that ambiguity shapes national coastal policy in Indonesia and what it means for post-2030 indicators.
Methods: Using Foucauldian governmentality, it analyses how arguments about coastal hazards are built and justified in Indonesia's 2025-2029 National Medium-Term Development Plan (RPJMN). It traces these arguments back through reports and presentations of the National Capital Integrated Coastal Development (NCICD) programme, plus indicator metadata, meeting minutes and supporting reports behind the plan. Comparing documents over time shows how the framing changes.
Results: The documents present ambiguous hazards as cascading impacts under the “sinking city” label, increasing urgency across successive versions. This framing supports the shift from the NCICD in Jakarta to a Giant Sea Wall along Java’s entire north coast, now a national strategic project within the RPJMN. Furthermore, to ensure the project’s smooth implementation, the RPJMN frames future public dissent as a strategic risk.
Conclusions: The post-2030 agenda should add indicators on participation, knowledge recognition and power. Communities should co-design them and keep them open to contest. This lets indicators record slow coastal harm and the governance quality that responds to it.

Title: Orchestration as a Spatial Project: From Global Agendas to the Geography of Transnational Climate-Biodiversity Action
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Organisations: German Institute of Development and Sustainability
Keywords: climate-biodiversity integration, transnational governance, forest conservation, forest restoration, remote sensing
Abstract_Text: This paper investigates transnational climate–biodiversity governance as a spatial project, focusing on how global agendas shape the geographical targeting of forest interventions. It asks how global conceptions of climate-biodiversity space in forests are formulated, translated and reconfigured by transnational initiatives, and materialized through place-based implementation. Building on work on orchestration, governmentality and socially produced space, we develop the concept of orchestrative spatial rationalities (OSRs) to analyze the spatial problem definitions and governance prescriptions embedded in global environmental agendas. We trace whether these rationalities are taken up, concretized or discarded in initiative-level spatial rationalities and subsequent spatial patterns of implementation. Empirically, the paper combines qualitative and quantitative text analysis of the Global Climate Action Agenda and Global Biodiversity Framework with analysis of 70 transnational initiatives and 220 projects. A novel geospatial dataset is used to assess the characteristics and distribution of implementation areas, contrasting spatial practice with orchestrative intent.

Title: Evaluating corporate social responsibility disclosures on sustainable development goals and rural development among South Africa financial firms
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Keywords: Leave No One Behind, social vulnerability, Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
Abstract_Text:
Objective
The study evaluated Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) disclosures on the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and rural development among South African firms listed in the financial sector of the Johannesburg Securities Exchange (JSE). Motivated by limited and fragmented evidence linking CSR, SDGs, and rural development, particularly in a context where 31% of South Africa's population reside in rural areas and face persistent financial exclusion.
The study; analysed how firms characterised the connectivity between SDGs and integrated report content elements over time; identifying the specific SDGs disclosed between 2017 and 2024; determining whether disclosures reflect improvements or inhibitors in achieving SDG and rural-development outcomes; and examined disclosure variances against the Nedbank Group benchmark using the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) matrix for the 2024 financial year.
Method
The study utilised a post-positivist paradigm adopting a quantitative content-analysis design. The sample comprised the entire JSE financials sector, whose disclosures were tracked longitudinally over the eight-year period. Audited integrated annual and supplementary reports were downloaded from each company website and cross-referenced against the JSE and Bloomberg platforms. Coding followed Klaus Krippendorff's four-step content- analysis approach of unitizing, sampling, recording, and reducing, operationalised through a codebook adapted from the integrated-reporting content elements and seventeen SDGs. Using Atlas.ti 24, coders identified SDG references and scored each qualifying disclosure on a binary (1/0) scorecard. Research objectives one to three were addressed through deductive reasoning and hypothesis testing, while objective four benchmarked disclosures against the GRI matrix.
Key Results
The findings revealed the extent of SDG and rural-development disclosures, identified, which SDGs financial firms prioritise, and highlighted areas that inhibit progress toward rural development.
Conclusion and relevance
The study contributes to accounting and sustainability scholarship by providing empirical evidence on CSR–SDG connectivity in the South African financial sector and the sector’s role in advancing rural development.

Title: Diverse Metrics for Tracking Sustainability: A Comparative Assessment of National SDG Monitoring Frameworks
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: Sustainability assessment, SDG monitoring methodologies, Sustainability indicators, National indicator frameworks, Cross-national comparison
Abstract_Text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a global framework for sustainable development; however, countries have adopted diverse methodologies to monitor progress towards these goals. Although previous studies have largely compared sustainability outcomes or national performance, comparatively little attention has been given to the methodological approaches underlying national SDG monitoring systems, particularly across countries with different levels of development. This study compares and critically analyzes the SDG monitoring methodologies adopted by India, Japan, Germany, and Vietnam. A three-dimensional analytical framework comprising the broader national context, monitoring framework design, and interpretation mechanisms was developed to systematically examine differences in indicator selection, normalization, weighting, aggregation, trend assessment, reporting, and communication strategies. The comparative analysis demonstrates that although all four countries monitor the same Sustainable Development Goals, they employ substantially different methodological approaches reflecting their respective governance structures, institutional capacities, policy priorities, and national contexts. India and Vietnam rely on composite indices based primarily on arithmetic aggregation, Japan employs geometric aggregation at the goal level, while Germany evaluates indicators individually through trend-based assessments without constructing a composite index. These methodological choices involve important trade-offs between scientific rigor, interpretability, policy relevance, and communication effectiveness. The study further highlights methodological limitations associated with normalization, equal weighting, and aggregation of heterogeneous sustainability indicators, while emphasizing the strengths of context-specific monitoring frameworks. Rather than identifying a universally superior methodology, the findings demonstrate that national SDG monitoring systems can be strengthened through comparative learning, enabling countries to adapt methodological lessons from one another while remaining aligned with their own national objectives and institutional contexts. The study contributes to the SDG literature by shifting the focus from comparing sustainability outcomes to comparing the methodologies used to measure them, providing insights that support the continued improvement of national SDG monitoring systems.

Title: Boring Objects Bureau: A New Approach to Desirable Sustainability
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Reuse, repair, products, design, desirable
Abstract_Text:
The Boring Objects Bureau is a design studio for creating desirable new approaches to product sustainability.
The motivation to create the Bureau was from seeing how sustainability initiatives in our everyday products are increasingly met with consumer apathy, with familiar approaches such as improved repairability or recycled content appealing only to committed buyers rather than the broader public.
This outlook combines with the costly and complex process of obtaining product sustainability certifications and their modest marketing value, leading companies to treat sustainability as a virtue add-on, rather than a business necessity. As a result, sustainability initiatives in consumer products have lost momentum, adding to the global delay in achieving the 2030 SDG goals.
As a new way to reach people, how can we draw on conceptual design and the fine arts, fields that explicitly communicate and connect with audiences, to shape sustainable offerings that are appealing in their own right? Could this approach define a new era for sustainable initiatives beyond 2030 and produce proposals that appeal to companies, the public, and the environment?
The Bureau's first investigations include the smartphone and the plant pot, products with different expectations with regards to repair and replacement. In response, the Bureau created a series of digital, physical, and hybrid proposals.

Title: The Idle Margin: Why Everyday Conservation Goes Undone
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Keywords: vehicle idling, sustainable mobility, behavioural interventions, air pollution, field experiment
Abstract_Text:
Vehicle idling wastes fuel and generates avoidable air pollution, yet drivers often fail to switch off their engines even when doing so saves money. This paper examines whether information, financial incentives, and real-time reminders can reduce this everyday source of urban emissions.
I conduct a large-scale randomised field experiment involving 6,621 vehicles in Pakistan. Using high-frequency GPS data, I measure vehicle idling and compare interventions providing personalised information about private fuel savings, additional social information, financial incentives, and an in-vehicle reminder device.
Personalised private-cost information reduces idling by approximately 1.8 minutes per vehicle per day, a 9% reduction relative to the control group. Adding social information or financial incentives yields little additional improvement. Counterintuitively, the real-time reminder increases idling relative to a comparable group without the device, suggesting that technological assistance can undermine preventive self-monitoring.
These findings demonstrate that low-cost information interventions can generate meaningful and persistent improvements in everyday environmental behaviour. However, additional information, financial incentives, and automated reminders do not necessarily enhance conservation. The results highlight the importance of behavioural frictions in designing scalable policies for sustainable urban mobility and air quality.

Title: From Germany to Nepal: Diaspora-Led Community Health Action for Health Equity and Sustainable Development
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Health equity; diaspora; community health; rural health; maternal health; menstrual health; SDGs; Nepal.
Abstract_Text:
Health inequalities in remote communities are shaped by distance from health facilities, limited diagnostic services, shortages of trained health professionals, poverty, gender inequality and lack of health information. Addressing these challenges requires more than short-term medical assistance; it requires partnerships that strengthen local capacity and community ownership.
My paper presents the experience of Nepali Samaj e.V., a diaspora organisation established in Germany in 2003, working with local partners including Manaslu Rural Development Society Nepal and Solukhumbu Polytechnical Academy to improve health and well-being in underserved communities in Nepal. It examines three complementary interventions.
First, mobile health camps bring multidisciplinary services directly to communities facing geographical barriers to healthcare. A camp in Chumnubri, Gorkha District, in April 2024 provided dental, paediatric, gynaecological, internal-medicine and ophthalmological services, including ultrasound and cataract surgery. Across documented health-camp activities, 1,443 patients received care and more than 2,000 examinations were conducted, including 58 cataract operations, 233 tooth extractions and 86 visual aids.
Second, a maternal-health project in Madhesh Province combined mobile ultrasound technology with training for frontline nurses and midwives. Twelve nurses from 12 health facilities were trained; 457 ultrasound examinations were conducted for 270 pregnant women, 19 women were referred, and eight significant pregnancy complications were identified. Knowledge assessments showed a 49% average improvement.
3rd, Project 28 addresses menstrual health, hygiene and menstrual poverty through awareness raising, education, product training and exploration of appropriate menstrual-health solutions in remote mountain communities.
Together, these initiatives demonstrate how diaspora partnerships can move from access to capacity and agency: bringing services closer to underserved populations, strengthening local health workers and enabling communities, particularly women and girls, to make informed health decisions. The paper highlights contributions to SDG 3, SDG 5, SDG 10 and SDG 17, and discusses lessons for health equity and the post-2030 sustainable development agenda.

Title: Digital sovereignty for just sustainability futures? Data autonomy, global dependencies, and democratic alternatives in the age of AI
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: Trustworthy AI, information integrity, data autonomy, and sustainability impacts of AI
Organisations: Stahl, Dr. Titus | University of Groningen
Keywords: digital sovereignty, data autonomy, artificial intelligence, sustainability
Abstract_Text:
Artificial intelligence can both promote and undermine the transition to a sustainable society, depending on who can determine legal frameworks, ownership regimes and the values driving its development. A transition towards a sustainable and equitable global society therefore raises questions of power, control and geopolitical dependency. As global powers compete over AI and the data, computing power and infrastructures on which it depends, states and societies face a difficult question: is digital sovereignty necessary and sufficient for self-determination, or does AI come with dependencies that undermine the pursuit of sustainability and social equality?
This interdisciplinary panel addresses this question by bringing legal, political-economic, philosophical and sociotechnical perspectives into dialogue. Cases examined include EU sustainability reporting that relies on US-based cloud providers and consultancies; Dutch universities seeking data autonomy amid hyperscaler dependence; the design and deployment choices through which public-sector AI governs citizens; and the planetary datafication on which sustainability knowledge depends.
The papers examine, in particular, whether digital sovereignty, understood as relying on domestic infrastructure and formal jurisdiction, is sufficient for self-determination. Formal sovereignty can still leave consequential choices about how people are governed in private hands, and thereby enable domination. Moreover, datafication, even when it is formally sovereign, runs the risk of reenforcing inequalities and environmental harms.
The panel therefore asks not only who controls AI, infrastructure and sustainability data, but what forms of collective governance (if any) can make these components serve just and sustainable futures. The papers explore alternatives, ranging from democratic constraints that keep AI-mediated power accountable and revisable, to degrowth policies, better strategies to make use of data, digital commons, and transnational digital solidarity. Drawing on the Sustainable Development Goals' 2030 horizon, it asks what governance of AI and data can advance sustainable development by and beyond 2030.
Driven increasingly by AI, datafication - the collection, processing, storage and circulation of data as primary organizing force of contemporary society – is central to sustainability interventions around the world, in specific locales and at a planetary scale. Without datafication, as it is, among others, enabled through remote sensing technologies, underwater cameras, or animal trackers, we would not know about the planetary boundaries, for example, and we would not know that we are rapidly transgressing (most of) them. Similarly, it is difficult to imagine how we can identify pathways out of the sustainability crisis without datafication, all while we are increasingly aware that datafication is a driver of inequalities, new forms of exploitation and also environmental destruction. Data centers, as the material backbones of datafication, are widely recognized for their negative impacts on the people and environments in their immediate vicinity. Digital sovereignty initiatives, on the other hand, point towards, and seek to address, the inequalities inherent in access to, and control over, datafication processes. As also reflected in the panel abstract itself, our relationship with datafication is essentially schizophrenic – we know about the problems but hope we can fix them through particular interventions such as better governance frameworks or investments in technologies that improve the environmental footprints of data centers. This paper presents a provocation to this approach: It argues that attention to the details of datafication distracts from, and thus actually fuels, the dynamics at the heart of the sustainability crisis itself: the continued, planetary expansion of capitalism as the dominant political economic system. It presents a degrowth perspective on planetary datafication, as central to broader degrowth initiatives that aspire towards a more radical response to the sustainability crisis.
How does the EU, and Europe more widely, balance Digital Sovereignty and its Green Deal agendas? This paper ties together Digital Sovereignty with the on-going development and enforcement of EU sustainability reporting requirements. By 2029 firms in the EU must produce, process and submit detailed sustainability reports following EU Regulation on the Traceability of Transfers of Funds (TFR), the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and the Taxonomy Regulation. Varying in their stages of adoption, the implementation of these frameworks is uncertain given the backlash against sustainable corporate reporting generally, and particularly of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices. EU policy-makers have indicated some relaxation and watering-down of these commitments underpinning the European Green Deal. The EU’s push to report emissions and enact the green-digital transition more broadly may lead firms and entire industries it seeks to develop as part of Digital Sovereignty ambitions to sidestep the region. Internationally, the soft power of the so-called “Brussels effect” of exporting legal frameworks to other regions may ultimately be diminished, to the detriment of a world also coping with green-digital transitions. However, EU sustainability goals rely either on data provided by US-based multinational cloud service providers such as Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, or on data estimates produced by consultancy firms such as Accenture. The presentation will examine 1) the provision and supply of sustainability data as well as 2) the take up and demand for such data in the private and public sectors in the context of 3) EU and member-state governance of European Digital Sovereignty and the Green Transition. It seeks to understand how trajectories towards digital sovereignty and the green transition can be mutually reinforcing.
AI and the cloud infrastructures on which it runs can both enable and constrain the transition to a sustainable society, depending on who controls ownership regimes and the values driving digital development. Universities exemplify this tension: they generate the knowledge needed for just sustainability transitions, yet their research, teaching, and administration increasingly run on cloud services provided by a handful of big tech companies. In times of heightened geopolitical competition, this dependency raises difficult questions of power, control, and (individual/collective) self-determination: can universities pursue values such as academic freedom, sustainability, and social equality on infrastructures they do not control?
This presentation examines how Dutch universities have sought to enhance data autonomy despite their reliance on hyperscalers. Drawing on a tripartite framework of regulatory, strategic, and value-oriented strategies, and on interviews with Chief Information Officers alongside policy document analysis, it shows how institutions combine legal compliance and contractual safeguards with collective procurement, open standards, and shared infrastructures such as the national cooperative SURF. The findings reveal that while regulatory and strategic strategies are maturing, value-based strategies remain largely absent, leaving questions of public value, meaningful participation, and sustainability under-addressed. The Dutch case offers lessons for universities and other public institutions in small and medium-sized countries confronting dependencies that digital sovereignty alone cannot resolve. It points towards alternatives grounded in digital commons, shared infrastructures, and collective governance that can make AI and digitalization serve just and sustainable futures beyond 2030.
The call for digital sovereignty is motivated by an observation that we are dependent on a small number of AI companies. However, what is it exactly that we, as citizens, must control in order for digital sovereignty to be democratically meaningful? Proposals for digital sovereignty include calls for domestic infrastructure and formal jurisdiction. However, as we will argue, these proposals can be realised, but still leave important decisions about how people are governed by AI systems in private hands. This talk looks at this problem in the context of public-sector AI.
Small changes in a threshold, update routines or variables used in public-sector AI can have large effects on how people are governed. We call these choices material system choices (MaSCs). They are choices in the design, configuration, deployment and updating of AI systems that determine who is subjected to AI-mediated public power, on what grounds, and with what consequences. These choices are often made by different actors across different institutional layers (vendors, officials, experts, etc.).
We argue that, when people do not have institutional ways to constrain the MaSCs that determine how people are governed, this has the structure of domination in a neo-republican sense. We show that power over MaSCs can avoid domination only if that power is institutionally constrained through addressability, publicly assessable standards, and structural revisability.
These conditions present a question for thinking about digital sovereignty. Can a state become less dependent on foreign AI providers but fail to give citizens meaningful control over the important choices that govern them? And, from the other direction, is that kind of control possible without full independence? This means that we should look beyond control over technology, and ask whether the relevant MaSCs remain subject to meaningful democratic control.
The digital transition will not automatically be a sustainable one. Rather, there is the danger that this transition will lead to forms of domination by agents who will use their power to pursue interests which are incompatible with sustainability. Both in the literature and in recent EU digital policy discourse, “digital sovereignty” is emphasized as a strategy to avoid digital domination and thus make sustainable digital transitions possible. While the meaning of “digital sovereignty” is vague, it is often read to imply policies that lead to the emergence of competitive digital infrastructures located within the jurisdiction of a given polity, and thus allow for effective regulation by that polity. The paper argues that this regulation-focused and implicitly nationalist or regionalist vision of digital sovereignty remains insufficient, since it misunderstands the nature of digital platform power. As the dominating structure of current platforms not only works through direct control but also through shaping the competitive environment, strategies for sustainable digital transitions that exclusively rely on attempts to bolster regulatory capacity through digital sovereignty are not only empirically likely to fail but will also tend to undermine their own normative ambitions.This is the “digital sovereignty dilemma”: On the one hand, the promotion of competitive national alternatives will often require copying the unsustainable strategies of the existing players. On the other hand, genuinely different, sustainable models risk remaining uncompetitive in the absence of a transnational push towards alternatives. In response to this dilemma, I develop a strategy of transnational digital solidarity in the service of sustainable digital commons. Instead of governments subsidizing competing, but structurally identical platforms within each given jurisdiction, the cause of sustainability is better served by supporting alternative, democratic governance models and technology choices across national boundaries.

Title: Forecasting Sustainable Development Progress in BRICS+ Economies: Country-Level Projections to 2030
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Authors: Yadav, Rajnish; Anand, Shweta; Singh, Kavita
Keywords: SDG, Sustainability, BRICS+, Agenda- 2030, SDG progress, Sustainability policy.
Abstract_Text:
As the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) approaches, understanding how sustainable development is progressing across emerging economies has become increasingly important. This study examines historical trends in the SDG Overall Score (SDGO) across 11 BRICS+ economies and projects their potential trajectories up to 2030. It aims to identify differences in national progress and contribute evidence to discussions on accelerating sustainable development beyond the current SDG framework.
The study uses annual SDGO data for Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates over 2000–2025, comprising 286 country-year observations. Country-specific linear trend regression and exponential smoothing (ETS) are evaluated as alternative forecasting approaches. Their predictive performance is assessed using mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) across alternative validation periods. The selected approach is then used to generate country-level projections for 2026–2030.
Preliminary findings indicate that SDGO has generally improved across the selected economies, although the pace of progress differs considerably. In the 2020–2025 validation period, ETS achieved an MAE of 0.945 and an RMSE of 1.267, compared with 1.000 and 1.402, respectively, for the linear trend model. However, a second validation exercise produced mixed results, indicating that model performance depends on the evaluation period. Initial trend-based projections suggest continued improvements through 2030, with different trajectories across countries.
The findings highlight the value of country-level forecasting for identifying differences in sustainable development progress and informing forward-looking policy discussions. By examining both historical performance and future trajectories, the study offers a practical evidence base for monitoring SDG progress, identifying countries requiring greater policy attention, and considering priorities for a more effective and inclusive sustainability agenda beyond 2030.

Title: Technology, Digital Media, and Attention: Towards a Globally Relevant Evidence Base for Responsible Digitalization
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Wiradhany, Wisnu; Parry, Douglas; Baumgartner, Susanne; Nieuwenstein, Mark
Organisations: Atma Jaya Catholic University of Indonesia
Keywords: technology and digital media, smartphones, social media, attention, distraction
Abstract_Text:
As technology and digital media (TDM) become increasingly embedded in everyday life, concerns about their potential effects on attention and cognitive effort have not only become prominent in public debates about responsible digitalization, but also resulted in use restriction policies implementation. Meanwhile, these actions have been implemented despite uncertainty about the strength, consistency, and generalizability of the underlying empirical evidence, and comprehensive assessments on their potential benefits. To take stock of the research landscape that is currently informing global digitalization policies, we reviewed a decade of experimental research on the effects of TDM on attention (108 studies; Ntotal = 11,811).
Our findings reveal a conceptually and methodologically discordant and uneven research landscape. Studies investigate diverse technologies, digital activities, and attentional outcomes, making findings difficult to compare and integrate. Much of the experimental evidence concerns immediate effects on task performance rather than enduring changes in attentional abilities. Moreover, experimental designs often lack clear theoretical grounding or appropriate control conditions, limiting the generalization or attribution that the effects stemmed from TDM instead of known cognitive mechanisms. Lastly, most studies were conducted in North America and Western Europe, which reflects the longstanding geographic concentrations in psychological and communication research, even though we found encouraging signs of geographic diversity.
Together, these findings highlight important barriers to evidence-informed technology governance, and suggest a disconnect between broad public claims about the effects of TDM and what the existing evidence can establish. Moving forward, we believe that the development of a more globally relevant understanding of these effects requires not only better theorization and experimental designs for future empirical data collection, but also better representation and contextualization of the effects.

Title: Driving Sustainable Development from Africa: Scaling Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) Start-ups in sub-Saharan Africa
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Wachira, Mumbi; Ndiritu, Simon; Ben, Probst; Hilary, Ndambiri
Keywords: Carbon Dioxide Removal, Start-ups, sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract_Text: Carbon Dioxide Removal (CDR) is in an emergent phase in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). CDR entails the deliberate removal of CO₂ from the atmosphere and durably storing it in geological formations, terrestrial or ocean reservoirs, or long-lived products. It poses unique opportunities for SSA to meet Net Zero pledges by 2050. Presently, global energy transition plans overlook SSA, though its share of global emissions could quadruple by 2060. This study examines the conditions that CDR start-ups in SSA need to scale, and how CDR can drive sustainable development from the continent. Using a mixed methods approach, we combine an indicator-based assessment of 9 SSA countries with a survey of 56 CDR start-ups. The assessment spans regulatory frameworks, finance, renewable energy, social inclusion and carbon market readiness. We analyse the data using readiness indices, nonparametric tests and regression. As of 2025, no African country has explicitly integrated CDR into its formal climate commitments, however, carbon market regulations are advanced in Ghana, Kenya and Rwanda. CDR start-ups display moderate readiness to scale, with an enterprise readiness index of 58.5 out of 100. Their strengths lie in business model clarity and value proposition, while access to capital remains a critical constraint for 81% of the start-ups surveyed. Additionally only 27% of projects generate carbon credit revenue. Biochar is the most common and advanced CDR pathway, generating co-benefits with smallholder farmers. Engineered pathways for example, direct air capture remain at the pilot stage with limited revenue, despite removal targets of 100,000 tCO₂ or more annually. Scaling CDR in SSA depends on conditions beyond the start-up: blended and concessional finance for working capital, national climate strategies that recognise removals, and local verification capacity. CDR can link climate action with rural livelihoods, renewable energy and green jobs positioning the region as a producer of scalable climate solutions.

Title: Agri-food system emissions and climate mitigation pathways. Topical review of CGIAR’s decade of climate research
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Authors: Vaidya, Shrijana; Mehar, Mamta; Mukherjee, Aditi
Keywords: agri-food system, climate change, emissions, mitigation, land use change
Abstract_Text:
Agri-food systems account for about one-third of the total anthropogenic GHG emissions. These emissions arise across the entire agri-food system, such as from crop and livestock production to land-use change associated with agricultural expansion, deforestation, peatland degradation, as well as pre- and post-production processes. Extensive research has been carried out within CGIAR on agri-food emissions and mitigation pathways. However, this evidence remains fragmented across repositories and has not been synthesised comprehensively.
We conducted a topical review of peer-reviewed articles published between 2012 and 2023 across eight CGIAR repositories: CGSpace, CIFOR-ICRAF, IRRI, IFPRI, CIMMYT, MELSpace, WorldFish, and ICRISAT. Of 5,713 climate-related articles screened, we identified 386 studies on agrifood system emissions and 502 studies on climate mitigation.
Within emissions, our findings show that deforestation and land use change have the highest evidence base, followed closely by agricultural practices. Comparatively, fewer studies focused on emissions resulting from energy use from pre- to post-production. Within each of these subthemes, evidence is clustered around a dominant topic, with conversion of natural forest dominating within deforestation and land use change, crop production within agricultural practices, energy use in post-production processes within pre- to post-production, and food loss and waste.
Similarly, within mitigation, CO2 mitigation in agriculture and forestry has the highest evidence base, followed by CO2 mitigation across the value chain, from pre- and post-production to consumption, CH4 mitigation, and N2O mitigation. Within each subtheme, evidence clustered around a dominant topic, with fertiliser and soil-related mitigation for N2O mitigation, livestock-related mitigation for CH4 mitigation, C sequestration for CO2 mitigation, and reducing energy use for CO2 mitigation across the value chain.
By mapping the evidence, this review identifies where the CGIAR climate research is concentrated and where the gaps remain, and provides a foundation for more balanced, evidence-informed agri-food system emissions and mitigation research.

Title: Learning from Historical Transformations for Informing Transformational Climate Adaptation Today
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Authors: Koren, Judith; Mukherji, Aditi; Harley, Alicia G.
Keywords: Transformational adaptation, Equity, Climate adaptation, Development, Global South
Abstract_Text: Transformational adaptation is increasingly treated as essential to climate-resilient futures, yet the concept itself remains poorly defined. This ambiguity has raised concerns among Global South representatives involved in climate negotiations, prompting debates over what matters most: the distinction between incremental and transformational adaptation or the goals that adaptation should serve, such as climate risk reduction, scalability, the avoidance of maladaptation, and the pursuit of equity and justice. Drawing on concepts of transformation from sustainability science and socio-technical transitions research and applying those to understand empirical examples of past societal transformations, the paper argues that history offers lessons that the adaptation community can use. Using an adapted Multi-Level Perspective (MLP) framework, this paper assesses six societal transformations since the 1960s across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. The analysis shows that transformational outcomes arise through multiple pathways; that transformation requires interaction between interventions, context, and institutions and needs dedicated resource support, including finance, capacity, and technology; that transformation is inherently political; and that transformational outcomes are not always positive, especially for marginalised groups. These findings offer practical guidance for pursuing transformational climate adaptation outcomes and support Global South calls for equitable access to the means of implementation, particularly finance for doing so.

Title: Climate vulnerability and sustainable adaptation of rural livelihoods: Evidence from wheat farmers in Kermanshah, Iran
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Authors: Mehraban, Ramesh; Rezaei, Rohollah; Mojarradi, Gholamreza; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: Climate vulnerability, climate change adaptation, rural livelihoods, maladaptation, community-based climate action
Abstract_Text:
Climate change poses a growing challenge to rural livelihoods in semi-arid regions, where wheat production is particularly sensitive to climatic variability and extreme weather events. Understanding the factors that shape farmers’ vulnerability and identifying feasible adaptation strategies are essential to sustaining agricultural livelihoods and strengthening rural resilience. This study investigates climate-related livelihood vulnerability among wheat farmers in Kermanshah County, western Iran, and identifies strategies that could support more sustainable adaptation.
The study uses a mixed-methods design informed by the Sustainable Livelihoods Framework and the IPCC vulnerability framework. The qualitative phase involved 20 experts from the Agricultural Jihad Organization and the meteorological administration. SWOT analysis was used to identify potential adaptation strategies, which were subsequently prioritized using the Quantitative Strategic Planning Matrix (QSPM). Five strategies emerged from this process: climate information dissemination networks and intelligent extension systems; cluster-based land management; participatory marketing and processing industries; crop insurance and financial support; and complementary skills and livelihood diversification. The first two strategies received the highest priorities in the QSPM assessment.
The quantitative phase draws on questionnaire data collected from 473 wheat farmers in Kermanshah County. The questionnaire addresses farmers’ perceptions of climate change, exposure to extreme climatic hazards, livelihood sensitivity, household livelihood assets, adaptive capacity, perceived vulnerability, and the livelihood impacts of climate change, alongside farmers’ individual and agricultural characteristics. Analysis of these data is ongoing.
By combining expert-based strategy prioritization with a household-level assessment of climate vulnerability, the study seeks to connect locally identified adaptation priorities with the livelihood conditions of wheat-farming communities. The findings are intended to inform context-specific adaptation planning and support more resilient and equitable rural development beyond 2030.

Title: Revealing the hidden costs of Dutch livestock production: a provincial true cost accounting analysis
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Hendriks, Gert-Jan; Zhang, Jingyu; Pradhan, Prajal
Keywords: True cost accounting, Hidden costs, Livestock production, Netherlands, Provincial
Abstract_Text: Hidden costs are costs that are not reflected in market prices but are instead borne by society, the environment, or future generations. In the Netherlands, the hidden environmental costs of livestock production were estimated at €8.5 billion in 2022, making it the sector with the highest hidden environmental costs in the country. Although national cost calculations are available, their distribution across provinces remains unclear. This study, therefore, applies a true cost accounting framework to examine the scale and composition of hidden costs across the twelve Dutch provinces. The analysis covers domestic livestock production and associated feed production up to the farm gate, using environmental, health, and social indicators to assess their associated impacts. Data from Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek and Emissieregistratie are combined with literature-based estimates and proxies to quantify these impacts at the provincial level. Selected impacts are then translated into monetary costs using valuation factors specific to the Netherlands, drawn from publicly available literature. By incorporating health and social impacts alongside environmental impacts and examining how costs vary across provinces, this study offers a more comprehensive overview of the hidden costs of livestock production in the Netherlands.

Title: Social Media Addiction and Stress Symptoms Among Senior High School Students in Indonesia
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: Nuraisyah, Ayu; Muthmainnah, Muthmainnah; Rizky Arifiani, Britsni; Nailufar Manto, Adya
Keywords: Social media addiction, Stress level, Adolescents, FoMO, Well-being
Abstract_Text:
Social media use among adolescents is increasing alongside advances in digital technology. Fear of Missing Out (FoMO) encourages adolescents to stay constantly connected to social media, which may affect their psychological well-being, including the emergence of stress symptoms. Excessive social media use may also raise the risk of social media addiction among adolescents.
This study aimed to examine the relationship between social media addiction and stress symptoms among adolescents at a senior high school in Indonesia. A quantitative cross-sectional design was used. The sample consisted of 110 students selected through cluster sampling across grades 11 and 12 in the science and social studies programs. Social media addiction was measured using the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS), and stress symptoms using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale (DASS-42). Data were analyzed using Spearman’s Rho Test.
Most respondents were in the normal category for social media use (n = 64, 58.2%) and had normal stress levels (n = 68, 61.8%). Spearman’s Rho showed a p-value of 0.003 (<0.05) and a correlation coefficient of 0.285, indicating a weak, positive relationship. A relationship was found between indications of social media addiction and stress symptoms among adolescents. Higher indications of social media addiction were accompanied by a greater tendency toward stress symptoms.

Title: The Policy–Action–Target–Metrics (PAT&M) Framework for Advancing SDGs integration: From Sustainability Reporting to Sustainable Transformation
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Methods and processes for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Ratkai, Dr. Melinda | Hotelschool The Hague
Keywords: sustainability reporting; PAT&M; ESG maturity; sustainability assessment; organisational capabilities; sustainable transformation
Abstract_Text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide internationally recognised sustainability objectives, yet organisations often struggle to translate commitments and reporting requirements into measurable organisational change. This paper introduces the Policy–Action–Target–Metrics (PAT&M) framework as a diagnostic approach for assessing the organisational embeddedness of environmental, social and governance (ESG) and SDG-related topics. Derived from the disclosure architecture of the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), the framework distinguishes between policies that formalise intentions, actions that operationalise commitments, targets that define measurable and time-bound objectives, and metrics that monitor effectiveness and progress. By shifting the emphasis from external disclosure to organisational integration and self-assessment, PAT&M identifies where sustainability maturity remains commitment- or activity-oriented and where it has developed into a measurable management capability. A pilot application to workforce sustainability in a hospitality SME found 89% alignment for Policies and Actions but only 14% for Targets and Metrics, indicating that extensive sustainability activity may coexist with limited capacity to measure outcomes and monitor progress. The framework supports SDG Target 12.6 by examining the organisational substance behind sustainability reporting. It can also be applied across any other ESG and SDG topics. PAT&M is not proposed as another rating or reporting standard, but as a structured methodology for organisational self-diagnosis, comparative research and longitudinal monitoring. It contributes to the post-2030 sustainability agenda by clarifying how reported commitments can become embedded in organisational capabilities, decision-making and sustainable transformation.

Title: When Fewer Children Mean Unequal Opportunities: Demographic Decline and the Sustainability of Rural Education in Moldova
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: National Institute for Economic Research, ASEM
Keywords: demographic decline; rural education; educational inequality; school-age population; educational sustainability; territorial disparities; Republic of Moldova; Sustainable Development Goals; post-2030 agenda.
Abstract_Text: Demographic decline poses significant challenges to the sustainability of education systems, particularly in rural areas where population ageing, migration and declining birth rates may intensify territorial inequalities. The Republic of Moldova provides a relevant case for examining how demographic transformations affect educational provision and the capacity of local communities to ensure equitable access to quality education. This study aims to investigate the relationship between demographic change and the sustainability of rural education, focusing on school-age population trends, territorial disparities and the implications for educational planning beyond 2030. The research proposes a quantitative, longitudinal and territorial approach based on demographic and educational statistics, complemented by comparative analysis across rural and urban areas. Key indicators include changes in the school-age population, student enrolment, school distribution and access to educational services. Where data availability permits, alternative demographic scenarios will be used to explore potential challenges for school network planning and resource allocation through 2040. The study seeks to identify territories where demographic contraction may create the greatest risks to educational accessibility and to examine how education policies can balance institutional efficiency with equal opportunities for students. Particular attention is given to the potential consequences of school consolidation for children in remote and disadvantaged communities. By connecting demographic analysis with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education), SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), the research aims to contribute to discussions on resilient and inclusive education systems. Its expected contribution is an evidence-based framework for integrating demographic projections into educational planning and for informing the post-2030 sustainable development agenda.

Title: Balancing climate finance between prevention and recovery: economy-wide effects of the European adaptation investment and post-disaster transfers on regional welfare and equity
