Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Dunne, Shane; Chatzivasileiadis, Theodoros; Ivanova, Olga; Filatova, Tatiana
Keywords: climate finance, climate adaptation, cohesion policy, regional inequality, computable general equilibrium
Abstract_Text:
Climate-driven flooding is projected to widen economic disparities between European regions. The European Union (EU) has two principal instruments to counter this: the EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF), which provides post-disaster recovery transfers, and Cohesion Policy investment in climate adaptation, which aims to prevent damage before it occurs. Neither has been quantitatively evaluated for its effects on the regional economies it is meant to protect.
We provide the first ex-ante macroeconomic assessment of both instruments against projected river flooding and sea-level rise over 2025-2050, using the EU-EMS spatial computable general equilibrium model across 242 regions (NUTS-2). We replicate the EUSF's statutory award formula and calibrate Cohesion Policy adaptation spending to observed project-level data.
Under a 2°C warming scenario, flooding causes about €300 billion in discounted EU-wide welfare losses. At current funding levels, the EUSF recovers 1% of these losses and Cohesion Policy 1.9%. Per euro of EU funding, place-based prevention under Cohesion Policy delivers about 4.6 times more household welfare than the place-blind recovery transfers of the EUSF and modestly reduces regional inequality, which the EUSF leaves virtually unchanged. In a budget-neutral reallocation of the combined funding envelope, shifting money from recovery towards prevention improves both efficiency and equity. Targeting regions that are both highly exposed and below 75% of average EU GDP per capita yields the largest equity gain of all designs tested, with near-maximal efficiency.
In EU adaptation finance, efficiency and equity are therefore complements rather than trade-offs. With Cohesion Policy facing proposed cuts in the 2028-2034 EU budget, reducing its adaptation allocation would forgo these gains. Directing adaptation finance to the regions most at risk and least able to adapt autonomously can advance climate action and reduced inequalities (Sustainable Development Goals 13 and 10) together, beyond 2030.

Title: Climate adaptation in a polarized development context: Wildfire governance and community resilience after the 2021 Mediterranean fires
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Climate adaptation, Wildfires, Community resilience, Climate-development nexus
Abstract_Text:
The 2021 wildfire season marked a turning point across the Mediterranean, with extreme fires affecting Turkey, Greece, Italy, and other countries. These events exposed growing climate vulnerabilities while raising questions about preparedness, governance, and communities’ capacity to adapt to increasingly severe wildfire risk.
Drawing on a five-year comparative project on communities affected by extreme wildfires across five countries, this paper examines the aftermath of the 2021 megafire in southwest Turkey. Based on interviews with residents, practitioners, and experts, and on repeated fieldwork conducted between 2021 and 2026, it explores how people interpreted the disaster, assigned responsibility, and prepared for future wildfire seasons amid political polarization, contested development priorities, and uneven trust in public institutions. The findings are subsequently compared with experiences from other Mediterranean wildfire regions to explore how governance conditions and development pathways influence adaptation, preparedness, and resilience in the face of escalating climate risk.
The findings show that experiences of wildfire shaped how communities interpreted risk, related to public authorities, organised collective action, and developed practices of preparedness. While the fires generated new forms of solidarity and community-based engagement, they also revealed tensions around responsibility, unequal capacities to prepare for future risks, and the difficulty of sustaining collective action beyond emergencies.
The paper argues that building societal resilience requires greater attention to the social and political dimensions of climate adaptation, including trust, participation, and community capacity. It contributes to debates on the climate change-development nexus by demonstrating how adaptation pathways are shaped by governance conditions and development trajectories at the local level. In doing so, it speaks directly to SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 16 (Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions), highlighting the importance of inclusive and community-based approaches to resilient, just, and equitable transformations beyond 2030.

Title: ECOLOGICAL AND HUMAN HEALTH RISKS ASSOCIATED WITH HEAVY METAL PRESENCE IN THE MUNI LAGOON – WINNEBA, GHANA.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Keywords: Heavy metal contamination; Muni Lagoon; Ecological risk assessment; Human health risk; Cadmium bioaccumulation
Abstract_Text:
The Muni Lagoon, a Ramsar site in Ghana, faces increasing threats from heavy metal contamination associated with anthropogenic activities, potentially endangering its ecosystem and surrounding communities. This study assessed the ecological and human health risks associated with cadmium (Cd), zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), chromium (Cr), iron (Fe), and lead (Pb) in lagoon water, sediment, and fish.
Physicochemical parameters and heavy metal concentrations were evaluated against World Health Organization (WHO) and United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) guidelines. Contamination factor, degree of contamination, enrichment factor (EF), and pollution load index (PLI) were used to characterize contamination. Ecological risks were assessed using the potential ecological risk index (RI), while human health risks from consuming black-chin tilapia (Sarotherodon melanotheron) were evaluated using target hazard quotient (THQ), hazard index (HI), and carcinogenic risk assessments.
Results revealed heavy metal contamination in water and sediment, with iron concentrations of 7.23 mg/L in water and 1,165.57 mg/kg in sediment, cadmium concentrations of 0.0521 mg/L and 67.68 mg/kg, respectively, and lead at 0.011 mg/L in water. Cadmium contributed most significantly to contamination. Although the PLI was below 1, EF indicated extremely high enrichment of cadmium and lead, moderate enrichment of zinc, and minimal enrichment of copper and chromium. The RI of 10,100.22, exceeding the 720 threshold, indicated substantial ecological risk, primarily driven by cadmium. THQ and HI values were below 1 for adults and children, suggesting no significant non-carcinogenic risk overall. However, the carcinogenic risk assessment indicated potential risks associated with cadmium and chromium exposure among children, warranting further investigation. Fish condition factors suggested generally good fish health.
Heavy metal contamination in the Muni Lagoon was likely due to human activities, highlighting the need for effective remediation strategies and protective boundaries to prevent further pollution and encroachment

Title: Synergy and Trade-off in Cross-City Interactions between Digital-Intelligent Development and the SDGs
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: digital-intelligent development; Sustainable Development Goals; cross-city interaction; synergy and trade-off
Abstract_Text: The advancement of digital-intelligent transformation and the pursuit of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are not processes confined within individual cities, as spatial linkages among cities may cause the interaction between the two to unfold as a cross-city pattern of synergies and trade-offs. However, existing studies mostly focus on the within-city coupling coordination between digital-intelligent development and the SDGs, leaving the following questions systematically unexamined: which dimensions of digital-intelligent development interact with which SDG indicators across cities, whether the interaction is synergistic or trade-off in direction, and whether the interaction pattern differs systematically under geographic versus economic spatial linkages. Using a sample of prefecture-level and above cities in China, this study first employs a Spatial Durbin Model to identify the spatial spillover effects of each digital-intelligent dimension on SDG indicators and to determine the existence and direction of cross-city interaction. A spatial interaction index is then introduced to decompose the interaction into synergy and trade-off effects, and the synergy-to-trade-off ratio is compared under geographic and economic spatial weight matrices respectively, testing whether the relative structure of synergy and trade-off varies with the channel of spatial association. This study extends the interaction between digital-intelligent development and the SDGs from the intra-city level to the inter-city level, revealing that a single city's coordination performance may obscure the synergy and trade-off structures between cities, thereby providing a basis for differentiated governance at the regional scale.

Title: Beyond 2030: What Can the Global Ethical Stocktake Teach Us About Our Common Future?
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Authors: Figueira, Luana; Galvão, Thiago; Ewandyr, Hérica
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals, Global Ethical Stocktake, COP30, Post-2030 Agenda
Abstract_Text:
After more than a decade of implementation, the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) reveal persistent gaps between global commitments and their realization, raising questions about the limitations of existing governance frameworks and the reforms needed beyond 2030. One beacon on this pathway emerges with the Global Ethical Stocktake (GES), incorporated as one of the Leadership Circles of the Brazilian Presidency of COP30, held in the Brazilian Amazon. The GES offers an important living experience for rethinking governance through global goals. By bringing, through social mobilization, ethical reflection into global governance, the GES raises questions about the responsibilities, power relations and political choices underlying the persistent gap between global commitments and effective action. The consequences of this gap fall disproportionately on women, children and racialized populations, despite their lower contributions to global carbon emissions.
Methodologically grounded in an interdisciplinary perspective and an ethnographic approach, this presentation brings together researchers engaged with the 2030 Agenda through anthropology, international relations and public administration. The analysis draws on institutional documents, event records, speeches and interviews, as well as observations of the practices and interactions of the actors and institutions involved. It situates these actors within the institutional processes and networks through which the GES was articulated, while also considering the researchers’ own engagement as part of the field under study.
It systematizes the GES’s contributions and critically examines their implications for the SDGs, with particular attention to structural barriers and innovative negotiation strategies for overcoming the limitations of conventional governance approaches. The presentation discusses how this experience can inform institutional reforms and cultural change, contributing to a post-2030 sustainability agenda centered on ethnic-racial justice and capable of confronting the political and economic conditions that reproduce unsustainable patterns of development.

Title: Weaving organizations into living systems: Two strategies of interconnectedness in regenerative organizing
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: de Vries, Melanie; Poldner, Kim; Velzing, Evert-Jan; Estrada, Isabel; Rijsdijk, Liesbeth; Drupsteen, Linda
Keywords: regenerative organizing, business models, circular economy, bioeconomy
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Regenerative organizing is a nascent phenomenon that moves beyond reducing negative impact toward contributing to the health of social-ecological systems. Research emphasizes that actors in these systems are highly interconnected and that their activities must be brought together. Yet an important challenge remains underexplored: how organizations, given limited resources and managerial attention, strategically cultivate, govern, and adapt their interconnections with human and non-human actors to support regeneration. Our objective is therefore to describe how organizations cultivate interconnections with actors in social-ecological systems to enact regenerative dynamics.
Methods: We conducted an inductive, theory-building multiple case study of 12 theoretically sampled cases across multiple levels, using regenerative organizing as a sensitizing concept. The Dutch biobased construction sector is an ideal setting: it faces strong regulatory and market pressures to transform and using regionally grown materials could enhance community and ecological health but requires radical change.
Key results: We show how the organizational processes of knowing, deciding, and acting of regenerative organizations both shape and are shaped through interconnections with multiple actors. We identify two distinct strategies through which organizations cultivate regenerative dynamics: (1) Interconnect to adapt, involves cultivating interconnections with incumbent industry actors to gradually redirect existing degenerative dynamics toward regenerative ones from within the existing system; (2) Interconnect to transform, focuses on building deep interconnections with a specific place and its human and more-than-human inhabitants to initiate new regenerative dynamics.
Conclusion: Achieving sustainable development by and beyond 2030 requires organizations that do more than reduce harm. Regenerative organizations show what this can look like: they reimagine how they are interconnected with the social-ecological systems they are part of, and nurture healthy relationships among humans and between humans and nature. Our study shows that regenerative organizing can take shape through two strategies, each contributing in its own way to sustainable development.

Title: Integrated Multi-Hazard Coastal Vulnerability to Shoreline Erosion and Sea-Level-Rise Flooding in Akplabanya and Anyamam, Ghana.
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Institute for Environment and Sanitation Studies
Keywords: Coastal erosion; Sea-level rise; Coastal vulnerability; Multi-hazard assessment; Ghana
Abstract_Text: Coastal communities in Ghana are increasingly vulnerable to shoreline erosion and sea-level-rise (SLR)-induced flooding, yet assessments often examine these hazards separately and rarely integrate biophysical and socioeconomic dimensions at local scales. This study assesses multi-hazard coastal vulnerability in Akplabanya and Anyamam in the Ada West District of Ghana by integrating shoreline erosion dynamics, projected SLR flooding, and socioeconomic vulnerability indicators within a place-based framework. A spatially integrated vulnerability approach was employed, combining Digital Shoreline Analysis System (DSAS) linear regression rate (LRR) analysis, IPCC-based SLR inundation modelling, and survey-derived vulnerability indicators from 97 households within a grid-based analytical framework. Results indicate persistent shoreline retreat in both communities, with mean erosion rates of −1.8 ± 0.23 m yr⁻¹ in Akplabanya and −2.0 ± 0.23 m yr⁻¹ in Anyamam. SLR projections revealed progressively increasing inundation, with Akplabanya experiencing 0.17–3.1% inundation across near- to late-century scenarios, while Anyamam exhibited substantially greater exposure ranging from 0.6% to 32.54%. Integrated vulnerability assessment showed markedly higher overall vulnerability in Anyamam (0.794) than in Akplabanya (0.191), driven primarily by greater exposure and comparatively lower adaptive capacity. The findings demonstrate that vulnerability is shaped not only by hazard occurrence but by the interaction between physical hazard conditions and place-specific socioeconomic characteristics. By integrating shoreline erosion, SLR flooding, and social vulnerability within a comparative framework, this study provides empirical evidence supporting multi-hazard and place-based approaches to coastal adaptation and disaster risk reduction in Ghana.

Title: Pooling Climate-Peace Finance in a Fragmenting Region: ECOWAS, the AES and the Limits of Regional Agency
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Keywords: Climate finance, peace and security, multipolarity, conflict sensitivity, regional agency
Abstract_Text:
Fragmentation deepens within West Africa. The shift from a post-Cold War unipolar to a multipolar global order coincides with a time of increased interstate wars globally, resulting in an increase in military expenditure while climate finance stagnates or declines. Climate change risk compounds irregular migration, pastoralist-farmer conflicts, insurgencies, resource scarcity, and weakening state capacity. The withdrawal of Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso from ECOWAS to form the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) complicates and fragments the regional political, security, and climate financial mobilization framework at a period of multilateral retrenchment that reduces external support.
This paper interrogates the conditions under which a pooled climate-peace finance can operate in West Africa despite fragmentation and what it reveals about the limits of regional agency. The paper argues that climate finance within the sub-region remains largely conflict-blind, revealing adaptation and mitigation metrics with little to account for how funding may interact with conflict dynamics, demanding the necessary inclusion of conflict sensitivity in regional financial frameworks.
From a comparative approach, the paper combines documentary analysis with remote expert interviews examining AES and ECOWAS instruments and climate fund projects. The paper examines four pooling arrangement tests, including political will, financial capacity, institutional capacity, and conflict sensitivity. Noting the influence of emerging powers in West Africa, the research underscores their complementary role in multilateral financing rather than replacing the established multilateral system.
The paper reveals that the AES and ECOWAS climate financing frameworks do not align with the changing subregional realities in the context of a multipolar global order. This situation restricts the ability of both institutions to raise climate funds effectively. Moreover, member states have loosely acknowledged and operationalized the climate change, peace, and security nexus as a financial mobilization strategy, which limits resilient prospects.

Title: Sentinel Terra: Integrating Satellite Remote Sensing and Critical Slowing Down Indicators for Early Detection of Ecosystem Destabilization in Coastal Wetlands
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Keywords: Ecological resilience, Critical slowing down, Satellite remote sensing, Ecosystem tipping points, Coastal wetlands
Abstract_Text:
Coastal wetlands are increasingly exposed to interacting climatic, hydrological, and anthropogenic stressors that can reduce ecological resilience and induce nonlinear regime shifts. Conventional monitoring approaches frequently identify degradation after substantial ecosystem change has occurred, limiting opportunities for preventive intervention. This study presents Sentinel Terra, an interpretable geospatial early-warning framework integrating multispectral satellite observations, ecological time-series diagnostics, and spatial risk modelling to investigate potential ecosystem destabilization in Karavasta Lagoon, Albania.
The framework processes Sentinel-2 surface reflectance imagery into cloud-reduced seasonal composites and derives the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Normalized Difference Water Index (NDWI), and Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) to characterize vegetation condition and hydrological variability. Matched-season interannual comparisons quantify spatial changes in ecological indicators. Temporal diagnostics are informed by critical slowing down theory, using rolling variance and lag-1 autocorrelation to examine statistical signatures potentially associated with declining recovery capacity. Normalized vegetation, hydrological stress, and change indicators are integrated into an interpretable composite risk formulation to generate spatially explicit maps of relative ecosystem vulnerability.
The Karavasta Lagoon pilot produces vegetation-condition maps, 2020–2024 change visualizations, and exploratory spatial risk surfaces, illustrating how heterogeneous ecological conditions can be assessed within a common analytical workflow. The framework additionally incorporates temporal warning diagnostics to investigate potential destabilization trajectories. These indicators are treated as signals requiring ecological interpretation rather than definitive evidence of an approaching tipping point.
Sentinel Terra provides a reproducible, satellite-based approach for linking ecological condition monitoring with resilience-oriented environmental assessment. Further validation against in-situ hydrological measurements and longer observational records is required before reliable forecasting can be established. The proposed framework offers a foundation for supporting earlier, spatially targeted wetland conservation and adaptive management.

Title: Fairer and more responsible director pay policies to curb the growing income gap in South Africa
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Keywords: executive remuneration; fair pay; King V; South Africa; SDG 10
Abstract_Text: Director pay policies can be directly linked to Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities) by ensuring that executive compensation is fair, transparent, performance-based and aligned with long-term corporate sustainability objectives. Regulators and policymakers recognise the need to balance economic growth with environmental and social responsibilities, given evident inequalities in South Africa. The country’s income gap is growing due to high unemployment, unequal distribution of wealth and stalled economic growth. The King V Report on corporate governance recommends that executive pay should be linked to verifiable performance outcomes across the triple bottom line while maintaining a justifiable wage gap. The Companies Amendment Act further ensures that listed companies in South Africa account for responsible pay practices, by introducing mandatory pay gap disclosure and binding say on pay in 2024. Semi-structured in-depth interviews were thus conducted with 14 board members, board committee members and remuneration advisors to explore the implications of stricter legislation and heightened sustainability guidance for responsible pay practices in South Africa. Thematic analysis was conducted on the interview transcripts and due attention was given to trustworthiness criteria. The findings show that principles-based governance guidance offers companies flexibility to tailor remuneration policies to corporate sustainability strategies. Sustainability frameworks and disclosure standards play a more nuanced role in shaping remuneration practices, given sector- and organisation-specific considerations. Stricter legislation drives fairer and more responsible pay practices. As executive remuneration takes on a distinctly ethical dimension within a highly unequal corporate context, remuneration policies should be tied to sustainable value creation to enhance pay equity. By engaging with stakeholders, remuneration committees could identify material context-specific sustainability considerations and incorporate relevant, measurable sustainability targets when setting director pay.

Title: School Context Matters: Acceptance of an Edutainment-Based Adolescent Health App Through the UTAUT2 Lens
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Muthmainnah, Muthmainnah; Nurmala, Ira; Putri Andiani, Tasya Azelya; Agus Salim, Lutfi; Thi Nguyễn, Thanh Thảo
Organisations: Muthmainnah, Dr. Muthmainnah | Faculty of Public Health Universitas Airlangga
Keywords: adolescent health; digital health; edutainment; technology acceptance; UTAUT2
Abstract_Text:
Background: Digital technologies offer opportunities for adolescent health promotion, yet their misuse may contribute to health-risk behaviours. *Konco SREGEP* is an edutainment-based health promotion application designed to support the prevention of adolescent risk behaviours. Understanding its acceptance across educational settings can inform context-sensitive implementation. This study compared acceptance of *Konco SREGEP* between students in general-curriculum and religious-curriculum schools using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2).
Methods:An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted in two schools representing these educational settings. Eligible students had previously been exposed to "Konco SREGEP". Simple random sampling was used, with a minimum required sample of 67 students. Data were collected through an online questionnaire assessing nine UTAUT2 constructs: performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, price value, habit, behavioural intention, and use behaviour.
Results: Statistically significant differences between the two school settings were identified in social influence, facilitating conditions, habit, and behavioural intention. These findings highlight contextual variation in the social and practical conditions surrounding application acceptance and students’ intentions to use it.
Conclusions: Acceptance of "Konco SREGEP" varied across educational settings in four UTAUT2 domains. Implementation strategies should consider school context and engage teachers, families, and peers to support routine application use. The findings inform the contextual adaptation of digital adolescent health promotion; longitudinal research is needed to determine whether acceptance translates into sustained engagement and reduced health-risk behaviours.

Title: Five integrated pathways for transforming food systems toward resilience, sustainability, and food security
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: Sapkota, Tek; Alexander, Peter; Odingo, Alice; Fanzo, Jessica; Merçon, Juliana; Fuller, Jessica; Fontefrancesco, Michele Filippo; Reisch, Lucia A.; Noble, Katie
All_Countries: Italy, Kenya, Mexico, Norway, United Kingdom, United States
Keywords: food systems transformation, resilience, integrated sustainable transformation, climate change, food security
Abstract_Text:
Food systems sit at the intersection of natural and human systems. They are a major driver of climate change, biodiversity loss, land degradation, and pollution, and are increasingly exposed to them. Food production and consumption account for about one-third of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, and the unpriced environmental, health, and social costs of food systems are estimated at US$15–20 trillion a year, about twice the market value of food consumed. More than 700 million people still face hunger. The 2026 disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, which affected nearly one-third of global fertilizer trade, shows how concentrated supply chains expose import-dependent regions to shocks.
This contribution builds on the food systems transformation chapter of the Seventh Global Environment Outlook (GEO-7) of the United Nations Environment Programme, written by the same group of authors and updated with recent evidence. We present five interlinked pathways for integrated sustainable transformation: (1) shifting toward healthy and sustainable diets; (2) sustainably intensifying crop, livestock, and aquatic production without expanding farmland; (3) reducing food loss and waste and increasing circularity; (4) developing novel foods and production processes; and (5) restructuring food markets, corporate governance, and trade.
The pathways reinforce one another but also involve trade-offs, notably for affordability, nutrition in low-income settings, livelihoods, and competition for land. Scenario-based estimates indicate that combined action could deliver substantial climate mitigation, reduce agricultural land demand, and lower diet-related disease. Realized benefits, however, depend on adoption, costs, energy systems, regulation, consumer acceptance, and governance capacity. Building resilience therefore requires coordinated action across scales and sectors: repurposing agricultural and fisheries subsidies, true-cost pricing combined with social protection, coherent trade policy, and investment in research, extension, and local knowledge. Combined, these levers can strengthen resilience across natural and human systems and accelerate a just transformation of food systems.

Title: From sustainability reporting to action: Integrating the Sustainable Development Goals into university governance
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Rebane, Sille; Pehme, Sirli; Kapak, Siret
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals, sustainability governance, carbon footprint, sustainability reporting, higher education
Abstract_Text:
Universities play an important role in advancing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through education, research, campus operations, and institutional governance. However, translating sustainability commitments into measurable actions remains a challenge. This contribution presents the experience of the Estonian University of Life Sciences in developing an integrated approach to sustainability monitoring, reporting, and action planning, highlighting opportunities and challenges for institutional SDG implementation.
The case study draws on the university's Green University initiative, institutional sustainability data collection, carbon footprint assessments conducted since 2022, and the development of a carbon footprint reduction and resource efficiency action plan. The approach combines cross-departmental collaboration, identification of key environmental impacts, SDG-related data collection, and the preparation of an institutional sustainability report. Particular attention is given to integrating sustainability objectives into university governance and operational decision-making.
The university has established a systematic approach to carbon footprint assessment, enabling the identification of major emission sources and priority areas for improvement. A practical action plan has been developed, defining responsibilities, implementation timelines, and annual review procedures. In parallel, the first institution-wide SDG-based sustainability report is being prepared to improve transparency and provide a basis for monitoring progress. The process has highlighted challenges related to data availability, coordination across university units, and measuring the impacts of activities that cannot be directly expressed in carbon dioxide equivalents.
The case demonstrates how universities can move from fragmented sustainability initiatives towards more coordinated institutional approaches. Linking carbon accounting, SDG reporting, and practical action planning can strengthen accountability and support evidence-informed decision-making. Beyond 2030, universities can contribute to sustainable development by embedding continuous monitoring, institutional collaboration, and adaptive management into their everyday operations.

Title: SDGs in heartprint projects – PtX-Lab-Challenge as door-opener towards sustainability commitment in energy transition
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Organisations: Gerner, Dr. Martin | TUD Dresden University of Technology
Keywords: service learning, tangible, relevant, strategic, PtX-Lab-Challenge
Abstract_Text: Some people doubt that simply adhering to research findings changes behaviour; this challenges an evidence-based promotion of the SDGs, especially where messaging primarily centres on wicked problems and excessive burdens, such like environmentalfootprints. Deficit-oriented facts should therefore increasingly be replaced by positive, intuitive approaches highlighting what people can actively contribute (handprint). Yet, their real impact remains vague, since knowing and acting do not automatically result in changing prevalent traits. Theheartprintconcept addresses this knowledge–action gap by highlighting civil-engagement projects that turn individual willingness into collective self-efficacy, thus calling for capacity-building and higher-education programmes to be redesigned around ownership and transformational SDG competencies.How may experiences of implementing SDGs through a service-learning course like praxiSDG boost a post-2030 agenda?We argue that SDGs do matter when being madetangible,relevantandstrategic. In our service-learning coursepraxiSDGand thePtX-Lab-Challengewe provide in-depth commitment and project-oriented interplay of stakeholders bridging the divide between academic and community contexts. ThroughpraxiSDGwe do invite like-minded campus-community members to collaboratively work on real-world challenges at level-playing field. Engaging with SDGs gets inspirational once turned into a strategic opportunity through value-adding partnerships. This vibe gets perceptible in co-creative steps of solution-based win-win situations that show levels of high ambition and interdependency of stakeholders. Please feel encouraged to join our interactive hub session! We invite you to immerse into our SDG-7 heartprint project ofPtX-Lab-Challenge, conjointly powered byPtX Lab Lausitz. Let’s experience and exchange views on how to raise the SDGs’ profile by making them tangible, relevant and strategic among authentic partners. Setting new horizons of co-creation, co-operation and ownership we are eager to share our lessons learned in energy transition!

Title: Resist, accept and direct in protected areas: Forest climate change adaptation choices in Natura 2000 areas in Lower Austria
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: climate adaptation, forestry, Natura 2000, political economy
Abstract_Text: Droughts, increasing temperatures and a growing number of extreme events put significant strain on Austrian forests. Those whose livelihoods depend on forestry must find sustainable ways to adapt their forests to these changing climatic conditions. However, local implementation efforts are embedded within complex and potentially conflicting regulatory multi-level governance arrangements and influenced by individuals' motivations and interests. Protection regimes such as Natura 2000 introduce an additional layer of complexity. This paper analyses the adaptation strategies of forest owners and foresters in protected areas, using the Resist-Accept-Direct (RAD) Framework as an analytical lens. Further the study analyses how forest actors’ decision-making is influenced by preferences, organisational objectives, and political-economic conditions. Empirically, this qualitative case study is based on management plans, site visit reports and six semi-structured interviews with local forest owners and foresters in Kamptal, Lower Austria. Our analysis shows, that forestry businesses in Kamptal use and experiment with different adaptation measures. Despite acting under similar ecological and political conditions, business-specific tendencies towards accept- or direct-oriented adaptation approaches were identified. Importantly, stated strategic preferences did not always translate into implemented measures, indicating that adaptation pathways are mediated by regulatory uncertainty, resource constraints and perceived legal risk. Natura 2000 does not alone determine whether forest actors resist, accept or direct ecological change. Instead, institutional, economic and relational conditions as well as local interpretations of conservation requirements shape which RAD choices become feasible and legitimate in practice. The findings are relevant to SDGs 13, 15, 16 and 17 and provide lessons for post 2030 sustainability governance: conservation policies need to protect biodiversity while remaining capable of responding to unavoidable ecological transformation through stronger incorporation of local stakeholders and a shift from static conservation to a more adaptive, learning-oriented conservation approach.

Title: Digital Sustainability Communication in the Fashion Industry: Brand Strategies and Consumer Perceptions in the Context of SDG 12
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Tunç Zengin, Dr. Mehtap | Istanbul Bilgi Uni
Keywords: sustainability communication, fashion industry, consumer perceptions, SDG 12, 5R framework
Abstract_Text:
Objective:This study investigates how Turkish clothing brands communicate sustainability through digital media and how consumers perceive these messages in relation to responsible consumption. Integrating the 5R principles—Reduce, Repair, Reuse, Recycle, and Reimagine—with Sustainable Development Goal 12 (SDG 12), the study examines sustainability communication across environmental, social, and economic dimensions.
Methods:The study adopts a qualitative research design combining content analysis of digital communications from eight Turkish clothing brands with semi-structured interviews with ten university students. The brand sample comprises four medium- to large-scale clothing brands and four smaller brands associated with slow-fashion approaches. Digital content published between September 2023 and January 2025 was analyzed using MAXQDA. The interviews explored participants’ sustainability awareness, engagement with 5R practices, and perceptions of selected brand messages, particularly whether these messages were considered credible or primarily marketing-oriented.
Key results:The preliminary content analysis indicates that environmental issues receive greater emphasis than social and economic dimensions. Within the 5R framework, Reimagine and Reduce are more prominently represented, while Repair and Reuse receive comparatively less attention. The interview component complements these findings by examining how consumers interpret sustainability messages, evaluate their credibility, and relate them to their own consumption practices.
Conclusions:By bringing brand communication and consumer perceptions together, this study provides a multidimensional perspective on sustainability communication in the fashion industry. It highlights the importance of connecting sustainability claims with clear, credible, and actionable information that supports responsible consumption. The findings may inform more transparent communication strategies and contribute to discussions on advancing SDG 12 beyond 2030.

Title: From Migration to Mitigation: Remittances and Household Decarbonisation in Nepal
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Remittances, household decarbonisation, just Transition, net-zero pathways
Abstract_Text:
Achieving net-zero emissions in developing economies requires not only expanding clean energy infrastructure but also enabling households to adopt low-carbon technologies. While migrant remittances are widely recognised for their contributions to household welfare and economic development, their potential role in accelerating household energy transitions remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates whether and how remittances influence household energy choices and the adoption of cleaner technologies in Nepal, a remittance-dependent economy committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2045.
The study conceptualises remittances as a potential source of private transition finance that can relax liquidity constraints and enable households to invest in technologies with relatively high upfront costs. However, increased income does not necessarily translate into decarbonisation, as rising purchasing power may also increase fossil fuel consumption. The research therefore examines whether remittance-receiving households are more likely to transition away from traditional biomass and fossil fuel-dependent energy use towards cleaner alternatives, including electric cooking, energy-efficient appliances, and electric mobility.
Using nationally representative household data from the Nepal Living Standards Surveys, the study proposes an econometric analysis of remittance receipt, household energy choices and technology adoption, accounting for socioeconomic characteristics and changes over time. It will also explore how outcomes vary across rural and urban households and how Nepal’s evolving clean energy policy environment may condition these relationships.
By connecting migration economics with household decarbonisation, the study seeks to extend understanding of how private financial flows can complement public climate policies. Its findings are expected to inform policy approaches that align remittance utilisation with clean energy investment, including targeted subsidies and remittance-linked green finance. The research also contributes to understanding of just transitions by examining household financial resources that can support inclusive pathways towards low-carbon development in remittance-dependent economies.

Title: 'If trees can walk, people can change': Impacts of a radical imaginative experiment on the scaling of urban Nature-based Solutions
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Keywords: Nature-based Solutions; Prefigurative actions, Scaling mechanisms; Urban experiments; Transformative change
Abstract_Text:
Over the last decade, Nature-based Solutions (NbS) have become widespread, cost-effective and multifunctional responses to many of today's wicked urban problems. Despite cities establishing ambitious targets, the implementation of urban NbS is lacking behind. Facing structural institutional and societal constraints, urban nature suffers from a weak narrative that requires deeper changes in order to shift human-nature relationships and scale.
To this end, this research looks into the potential of prefigurative urban experiments to challenge these structural barriers and instigate transformative change. Embodying alternative futures in the present, these prefigurative actions facilitate imagination through collective sensory experiences, and encourage critical reflections on the status quo. Despite this potential, little empirical evidence exist of the long-term impacts of prefigurative experiments on transformative change.
Henceforth, using a theoretical framework around 'scaling up, deep and out', this research revolves around a retrospective case study. Over the summer of 2022, the city of Leeuwarden hosted a radical urban greening art project named 'BOSK'. Featuring over 1000 trees that were moved around the inner city for 100 days, this project aimed to shift human-nature relations and show how urban nature can transform urban environments.
Applying a learning history approach, this research captures the reflections of different actor groups on their experiences of BOSK and its impact in the years thereafter. To this end, narrative interviews were used to investigate the long-term traces that BOSK left in policies, practices and mindsets of local actors, and the mechanisms that enabled or hampered the scaling of these impacts. Doing so, this research aims to learn how prefigurative experiments such as BOSK can contribute to scaling urban NbS.

Title: Unequal Access to National Health Insurance Scheme Coverage in Ghana: Causes and Consequences for well-being and sustainable development.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Organisations: Aikins, Prof. Eric Kojo Wu | University of Cape Coast
Keywords: National Health Insurance Scheme, Universal Health Insurance Coverage, Youth, Spatio-economic Development, Economically Disadvantage
Abstract_Text:
The National Health Insurance Scheme was established in 2004 to contribute to sustainable and healthy workforce production in Ghana (Darkwah, 2022). With an initial coverage of 6.74 percent the scheme grew to about 34 .0 percent coverage in 2010 and 52.7 percent in 2020 (Strupat, and Klohn, 2018: Alagidede, Baah-Boateng and Nketiah-Amponsah, 2013). Currently, the NHS coverage in Ghana has increase from 57 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2026 (Information Services Department, 2026).
The 30 percent of the population that are currently uncovered have limited access to effective healthcare mainly due to their general low level of education, low income, and cultural beliefs and practices.
The study employed a systematic review methodology, involving a review of global, Government of Ghana, and local health insurance coverage reports and related literature, to assess the problem of the relatively low NHIS coverage among the economically disadvantaged persons in Ghana. The study observed about 20 percent improvement in NHSI coverage between 2024 and 2026 period that if well maintained and intensified could result in universal coverage by 2030. Also, it examines the barriers to NHIS enrolment and provides the following policy strategies for expanding NHIS coverage towards the achievement of universal health coverage in Ghana by 2030:
1. The Government of Ghana could encourage the creation of small-scale enterprises capable of generating sustainable income to the under privileged population,
2. The Government of Ghana could bridge the gap between urban-rural spatio-economic development that could attract rural youth to rural areas,
3. The NHIS and the Government of Ghana expand the coverage of free care to cover the youth of school going ages that could defer payment of coverage till the youth completes their levels of education and get employed. Their past and current coverage will then be paid upon getting employed.

Title: Climate Shocks and Fiscal Resilience in Africa: Implications for Sustainable Development Beyond 2030
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Isah, Kazeem O.; Zerihun, Mulatu F.; Nyati, Malibongwe C.
Organisations: Isah, Dr. Kazeem | Tshwane University of Technology
Keywords: Climate shocks; Fiscal resilience; Sustainable development; Fiscal capacity; Africa
Abstract_Text: Climate shocks pose growing challenges to sustainable development, particularly in African economies where climatic vulnerability coincides with limited fiscal resources. While their implications for economic growth are increasingly documented, less is known about how these disturbances affect public finances and whether countries’ fiscal positions before a shock influence subsequent outcomes. This study examines the macroeconomic and fiscal consequences of climate shocks across 51 African economies over 2000–2023, focusing on the role of pre-shock fiscal capacity in shaping fiscal resilience. Using country-specific temperature and precipitation anomalies alongside historical macroeconomic and fiscal data, the analysis employs two-way fixed-effects models and panel local projections to investigate the contemporaneous and dynamic responses of economic growth, inflation, government revenue, fiscal balances and public debt. The findings reveal that below-normal precipitation is associated with weaker economic growth, while heat shocks are followed by a delayed deterioration in government revenue, reaching an estimated decline of 0.81 percentage points of GDP after three years. Importantly, countries entering heat shocks with weaker primary balances experience larger subsequent revenue losses, whereas the evidence that higher initial public debt systematically amplifies fiscal vulnerability is less consistent across alternative specifications. These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing accumulated debt from the fiscal capacity available before climatic disturbances occur. They suggest that strengthening domestic revenue mobilisation and preserving fiscal flexibility could improve governments’ ability to withstand climate-related pressures. For African economies, integrating climate-risk considerations into fiscal planning is therefore essential to protecting development financing, supporting adaptation and sustaining progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals and beyond 2030.

Title: Gathering the low-hanging fruits: Mapping price-based flexibility opportunities for smart energy hubs
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Tromp, Edrick; Zabala Figueroa, Alejandro; Medjroubi, Wided
Keywords: Price-based demand response, Grid congestion, Smart energy hubs
Abstract_Text:
Grid congestion increasingly limits electricity access for new developments, business expansion, and
renewable generation, creating a bottleneck for decarbonisation and economic growth. Electrification
of transport, heating, and industrial processes intensifies this pressure, while infrastructure expansion
requires substantial time and investment. Exemplary, the Dutch network operators project C 212 billion
in net electricity infrastructure investment over 2026–2040, expressed in 2026 prices. Furthermore,
grid congestion varies across regions, highlighting the need to identify where demand flexibility could
most effectively relieve network constraints and support local economic activity. To provide insights into
where demand flexibility could most effectively alleviate grid congestion and support local economic
activity, this study proposes a spatial framework for identifying promising municipalities for smart energy
hub development. These hubs could coordinate flexible electricity demand, local renewable generation,
and energy storage, supported by targeted incentives to encourage participation. We hypothesise that
areas with a larger share of industrial electricity demand, stronger short-term demand responsiveness
to electricity prices, and more severe grid congestion are particularly promising locations for energy
hubs, especially where industrial processes offer flexibility to shift or adjust consumption during periods
of congestion. To test this hypothesis, we will first map municipal DSO level non-residential electricity
demand and sectoral composition using available data. We will then estimate municipal-specific demand
responsiveness to electricity prices, accounting for weather, calendar effects, and energy prices. Then
municipal price-based demand response are analysed across municipalities to identify possible sectoral
effects. Spatial congestion indicators will characterise capacity constraints, connection queues, and
reported congestion periods. These indicators will be combined with supply-demand mismatches and
demand response indicator to rank candidate hub locations. The resulting framework aims to guide energy
hub development and geographically targeted flexibility incentives that support industrial competitiveness

Title: Cross-cultural perspectives on sustainability strategies and reporting in the compressed-air industry: A comparative study of India, Italy, and Sweden
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Militaru, Andreea Maria Gabriela; Fleaca, Elena; Ionita, Ioana Ruxandra
Organisations: National University of Science and Technology POLITEHNICA Bucharest
Keywords: Sustainability reporting, Cross-cultural comparison, Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG), Sustainable industrial development
Abstract_Text:
Objective:This study examines sustainability strategies and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting practices in the compressed-air industry through a cross-cultural comparison of two corporate groups: ELGi Equipments, headquartered in India and including its Italian subsidiary, Rotair SpA, and Atlas Copco, headquartered in Sweden. The research aims to identify similarities and differences in sustainability approaches and reporting practices, considering the influence of national cultural characteristics and regulatory environments.
Methods:The research adopts an exploratory comparative case study approach combining primary and secondary data. Primary information was collected during a field visit to Rotair SpA in Italy. Secondary sources include corporate sustainability reports, publicly available strategies, and scientific literature. The analysis examines environmental, social, and governance disclosures, with particular attention to energy efficiency, emissions reduction, reporting transparency, and governance practices. Selected Hofstede cultural dimensions, particularly Power Distance and Uncertainty Avoidance, provide a contextual framework for interpreting differences across India, Italy, and Sweden.
Key Results:Preliminary findings indicate differences in sustainability reporting maturity between the two corporate groups. Atlas Copco demonstrates more developed reporting practices, particularly regarding double materiality assessment, external assurance, and alignment with European sustainability reporting requirements. ELGi demonstrates sustainability commitments and initiatives, although opportunities remain to improve reporting transparency and comparability. Similar challenges in social disclosures are observed across both groups. The comparison suggests that regulatory requirements and national cultural characteristics may help explain differences in reporting approaches, although direct causal relationships cannot be established.
Conclusions:The study highlights the importance of transparent ESG reporting, responsible governance, and energy-efficient technologies in supporting sustainable industrial transformation. The comparative approach provides insights into how to improve sustainability practices across different organisational and national contexts. By addressing industrial energy efficiency, emissions reduction, and reporting credibility, the research contributes to sustainable development priorities for 2030 and beyond.

Title: Gendered Effects of Climate Change in Zimbabwe: Experiences of Smallholder Rural Women Farmers in Chiredzi District.
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: climate change, gendered effects, smallholder farming, rural women, Zimbabwe
Abstract_Text: This study examines the gendered impacts of climate change on the livelihoods of rural women farmers in Chiredzi District, Zimbabwe. Adopting a qualitative research design, the study draws on data collected through in-depth interviews, key informant interviews, and focus group discussions. The data are thematically analysed through the complementary theoretical lenses of liberal feminism, radical feminism, and feminist standpoint theory. The findings demonstrate that patriarchal structures, gendered socialisation, limited access to civil rights and productive resources, and women’s marginalisation from knowledge production and decision-making processes significantly constrain their capacity to sustain, diversify, and adapt their livelihoods in response to climate-related shocks. These structural and institutional inequalities not only limit women’s agency but also generate compounding social and economic vulnerabilities that heighten their exposure to climate risks. Given that women constitute key actors in agricultural production and household food provisioning in Chiredzi, climate-induced disruptions to agricultural activities have particularly pronounced consequences for their livelihoods and well-being. The study highlights women’s vulnerability to climate change is intensified by pre-existing gender inequalities embedded within social, cultural, economic, and institutional systems. Therefore, policy and social reforms are crucial. The results provide broader insights into the challenges and vulnerabilities experienced by women farmers across Zimbabwe.

Title: Digitalisation for sustainable chemistry education: Integrating green chemistry metrics and artificial intelligence into an electronic laboratory notebook
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Authors: Nwafor, Peace C; Gurung, Shason; van Krimpen, Philip; Jolley, Katherine; Hirst, Jonathan D
Organisations: Nwafor, Dr. Peace C | Anglia Ruskin University
Keywords: Green chemistry, Artificial intelligence, Electronic laboratory notebooks, Sustainability assessment, Chemistry education
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Integrating green and sustainable chemistry into undergraduate education is essential for advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production). Artificial intelligence (AI) and digitalisation offer opportunities to embed sustainability assessment into laboratory workflows, enhance decision-making, and develop industry-relevant digital competencies. This study evaluates the potential of an AI-enabled electronic laboratory notebook (ELN) to support sustainable chemistry education.
Methods: AI4Green4Students, a pedagogically tailored ELN, was developed through an iterative, user-centred design process informed by instructor and student questionnaires and interviews. The platform integrates structured experimental data capture, hazard assessment, green chemistry metrics, solvent selection guidance, and machine learning-assisted reaction prediction. Its implementation in a third-year MSci organic chemistry laboratory course was evaluated through student feedback, instructor observations, and assessment of laboratory records and project reports.
Key results: Instructor evaluation indicated that integrated feedback, automated notifications, and approval workflows improved experimental planning and supported timely intervention before laboratory activities. Structured templates facilitated more complete, consistent, and professionally presented experimental records compared with template-free documentation. Students using the ELN demonstrated greater engagement with sustainability considerations, including solvent selection, reaction conditions, and green chemistry metrics. Assessment of project reports indicated more critical and consistent integration of sustainability principles than among students completing equivalent projects without the ELN. However, usability challenges, including extensive mandatory data entry and device limitations, highlighted barriers to wider adoption.
Conclusions: AI-enabled ELNs offer opportunities to integrate sustainability assessment, digital literacy, and evidence-based decision-making into chemistry education. Addressing usability and implementation challenges is essential for wider adoption. This approach supports progress towards SDGs 4, 9, and 12 by 2030 while providing a transferable framework for sustainable laboratory practices beyond 2030.

Title: Inequal Exchange Between the United States and the Global South
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Understanding climate change and climate actions for human security
Organisations: Twichell, Joe | Energy and Environmental Science
Keywords: Unequal Exchange, United States, Global South, MRIO
Abstract_Text: This project has the goal of exposing the unequal trade between the United States and the Global South. This will be done using Multi-Regional Input-Output (MRIO) tables to find where the value added is flowing, while also looking at where the environmental impacts are imbedded. We expect to see that the United States is richer than these nations due to unfair trade deals, getting the majority of the value while harboring less of the pollution. After this is visualized with the MRIO data, the scope can be focused in on the trade between the US and one specific country (to be decided by calculated value exchange), and the history between them. This will tie the data to the real world cause of the imbalance.
