Title: Governance Architectures for Energy, Mineral, Waste and Climate Transitions in Sub-Saharan Africa
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: de Wit, Martin; du Plessis, Anel; Esler, Karen; Midgley, Guy; Williams, Samantha
Organisations: de Wit, Prof. Martin | Stellenbosch University
Keywords: governance architecture, energy transition, critical minerals, environmental burden, sub-Saharan Africa
Abstract_Text: Sub-Saharan Africa will add close to a billion people by 2050, and most of the energy, mineral, urban and waste infrastructure they will use has not yet been built. Choices made before 2035 will therefore lock in the region's environmental footprint and its development path for decades. Research has mostly treated energy, critical minerals, waste and climate finance as separate sectors. This perspective treats them as one governance problem. We define governance architecture as the arrangement of rules, organisations and power relations that decides who controls natural resources, where the income from them goes, and who can check abuses of that control. We place 49 sub-Saharan countries in a two-axis scenario space of accountable resource governance capacity and transition burden. We then explore four conditional pathways to 2050: a Green Shift and a Brown Shift, in which governance and environment move together, and two trade-off pathways, Developmental Brown and Green Authoritarian, in which they move apart. Robustness checks show that 71% of the region's population live in countries currently in the weak-governance, heavy-burden quadrant. We argue that the trade-off pathways are the most policy-relevant, and we derive testable propositions about the minimum accountability conditions and safeguards that keep transitions from becoming extractive or authoritarian.

Title: From Speculative Visions to Pathways for Sustainable Transformation
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Keywords: Speculative futures, Post-2030 sustainability, Future sustainability priorities, Doctoral research, Sustainable transformation
Abstract_Text:
How might the world look 50 years from now if we succeed in addressing today’s sustainability challenges, and what if we do not? This innovative session builds on the SENSE PhD Symposium 2026,Reimagining Sustainability: Connecting Systems, Challenges and Future Pathways, organised by the SENSE (Socio-Economic and Natural Sciences of the Environment) Research School, an interdisciplinary network connecting sustainability researchers across institutions and disciplines.
The session will bring conversations initiated at the symposium to a wider community of experts, extending the discussion on interconnected environmental, social, economic, technological and governance challenges and the futures we want to shape beyond 2030. A starting point will be the symposium’sVoices from the FutureGallery, which invites SENSE researchers and PhD candidates to explore possible futures through creative contributions, including stories, images, illustrations, headlines and other speculative forms. These visions challenge present-day assumptions, explore alternatives and open up new ways of thinking about sustainability.
The session will take the form of facilitated roundtable discussions, bringing together participants from different disciplinary and institutional backgrounds. Using selected Gallery contributions as prompts, participants will critically examine imagined futures, identify trade-offs and overlooked perspectives, and discuss the transformations and forms of cooperation needed to realise desirable outcomes. Working backwards from these visions, participants will collaboratively identify key milestones, decisions and research priorities that could translate long-term aspirations into present-day action. A collective synthesis will bring these discussions together into a shared pathway framework, outlining priorities and opportunities for sustainable transformation beyond 2030.
At the heart of the session is the role of doctoral researchers as emerging knowledge producers and key actors in sustainability transformations. Connecting their creative visions and perspectives with those of a broader expert community will help challenge established ways of thinking, foster interdisciplinary collaboration and develop pathways towards more just, resilient and sustainable futures.

Title: Data as critical infrastructure and asset for SDG localisation and reporting: perspectives from South African municipalities
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: digital governance, big data, data governance, SDG localization, Voluntary Local Reviews
Abstract_Text:
Local governments are expected to review progress on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), yet the data for doing so are organised around national surveys and sectoral administration, not municipal boundaries. This paper treats data as critical infrastructure and a public asset for SDG localisation, drawing on a UN DESA-supported programme in South Africa that paired a national data platform with municipal Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs).
Three strands are combined: an assessment of 30 draft VLRs against the eight UN DESA/UNECA building blocks; an indicator-level audit of municipal data availability for the 339-indicator localised SDG framework before and after the National Strategic Hub (NSH) re-aggregated crime, education and spatialised tax data to municipal level; and the alignment of Service Delivery and Budget Implementation Plan (SDBIP) indicators to SDG targets in five pilot municipalities.
VLR maturity was high (mean 20 of 24) but coverage narrow: median seven of seventeen goals, methodology sections often absent, "leave no one behind" rarely evidenced with disaggregated data. These gaps tracked data availability. Before NSH, municipal-level data existed for 7% of SDG 9 indicators, 18% of SDG 4 and 28% of SDG 16; re-aggregation to municipal boundaries raised projected coverage to roughly 45–70%. Aligning 1 274 SDBIP indicators (84% from the departmental layer) showed that municipalities already held evidence for 10 to 16 goals each, well beyond the one to six they chose to review, and allowed R2.4 billion of capital expenditure to be traced to SDG targets. Persistent gaps were misaligned administrative boundaries, erratic regulatory reporting and missing disaggregation.
Data infrastructure determines what gets reviewed. A post-2030 agenda should fund national platforms that re-aggregate administrative data to local boundaries, treat municipal performance data as an SDG asset, and secure data stewardship across political and fiscal cycles.

Title: Does ESG Disclosure Really Pay Off? Unpacking Within-Firm Dynamics and Between-Firm Heterogeneity in Saudi Arabia
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Organisations: Sharawi, Dr. Dr.Hossam | Jeddah International College
Keywords: EESG disclosure, Sustainability assessment, Corporate financial performance, corporate accountability, SDGs beyond 2030
Abstract_Text:
This study examines whether environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure is associated with stronger corporate financial performance and explores its implications for assessing corporate contributions to sustainable development. Drawing on stakeholder, legitimacy, and resource-based theories, the research distinguishes between persistent differences across firms and changes in disclosure practices within firms over time. The analysis covers 75 Saudi-listed companies across 17 industries during 2021–2025, comprising 375 firm-year observations. ESG disclosure is measured using a researcher-developed index informed by established literature and systematic annual-report content analysis. The empirical framework combines pooled ordinary least squares, firm fixed-effects models, and within–between panel estimations, supported by firm-clustered standard errors and robustness checks.
The findings indicate a positive association between ESG disclosure and corporate profitability in pooled and between-firm estimations, whereas the within-firm relationship is statistically insignificant. However, formal coefficient-comparison tests do not establish a statistically significant difference between these relationships. These findings caution against interpreting greater ESG disclosure as evidence of immediate financial gains or substantive sustainability improvements.
The study contributes to sustainability scholarship by integrating a context-sensitive, researcher-developed ESG disclosure index with a longitudinal analytical framework that separates firm-level heterogeneity from temporal changes in reporting behavior. Economically, the findings inform investment decisions and corporate sustainability strategies by clarifying the limitations of disclosure-based financial assessments. The findings also underscore the importance of credible sustainability disclosure, corporate accountability, and more comprehensive approaches to sustainability assessment. In relation to SDGs 8, 12, and 16, the study offers relevant insights for the post-2030 development agenda by highlighting the need to distinguish corporate reporting practices from measurable financial outcomes and independently verified sustainability performance.

Title: Water Security in Kuwait: Exploring a Water Citizenship Approach to Sustainable Water Futures
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Organisations: Bilgen, Dr. Arda | London School of Economics and Political Science
Keywords: water security, water governance, water scarcity, civic responsibility, Kuwait
Abstract_Text: Kuwait faces critical water security challenges driven by extreme freshwater scarcity, near-total reliance on energy-intensive desalination, and some of the world’s highest per capita water consumption rates. While technological interventions have expanded supply, they often intensify environmental pressures and overlook the social and behavioural dimensions that shape water use. This study introduces a Kuwait-specific framework of ‘water citizenship’ to examine how identity, cultural values, and governance structures influence water practices and public engagement. Using a qualitative approach grounded in constructivist grounded theory, the research draws on interviews, participant observation, and policy document analysis to capture the complex interplay between individual behaviour, social norms, and institutional frameworks. Initial findings reveal persistent gaps between water awareness and everyday action, limited avenues for meaningful citizen participation, and policy narratives that emphasise supply-side solutions over societal involvement. These patterns suggest that addressing water challenges in Kuwait requires more than technical fixes; it necessitates cultivating a sense of civic responsibility and embedding water conservation within cultural and social practices. By linking identity, values, and governance to practical strategies for engagement, the study offers a conceptual model for integrating behavioural change, cultural meaning, and public participation into sustainable water management. This approach not only provides insights for Kuwait but also contributes to broader debates on water governance in arid urban contexts, highlighting the critical role of socially informed, participatory approaches in building resilient and sustainable water systems.

Title: Beyond 2030: Corporate Net-Zero Commitments and Local Sustainability Implementation in Scottish Grocery Retail
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Integrated sustainability assessment of progress made on the SDGs
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals; Net Zero; Life Cycle Assessment; Scope 3 Emissions; Sustainability Governance
Abstract_Text:
As the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) approach their 2030 deadline, assessing the effectiveness of sustainability commitments and their implementation at the local level is increasingly important. This study examines the gap between corporate net-zero commitments and operational sustainability practices in Scotland's grocery retail sector, providing evidence to inform integrated sustainability assessment frameworks beyond 2030.
A quantitative, cross-sectional observational study was conducted across 20 grocery retail stores in Edinburgh, representing the retail giants like Aldi, Lidl, Sainsbury's and Tesco. The research integrated Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), Material Flow Analysis (MFA), Scope 1–3 greenhouse gas accounting and 113 operational sustainability variables. Four composite sustainability indices were developed to assess energy transition, material flows, decarbonisation readiness and circular governance. Scenario modelling evaluated six potential decarbonisation interventions against Scotland's 2045 net-zero target.
The findings identified gaps between corporate sustainability commitments and store-level implementation. Scope 3 emissions accounted for approximately 73.6% of estimated total emissions, while upstream product emissions dominated the life cycle assessment. The study also identified limited carbon labelling, insufficient store-level net-zero communication and uneven sustainability infrastructure. Scenario modelling suggested that a 20% shift towards plant-based products could reduce modelled emissions by approximately 20.8%, highlighting the importance of supply-chain interventions alongside operational improvements.
These findings highlight the limitations of relying exclusively on corporate level sustainability disclosures to evaluate progress towards SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action). The study recommends integrating measurable local sustainability indicators, supply-chain emissions accounting and scenario-based assessment into post 2030 monitoring frameworks to strengthen transparency, accountability and evidence-based implementation.

Title: The perspectives of primary care healthcare professionals on interventions aimed at reducing the environmental impact of medicines: a mixed-methods systematic review as part of the PREWAPHARM project
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Environmental health and emerging pollutants, including regulatory and governance responses, and policy translation of exposure science
Authors: Culkin, Laura; Cardon, Helena; Taxis, Katja; Boussery, Koen; Ryan, Cristín
Keywords: Primary care, perspectives, interventions, medicines, environmental impact
Abstract_Text:
Introduction: Healthcare accounts for approximately 4-5% of global greenhouse gas emissions, with medicines contributing substantially to this footprint. Pharmaceuticals enter the environment throughout their lifecycle, contributing to water pollution, which can have adverse ecological effects and contribute to antimicrobial resistance. Primary care is well positioned to implement interventions to reduce this environmental impact. However, the success of such interventions depends partly on the healthcare professionals (HCPs) expected to deliver them.
Aim: To synthesise primary care HCPs’ perspectives on interventions designed to reduce the environmental impact of medicines.
Methods: MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science and CINAHL were systematically searched for qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods studies exploring primary care HCPs’ perspectives on relevant interventions. No language or date restrictions were applied. Screening, data extraction and quality appraisal were performed independently and in duplicate. Quantitative data were ‘qualitised’ and integrated with qualitative findings using a convergent integrated synthesis approach as per JBI guidance.
Results: Twenty-nine studies were included: 17 qualitative, 11 quantitative, and 1 mixed-methods study. Findings were synthesised across intervention groupings: targeted medication interventions, medicines optimisation strategies, pharmaceutical waste management, educational interventions, and general perspectives not attributable to any one intervention type. HCPs generally expressed positive attitudes towards interventions, particularly when they aligned with best clinical practice, e.g., medication reviews. Consistently, patient safety and clinical considerations were prioritised over environmental concerns. Common
implementation barriers included insufficient education, limited resources, inadequate support and financial constraints. Key facilitators included education, necessary resources, financial incentives and supportive policy measures.
Conclusion: Primary care HCPs are generally supportive of environmental interventions, but implementation is hindered by organisational and system-level barriers. Aligning environmental objectives with existing clinical best practices, while addressing implementation barriers, may facilitate integration into routine primary care.
This project has received funding from the European Union’s Interreg NWE program under grant no. NWE0400548 (PREWAPHARM).

Title: Resilience for Growth: Policy Narratives of Climate Adaptation in Indonesia's Industrial Development
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Keywords: policy narratives, climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, industrial development, industrial estate
Abstract_Text: Indonesia confronts intensifying climate and disaster risks even as it pursues an industrial growth agenda that concentrates development in its most hazard-exposed coastal and urban landscapes. While climate change adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and industrial estate development are each governed by extensive policy architectures, little is known about how these domains converge in the pursuit of climate-resilient industrial development. This article examines how Indonesian policy constructs climate adaptation in industrial estates and industrial development, treating policy documents not as neutral technical instruments but as purposeful narratives that shape which interventions appear necessary and legitimate. Drawing on the Narrative Policy Framework, it applies qualitative content and thematic analysis to nineteen national policy and planning documents published between 2007 and 2025, coded in NVivo and organised into seven thematic domains. The analysis surfaces five recurring contradictions: adaptation framed as an economic safeguard; risk acknowledged without altered spatial planning; governance centralised in design yet decentralised in burden; an increasing regulatory apparatus that outpaces implementation; and green industrialisation advanced alongside extractive down streaming. Together these reveal that adaptation governance in Indonesian industrial estates is not merely a technical exercise in managing environmental risk, but a political and economic process that tends to legitimise existing patterns of growth.

Title: Diagnosing the Gap Between Urban Rail Investment and Sustainable Mobility Outcomes: Spatial Evidence from Palembang, Indonesia
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Keywords: Sustainable mobility, Urban rail, Spatial alignment, Urban development, Spatial Diagnostic Framework
Abstract_Text:
Urban rail investment is increasingly promoted as a strategy for sustainable urban mobility, yet infrastructure provision does not necessarily deliver the anticipated transport outcomes. This study examines how spatial alignment between rail infrastructure, metropolitan demand, urban growth, and station-area accessibility may explain urban rail underperformance. Drawing on the Palembang light rail system in Indonesia, the research investigates the spatial conditions underlying the gap between planned investment objectives and realised transport performance.
The study develops a Spatial Diagnostic Framework comprising three dimensions: Demand–Structure Alignment, Growth Trajectory Alignment, and Network–Urban Form Interface. The framework assesses population and activity distributions, urban growth trajectories, corridor positioning, street-network connectivity, and pedestrian accessibility across metropolitan, corridor, and station-catchment scales.
Preliminary findings reveal uneven spatial alignment along the Palembang light rail corridor. Concentrations of population and urban activities do not consistently coincide with emerging growth areas, while street-network connectivity and pedestrian accessibility vary across station catchments. These patterns indicate spatial mismatches between infrastructure provision, existing urban demand, and development trajectories, which may contribute to the system's underperformance.
The study identifies spatial alignment as an important dimension in understanding urban rail underperformance. The proposed framework offers a systematic approach to assessing the relationship between transport infrastructure and urban development, complementing operational and institutional analyses. Its application to Palembang provides an initial basis for examining similar challenges in other rapidly urbanising cities. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 11 by informing evidence-based urban transport planning and sustainable urban development towards and beyond 2030.

Title: Optimising SDG progress in Australia through the combination of System Dynamics modelling and Reinforcement Learning algorithms
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Authors: Sperone, Edoardo; Allen, Cameron; Malekpour, Shirin; Asadikia, Atie
Keywords: System Dynamics Modelling, Reinforcement Learning, SDGs, Optimisation, Decision-making
Abstract_Text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) form an interconnected system in which progress on one goal can accelerate or undermine progress on others. Policymakers therefore need to know which interlinkages exist, and also which combinations and sequences of interventions maximise progress across goals over time. System Dynamics (SD) models capture broad, causally structured SDG interactions, but they are designed to explore “what-if” scenarios rather than to optimise. Optimisation-based models, by contrast, typically cover only a narrow subset of goals. This study addresses the gap by coupling SD with deep Reinforcement Learning algorithms such as SAC and PPO to find strategic interventions that maximise sustainable development progress over time based on SDG interlinkages. We use the iSD-Australia model, which covers all 17 SDGs and has been calibrated against over 30 years of national historical data. At each annual time step to 2050, an RL agent adjusts policy levers such as government expenditure, taxation or private investment. These adjustments stay within bounds on feasible annual change, and the agent is rewarded according to the model’s SDG performance indicators. We also compare alternative reward formulations, such as maximising aggregate SDG progress versus prioritising lagging goals, to show how normative choices shape optimal pathways. This way, we outline optimised trajectories for Australian SDG indicators to 2050, the policy levers and timings that act as leverage points, and synergies and trade-offs that the agent exploits or must navigate. Sensitivity analysis tests whether the learned strategies hold up under parameter uncertainty. The framework shows how AI can move SDG modelling from scenario exploration towards decision support.

Title: The Next Global Prosperity Priorities
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Hunt, Dr. Peter | University of New South Wales
Keywords: Sustainable Development, Economic Growth, Political Participation, Equity, Prosperity
Abstract_Text:
What are the lessons learnt from analysing the achievements and failures of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and what is now needed to ensure a sustainable future for humanity?
Our Common Future (1987) conceptualised sustainable development with the notion of intergenerational equity, stating that “Humanity has the ability to make development sustainable – to ensure that it meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations…” and stated that a new approach to economic growth aided by political systems is necessary to secure effective participation. These notions were central to the formation of the SDGs. They were globally accepted and established as appropriate environmental, social and economic goals. The SDGs were designed to reflect the variety of contemporary principals of sustainable development applicable from 2015 to 2030. As the 2030 deadline approaches many of the goals will not be achieved and we have witnessed a disparity across and within some nations in their desire and ability to reach the goals. Whilst some nations have embraced the SDGs, many contemporary economic and political systems have diverged away from the SDGs.
This empirical research reflects on the establishment of the concept of sustainable development, analyses and evaluates the reported performance of the SDGs. This critique enables the establishment of the next sustainable development priorities and critical pathways.
A new set of urgent priorities are now required to ensure a sustainable future. The key priorities now include the environmental and economic impacts from climate change, with energy, food and water security, and the societal issues around the evolving human population demographics and the desire to create global social equity. To achieve appropriate sustainable development outcomes beyond 2030, priorities focussed on global prosperity need to be set, policy commitment needs to be established, and the economic benefits need to be promoted.

Title: Evolving Path of Global Sustainable Development Governance
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Furman, Eeva; Schönach, Paula; Rantala, Salla
Keywords: agency, global, UN, multi-actor, multilevel
Abstract_Text:
Over time, sustainability challenges have become more interconnected and complex with global megatrends from shifting geopolitics, digitalisation, the concentration of wealth to threefold ecological crisis of climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution. This context has heightened the need to advance sustainable development at the global level, resulting in a dynamic and evolving governance architecture. How has this materialized over the years? Where to move next?
Our presentation examines global sustainable development governance as a platform for agency. We highlight the role of the United Nations and evaluate how actors across scales—from local to global—have shaped this governance landscape. We elaborate on what kind of institutions, networks and groups have taken agency and use some cases from literature to flesh this out. In recent years, major geopolitical turbulence has intensified structural challenges and increased pressure while eroding collective capacity to respond. We therefore ask whether existing forms of agency are sufficiently robust and appropriately targeted.
We conclude by outlining new approaches which potentially could mobilize action and open regenerative paths to global sustainable development governance.

Title: From Global Goals to National Realities in Pakistan: Fiscal Constraints and Lessons for the Post-2030 Agenda
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Asad, Prof. Saeed Ahmad | COMSATS University Islamabad, Pakistan
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals, Fiscal Constraints, Sustainability Governance, Institutional Resilience, Climate Finance, Post-2030 Agenda
Abstract_Text:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) aim to steer national development towards prosperity, social inclusion and environmental sustainability, yet their influence remains limited in climate vulnerable states facing fiscal constraints and institutional instability. Pakistan ranks 131stout of 169 states and SDG score index of 59.3, placing it last in South Asia. Although, the country has made progress for mainstreaming SDGs including automated SDGs tagging across national project life cycles, overall progress remains limited with reported advancement on 19% of the targets. Major challenges remain for SDG 4 (26 million children out of school), SDG1 (poverty), SDG2 (food security), and SDG5 (gender equality). These challenges are aggravated by an annual SDG financing gap of US$60 billion and rising debt-servicing pressures that constraint social investment. Against this backdrop, Pakistan provides a case for examining why global sustainability commitments have not translated into sustained national implementation.
The paper draws on SDG policies, national reviews, financing, and monitoring frameworks. It also examines debt, development priorities, and Govt. responsibilities. It notes that fiscal challenges, and fragmented monitoring systems have compromised the effect of SDGs in Pakistan. Implementation discontinuity, bureaucracy, political transitions, and fragmented local data weakened planning and accountability. The analysis proposes four mechanisms for the post-2030 sustainability agenda; 1. Fiscal reality, connecting global targets with expenditure frameworks, public spending, and innovative development financing; 2. Institutional durability, continuing implementation and monitoring processes under administrative and political transitions; 3. Territorial responsiveness, through relevant local indicators and stronger links between subnational priorities, budgets, and outcomes; 4) Accountability, through accessible data systems and clear implementation monitoring. Debt-swaps and SDG-aligned climate finance, tailored to national capacity and fiscal conditions should be considered. Post-2030 framework must align global ambitions with national financing, institutions, and accountability. These principles may steer global sustainability agendas in vulnerable, fiscally constrained countries.

Title: Beyond scavenging: Hooded vulture ecosystem services in strengthening Human and environmental resilience for sustainable development in Burkina Faso
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Authors: DABONE, Clément; OUEDA, Adama; WEESIE, Peter D M
Organisations: DABONE, Dr. Clément | University Thomas SANKARA
Keywords: Ecosystem services, Vultures’ conservation, Human well-being, Sustainable development, Burkina Faso.
Abstract_Text:
Throughout Africa, Hooded vultures provide essential ecosystem services by feeding on animal carcasses and human organic waste. This supports ecosystem balance and contributes to human well-being and environmental resilience. However, they have declined sharply in number across Africa due to both intentional and unintentional poisoning, and the use of their body parts for belief-based practices. In Burkina Faso, we have assessed an important ecosystem service provided by Hooded vultures to elucidate their contribution to socio-ecological resilience, and identify conservation strategies supporting sustainable human development.
To meet this objective, we quantified the amounts of animal carcasses and organs deemed unfit for human consumption that were removed by Hooded vultures and estimated the economic value of this natural waste-removal service across five abattoirs located in different towns. We have found that a daily average of 110 Hooded vultures visited the five surveyed abattoirs. Over a single year, these five abattoirs generated a total of 83 tonnes of animal carcasses and organs, which were removed by Hooded vultures at no direct cost. The estimated economic value of this ecosystem service amounted to €306,000 in just one year. By removing animal carcasses and recycling organic matter from abattoirs, throughout towns and townships as well as in more natural settings, Hooded vultures support ecosystem balance and potentially reduce environmental and public health risks associated with carcass accumulation. We therefore recommend the establishment of supplementary feeding sites in and around abattoirs which could ensure safe food availability, mitigate poisoning risks, and reduce the environmental and human health risks. This conservation strategy extends well beyond mere biodiversity protection, particularly in developing countries, where towns often lack effective systems for the collection, management, and processing of animal carcasses. It will make a significant contribution to human well-being, and sustainable development in Burkina Faso over the coming decades.

Title: From Ambition to Evidence: Benchmarking the Corporate Transition
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Keywords: Corporate Accountability, CSRD, Net-Zero Transition, ISSB, SBTi
Abstract_Text:
Nearly 2,000 companies, representing USD 36.6 trillion in annual revenue, have pledged net-zero, yet only a fraction show credible follow-through (Net-zero Tracker, 2025). Closing this gap is a shared challenge for corporations and the scientific infrastructure underpinning the standards, data and verification systems that would make pledges credible. Voluntary frameworks such as the Science Based Targets initiative and mandatory regimes such as the EU's European Sustainability Reporting Standards have both recently been revised from the perspective of flexibilizing company reporting and engagement. While this helps to build a common reporting ground,a shared scientific base for measuring progress, credibility of actions and capital investments is still lacking. A recent Nature Sustainability Perspective (Gudipudi et al., 2026) maps some of these challenges.
The session, co-chaired by Ramana Gudipudi and Luis Costa. Ramana Gudipudi then presents the evidence and the proposal for industry-specific, peer-reviewed net-zero blueprints that translate global climate targets into firm-level, sector-specific benchmarks. Luis Costa (World Benchmarking Alliance) presents recent analysis benchmarking the transition plans of the world's most influential companies, based on emissions performance, the robustness of transition planning and the alignment of capital expenditure with decarbonisation targets - showing how far current practice sits from credible pathways.
A moderated roundtable follows, bringing together the speakers with Panji Putra (Henkel), on implementing net-zero and GHG accounting inside a global manufacturer; Niskua Igualikinya (European Climate Foundation), on how philanthropy can fund the missing scientific infrastructure; and Franco Ruzzenenti (University of Groningen), on how complex-systems modelling can build sector-specific pathways at scale. The session aims to identify concrete next steps: industry-specific benchmarks, independent verification and blended funding models for turning pledges into evidence-based action.
Corporate net-zero pledges have proliferated, yet evidence increasingly suggests that most fall short of real-world impacts. This reflects not a lack of ambition but a lack of scientific foundations needed to ensure credibility and integrity in corporate climate action. This uncertainty underpins a trillion-dollar question: how capital and policy mechanisms can be directed towards actions that genuinely reduce emissions. A scientific infrastructure built around four interconnected research frontiers can close this gap, making corporate climate commitments credible, comparable and policy-relevant at scale. This could redirect trillions of dollars in investments towards genuine climate action.
Corporate climate commitments are now widespread, but evidence that they translate into credible, funded and socially responsible transition plans remains thin. This talk presents the World Benchmarking Alliance's (WBA) 2026 Climate Benchmark, which assesses the transition plans of 2,000 of the world's most influential companies. Together, these companies generate USD 53 trillion in revenue and account for 54% of global emissions.
Building on the Assessing low-Carbon Transition (ACT) methodologies applied to 450 companies in high-emitting sectors between 2020 and 2024, WBA extended the approach to all sectors through a unified framework, ACT Core. Companies are assessed on the credibility and integrity of their transition plans across six areas: emissions reporting and target definition, planning for the low-carbon transition, governance and policy, low-carbon investments, current target alignment, and performance. A complementary Just Transition assessment examines whether plans account for workers and communities. The methodology is built around publicly disclosed information, enabling comparison at scale while retaining a performance-oriented focus.
The results reveal a gap between ambition and delivery. Only 5% of companies integrate impacts on workers and communities into their climate transition plans, and just 4% set measurable targets to manage them. At the same time, leading companies across 19 industries are allocating 30% to climate solutions; if replicated more widely, this shift could mobilise at least USD 1.3 trillion for the transition without technological breakthroughs.
The talk will discuss the methodological choices behind the benchmark, the limits of disclosure-based assessment, and how the publicly accessible data can help researchers, investors and policymakers hold corporate transition planning to account and test whether credible plans translate into measurable decarbonisation. Attendees will gain a clearer view of where corporate transition planning is strong, where it falls short, and which questions the data can and cannot yet answer.
Corporate net-zero commitments are now common, but investors, researchers and policymakers increasingly ask whether they are backed by credible, funded and verifiable transition plans. This contribution offers the view from inside a multinational: Henkel, a global consumer goods and adhesives company with operations and supply chains across many regions.
Henkel has committed to net-zero greenhouse gas emissions across its value chain by 2045, aligned with the Science Based Targets initiative's Corporate Net-Zero Standard and a 1.5°C pathway. The plan combines a 90% absolute reduction in Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions by 2045 against a 2021 baseline with interim 2030 targets: a 42% cut in Scope 1 and 2 emissions, a 30% cut in Scope 3 emissions, and 100% renewable electricity. By 2025, absolute emissions across all three scopes had fallen 29% against the baseline, and 97% of electricity consumed globally came from renewable sources. Henkel intends to address the remaining 10% of unavoidable emissions through high-quality carbon removal.
The talk uses this case to examine what it takes to move from ambition to delivery. It discusses where progress has come fastest, such as renewable electricity and site-level energy management, and where it is harder: Scope 3 emissions, replacing fossil-based feedstocks, and improving supply chain transparency. It also reflects on how packaging circularity targets interact with the climate agenda, and how companies should treat emissions that cannot be eliminated.
Finally, the contribution considers how external assessments, including independent benchmarks of corporate transition plans, are experienced by the companies they evaluate: what they help clarify, what they miss, and how they could better support the transition. Written for a panel discussion between company, benchmarking and research perspectives, it aims to identify what evidence would make corporate transition plans more credible and comparable for all stakeholders.
Corporate transition plans are typically assessed one company at a time: targets, governance, investment and progress. Yet the emissions these companies are responsible for arise from interconnected systems of suppliers, customers, energy carriers and markets. A plan that looks credible for a single firm may not add up when the same logic is applied across an entire economy. This contribution asks what a systems perspective can add to how corporate decarbonisation is planned, measured and benchmarked.
Drawing on research in complex systems, network theory, energy modelling and industrial ecology, the talk addresses three questions. First, how do efficiency gains and emission reductions made within one company propagate through value chains, and when are they offset elsewhere through rebound effects, burden shifting or displaced demand? Second, how should Scope 3 targets be understood when one company's supply-chain emissions are another's operational emissions, and how can double counting and gaps be avoided when many firms report at once? Third, what do assessments of thousands of companies, such as the 2,000 influential firms covered by the World Benchmarking Alliance, which together account for over half of global emissions, imply about whether the sum of corporate plans is consistent with global climate goals?
The contribution is framed as a research agenda and a set of questions for discussion with the company and benchmarking practitioners on the panel. Which network-based indicators could complement disclosure-based scores? How could rebound and system-wide effects be considered when evaluating transition plans? What data would companies need to share to make this possible? By connecting corporate-level benchmarking with system-level modelling, the session aims to help make transition plans not only credible for individual firms, but collectively consistent with the transformations required beyond 2030.

Title: Occupational health in the hotel cleaning jobs
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: Health Inequalities, Well Being Determinants, Population Health, Occupational Wellbeing
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
Hotel work is characterized by hard work, long hours and low wages which are typically offset by social interactions and guest contact. This study focuses on housekeeping work, physically impactful jobs in which social interactions and guest contact are often absent. These jobs are primarily taken up by women, and often by people from minority groups. Housekeepers frequently report musculoskeletal injury and the lowest job satisfaction in the hotel industry, and hotels struggle with sick leave and to keep their housekeeping departments staffed. The objective of this study is therefore to make housekeeping work more decent (SDG8), thereby contributing to good health and wellbeing (SDG3) and ultimately to reduce gender inequalities (SDG5).
Methods:
This study evaluates two innovations aimed at improving the physical conditions of housekeeping workers while changing beds. They are an exoskeleton that housekeepers can wear to support their back and a bed lift that raises reduces the unhealthy positions adopted while making a bed. Innovations were tested at a test hotel in a 2x2 design with 28 participants. Both objective (back posture and completion time) and subjective evaluations (NASA task load scale) were collected.
Results:
Results show how both innovations increase time spent in healthy positions, while also lowering physical load, frustration and back discomfort for housekeepers, while not compromising performance or completion time.
Conclusions:
While the results point out that ergonomic innovations can improve working conditions and occupational wellbeing, it also raises new questions. As these two solutions were readily available, what is keeping hotel companies from improving health conditions for their employees? To progress towards healthier societies, the results from the current study could be used to inspire decision makers in the hotel industry to identify barriers and opportunities to make housekeeping work more sustainable.

Title: Safeguarding Human Rights Through Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse Regulation : A Roadmap For ASEAN Human Rights Integration Through Technological Governance Inspired by European Convention of Human Rights and European Union Legal Framework
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: ASEAN, Human Rights, Artificial Intelligence (AI) Regulation, Metaverse Governance, European Supranational System, Technological Governance
Abstract_Text:
Southeast Asia faces a double-edged sword as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Metaverse continue to rapidly develop. These technologies provide unprecedented opportunities for economic development and social connection, but could also exacerbate digital inequality, increase surveillance, and diminish privacy. This study proposes a roadmap for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to actively safeguard human rights as digital ecosystems like AI and Metaverse continue to evolve. Grounded in regulatory theory, technological governance, regional integration, and international human rights law, this study explores ASEAN’s possibility to construct an effective governance framework on AI and Metaverse. It suggests that ASEAN may establish a cohesive regional framework similar with EU and Council of Europe supranational legislative system such as EU Artificial Intelligence Act and EU Charter of Fundamental Rights to integrate human rights protections and mitigate its non-interference stance via a hybrid model.
This study employs comparative legal methodology providing doctrinal analysis of primary and secondary sources, namely ASEAN Human Rights Declaration, European Convention on Human Rights and other EU legal instruments such as GDPR and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act alongside relevant ECtHR case law and other digital regulations. The study shows that while ASEAN's non-interference principle and consensus fall short, Europe provides a reference of enforceable risk-based regulation with strong human rights protections. The study recommends that establishing ASEAN binding regional instrument on tech governance and monitoring digital rights, is both timely and achievable.
This research concludes that ASEAN’s actionable roadmap requires a hybrid governance model effectively customizing elements of EU's and ECHR's rights-based frameworks into ASEAN's socio-political landscape. With common minimum standards, platforms for multi stakeholder dialogue, and evolving principle-based regulations covering AI and Metaverse, ASEAN can address human rights risks while driving regional integration and serving as a beacon globally.

Title: Thinking and Doing Green: Applying Planetary Health and Systems Thinking in Health Research, Education and Practice.
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Keywords: Planetary Health, Sustainable Healthcare, Systems Thinking, Health Education, Research Practice
Abstract_Text:
Sustainable Development Goal 3 aims to ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for people of all ages. Human health is closely connected to the environment, making it impossible to separate human well-being from the health of the planet.
This connection is the focus of Planetary Health, an emerging interdisciplinary field that explores how human activities affect natural systems and, in turn, influence health outcomes. Planetary Health encourages a broader understanding of health that considers environmental change and its implications for research, education and healthcare.
While healthcare plays a crucial role in preventing, maintaining, and restoring health, it also contributes significantly to environmental problems through resource use, greenhouse gas emissions, and waste production. Promoting sustainability within healthcare is therefore essential, both to reduce environmental harm and to protect current and future population health. Sustainable healthcare can create a positive cycle: healthier environments can reduce disease burdens and healthcare demand, while lower-impact healthcare systems help preserve environmental conditions that support good health.
At the University Medical Center Groningen, efforts are focused on both mitigating environmental change and adapting to its health-related consequences. As part of this commitment, planetary health principles are increasingly being incorporated into the education of medical, dental, and health science students. The goal is to support the development of sustainable approaches to health research, prevention, and patient care.
We developed an interactive workshop to help participants integrate sustainability into their own research practices. Following a short introduction to planetary health, participants engage in two parallel activities. In Thinking Green, they examine their research from a sustainable perspective. In Doing Green, they identify ways to make their research activities more sustainable. Through discussion and knowledge exchange, participants learn from one another.
The workshop is relevant for healthcare researchers, educators, students, professionals and policymakers committed to sustainable change.
Duration: 1.5 hours

Title: Tracking transnational action across climate, biodiversity and sustainable development through databases: gaps, policy relevance and research priorities
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Keywords: Transnational cooperation, Sustainability governance, Databases, decision-making, Evidence-informed policy
Abstract_Text:
A growing number of databases now document transnational cooperative initiatives involving businesses, civil society, governments, international organisations and other actors across climate, biodiversity and sustainability governance. These databases offer a foundation for evidence-based decision-making, yet, fragmentation and limitations in data findability, accessibility, interoperability and reusability constrain their potential. Addressing these challenges, alongside exploring new tools, including AI, could help better leverage existing data and databases to inform research, policy analysis and impactful action on the ground.
This roundtable brings together researchers working with databases on cooperative initiatives across climate, biodiversity and sustainable development to take stock of the current landscape, share ongoing work, and explore opportunities for collaboration. We will discuss what existing databases and analyses currently tell us about transnational action, how this evidence is being used to inform policy and research agendas, and where important knowledge gaps remain.
The discussion will focus on data coverage, quality, comparability and interoperability, as well as the transparency and reliability of AI assisted and conventional data collection. Particular attention will be paid to persisting gaps and underrepresentation in existing databases, how biases may shape findings, and how uncertainty may be communicated to decision-makers.
The roundtable aims to identify opportunities to strengthen the relevance and usability of existing databases for research, policy and action. By bringing together complementary datasets, analytical approaches and research communities, we seek to explore how we can better leverage existing data, foster collaboration, and generate evidence that helps direct attention and resources towards areas where additional action is most needed.

Title: Community perspectives on climate and land-use change drivers of medicinal plant availability in Ghana’s mangrove forests: Evidence from the Greater Amanzule Wetland ecosystem
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Organisations: Adarkwah, Dr. Francis | University of Ghana
Keywords: medicinal plant, mangrove ecosystems, climate-related drivers, traditional ecological knowledge, community-based management
Abstract_Text: This study examines community perceptions of how climate-related and land-use drivers influence the availability of medicinal plant ecosystem services in the Greater Amanzule mangrove wetland in Ghana. We used a mixed-method approach, combining household surveys (n = 401), logistic regression, focus group discussions, and key informant interviews to assess local perceptions of environmental pressures and community responses. The results show that coastal flooding and rising temperature were positively associated with perceived medicinal plant availability, with predicted probabilities 9.6 and 9.0 percentage points higher, respectively, among respondents who identified these drivers. These findings reflect community perceptions of climate-related change rather than measured ecological effects on the availability of medicinal plants. In contrast, excessive chemical use, overexploitation, illegal mining, and deforestation were significantly associated with lower community-reported availability. Qualitative findings corroborate these patterns and highlight how communities interpret, respond to, and manage these impacts through mangrove reforestation, monitoring, and local enforcement, despite weak formal policy implementation. The findings highlight the value of examining medicinal plants as a distinct mangrove provisioning service and linking perceived environmental drivers to community management responses. They also illustrate how household survey analysis and local ecological knowledge can complement each other where ecological monitoring data are unavailable. Sustaining this service could be supported through formal legal protection of the wetland, recognition of community conservation rules through district bylaws, reduced chemical use in farming near mangroves, and the inclusion of medicinal plant species in restoration and district planning. The study contributes to a broader understanding of how communities perceive environmental changes affecting mangrove medicinal plant ecosystem services and how community-based practices can inform ecosystem service governance beyond Ghana.

Title: Nonlinear relationships between urban multi-dimensional risks and sustainable development: evidence from Chinese cities
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Authors: Ye, Qinhan; Zhang, Junze; Wang, Shuai; Fu, Bojie
Keywords: urban multi-dimensional risks, Sustainable Development Goals, explainable machine learning, nonlinear relationships
Abstract_Text:
Objective:Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) faces multiple pressures, while regional differences in resources, infrastructure and socioeconomic conditions shape local risk profiles. We examine how urban multi-dimensional risks relate to different goals across risk levels and economic contexts, identifying key risks and nonlinear response changes to inform differentiated monitoring and sustainability strategies.
Methods:We analyse panel data for 283 Chinese prefecture-level administrative units during 2000–2022, covering spatial exposure, supply disruption, social vulnerability and market volatility. Spatial comparisons, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) models and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) assess risk importance, interactions with GDP per capita, and nonlinear associations with 16 SDG scores and a composite index. Segmented regression and bootstrap resampling of cities assess response shapes and breakpoint stability.
Key results:Risk profiles varied geographically, with lower-income cities generally facing higher risks. Social vulnerability and supply disruption were the most important risk dimensions for the composite SDG index, accounting for 17.25% and 13.99% of total SHAP importance. Higher GDP per capita was associated with more negative SHAP interaction contributions to the composite SDG index at high social vulnerability (80–95) and relatively low supply disruption (25–60). Higher risk could coincide with improving SDG contributions, while further increases were associated with reversals or faster declines in some relationships. These patterns highlight the need to identify the risk ranges where individual goals become more sensitive. Seven goals, including food, water and energy, showed accelerating declines or reversals from increasing to decreasing SHAP contributions within a narrow supply-disruption range (58.82–64.03), highlighting a common risk range for coordinated monitoring across goals.
Conclusions:Urban sustainability assessment should consider risk dimensions, economic context and nonlinear response patterns together. These findings can inform differentiated risk monitoring and joint assessment of goals with clustered breakpoints towards 2030 and beyond.

Title: Who pays for adaptation? Splitting the climate bill across risk owners in the Netherlands
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Organisations: Ivanova, Dr. Olga | The Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency (PBL)
Keywords: climate finance, multilevel governance, regional climate action, climate-economic modeling, social vulnerability
Abstract_Text: Existing adaptation assessments rarely move beyond national cost aggregates to ask who bears adaptation costs and whether they can afford them. This paper examines the distributional incidence of the climate bill, defined as adaptation investment plus residual damage, across risk owners and municipalities in the Netherlands. We develop a spatially explicit, bottom-up cost assessment covering all 342 Dutch municipalities, 54 adaptation measures and six risk owners, allocating costs on the basis of ownership and management responsibility. Residual damage is derived from a national multi-hazard damage model updated to the latest climate projections. Both are expressed in net present value and compared with risk-owner-specific financial capacity, calibrated to national accounts, across two climate and four socio-economic scenarios. Aggregate adaptation costs range from EUR 58 billion under moderate to EUR 167 billion under high-end warming, with households bearing nearly half, predominantly for foundation repair on compressible soils. While the aggregate burden is modest relative to national capacity, its incidence is highly uneven and regressive. Household burdens amount to 1.2–4.5 percent of financial capacity nationally but approach 8 percent in the most exposed decile of municipalities, and municipalities and water boards would need 11–17 percent of own revenues. Burdens concentrate in small coastal, deltaic and peat municipalities, where climate impacts erode the property-tax base. Inaction does not eliminate these costs but shifts them to residual damage, approximately 81 percent of which is currently uninsurable, while a twenty-year delay adds about EUR 50 billion in avoidable damage. We conclude that the binding constraint on adaptation is distributional and fiscal rather than aggregate. Adaptation governance beyond 2030 therefore requires explicit cost-allocation rules, including climate-sensitive intergovernmental transfers, targeted support for low-capacity households and ex-ante risk-sharing arrangements for uninsurable losses. The framework is transferable to other national contexts.

Title: Steering AI to Accelerate the Sustainable Development Goals: Sustainability, Impact Assessment, Responsible Governance and Global Cooperation
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Organisations: Chen, Prof. Min | Nanjing Normal University
Keywords: AI, geography, sustainability science, interaction, public policy
Abstract_Text:
This session examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), focusing on how AI can both enable and inhibit progress towards sustainable development. AI can support agricultural monitoring, ecosystem management, climate action, health services, and SDG modelling. At the same time, its development and use can intensify resource consumption, generate electronic waste, reproduce biases, amplify misinformation, and deepen inequalities in access to computing infrastructure and expertise. These enabling and inhibiting effects may coexist: advances towards AI may undermine or facilitate SDG, while benefits in one region or over one period may entail costs elsewhere or in the longer term. Understanding the AI–SDG relationship therefore requires examining not only AI potential applications, but also the conditions under which AI produces positive or negative outcomes, how these outcomes are distributed across space and time, and how they interact across SDGs.
Bringing together perspectives from AI, geography, sustainability science, and public policy, the session aims to provide an interdisciplinary platform for examining the complex relationships between AI and sustainable development. Discussions may address a broad range of interconnected issues, such as sustainability considerations across the AI lifecycle, the enabling and inhibiting effects of AI on SDG progress across different spatial and temporal scales, the implications of AI safety and governance, and the role of knowledge sharing and regional cooperation in shaping equitable and sustainable outcomes.
