The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) form an interconnected system in which progress on one goal can accelerate or undermine progress on others. Policymakers therefore need to know which interlinkages exist, and also which combinations and sequences of interventions maximise progress across goals over time. System Dynamics (SD) models capture broad, causally structured SDG interactions, but they are designed to explore “what-if” scenarios rather than to optimise. Optimisation-based models, by contrast, typically cover only a narrow subset of goals. This study addresses the gap by coupling SD with deep Reinforcement Learning algorithms such as SAC and PPO to find strategic interventions that maximise sustainable development progress over time based on SDG interlinkages. We use the iSD-Australia model, which covers all 17 SDGs and has been calibrated against over 30 years of national historical data. At each annual time step to 2050, an RL agent adjusts policy levers such as government expenditure, taxation or private investment. These adjustments stay within bounds on feasible annual change, and the agent is rewarded according to the model’s SDG performance indicators. We also compare alternative reward formulations, such as maximising aggregate SDG progress versus prioritising lagging goals, to show how normative choices shape optimal pathways. This way, we outline optimised trajectories for Australian SDG indicators to 2050, the policy levers and timings that act as leverage points, and synergies and trade-offs that the agent exploits or must navigate. Sensitivity analysis tests whether the learned strategies hold up under parameter uncertainty. The framework shows how AI can move SDG modelling from scenario exploration towards decision support.
Focusing on mainland China, we investigate the trade-offs and synergies between food supply, water resource use, and environmental sustainability associated with cropland use change. We analyze the effects of cropland spatial reorganization on grain production and the geography of food supply and demand, identifying the main pathways to increased grain production and their regional variation. We assess the water resource costs of these pathways, with particular attention to how precipitation, surface-water irrigation, and groundwater irrigation support production stability and whether this support is sustainable. The analysis also examines how changes in grain production affect soil carbon dynamics, nutrient use, and pollution risks. Building on these findings, we explore regional management strategies that balance food supply, resource conservation, environmental protection, and production resilience. This research provides a scientific basis for cropland conservation, the spatial optimization of agricultural production, and coordinated management across sectors.
In the context of the flourishing development of the Belt and Road Initiative, it is of great significance to study the impact of energy transition on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) in the countries along the Belt and Road. Based on the geographic perspective, this study focuses on how the energy transition model promotes the realization of SDGs in the countries along the route. Using the SDGs indicator system framework, the study precisely quantifies the contribution of energy transition (SDG 7) to the SDGs in terms of environmental (SDG 13), economic and social (SDG 8) dimensions. At the same time, the multi-regional input-output method is used to analyze the cross-regional economic linkage effect triggered by the energy industry change. The study shows that the promotion of clean energy not only reduces carbon emissions, optimizes the ecology, and contributes to the achievement of SDG 13, but also promotes the construction of new energy sources, stimulates employment and economic growth (SDG 8), and makes energy more accessible to the public, thus contributing to the achievement of SDG 7. However, in the face of extreme weather, geopolitical conflicts and other shocks, it is urgent to explore the path of energy strategy adjustment to achieve SDGs resilient development in the countries along the route, and this study aims to provide a scientific basis for this.

Title: Interactions between climate mitigation and SDGs in countries’ Long-Term Strategies
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Herman, Sophia; Bellanca, Margherita; King, Lewis; van den Bergh, Jeroen
Keywords: Sustainable Development Goals, Long-Term Strategies, Climate mitigation, Co-benefits, Content analysis
Abstract_Text: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide a useful framework for understanding the relationship between climate action and broader development priorities. While climate mitigation can generate synergies across multiple goals, it can also involve competing objectives. Yet the way in which governments represent these interactions in their national climate strategies remains poorly understood. The long-term strategies (LTSs), submitted by countries under the Paris Agreement, provide a basis for examining these interactions. With a horizon typically to 2050, governments have the opportunity to outline the social and economic changes that mitigation involves, beyond emission reductions. Through a systematic content analysis of 84 LTSs submitted to the UNFCCC, we examine which SDGs countries associate with mitigation, whether these interactions are framed as co-benefits or trade-offs, how SDG emphasis varies across income and emission groups, and across different national characteristics. Co-benefits account for 88% of interactions, but attention is focused on a subset of goals. Four goals - Decent Work and Economic Growth, Good Health and Well-being, Sustainable Cities and Communities and Life on Land - account for roughly two-thirds of the interactions. By contrast, five goals - Quality Education, Gender Equality, Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure, Peace, Justice and Strong Institutions and Partnerships for the Goals - account for only around 6%. Across income and emission groups, governments emphasise broadly similar SDGs as co-benefits of mitigation, while trade-offs vary more substantially. Food security is more dominant in upper-middle- and lower-income countries, while economic growth is a major topic among upper-middle-income countries, and sustainable cities mostly appear in high-income countries. National conditions, including air pollution, unemployment and inequality, are associated with differences in SDG emphasis. By showing which development priorities governments connect to climate mitigation and which receive limited attention, this study contributes to understanding how climate and development agendas are linked in national policy.

Title: Addressing global biodiversity loss footprint inequality through equitable consumption strategies toward Global Biodiversity Framework
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Authors: Tang, Hui; Li, Ruoqi; Shan, Yuli; Hubacek, Klaus
Keywords: Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, Inequality, Biodiversity, Sustainable consumption
Abstract_Text: Halting biodiversity loss requires reducing global footprints of consumption in an equitable manner, consistent with Target 16 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). Yet the distribution of global biodiversity loss footprints (BF) across consumer groups remains poorly understood. Combining a species-area relationship model with the environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model, we quantify BF of 201 consumer groups across 164 countries and estimate the inequality in BF using the biodiversity loss footprint Gini (BF-Gini) coefficient. Results show that the wealthiest 10% of consumers are responsible for 30% (26%‒35%, 95% confidence interval) of global BF in 2023, while the poorest half contribute only 25% (21%‒31%, 95% confidence interval). Inequality in global BF is substantial, indicated by a BF-Gini coefficient of 0.57 (0.55‒0.66, 95% confidence interval), and is most pronounced in the consumption of forestry and logging products, and services. This inequality persists within countries and generally declines as countries grow more affluent. Strategies to promote equality toward Target 16 are further explored by targeting overconsumption of the wealthiest and pairing top-end reductions with consumption floors for the poorest. Targeting overconsumption of the wealthiest presents dual benefits, reducing the global BF by 24% and BF-Gini coefficient by 12% relative to the 2023 baseline. Pairing top-end reductions with consumption floors leads to a larger reduction in BF-Gini coefficient to 14%, with the cost of 20% less cut in BF compared to top-end reductions alone. Cross-group consumption transformations remain essential for steering the global BF toward an equitable manner under KMGBF.

Title: From laboratory waste to resource: establishing monostream plastic recycling in academic research laboratories.
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Bonsing-Vedelaar, Silke; Matei, Alexandra; Heinemann, Matthias; Elzinga, Nils
Keywords: Material efficiency, Circularity, Laboratory sustainability, Plastic waste recycling, Waste management
Abstract_Text:
Objective
Single-use plastics in laboratories account for approximately 2% of global plastic waste, yet they are rarely recycled. In our laboratories, plastic consumption reached up to 25 kg per person annually. Following the implementation of targeted reduction measures, this was reduced to 18 kg per person; a substantial amount that is still incinerated. These plastics are rarely recycled, as they are generally considered biohazardous, mixed types fuse into unrecyclable clumps during autoclaving, and standard facilities cannot process the smaller items typical of laboratory use. As most single-use plastics from microbio/biochemical labs are not exposed to harmful chemicals and are sterilized post-use, the remaining plastic waste provides a safe source for plastic recycling.
Method
At the University of Groningen, in collaboration with our biosafety department, we initiated a pilot project to separate plastics into single-polymer streams prior to autoclaving. For effective recycling, different types of plastics must be separated to ensure the quality of the resulting recycled material. From common laboratory plastics, we selected three recyclable single-polymer materials, polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and high-density polyethylene (HDPE). We developed an intuitive separation protocol to ensure consistent sorting of waste items and we quantified the recycled output by weighing the autoclaved plastics for each polymer type.
Key results
In its first year, the initiative diverted 4 kg of plastic per person from incineration to recycling. Building on this successful pilot, the initiative has expanded across multiple laboratories, with the long-term goal of university-wide implementation and inspiring broader adoption across the research community.
Conclusion
Separating laboratory plastics by polymer type prior to autoclaving is a practical, biosafety-compliant route to recycling waste that would otherwise be incinerated. When combined with continued single-use plastic reduction, broader institutional adoption could meaningfully advance circular economy goals and contribute to reducing the environmental footprint of laboratory research.

Title: Spatial analysis for sustainable island energy transitions: Lessons from Ameland, The Netherlands
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Keywords: Energy transition, Smart grids, Community resilience, Sustainable resource management, GIS
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Achieving the SDGs and advancing post-2030 sustainability strategies will require effective planning for renewable energy infrastructure. Small islands are ideal case studies showing integrated transformation across social, technological, and environmental systems. This study uses Ameland (A Dutch Wadden Island recognized for its community-driven green projects, clean energy, and smart girds) to examine how spatial analysis can guide energy transitions.
Methods: This research develops GIS mapping with insights from scientific literature, policy data, and knowledge gained through participation in the Ameland Summer school on Public Participation in Sustainable Transitions. The model merges Spatial information on renewable energy infrastructure alongside community projects, stakeholder engagement. Spatial analysis is used to examine the relationships between technical energy networks interact with local public participation within the energy transition.
Key results: The finding highlights spatial analysis as a critical integrative tool for designing resilient energy strategies. Preliminary results showed that GIS mapping can improve the visualization of renewable-energy assets, local networks, and public policy structures while mapping the spatial interactions between infrastructure and community participation. The Ameland case illustrates how spatial planning can connect renewable energy infrastructure with community initiatives and support collaborative decision-making.
Conclusions: Sustainable energy transitions must integrate environmental, technical, with human elements rather than focusing on technological solutions. The Ameland case study highlights the potential of geospatial mapping tools to advance community-led energy transitions, optimize planning, and boost resilience in island contexts. Through linking initiatives within SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 13 (Climate Action), this framework contributes actionable lessons for sustainable development agendas through 2030 and provides scalable insights for sustainability planning decades that follow.

Title: Time-use patterns reveal carbon footprint disparities among US households
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Authors: Liu, Ludi; Li, Ruoqi; Fang, Shuai; Shan, Yuli; Hubacek, Klaus
Keywords: Time Use, Lifestyles, Cluster analysis, Multi-Regional Input-Output model
Abstract_Text: How people spend their time shapes their consumption and the embodied carbon emissions, yet existing studies have mostly used time to describe the lifestyles of predefined socio-economic groups rather than to characterize lifestyles by time use itself. Here we cluster more than 9,000 US households in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics into five time-use patterns based on their time-use behavior records, and compare their per capita carbon footprints estimated by linking expenditure data to a Multi-Regional Input-Output model. Time-use patterns differentiate carbon footprints independently of income. Within the same income decile, per capita footprints differ by up to 53% across patterns, and the gap widens with income. Households spending most of their time at home without paid work emit the most and those combining full-time work with intensive childcare the least, consistently across the income distribution. The gap arises mainly from housing-related consumptions, where footprints respond more to free time than to income. Time use thus reveals footprint differences beyond socio-economic status, identifies high-footprint households and time-sensitive consumption categories, and can support time-related mitigation measures such as working time reduction.

Title: Share the gains, mind the pains: The double-edged promise of benefit-sharing in PtL-SAF Supply Chains
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Kamrad, Sophie; Hock, Martin; Shetye, Niyanta Avadhut; Schmermer, Felix
Keywords: Energy Extractivism, Sustainable Aviation Fuels, Green Hydrogen, Global Value Chains, benefit-sharing
Abstract_Text: The European Union’s (EU) ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation mandates the use of Power-to-Liquid (PtL) for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) derived from green hydrogen from 2030 onwards. To meet this demand, the EU will depend on green hydrogen imports, including imports from the Global South (GS). However, these emerging Global Value Chains (GVCs) risk replicating historical patterns of extractivism, unless local communities avail the benefits arising from PtL projects. As a premium hydrogen derivative, PtL-SAF may offer substantial potential for high value creation, yet benefit-sharing within these GVCs remains understudied. Hence, this paper examines where along the PtL-SAF value chain benefits can be arranged. To achieve this, we employ a multi-layered methodology. Firstly, we conduct a literature review of benefit-sharing in renewable energy sector and industrial complexes (e.g. Fischer-Tropsch Plants and refineries) to categorise them into monetary and non-monetary benefits. We then assess entry points of benefit-sharing in GVC constellations consisting of possible trade flows in which products such as renewable energy/ green hydrogen (H2)/ methanol/ syncrude/ PtL-SAF could be exported from GS to the EU. And lastly, we identify which benefits can be included in each constellation that could complement the post-2030 agenda particularly on just climate transition. The paper also concludes with a critical discussion on the unintended negative consequences of conventional benefit-sharing models which could affect sustainability beyond 2030. The authors argue that without stakeholder engagement, local sustainability, co-designed benefit-sharing mechanisms, and dispute mechanisms conventional benefit-sharing mechanisms risk exacerbating inequalities and intra and inter communal discords. By framing benefit-sharing opportunities and their entry points in PtL-SAF GVCs, the paper provides a clear picture of how developing PtL-SAF GVCs have multiple dimensions on sustainability beyond 2030 rather than just mitigation.

Title: Game of Tonnes: The Clash between Emissions Trading and Carbon Offsets
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate governance, finance, and negotiation for sustainable development
Authors: Shetye, Niyanta Avadhut; Hock, Martin; Schmermer, Felix
Keywords: International Carbon Markets, Aviation emissions, Market-based Mechanisms
Abstract_Text:
Governments worldwide are increasingly deploying market-based mechanisms (MBMs) for achieving net-zero pathways in aviation, yet the sector remains only partially covered, exposing a climate governance gap. As of 2026, only eight emissions trading systems (ETS) domestic aviation emissions, while international flights are covered under ICAO’s Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA). Despite these MBMs, international aviation emissions grew by 6.3% in 2024. Hence, the EU has proposed extending its ETS to international aviation up to 5000km measured from Frankfurt airport in 2029, a regulatory shift that fundamentally alters aviation emission governance.
The objective of this paper is to examine how these increasingly intersecting MBMs can deliver genuine emission reductions for international aviation. Methodologically, we employ a narrative literature review paired with legal and policy analysis to synthesize the evolution and interactions between MBMs beyond 2030. Our key findings show that both EU ETS and CORSIA in its current stages are insufficient to address aviation emissions, we also find that the inclusion of Article 6 credits from Paris Agreement in CORSIA could offer high integrity credits for the aviation industry. Moreover, the paper sketches the complex and overlapping interactions within this evolving landscape of MBMs for addressing aviation emissions. The study also maps out the systematic frictions and regulatory interfaces between domestic and international frameworks. Specifically, we narrate the post 2030 trajectory of the expanded scope of EU ETS, domestic ETS covering aviation emissions, CORSIA, and the interaction where Article 6.4 credits will be eligible for CORSIA compliance. The paper concludes by sketching the post 2030 landscape of MBMs for international aviation emissions while also providing unique policy perspectives on the current and future interactions between European and International climate law, offering a roadmap to align market instruments with Paris compatible pathways for international aviation emissions beyond 2030.

Title: Economic Assessment of the Back End of Nuclear Energy: Fuel Cycle Strategies, Radioactive Waste Management, and Deep Geological Disposal Costs
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Etemadi, Mediya; Kalantar-Nayestanaki, Nasser; Van den Broek, Machteld; Medjroubi, Wided; Miocic, Johannes
Keywords: Nuclear Energy; Nuclear Fuel Cycle; Back-End Economics; Radioactive Waste Management; Deep Geological Repository; Net-Zero Energy Systems
Abstract_Text:
Nuclear energy can contribute to climate change mitigation by providing reliable, low-carbon electricity. However, its long-term economic sustainability partly depends on nuclear fuel cycle strategies and radioactive waste management costs, particularly those of deep geological repositories (DGRs).
This study assessed the economics of alternative nuclear fuel cycle strategies and the factors influencing geological disposal costs, focusing on their relevance to the Netherlands. First, a literature review compared once-through (OTC), twice-through (TTC), and advanced fuel cycles (AFC) in terms of levelised fuel cycle costs (LFCC) and radioactive waste generation. Cost estimates were normalised to 2024 USD/MWh, accounting for differences in cost boundaries, technological assumptions, and waste management approaches. Waste quantities were also compared to assess trade-offs between economic performance and waste generation. Key technical and economic parameters affecting fuel cycle costs and the competitiveness of different strategies at varying production scales were examined.
Second, DGR cost estimates from different countries and geological host rock formations were compared to identify key cost drivers and assess their applicability to the Netherlands. The analysis considered repository capacity, nuclear electricity production, geological conditions, and cost estimation methods. Reported costs were harmonised to 2024 USD/MWh of electricity generated and used to estimate potential DGR costs in the Netherlands, including the influence of repository capacity and geological characteristics.
By integrating evidence on fuel cycle economics, waste generation, and geological disposal costs, this study provided insights into the economic trade-offs between fuel cycle strategies and the factors influencing long-term disposal costs. The key findings and their implications for nuclear fuel cycle strategies and geological disposal costs will be presented and discussed during the oral presentation.

Title: Coordinated operation of electricity, heat and hydrogen in urban energy units under supply–demand uncertainty
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Shi, Lin; Zabala Figueroa, Alejandro; Medjroubi, Wided; Zhao, Huiru; Zhai, Yuxin; Li, Bingkang; Wang, Yuwei; Li, Qianqian
Keywords: Urban energy units; Electricity–heat–hydrogen systems; Hydrogen flexibility and trading; Supply–demand uncertainty; Distributionally robust optimization.
Abstract_Text:
Uncertainty in renewable generation and electricity and heat demand complicates the coordinated operation of urban energy units, while hydrogen conversion, storage, and trading provide additional operational flexibility. The trade-off between using hydrogen for internal energy supply and exchanging it in with external markets remains insufficiently understood. This study proposes a coordinated electricity–heat–hydrogen operational optimization framework under joint supply–demand uncertainty, using representative urban energy units in a city in the Netherlands as a case studies. Open geodata, building characteristics, energy statistics, and meteorological data will are integrated to generate hourly electricity and heat demand and renewable generation profiles. Climate scenarios are incorporated to examine changes in future supply–demand conditions. For fixed equipment capacities, the framework optimizes electrolysis, hydrogen storage, fuel-cell operation, heat pumps, and electricity and hydrogen trading. It minimizes net operating costs while meeting all energy-supply requirements.
A Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization model is developed using joint samples that preserve supply–demand correlations and temporal dependencies. Its out-of-sample performance is evaluated through rolling-horizon operation . The Dutch case study compare different urban energy unit types, hydrogen trading arrangements, and uncertainty modelling approaches. The analysis is designed to quantify the incremental operational value of hydrogen flexibility and trading and identify the conditions governing hydrogen production, storage, internal use, and market exchange. The framework supports economically efficient and reliable operation of urban multi-energy systems under uncertainty.

Title: Beyond biodiversity: Integrating animal welfare into the post-2030 sustainable development agenda through tourism governance
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Organisations: Fennell, Prof. David | Centre for Animal-based Tourism (CAT)
Keywords: Sustainable development beyond 2030, animal welfare, animal-based tourism, sustainability governance, biodiversity conservation
Abstract_Text:
Objective:The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) recognise biodiversity conservation, ecosystem protection and sustainable livelihoods, yet animal welfare and the interests of individual animals remain insufficiently integrated into many approaches to sustainable development. As the international community considers how to advance sustainability beyond 2030, this contribution examines what animal-based tourism can reveal about this gap and how animal-inclusive principles could inform more holistic and regenerative approaches to sustainable development.
Methods:Drawing on more than 26 years of research by CAT Executive Director Dave Fennell in animal-based tourism, tourism ethics and sustainability, alongside CAT’s practice-based work, this contribution explores how animal welfare is considered within existing sustainability approaches. It draws on CAT’s Journeys to Justice framework and animal-based tourism literacy work to examine how animal welfare could be better reflected in sustainability assessment, governance and decision-making.
Key results:The contribution highlights a gap between commitments to biodiversity conservation and sustainable development and the welfare of individual animals. Tourism illustrates this challenge particularly clearly, as activities that generate economic benefits or support conservation objectives may still compromise animal welfare. It identifies opportunities to address this gap through more inclusive sustainability targets and indicators, stronger accountability, and education that helps tourism operators, policymakers and travellers make more informed decisions.
Conclusions:The post-2030 sustainable development agenda presents an opportunity to ensure that animal welfare is not overlooked in wider sustainability ambitions. Animal-based tourism provides a practical context for exploring how ecological, social and animal welfare considerations can be brought together. CAT’s frameworks offer a foundation for translating these principles into more responsible tourism practices and informing broader approaches to sustainable development.

Title: Women’s Gold and Global Value Chains: Building Inclusive and Resilient Shea Economies in West Africa
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Economic approaches beyond GDP, including circularity and  bioeconomy
Keywords: Shea butter; global value chains; women’s economic empowerment; sustainable transformation; rural livelihoods; West Africa
Abstract_Text:
Shea, often referred to as “Women’s Gold,” provides vital income for millions of rural women across West Africa and serves as an important raw material for the global cosmetics, personal care, and food industries. Growing demand for sustainably sourced ingredients makes the shea sector a valuable case for examining the connections between global value chains, rural livelihoods, gender equity, and sustainable economic transformation. However, despite women’s central role in shea collection and primary processing, much of the higher-value processing occurs outside Africa, raising concerns about value distribution and economic inclusion.
This paper examines the West African shea economy as a gendered global value chain, focusing on how corporate sourcing strategies, labour structures, trade patterns, and sustainability initiatives influence local development. Drawing on first-hand data from Beiersdorf AG and qualitative evidence from industry initiatives, including AAK’s Kolo Nafaso programme and the Global Shea Alliance, the study traces connections between women collectors in Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Côte d’Ivoire and multinational processors and consumer goods companies. It explores how direct sourcing, cooperative organisation, traceability systems, and corporate–community partnerships can support women’s economic participation and more sustainable production.
The findings highlight the gap between women’s essential contribution to the shea economy and their limited participation in higher-value market segments. Evidence from the Kolo Nafaso programme illustrates how direct sourcing, cooperative organisation, and sustainability initiatives can improve household incomes, strengthen women’s economic agency, and encourage environmentally sustainable production. The paper argues that more resilient shea economies require approaches that integrate environmental sustainability with equitable value distribution and expanded economic opportunities for rural women. By connecting global value chains with local social and environmental outcomes, this study contributes to understanding how inclusive sourcing and corporate sustainability partnerships can advance integrated and resilient sustainable development across West Africa

Title: Rethinking Occupational Exoskeletons: Moving Beyond Biomechanical Outcomes
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: van Laar, Daniek; Roossien, Charissa; Saakes, Daniel; Reneman, Michiel; Bieleman, André
Keywords: Sustainable employability, Healthy work, Healthy aging, Population health, Exoskeletons
Abstract_Text: Traditionally, work-related musculoskeletal pain and disorder (MSD) management has been dominated by a biomedical paradigm, primarily focussing on the physical load as main contributor. Early influential models identified biomechanical aspects, such as high force exertion, awkward postures, and repetitive tasks, as primary causal factors in MSD development. More recent work, however, reports no clear relationship between trunk flexion and the development or aggravation of low back pain among blue-collar workers. Despite these developments, workplace prevention strategies, interventions and research remain largely focused on identifying and reducing biomechanical risk factors. Occupational exoskeletons (OEX) are one such biomechanical intervention that has gained increasing attention for reducing physical workload during occupational tasks. OEX have been introduced to industrial settings, aiming to reduce high mechanical load using springs and dampers to release energy. Although the biomechanical aspects of OEX are relatively well studied, the existing evidence is mainly derived from laboratory studies with healthy participants. In contrast, research examining subjective outcomes in real-world occupational settings remains limited. Combined with limited attention to psychosocial risk factors in OEX research (e.g. expectations, attitudes, and workplace context) this underscores a gap in the literature, despite the relevance of these factors for user acceptance, sustained adoption and MSD-aetiology. To determine the true value of OEX for sustainable employability, it is essential to examine the interaction between physical and psychosocial influences on user experience. Therefore, this project adopts a biopsychosocial perspective to investigate OEX in occupational settings. Specifically, it examines in-field end-user experiences, effects of instructional framing on implementation and determining important facilitators and barriers to both end-users, managers and other professionals involved in the implementation process. This presentation integrates findings from a systematic review, an in-field experimental study, and a qualitative observational study, providing novel insights into the role of biopsychosocial factors in OEX implementation and sustainable employability.

Title: Exploring the Water-Energy-Food Nexus Potential of Urban Rooftops: A Review
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Ensuring food, water, and energy security and understanding their nexus
Authors: De Souza Coelho, Andre; Blunk, Andrew; O’Hara, Sabine
Organisations: University of the District of Columbia
Keywords: Rooftop Agriculture, Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA), Solar Energy, Green Roof, Input-Output Analysis
Abstract_Text: Long-term sustainability requires integrated approaches that recognize the interdependence of economic, social, and environmental systems. However, assessments often emphasize direct impacts while overlooking indirect and induced impacts of changes in technology and behaviors. This study explores the potential of integrating rooftop controlled environment agriculture (CEA), solar energy generation, and green roof stormwater management within a water-energy-food (WEF) nexus framework. Rooftops represent underutilized urban spaces where these functions frequently compete for limited space and policy support, despite opportunities for complementary benefits. Building on prior research applying input-output (I-O) analysis to assess the economic, social, and environmental impacts of CEA, this ongoing project introduces a Solar Green Rooftop Farm approach. A literature review examines opportunities, challenges, and interactions among rooftop food production, solar energy generation, and stormwater management. This review informs the development of an environmentally extended I-O modeling framework that incorporates direct and indirect supply-chain effects, as well as induced impacts associated with household expenditures, to evaluate integrated rooftop systems. Findings from our prior CEA modeling research identify opportunities for employment generation and reduced land and water use, alongside trade-offs related to energy demand and greenhouse gas emissions. The literature suggests that integrating solar energy could mitigate energy-related impacts, while green roof systems could improve stormwater management and provide pollinator habitats with potential benefits for food production. An additional pathway under investigation is the potential for renewable energy and stormwater-related credits to generate revenue that supports CEA business operations. The review examines these potential synergies alongside technical, economic, and regulatory constraints. The proposed framework advances an integrated understanding of the challenges and opportunities associated with multifunctional rooftop systems. By connecting resource efficiency with structural economic analysis of direct, indirect, and induced impacts, the research contributes to discussions on integrated urban sustainability assessment.

Title: From Expectations to Long-Term Use: A Roadmap for Understanding Occupational Exoskeletons in the Workplace
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Authors: van Laar, Daniek; Roossien, Charissa; Saakes, Daniel; Reneman, Michiel; Bieleman, André
Keywords: Sustainable employability, Healthy work, Healthy aging, Population health, Exoskeletons
Abstract_Text:
Musculoskeletal disorders (MSD) remain a major challenge across physically demanding occupations. Traditionally, MSD prevention has been dominated by a biomedical perspective, focusing primarily on biomechanical risk factors such as exertion, repetitive movements, and awkward postures. Consequently, workplace interventions have largely aimed to reduce physical workload and mechanical strain.
For example, occupational exoskeletons (OEX), are designed to support workers during physically demanding work hoping to reduce exertion and promote sustainable employability. However, existing research has mostly focused on short-term biomechanical outcomes in laboratory conditions with healthy participants. These studies offer only a partial understanding of how OEX function in occupational settings.
Successful implementation and sustained use of OEX depend on more than biomechanical performance alone. Factors such as expectations, attitudes, workplace culture, management support, perceived usefulness, and comfort may influence adoption and long-term effectiveness. Yet these factors have received limited attention within OEX research.
This project therefore adopts a biopsychosocial perspective on OEX, aiming to contribute to understand their impact on sustainable employability.
Project outline
Insight in facilitators and barriers
- Systematic Review: Synthesizing current evidence on facilitators and barriers for OEX implementation.
- Observational Study: Observing OEX use in the workplace.
The implementation process
- Experimental Study: Investigating the impact of information framing on short-term user experience and acceptance in occupational settings.
- Interview study: Establish an implementation timeline that compares successful long-term users with workers who discontinued OEX use, identifying critical moments that shape adoption trajectories.
OEX wear effects
- Perspectives Study: Exploring health professionals’ views on potential risks, benefits, opportunities, and challenges of in-field OEX use.
- Long-term Study: Evaluating prolonged OEX use through user experiences and electromyography measurements to investigate muscular adaptations and potential compensatory activation patterns.
By integrating biomechanical, psychological, social, and organizational perspectives, this project aims to generate practical recommendations for evidence-based implementation and sustainable adoption of OEX in work environments.

Title: Analysis of Multiscale Health Inequality Caused by Aviation Emissions
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: HAN, Yuxiao; SHEN, Huizhong; TAO, Shu
Organisations: Southern University of Science and Technology
Keywords: aviation emission, health inequality, adjoint model, reduction strategy
Abstract_Text: Aviation is one of the fastest growing modes of transport and a major source of emissions. Global passenger traffic is projected to reach 11 trillion passenger-kilometres by 2030. Aviation emissions can degrade air quality far beyond flight corridors, imposing substantial health burdens on exposed populations. However, these health impacts remain inadequately quantified, hindering the development of health informed emission control policies and the equitable allocation of responsibilities among countries. Here, we combined observed trajectories from 50 million flights with forward and adjoint models to attribute premature deaths to individual flights. Global aviation emissions in 2019 were associated with 87,600 premature deaths (95% uncertainty interval: 67,900–114,300), more than 300 times the number of fatalities from commercial aviation accidents. Although landing and take-off operations consumed only approximately 10% of total aviation fuel, they accounted for 35% of aviation-attributable premature deaths. Health impact indices varied by four orders of magnitude across routes, while the top 50 airports, which handled 17% of global air traffic, accounted for 63% of premature deaths. Both national aviation attributable health burdens and contributions were unequal, with Gini coefficients of 0.51 and 0.63, respectively. These findings identify the flights associated with the greatest health risks worldwide, establish emission-reduction priorities from a population health perspective, inform sustainable mitigation policies, and provide a basis for equitable international cooperation.

Title: A Comprehensive Analysis of Global Non-Methane Volatile Organic Compound Emissions from the Chemical Industry Using Plant-Level Data
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: LIU, Yiqi; SHEN, Huizhong; TAO, Shu
Organisations: Southern University of Science and Technology
Keywords: NMVOCs; chemical industry; plant-level data; point-source emissions; emission hotspots; sustainable development
Abstract_Text: Non-methane volatile organic compound (NMVOC) emissions from the chemical industry contribute substantially to ozone and secondary organic aerosol formation, posing challenges to air quality, public health, and sustainable industrial development. Based on plant-level data from 8,122 chemical facilities worldwide, this study developed a point-source emission inventory and investigated global trends, spatial heterogeneity, and major emission hotspots from 2010 to 2020. Global NMVOC emissions increased by 11.6%, from 2.82 Tg yr-1 in 2010 to 3.15 Tg yr-1 in 2020, after peaking at 3.62 Tg yr-1 in 2015. Over the same period, emissions from developed countries declined by 36.9%, whereas those from developing countries increased by approximately 20% and accounted for 92% of global emissions in 2020, indicating a continued shift of the global emission center toward rapidly industrializing regions. Emissions were highly spatially concentrated: Asia contributed 85% of the global total, while China alone emitted 1.5 Tg yr-1, equivalent to approximately 48%. China, Saudi Arabia, India, Iran, and Brazil collectively accounted for more than 71% of global emissions, with a country-level Gini coefficient of 0.87. Concentration was even greater at the facility level, as the top 1% and 5% of emitting plants contributed 32% and 61% of total emissions, respectively. These findings demonstrate the substantial mitigation potential of targeting high-emitting facilities and petrochemical clusters. Strengthening cleaner production, fugitive emissions control, and leak detection and repair, alongside differentiated regional policies, is essential for advancing both air quality improvement and sustainable industrial transformation.

Title: Sustainable hospital waste management in Austria, Ecuador, Nigeria, Uganda, and Ukraine: lessons for health beyond 2030
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Emeya, Irene; Cherneha, Maria; Chiluiza, Kevin; Odongo, Innocent; Yarantovskiy, Rodion
Keywords: Healthcare waste management, Circular economy, Climate-resilient health systems, Waste segregation and safe recovery, Multiple-case study
Abstract_Text:
OBJECTIVE: This research will compare healthcare waste-management practices in three hospitals in each of Austria, Ecuador, Nigeria, Uganda and Ukraine, yielding 15 cases. It aims to identify effective practices, examine organisational learning, and analyse errors, corrective actions and lessons learned. It will assess how local resource availability and disruptions influence waste-management decisions, and whether safely recovered materials from one hospital could be used as inputs for products required by another.
METHODS: A mixed-methods, multiple-case design will integrate a systematic literature review covering 2015–2026, reported according to PRISMA 2020 — a framework for transparent reporting of study identification, selection, appraisal and synthesis — with structured surveys and semi-structured interviews among healthcare providers and waste-management personnel in each country. Hospital-level comparisons will address waste segregation, collection, treatment, staff training, costs, regulatory compliance, waste reduction and continuity of services during disruptions. Cross-case thematic analysis and descriptive analysis of survey data will identify successful practices, implementation challenges and adaptive responses. Waste-stream mapping will evaluate opportunities, technical requirements and safeguards for safe inter-hospital circular material flows.
ANTICIPATED RESULTS: Findings are expected to show similarities and differences across the 15 hospitals, including effective approaches, recurrent failures and underlying conditions. Analysis will examine how resource availability, staff behaviour, regulation and emergency preparedness shape safe waste recovery and circular procurement. Results will differentiate climate-related disruptions from conflict-related damage, with particular attention to Ukraine.
CONCLUSIONS: Rather than ranking countries or hospitals, the research seeks to generate transferable lessons while recognising context-specific constraints. Findings aim to inform practical improvements in hospital waste management, safer inter-hospital resource exchange, and more equitable and climate-resilient healthcare systems by and beyond 2030, contributing to Sustainable Development Goals 3, 6, 12 and 13.

Title: Soft shores or hard lines? Community and expert valuation of grey, green and hybrid coastal protection in Bangladesh
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Authors: Sarker, Md Monzer Hossain; Gain, Animesh K.; Giupponi, Carlo
Organisations: Sarker, Dr. Md Monzer Hossain | University of Groningen
Keywords: Nature-based solutions, coastal adaptation, ecosystem services, multi-criteria decision analysis, Bangladesh
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Coastal adaptation is shifting from engineered defences towards nature-based and hybrid solutions, yet little is known about how affected communities value their wider benefits, or how robust such preferences are to expert judgement and decision uncertainty. We compared perceived ecosystem services of grey, green and mixed coastal protection on the climate-vulnerable central coast of Bangladesh.
Methods: We surveyed 150 households across three sites, each representing one strategy: embankments at Char Alexendar, mangrove plantations at Nijhum Dwip, and combined embankments and mangroves in Hatiya. Respondents rated 20 provisioning, regulating, supporting and cultural ecosystem-service indicators, structured within a Driver-Pressure-State-Impact-Response framework. Thirty-five experts weighted the indicators, and a multi-criteria decision support system ranked the strategies using simple additive weighting, weighted ordered weighted averaging to represent risk attitudes, and sensitivity, uncertainty and classification-tree analyses.
Results: Mixed strategies scored highest (0.88), closely followed by green (0.84), with grey infrastructure lowest (0.63). This ranking held at every site and under risk-averse, risk-neutral and risk-taking profiles. Mixed approaches excelled in erosion control, storm-surge protection, freshwater storage and agricultural production, whereas green approaches delivered stronger biodiversity, fisheries, carbon sequestration and cultural benefits. Changing stakeholder priorities shifted preferences only between mixed and green options; grey infrastructure never became the preferred alternative.
Conclusions: The key adaptation choice is not between hard and soft protection, but how to configure context-specific portfolios of engineered and ecological functions. Participatory, uncertainty-aware decision frameworks can guide such portfolios and help align the Bangladesh Delta Plan 2100, Nationally Determined Contributions and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, so that coastal investments jointly advance climate adaptation, livelihoods and biodiversity. This integrated approach offers a transferable pathway for delivering Sustainable Development Goals 13, 14 and 15 in densely populated deltas by and beyond 2030.

Title: Writing the Wadden as one system: co-producing storymaps for a social-ecological systems portal to support better decisions
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI and big data for decision-making and sustainable governance as a supporting decision tool
Authors: Sarker, Md Monzer Hossain; Sijtsma, Frans J; Jager, Wander; Oostra, Minne; Dobbelsteen, Michael van den
Organisations: Sarker, Dr. Md Monzer Hossain | University of Groningen
Keywords: Social-ecological systems, storymaps, knowledge co-production, science-policy interface, Wadden Sea
Abstract_Text:
Objective: Decisions in the Wadden Sea require a shared understanding of its social and ecological dimensions, yet research knowledge remains scattered across disciplines, projects and dashboards. Within the German-Dutch WADCouple programme, we are co-designing an online social-ecological systems portal and accompanying course for the trilateral Wadden Sea World Heritage region. We present its conceptual design and first lessons from co-producing content with researchers and stakeholders.
Methods: Building on Ostrom's social-ecological systems framework and a review of existing regional dashboards, we developed a seven-category structure spanning global context, landscape portrait, ecosystems, people and economy, landscape change, landscape appreciation and governance. Content is delivered through about 50 storymaps, each combining text, maps, a visual and a short video, linked to an interactive map viewer, expert interviews and a Massive Open Online Course (MOOC). At the research programme's mid-term meeting in Wilhelmshaven, Germany, we held a workshop on writing storymaps, asking researchers and stakeholders what knowledge decision-makers need, what knowledge stakeholders regularly miss, and whether stories and maps are understandable.
Results: The seven categories give researchers from five trilateral projects a common place to position their findings. Mapping planned stories onto them reveals which categories need commissioned content. The workshop translated the framework into practical guidance for authors: a shared storymap template of 500-1500 words with maps, a visual and a video, written for non-specialist readers. The same structure underpins the MOOC: a two-to-four-hour, video-based learning pathway that guides decision-makers along dedicated routes through the stories, with exercises on social-ecological links and a certificate.
Conclusions: Structuring research synthesis around social-ecological categories, rather than projects or disciplines, exposes knowledge gaps and helps researchers write for decision-makers. Pairing co-produced storymaps with guided online learning offers a transferable approach for building shared understanding in coastal and other transboundary commons beyond 2030.

Title: Listening to communities: linking food security, HIV care, and governance in Casamance, Senegal
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health as both an outcome and driver of sustainable development
Authors: Barclay-Derman, Noah; Benzekri, Noelle; Seydi, Moussa
Keywords: SDG and health interactions, Climate and environmental change, Multisectoral coordination, Food security and HIV, Community knowledge
Abstract_Text:
Health, food, and environment are experienced as one circumstance by the people most affected, yet the institutions responsible for them act separately. We present a pathway from community evidence to institutional design, drawing on three linked pieces of work in Casamance, Senegal, the region most affected by HIV in the country.
First, a community-based participatory study of 234 agricultural households in 13 communities (81% women) found that all participants reported environmental change, and 86% reported difficulty accessing food. Participants described deforestation, declining rainfall, and abandoned farmland, and proposed reforestation, sustainable agriculture training, and stronger environmental governance. Their observations aligned with regional climate data. Second, a pilot of a multisectoral nutrition-sensitive agriculture program among women living with HIV, implemented with a local NGO and health partners, found associations between participation and improved food security, viral suppression, and mental health. These findings are preliminary and associational.
Third, we apply Ostrom’s Institutional Analysis and Development framework to ask which institutional arrangements determine whose knowledge enters decisions on agriculture, food security, and HIV care. Senegal has built multisectoral arrangements in nutrition and HIV, so coordination exists on paper. The gap is institutional listening. Sectoral mandates, program-tied financing, administrative indicators that cannot register local knowledge, and representation gaps limit the channels through which communities can inform decisions with authority and resources attached. In the sources reviewed, no feedback route told communities what their input changed.
These findings point to implications for a post-2030 agenda: interconnected goals are necessary but insufficient without rules for community knowledge as evidence, shared cross-sector financing, indicators of interaction, and feedback loops. We close with the next step, a cluster-randomized trial beginning in 2027 that tests the integrated approach and will generate evidence on costs, scalability, and sustainability to inform what such institutional arrangements must deliver.

Title: Beyond thermal comfort: Designing resilient university housing for student wellbeing and learning in hot-arid climates
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Agbo, Godman; Adebowale, Moshood; Ibrahim, Turki
Organisations: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals
Keywords: Sustainable housing, urban resilience, social equity, well-being determinants, climate adaptation.
Abstract_Text:
Objective: University dormitories are more than residential facilities; they are everyday learning environments where indoor conditions can influence students’ wellbeing and academic routines. Yet sustainable housing assessments often overlook how environmental differences within buildings shape occupants’ behaviour. This study examines how dormitory microclimates influence study-space choices, behavioural patterns and self-reported academic performance, offering insights for more resilient and inclusive student housing in hot-arid climates.
Methods: A mixed-methods study was conducted in two male dormitories at King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals, Saudi Arabia. Data were collected through 88 student questionnaires, DesignBuilder/EnergyPlus simulations and three weeks of systematic observations. Thermal conditions, study-space preferences and behavioural patterns were examined using descriptive analysis, unsupervised clustering and ordinal regression.
Key Results: Simulations revealed uneven thermal exposure across rooms and floors, with hours above 26°C ranging from 65.2 to 197.9 in one dormitory and 79.6 to 195.5 in the other. Despite generally favourable thermal conditions in designated study rooms, 54.5% of students preferred studying in their dorm rooms, primarily for privacy, quietness and fewer distractions. Four distinct study-behaviour archetypes emerged, with statistically significant differences in self-reported academic performance (p = 0.003). Students also identified additional study rooms (64.8%) and improved thermal conditions (51.1%) as priorities.
Conclusions: The findings suggest that resilient student housing requires more than energy-efficient buildings and acceptable indoor temperatures. Equitable thermal conditions, acoustic privacy and accessible study spaces are essential to supporting diverse learning needs. By linking environmental performance with occupant behaviour, this research offers practical directions for targeted retrofits and inclusive housing design, contributing to Sustainable Development Goals 3, 4 and 11 and informing human-centred sustainable housing strategies beyond 2030.

Title: THE DAWN OF AN ECO-FRIENDLY WORLD
Theme_Title: Health, well-being, and societal foundations as key drivers of sustainable development
Topic_Title: Health equity, well-being, inner development, and societal foundations as societal outcomes
Keywords: social contract, eco-friendly, circular economy, true cost accounting, population/consumption explosion
Abstract_Text:
