Title: ClimaGraph RS: Integrating Ontologies, Knowledge Graphs, and Artificial Intelligence for Climate Education Grounded in Learning Theories
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI as an enabling technology for understanding sustainable development and twin transition
Authors: Schünke, Marco Aurélio; Barone, Dante Augusto Couto; Silva, Rodrigo de Cassio da
Organisations: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul
Keywords: Knowledge Graphs; Ontologies; Artificial Intelligence; Climate Education; Learning Theories; Territorial Resilience.
Abstract_Text:
Climate challenges require educational approaches that help students understand the relationships between environmental phenomena, territorial characteristics, social vulnerabilities, and adaptation strategies. However, access to scientific and geospatial data alone does not guarantee meaningful learning. This doctoral research proposes ClimaGraph RS, a computational and pedagogical model integrating ontologies, knowledge graphs, and artificial intelligence to support contextualized climate education.
The proposal draws on five educational perspectives: Piaget's active construction of knowledge, Vygotsky's social mediation and collaborative learning, Ausubel's meaningful learning, Freire's critical problematization of reality, and Papert's learning through the creation of meaningful artifacts. These foundations guide the development of Explainable Climate Investigation Pathways (TICE), organized around five interconnected components: investigative questions, territorial and temporal contexts, knowledge subgraphs, scientific evidence, and pedagogical mediation.
Methodologically, the research proposes developing interconnected climate-territorial and pedagogical ontologies to represent relationships among rainfall, rivers, terrain, soil, vegetation, environmental risks, school communities, and Nature-based Solutions. Artificial intelligence will support knowledge retrieval, evidence-based explanations, and pedagogical guidance while preserving teachers' central role in learning.
The 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, provide the initial context for investigating how students can connect scientific knowledge with environmental challenges affecting their communities. The proposed evaluation will examine the semantic consistency and traceability of the knowledge graph and its educational potential to foster systems thinking, evidence-based reasoning, collaborative knowledge construction, and critical analysis of climate adaptation strategies.
The expected contribution is a theoretically grounded model that transforms fragmented environmental information into meaningful, place-based learning experiences, connecting artificial intelligence, climate education, and sustainability to support the development of more climate-resilient communities.

Title: Mapping the Role of Artificial Intelligence in Local Renewable Energy Forecasting: A Review for Post-2030 Urban Decarbonization
Theme_Title: Artificial Intelligence, big data, and digitalization as enablers for sustainable development
Topic_Title: AI, big data, and digitalization for sustainable development by and beyond 2030, including opportunities and challenges
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Renewable Energy, Literature Review, Smart Grids, Post-2030 SDGs
Abstract_Text:
Objective:
As global efforts intensify to meet the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), municipal energy grids face increasing challenges in integrating variable renewable energy sources.
This paper reviews established literature examining how machine learning models improve short-term solar and wind energy generation forecasts at the local level to accelerate urban climate neutrality targets.
Methods:
We conducted a systematic literature search across major academic databases, targeting peer-reviewed studies on AI-driven local renewable energy forecasting, smart grid integration, and municipal decarbonization.
Selected foundational papers and empirical case studies were critically analyzed to synthesize prevailing methodological trends, technological capabilities, and systemic impacts on urban energy governance.
Key Results:
The reviewed literature demonstrates a strong consensus that advanced hybrid machine learning architectures significantly outperform conventional forecasting techniques in managing the intermittency of renewable sources. Established studies show that incorporating AI-driven predictions into municipal smart grids optimizes energy dispatch, enhances grid flexibility, and substantially reduces reliance on fossil-fuel backup systems. Additionally, documented evidence indicates that localized digital forecasting successfully translates overarching climate policies into practical, operational grid management.
Conclusions:
Digital tools and AI-driven forecasting frameworks are critical enablers for operationalizing SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities). By synthesizing established best practices and identifying current research gaps regarding technological adoption and regional scalability, this review provides a strategic framework to guide post-2030 sustainable energy governance and infrastructure resilience.

Title: From Planting to Sustainability: grassroots governance lessons from Gunung Halimun Salak National Park Buffer Zone, Indonesia
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Lessons learned from SDG governance and multi-stakeholder partnerships
Authors: Sari, Galih Kartika; Soekmadi, Rinekso; Masy'ud, Burhanuddin; Mulatsih, Sri
Keywords: Community-based restoration; farmer participation; social capital; multi-stakeholder partnership; policy coherence; SDG17
Abstract_Text:
The buffer zone of Gunung Halimun Salak National Park (TNGHS) in Indonesia is a transitional landscape where conservation interests meet local communities' socio-economic development. In this buffer zone, communities have a high dependency on the land, especially for agriculture, but farmers face land-ownership constraints, creating a challenge in reconciling conservation and socio-economic development. Meanwhile, its hilly topography and role as the upstream for several river basins also require limited land management to prevent disasters such as landslides or droughts. This study explores farmer-group participation in land restoration and draws lessons on how multi-stakeholder partnership and coordination can support both community needs and conservation objectives, in line with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 17. Mixed-methods research was conducted in four buffer zone villages in Sukabumi Regency, where the land restoration programme was implemented with the participation of 34 farmer groups. We surveyed 300 respondents and conducted in-depth interviews with 40 key informants. Questionnaire and interview data were analysed using quantitative and qualitative descriptive methods. The findings show that the economic benefits expected from the land are a key driver of farmers' involvement in restoration. They also show that social capital forms the foundation for collective action, while sustaining participation requires ongoing support, particularly during the early stages of the programme. The findings further indicated that farmers require capacity building in land productivity, market access, post-harvest processing, conservation, and sustainable land management. At the landscape level, the convergence of various sectors and interests demands coordination and collaboration between stakeholders, as well as policy alignment.
Community-based restoration sustainability requires partnerships linking farmers' interest in economic benefits with conservation objectives. These partnerships need support, capacity building, stakeholder coordination, and policy alignment. These lessons can inform policymakers to improve restoration governance that supports sustainable development up to 2030 and the post-2030 agenda.

Title: How Can Equity and The Concept of "Enough" Help Reimagine The Built Environment
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Actions for climate change adaptation to build societal resilience
Keywords: Environmental justice, built environment, urban design, particpatory model
Abstract_Text:
Conventional built-environment development has often approached nature as something to control or protect against, reinforcing a perceived separation between human and natural systems. This paradigm can contribute to ecological degradation and unequal distributions of environmental harm. This research aims to develop a model that reconceptualizes the built environment as part of nature, integrating existing ecological and net-zero interventions with participatory decision-making and a commitment to prioritizing communities experiencing disproportionate environmental burdens. Data centers serve as the initial application through which to explore this approach to more ecologically integrated and socially just development.
A multidisciplinary team of independent researchers across construction, renewable energy, and data-center infrastructure examined existing development practices, environmental and community impacts, and available interventions. This analysis informed a multi-solution model integrating ecological systems, community programming, and neighborhood benefits. The model has undergone technical expert review. A small-scale internet café and server pilot, powered by renewable energy and incorporating circular practices, is being developed to test the model and participatory methodology, including community-led programming decisions.
The resulting intervention model integrates renewable energy and water-conservation systems, community co-designed programming, local economic opportunities, and rooftop food production. Analysis of existing data-center approaches identified neighborhood repair and environmental justice as gaps in the approaches examined. The model's systems-level design applies the principle of “enough” to explore how appropriate scale and integrated interventions could support greater ecological feasibility while generating social, economic, and environmental benefits to surrounding communities.
The model proposes an alternative to development that prioritizes growth over local needs and ecological limits. Integrating ecological practices, community agency, and local economic benefits, it aims to support place-based resilience and climate adaptation. The planned internet café pilot will explore the model's operational feasibility, participatory processes, and community reception, informing further development of a more just and ecologically integrated approach to the built environment beyond 2030.

Title: A Smart, Solar-Powered, Low-Carbon Bioremediation and Sustainable Campus System for Petroleum-Contaminated Soil
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: National and local implementation of SDGs, including barriers and opportunities
Organisations: Muhammad Nawaz sharif university of multan
Keywords: petroleum-contaminated soil; bioremediation; phytoremediation; biochar; solar-powered sensors; carbon footprint
Abstract_Text: Petroleum-contaminated soil is a serious environmental problem, especially in hot and dry regions such as the United Arab Emirates, where high temperature, salty soil, low rainfall, and low organic matter slow natural cleanup. Common methods such as excavation and landfill disposal only move the pollution to another place and produce high carbon emissions. This study proposes EcoRemediate, a smart, solar-powered, and low-carbon system for treating petroleum-contaminated soil. The system combines three treatment methods: microbial bioremediation (biostimulation and bioaugmentation), phytoremediation with arid-tolerant plants, and biochar made from date-palm waste. A six-group experiment (clean control, contaminated control, microbial treatment, plant treatment, biochar treatment, and combined treatment), with at least three replicates per group, will test each method alone and together. Total petroleum hydrocarbon (TPH) will be measured at Day 0, 20, 40, 60, and 90 by GC-FID in the university laboratory. A solar-powered sensor network will record soil conditions such as temperature, moisture, and pH, and smart irrigation will use harvested rainwater. A carbon-footprint (CO₂) assessment will compare the biological treatment with excavation and disposal. The project also forms part of a sustainable campus model based on recycling, water and energy saving, and circular-economy practice, and it supports SDGs 6, 7, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15. The combined treatment is expected to reduce TPH more than untreated soil, with a lower carbon footprint than excavation and disposal. These expected results must be confirmed by laboratory measurements.

Title: What’s fair? Positional perspective and decision-making power in public participation: Evidence from a survey experiment on hydrogen pipelines and wind energy
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Roles of equity & justice for sustainable transformation and resilience
Authors: Rehage, Ruben; Squintani, Lorenzo; Perlaviciute, Goda; Diestelmeier, Lea
Keywords: energy justice, public participation, hydrogen, survey experiment
Abstract_Text:
Public participation is widely considered important for the acceptance and legitimacy of energy infrastructure. However, the growing (political) pressure to accelerate the energy transition raises questions about the extent to which citizens can influence infrastructure decisions. Previous research indicates that citizens wish to participate throughout the decision-making chain, while legal frameworks may constrain opportunities for influence for the sake of the efficiency of decision-making. Against this background, this study examines how different designs of public participation affect perceived procedural fairness of decision-making processes.
We employ a factorial survey experiment comparing participation arrangements across two energy technologies: hydrogen and wind energy. The experimental design systematically varies
1. decision-making power of affected citizens (binding vs. advisory),
2. assigned positional perspective (affected-and-included vs. non-affected-and-excluded), and
3. energy technology (hydrogen pipeline vs. wind energy).
Respondents’ baseline attitudes toward the respective technology and their trust in institutions are being measured as potential moderators. The primary outcome measure is perceived fairness of the decision-making process.
Data collection is currently under way with a quota-based (age, gender, education, region) sample of the adult population (N = 2000) in Germany. By the time of the conference, the results of this study can be presented and discussed.
The study contributes to research on procedural justice in sustainable energy transitions by examining how specific institutional characteristics of public participation shape fairness perceptions. Its findings aim to inform the design of participation arrangements that reconcile the need for accelerated infrastructure development with meaningful opportunities for citizen influence, supporting more inclusive and just energy transitions by and beyond 2030.

Title: Modelling urban electricity and heat demand using open-source data
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Measures for urban transformation, including sustainable mobility
Authors: Zabala Figueroa, Alejandro; Medjroubi, Wided; Ursavas, Evrim; Knies, Jürgen
Keywords: Urban energy planning, Bottom-up models, Open georeferenced datasets, Representative load profiles, Electricity and heat demand.
Abstract_Text: Developing sustainable, secure, and affordable energy systems is a central goal of energy planning worldwide. National decarbonisation strategies outline pathways towards this goal through targets for emissions reductions, renewable energy deployment, and changes in technology use such as sector coupling. Translating these targets into implementation, however, requires a detailed and systemic understanding of where technologies can be deployed as to be accommodated by the local infrastructure​. Regional and urban energy system analyses therefore provide an essential link between national ambitions and the spatial and operational conditions that shape their implementation. Bottom-up models support this link by representing local energy demand, resources, and infrastructure at high spatial and temporal resolution, enabling the assessment of transition scenarios​. A fundamental input to these models is a detailed representation of electricity and heat demand, the availability of which remains constrained by fragmented and inconsistent data. To address this gap, this study presents a method that integrates open georeferenced datasets, local statistical information, and representative load profiles to estimate hourly electricity and heat demand for individual buildings in urban areas. The method is applied to a German city, and the resulting annual demand estimates are compared with reported municipal values. The modelled totals are of the same order of magnitude as the municipal figures, providing an initial indication of the plausibility of the aggregated estimates. By generating spatially explicit demand profiles, the approach provides a foundation for analysing local technology deployment and infrastructure needs, supporting the translation of national decarbonisation targets into urban energy planning.

Title: Collective Shifts toward Animal-Friendly Food Choices: The Role of Social Tipping
Theme_Title: Lessons from the Sustainable Development Goals for sustainable development beyond 2030
Topic_Title: Missing links and reforms for a sustainable development agenda beyond 2030
Authors: Lendl-Lewisch, Leonore; Galiotto, Chiara; Epstude, Kai; Fennis, Bob; Riefler, Petra
Keywords: social tipping; animal welfare; benefit framing; sustainability; consumer behavior
Abstract_Text:
Social tipping points can be understood as thresholds “[...] at which a small quantitative change inevitably triggers a non-linear change [...] that inevitably and often irreversibly lead to a qualitatively different state of the social system” (Milkoreit et al., 2018, p. 10). Thus, social tipping points are of substantial importance for advancing the SDGs (Allen & Malekpour, 2023). Although social tipping dynamics have received increasing attention in climate research (e.g., Lenton et al., 2020; Otto et al., 2020), their potential as a communication strategy for promoting sustainable consumer behavior remains largely unexplored.
Against this background, we investigate whether messages portraying sustainable food consumption as part of a rapidly spreading social change can encourage more animal-friendly food choices. Building on empirical evidence from benefit framing research (Evans et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2025), we further explore whether self-benefits (vs benefits for others) amplify the effectiveness of such social tipping messages.
Our study focuses on animal welfare, an aspect of sustainability that is closely connected to several SDGs (Keeling et al., 2019) and considered relevant by consumers (Lendl-Lewisch & Riefler, 2026) but remains underrepresented in food sustainability research (Richter et al., 2024). By applying the concept of social tipping points to animal welfare communication, our work seeks to contribute to both sustainability communication and consumer behavior research.
We will conduct an online experiment in the Baltic states in November and December 2026 using a 2 by 3 factorial between-subjects design. Participants will be exposed to either a social tipping message or a control condition, combined with information emphasizing no benefits, self-benefits, or benefits for others. In a subsequent field study planned for 2027, conducted in collaboration with a Baltic food retailer, we will examine whether the observed effects extend to a real-world food-choice context.

Title: Beyond Geological Reserves: Value chain vulnerability assessment of India`s critical minerals for renewable energy transitions
Theme_Title: Navigating the climate change–development nexus for resilient, just and equitable transformations
Topic_Title: Climate change mitigation and net-zero pathways for a just transition
Authors: Manav, Shreya; Kumar, Anand; Magry, Muneer
Keywords: decarbonization, critical minerals, value chain, vulnerability assessment, energy transitions
Abstract_Text:
Global climate mitigation strategies-anchored in the Paris Agreement and the COP28 pledge to triple renewable energy capacity by 2030 depend on scaling low-carbon technologies. India has committed to achieve 50% non-fossil energy capacity by 2030 and net zero emissions by 2070. Meeting these targets requires an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy sectors, including solar photovoltaics, battery storage, and electric mobility. Consequently, this transition has led to an increased domestic demand for Critical Energy Transition Minerals (CETMs).
This study assesses India’s CETMs resource landscape by synthesizing datasets from the Indian Bureau of Mines and National Mineral Inventory reports. The United Nations Framework Classification (UNFC) method has been used to classify the reserves and total resources for 30 critical minerals, and their spatial distribution was mapped. Furthermore, we assess domestic capabilities across four value-chain stages, i.e., mining, processing, refining, and commercial manufacturing—categorizing readiness as established, partial, emerging, or absent.
Results reveal severe structural challenges across high-priority value chains. Key battery minerals—lithium, cobalt, and nickel—lack primary domestic mining, leaving midstream processing absent or entirely import-dependent. Crucially, despite holding 647.75 million tonnes of silicon reserves, India lacks industrial refining capacity, creating direct vulnerabilities for its renewable energy sector. This domestic gap is compounded by global market concentration and the changing geopolitical landscape.
Our findings demonstrate that possessing raw geological reserves does not ensure mineral supply security. To overcome these challenges, industrial policies must shift from extraction-focused incentives toward building domestic midstream refining capabilities and processing infrastructure. Furthermore, establishing strategic partnerships for technology transfer and mineral processing will be vital to insulate India's clean energy roadmap from global supply disruptions. Mitigating these risks is essential for fulfilling India's Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) and advancing Sustainable Development Goals 7 (Clean Energy), 9 (Industry & Innovation), and 13 (Climate Action).

Title: Integration of nature conservation and agriculture for biodiversity conservation. Insights from the Netherlands.
Theme_Title: Building resilience through integrated sustainable transformation across natural and human systems
Topic_Title: Sustainable landscape and seascape for nature's contribution to people
Keywords: biodiversity, nature conservation, agriculture
Abstract_Text:
Agriculture and nature are intertwined in multiple ways. Agriculture needs nature to function, but the large-scale industrialized forms of agriculture that are most common in Europe have a detrimental effect on nature at the same time. Growing acknowledgment about these effects is leading to more attention for (more) sustainable agri-food systems. In addition, it is widely recognized that protected areas alone are not providing a sufficient answer to the ongoing biodiversity decline. Therefore, we should look into possibilities to integrate nature conservation and agriculture for biodiversity conservation.
Using insights from transition studies and social-ecological systems, data from multiple sources (e.g. interviews, observations, policy reports) of different Dutch national parks and agricultural initiatives around nature-inclusive agriculture are analyzed. New initiatives in both Dutch national parks as well as (groups) of farmers developing nature-inclusive agriculture show a high potential for an integration of nature conservation and agriculture. But multiple ingrained and incumbent aspects of both sectors are inhibiting the larger uptake of such initiatives and with that the integration of nature conservation and agriculture.
These insights are relevant for achieving in particular SDG 12 (responsible production) and SDG 15 (life on land), as well as the targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Beyond 2030, integrating nature conservation and agriculture will be essential for long-term biodiversity recovery. Understanding what enables and inhibits such integration in the Dutch context offers lessons for other densely populated, intensively farmed regions facing similar challenges.
